Postoperative Digital Health Interventions After Non-Cardiac Surgery: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.abstract: Background: Recovery after non-cardiac surgery increasingly occurs at home, where clinical deterioration may go unrecognized. Digital health interventions may extend postoperative surveillance beyond discharge, but vary widely in components and clinician involvement. We evaluated their association with readmission and other outcomes. Methods: Five databases were searched from inception to December 12, 2025, for prospective randomized and observational studies comparing digital health interventions with standard care in adults after non-cardiac surgery. Readmission was the primary outcome; all-cause and major complications, emergency room (ER) visits, length of stay (LOS), and patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) were secondary. Interventions were grouped by whether a clinician reviewed patient-submitted data and had the ability to take action (active clinician involvement). Random-effects models pooled risk ratios (RR), mean differences (MD), and standardized mean differences (SMD). p values were adjusted for multiple comparisons (Benjamini–Hochberg). Results: In 38 studies (30 randomized, 8 observational; 7,494 patients), digital health interventions were associated with fewer readmissions (17 studies, n=3,944; RR 0.85, 95% CI 0.73–0.99, adjusted p=0.045), ER visits (RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.63–0.97), and major complications (RR 0.75, 95% CI 0.60–0.94), but not all-cause complications (RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.79–1.08) or LOS (MD −0.04 days, 95% CI −0.26 to 0.18). Pain and anxiety were lower and functional status, quality-of-life, and satisfaction scores higher (absolute SMD 0.41–0.69). Readmission risk was lower with active clinician involvement (RR 0.76, 95% CI 0.64–0.92) but not without it (RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.78–1.18; interaction p=0.029). Heterogeneity in interventions, cohorts, and outcomes was substantial (PROM I² 50–97%). Conclusions: Digital health interventions were associated with fewer readmissions, ER visits, major complications, and better PROMs, but not fewer all-cause complications or shorter LOS. The readmission association was concentrated in studies with active clinician involvement. Heterogeneity was substantial and certainty of evidence low to very low.

items.title: Quality of Recovery After Primary Breast Cancer Surgery: A Randomized, Two-Centre, Triple-Blinded Trial Comparing Erector Spinae Plane Block and Intravenous Lidocaine Infusion Within a Multimodal Analgesia Framework.
items.abstract: Background: The erector spinae plane block (ESPB) is widely used for primary breast cancer surgery (BCS), though its clinical benefits within optimized multimodal analgesia pathways remain uncertain. Intravenous lidocaine infusion (IVLI) offers a simple, reproducible alternative with potential systemic analgesic effects. This randomized, tripleblinded, placebo controlled, twocentre trial compared the quality of recovery after ESPB versus IVLI for BCS. Methods: Eighty adult patients undergoing primary BCS, with or without axillary dissection, were randomized to receive either ultrasoundguided ESPB (n=40) or intraoperative IVLI (n=40), in addition to a standardized multimodal analgesic protocol. The primary outcome was quality of recovery (QoR15) score at 24 hours. Secondary outcomes included postoperative pain scores, opioid consumption, adverse events, and rescue analgesia requirements. Results: Both interventions produced excellent postoperative recovery, with 24hour QoR15 scores approaching preoperative baselines with no significant difference between groups (mean (SD) 24-hour QoR score; ESPB vs. IVLI group, 137.7(17.9) vs. 136.3(8.8), p=0.61). Pain burden and analgesic requirements over the first 24 hours were similarly low, and no ESPB or lidocainerelated adverse events were observed. Conclusions: Within a standardized multimodal analgesic framework, postoperative recovery and analgesic outcomes did not differ significantly between IVLI and ESPB, suggesting that IVLI may offer a pragmatic alternative when regional anesthesia expertise is limited.

Rethinking the Responsible Adult Requirement after Ambulatory Anesthesia: Toward Risk-stratified Discharge
items.abstract: For decades, ambulatory anesthesia pathways have commonly required a “responsible adult” before discharge after sedation or anesthesia. In practice, this requirement may function as a binary eligibility criterion based on a patient’s social circumstances. However, the empirical evidence evaluating discharge without an escort remains limited and derives largely from observational studies. This Focal Point argues that carefully selected low-risk patients should be studied within structured alternative discharge pathways that preserve safe transportation, communication, observation, and rescue capacity. Such pathways should not permit self-driving or unrestricted solo discharge. The aim is to determine whether postanesthesia safeguards can be matched more precisely to patient, anesthetic, procedural, recovery, transport, and postdischarge risk while preserving conventional adult support for patients whose clinical circumstances warrant it.

Actuarial Validity and Financial Implications of Maximum Paid Anesthesia Time Based on Tolerance Limits for Log-Normal Distributions
items.abstract: Background: We investigate the policy implications of statistically valid upper limits on anesthesia durations. We test whether these tolerance limits categorized by claims data (procedure, surgeon, and facility) differ in practical consequence from limits calculated with data pooled among surgeons and facilities. We evaluate whether using valid tolerance limits at typical insurer sample sizes would differ functionally from no limits. Methods: Simulations had 100,000 replicates per configuration with 8 surgeons per hospital: equal n = 10 or 300 cases per-surgeon or unequal (geometric) median n = 10 and 60. The within-surgeon coefficient of variation was 36.2%. The between-surgeon variance accounted for 22.4% of total log-time variance (intraclass correlation). Five tolerance-limit methods (pooled Weibull generalized pivotal quantity, pooled nonparametric, per-surgeon log-normal, per-surgeon 3-sigma, and per-surgeon nonparametric) were evaluated by coverage probability (95% was correct), case-volume-weighted percentage bias (0% best), functional quantile (90 th for 90 th percentile), and payment satisfaction (100% ideal). Results: Pooled mixtures of cases by procedure were best fit by log-normal distributions. The noncentral-t–based log-normal tolerance limit, calculated per combination of procedure, surgeon, and facility, attained nominal 95% coverage in every configuration. Pooled Weibull and pooled nonparametric limits failed often (coverage 70.9%–79.2% and 62.9%–83.8%). The nonparametric method with all claim data attained 95.4%–97.1% coverage but was unavailable for 85% of surgeons at the realistic condition of unequal sample sizes, median n = 10. Applying the exact log-normal-based tolerance limits on 90 th percentiles functionally achieved percentiles ranging from the 92.1-97.4 th , with resulting payment satisfaction rates of 97.9%-100%. Conclusions: The per-surgeon log-normal 95% upper confidence limit for the 90 th percentile on log-transformed durations was the only valid method computable at realistic sample sizes. Applying those actuarially valid tolerance limits would pay ≈99.4% of historical case-time in full, thus functionally equivalent to retaining no paid time limit.

items.title: Prefrontal hemodynamic fluctuations and functional connectivity during propofol and sevoflurane anesthesia: A functional near-infrared spectroscopy study
items.abstract: Background: Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) measures cortical hemodynamics, yet its ability to characterize anesthesia-related functional changes remains unclear. Methods: This exploratory secondary analysis used prospectively collected data from 120 female patients undergoing gynecologic laparoscopic surgery under propofol or sevoflurane anesthesia (60 per group). Twenty-channel prefrontal fNIRS recordings covered wakefulness, induction, and maintenance. Deoxygenated hemoglobin-derived amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations (ALFF), functional connectivity (FC), network topology, and within- and cross-state FC similarity were assessed. Support vector machine, logistic regression, and random forest classifiers assessed discrimination between states. Results: During induction, ALFF increased by 89.8% to 202.2% with propofol and 75.2% to 242.0% with sevoflurane across five prefrontal regions (all P < 0.001). During maintenance, mean ALFF was below awake levels, with significant reductions of 20.0% to 40.1% in three regions under sevoflurane (all P ≤ 0.019). Induction-related FC changes were limited and regionally heterogeneous. Regional FC, modularity, and global efficiency showed no significant maintenance-versus-awake differences in either group. Within-state between-subject FC similarity was significantly higher during maintenance than during wakefulness only with sevoflurane (mean difference [MD], 0.110; 95% CI, 0.054 to 0.169; P < 0.001). Cross-state between-subject FC similarity was higher for awake–maintenance than awake–induction comparisons with propofol (MD, 0.072; 95% CI, 0.055 to 0.090) and sevoflurane (MD, 0.144; 95% CI, 0.126 to 0.161; both P < 0.001). Support vector machine classification of induction versus wakefulness yielded areas under the curve (AUCs) of 0.83 (95% CI, 0.75 to 0.90) for propofol and 0.85 (95% CI, 0.78 to 0.91) for sevoflurane; maintenance-versus-awake AUCs were 0.67 (95% CI, 0.58 to 0.75) and 0.76 (95% CI, 0.68 to 0.85). Conclusions: Prefrontal fNIRS detected widespread induction-related hemodynamic changes, but the present connectivity measures provided limited discrimination between maintenance of anesthesia and wakefulness.

items.title: Incidence, Mortality, and Coding Validity of Malignant Hyperthermia in a Large U.S. Hospital Cohort
items.abstract: Background: Malignant hyperthermia national incidence and mortality in the United States have not been estimated for the International Classification of Diseases, Tenth Revision period. Diagnosis codes cannot separate an acute event from susceptibility, and previous chart review found only about one in four coded cases were true events. The authors estimated incidence and mortality using intravenous dantrolene as a coding-validity instrument. Methods: This retrospective cohort study used Epic (USA) Cosmos, a de-identified multi-institutional dataset, greater than 2016 through 2024. Malignant hyperthermia was identified by International Classification of Diseases, Tenth Revision–Clinical Modification code T88.3. The primary definition matched the only previous U.S. national study (billing final, any listed, mimics excluded). Rates per million used a fixed panel of 201 hospitals contributing inpatient discharges every year, with trend tested by Cochran–Armitage test. Coding positive predictive value (PPV) was assessed by anchoring the diagnosis to inpatient intravenous dantrolene. Results: Incidence was stable at approximately seven per million discharges (pooled, 7.3; 95% CI, 6.7 to 7.9) with no significant trend ( P = 0.086), roughly half the most recent published estimate (13.3 per million, 2005). The treatment-anchored PPV was 24.3% (95% CI, 21.3 to 27.5), reproducing the chart-validated 23.4%. A 94% rise in broadly coded cases in 2024 attenuated at the primary definition (+9%) and was absent among treatment-anchored events (PPV, 14.6%). In-hospital mortality was 5.0% (95% CI, 3.7 to 6.8). Present-on-admission comorbidity burden was the only independent predictor of death (odds ratio, 1.08 per diagnosis; 95% CI, 1.04 to 1.12). Conclusions: In this large health system network, malignant hyperthermia incidence was approximately seven per million inpatient discharges and stable, with in-hospital mortality of 5.0%. Diagnosis coding overstates the condition. Anchoring to intravenous dantrolene reproduces the chart-validated PPV and yields a treatment-confirmed incidence of approximately 1.7 per million. The anchored estimate is robust to the coding inflation observed in 2024.

Disparities in Regional Analgesia Utilization for Rib Fractures: Hospital-Level Variation, Trends, and Clinical Outcomes in a Nationwide Retrospective Cohort Study 2016 to 2022
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Regional analgesia is recommended for rib fractures, but utilization remains low. The extent to which hospital-level factors drive utilization and influence patient outcomes is unclear. This study’s objective was to evaluate associations between hospital characteristics and regional analgesia receipt and outcomes. METHODS: Retrospective cohort study using the Nationwide Inpatient Sample (NIS) of adult hospitalizations (>18 years) between January 1, 2016, and December 31, 2022 with rib fractures. Exposures included hospital bed-size, ownership, teaching status and geographic region. Primary outcome was regional analgesia receipt. Secondary outcomes included in-hospital mortality and tracheostomy. RESULTS: 250,630 hospitalizations met inclusion criteria, of which 7,179 (2.9%) received regional analgesia. After adjustment, 23.9% of variation in utilization was attributable to between-hospital differences. Greater utilization was associated with large hospital bed-size (odds ratio [OR] 2.08; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.80–2.39), urban teaching-status (OR 1.39; 95% CI, 1.19–1.62), higher income-quartile (OR 1.21; 95% CI, 1.10–1.33), and private insurance (OR 1.24; 95% CI, 1.14–1.35). Lower odds were observed in private nonprofit (OR 0.75; 95% CI, 0.65–0.86) and for-profit hospitals (OR 0.42; 95% CI, 0.34–0.53) compared with government hospitals. Regional analgesia utilization varied geographically, with the highest utilization in New England. Private insurance, White race, highest income quartile, government ownership and urban teaching status were also associated with earlier receipt of regional anesthesia. Disparities by insurance and hospital characteristics either persisted or widened from 2016 to 2022. Regional analgesia was associated with lower mortality (OR, 0.52; 95% CI, 0.42–0.64) and tracheostomy (OR, 0.48; 95% CI, 0.36–0.63) in multivariable analysis. In instrumental variable analysis with leave-one-out hospital-year regional analgesia rate as the instrument, these associations were attenuated. CONCLUSIONS: Regional analgesia remains infrequently utilized for rib fractures, with marked variation across hospitals. Access and outcomes appear to depend substantially on where patients receive care. Understanding the institutional and provider-level factors underlying this variation represents an important target for future quality-improvement and implementation efforts.

items.title: Dual Guidance in Regional Anesthesia: Influence of Needle Electrode Configuration on Stimulation Success at the Sciatic Nerve: A Randomized, Controlled Pilot Trial
items.abstract: Introduction In contrast to ultrasound technology (US), peripheral nerve stimulation (PNS) for regional anesthesia was little improved in recent years. When using the combination of both techniques, PNS can give additional information for nerve localization to improve safety and success of regional anesthesia. There are influencing factors on the success rate of stimulation in PNS remaining uninvestigated in a clinical setting to date. This randomized controlled pilot trial evaluates the impact of shape and size of stimulation needles electrodes under dual guidance conditions. Methods In a randomized controlled clinical trial 35 participants undergoing lower limb surgery received a preoperative proximal sciatic nerve block in dual guidance technique. Use of facet needles with point shaped electrodes (N=19, facet group) were compared with tuohy needles with large electroconductive tips (N=16, touhy group). Stimulation success at minimal distance between needle tip and nerve was recorded. Block success and complications of regional anesthesia were assessed. Results In 87% of successful stimulation (20 of 23) an ultrasound-proven contact of needle tip and sciatic nerve was necessary to elicit a motor response. More successful stimulations could performed using facet needles (84%, 16/19) compared to tuohy needles (44%, 7/16, p=0.03). If stimulation was successful the number of successful sensory blockades was increased (78%, 18/23, p=0.02). No serious complications of regional anesthesia were recorded. Discussion This pilot trial suggests that stimulation needles with small electrodes may be more reliable in indicating a contact of needle and nerve, which may improve safety and success of proximal sciatic nerve blocks.

items.title: Real-Time Mean Arterial Pressure Forecasting During Cesarean Delivery: A Prospective Feasibility Study With Matched Nonconcurrent Controls
Anesthetic Technique and Hospital Length of Stay in Modern Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement: A Randomized Controlled Trial
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Observational studies have suggested that monitored anesthesia care (MAC) improves hospital throughput in transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR), though these findings largely reflect earlier practice patterns with longer hospitalizations, evolving care pathways, and limitations inherent to retrospective designs. METHODS: We conducted a single-center, prospective randomized controlled trial of 170 patients undergoing elective transfemoral TAVR. Patients were randomized 1:1 to MAC or general endotracheal anesthesia (GETA) with intraoperative transesophageal echocardiography. The primary outcomes were hospital length of stay (LOS), 30-day mortality, and intensive care unit (ICU) admission. The secondary outcome was paravalvular regurgitation (PVR). Other prospectively tracked perioperative efficiency metrics included procedure time and operating room time. RESULTS: There was no significant difference in hospital LOS between the two groups (median difference in LOS, MAC vs GETA: 0.02 days (95% confidence interval [CI], –0.09 to 0.15 days); P = 0.631). There were no 30-day deaths in either group. ICU admission rates ( P = 0.634) were similar between arms. No significant differences were observed in PVR rates ( P = 0.934), procedure time ( P = 0.142), or operating room time ( P = 0.439). CONCLUSIONS: In a modern TAVR program, anesthetic technique did not influence hospital LOS or other clinical endpoints during the study. These findings suggest that the efficiency differences previously associated with MAC may not persist in current TAVR practice. Anesthetic choice can be individualized without substantially altering hospital throughput in similar practice settings.

A Machine Learning–Based Early Warning System for Renal Replacement Therapy in the Intensive Care Unit
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Renal replacement therapy (RRT) is a life-saving intervention for acute kidney injury in the intensive care unit (ICU). The decision to initiate RRT remains highly complex and subjective. Accurate and timely predictions for the need of RRT initiation are crucial components of personalized care. Using time series patient data (vital signs, laboratory findings, medications, ventilator settings, intake/output, risk scores), we aimed to develop machine learning (ML) models for predicting future initiation of RRT. METHODS: Using data from the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care (MIMIC)-III, MIMIC-IV, and Electronic ICU Collaborative Research Database (eICU), we trained and internally validated models using dataset-specific training, validation, and test splits. We externally validated model performance using held-out eICU hospitals excluded from model development and a temporally distinct cohort of ICU patients admitted during the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic period (2020–2022). Models were developed for: (1) screening patients for prediction of the need for RRT after their first 12 hours in the ICU; and (2) real-time dynamic prediction of the likelihood of documented RRT initiation within the next 24 hours. RESULTS: Here, we summarize the results of the ML model aimed at screening patients for early prediction of RRT. In internal validation, the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) was 0.90 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.886–0.906) and the area under the precision–recall curve (AUPRC) was 0.53 (95% CI, 0.496–0.564) in MIMIC-III. Results were similar in MIMIC-IV and eICU. External validation on ICU patients admitted during the coronavirus disease (COVID) period yielded an AUROC of 0.90 (95% CI, 0.894–0.913) and an AUPRC of 0.57 (95% CI, 0.534–0.602). Additional hospital-level external validation across eight individual eICU hospitals showed AUROCs ranging from 0.86 to 0.91 and AUPRCs ranging from 0.35 to 0.52. Accuracy ranged from 0.78 to 0.84 across validation experiments. CONCLUSION: By accurately identifying patients at high risk for RRT initiation, the early prediction ML model could serve as a triage tool to prompt closer nephrology evaluation or optimization of fluid and hemodynamic management before overt renal failure develops.

Etomidate vs Propofol for Anesthetic Induction: Association With 30-Day Mortality and Postoperative Complications in a Propensity Score-Matched Retrospective Cohort Study
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Etomidate is commonly used for induction in hemodynamically unstable patients to preserve cardiovascular stability. However, concerns persist regarding potential adverse outcomes, including adrenal suppression and increased mortality. We evaluated whether intravenous anesthetic induction with etomidate was independently associated with adverse postoperative outcomes as compared to propofol induction. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of 155,667 adult surgical patients undergoing induction with etomidate or propofol at our academic health system. Patients younger than 18 years of age, those receiving preoperative mechanical ventilation, and those with American Society of Anesthesiologists physical status VI were excluded. The primary outcome was all-cause 30-day mortality; secondary outcomes included sepsis, acute coronary syndrome (ACS), cardiogenic shock, and acute kidney injury (AKI). Multivariable logistic regression adjusted for demographic, comorbidity, physiologic, and surgical factors. Given substantial baseline imbalance between induction groups, propensity score matching (1:1) using the same covariates was performed. Sensitivity analyses included adjustment for neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio, complete-case analyses, and interaction testing. RESULTS: A total of 155,667 patients met inclusion criteria, including 3846 (2.5%) who received etomidate and 151,821 (97.5%) who received propofol. Thirty-day mortality occurred in 1151 patients (0.74%). Unadjusted mortality was higher in the etomidate group (227/3846 [5.9%]) than in the propofol group (924/151,821 [0.61%]). After multivariable adjustment, etomidate use remained independently associated with increased 30-day mortality (aOR 1.44; 95% CI, 1.21–1.72; P < 0.001). Propensity score matching (n = 3832 per group) reduced the average standardized mean difference from 0.398 before matching to 0.023 after matching. The association persisted in the matched cohort (aOR 1.43; 95% CI, 1.14–1.78; P = 0.002), with observed mortality of 225/3832 (5.9%) among etomidate recipients and 157/3832 (4.1%) among propofol recipients, corresponding to an absolute risk difference of 1.8% and a number needed to harm of 56. In the matched cohort, etomidate was also associated with higher odds of sepsis (aOR 1.28; 95% CI, 1.08–1.52), acute coronary syndrome (aOR 1.24; 95% CI, 1.09–1.41), cardiogenic shock (aOR 1.56; 95% CI, 1.21–2.01), and acute kidney injury (aOR 1.27; 95% CI, 1.11–1.45). Post-induction hypotension was lower in the etomidate group (aOR 0.40, 95% CI 0.32–0.49; P < 0.001). Findings were consistent across sensitivity analyses. CONCLUSIONS: Etomidate induction was associated with increased 30-day mortality and major postoperative complications. Given the observational design, results should be interpreted with caution.

Anesthesia Care-Team Staffing Ratios in the United States: Anesthesia Time and Billing Units: A Retrospective Observational Study
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: The use of Certified Registered Nurse Anesthetists (CRNAs) in medically directed anesthesia care teams has expanded, but the implications for anesthesia time and billing units remain uncertain, especially in relation to staffing supervision ratios (number of CRNAs to anesthesiologist). METHODS: We conducted a retrospective fixed-panel observational study of unique surgical encounters spanning January 2018 through December 2024 using billing records from a large revenue cycle management company. The sample included encounters involving anesthesiologists, CRNAs, surgeons, and facilities across 47 states. We compared physician-alone cases with medically directed care-team cases using fixed-effects regression models. Outcomes included anesthesia minutes and anesthesia billing units (base, time, modifier, conditional, and total units). A Medicare subsample was analyzed for realized gross payments. Secondary analyses examined each encounter by the number of CRNAs the anesthesiologist medically directed simultaneously, that is, staffing ratios, to assess whether outcomes varied by level. Models adjusted for patient-, procedure-, surgeon-, facility-, and time-level factors. RESULTS: Care-team cases were associated with longer anesthesia time (adjusted difference +1.67 minutes; 95% CI, 1.11–2.23; P < .001) and higher total billing units (adjusted difference +0.11 units; 95% CI, 0.04–0.18; P = .003) than cases performed by an anesthesiologist alone. Both differences increased with the staffing ratio. Relative to physician-alone cases, anesthesia time was shorter with 1 CRNA directed (−2.52 minutes; 95% CI, −3.22 to −1.83), similar with 2 CRNAs (−0.13 minutes; 95% CI, −0.69 to 0.43), and longer with 3 CRNAs (+3.03 minutes; 95% CI, 2.40–3.66) and 4 CRNAs (+6.99 minutes; 95% CI, 6.18–7.80); total billing units followed the same pattern (1 CRNA, −0.23; 2 CRNAs, −0.02 [not significant]; 3 CRNAs, +0.21; 4 CRNAs, +0.50). In a Medicare subsample, gross payments differed little overall (−$3.53; 95% CI, −$5.13 to −$1.92) and followed the same staffing-ratio gradient (1 CRNA, −$10.44; 4 CRNAs, +$3.74). CONCLUSIONS: Medically directed CRNA care teams were associated with modestly longer anesthesia time and slightly greater billing-unit intensity than physician-alone care. These differences were small overall but increased with rising staffing ratios, indicating that the number of CRNAs directed concurrently is associated with measurable differences in anesthesia time and billing intensity.

items.title: Solutions to Reduce Burnout Syndrome Among Perioperative Healthcare Providers in Low-Resource Settings: A Qualitative Study
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Research from high-income countries indicates that perioperative care providers are at high risk for burnout, with potential downstream effects on patient safety. Adequate solutions to address burnout may be particularly important in low-income countries where the effects of burnout on staff motivation and migration are likely to be compounded by the current human resources crisis. This study aimed to explore solutions to address burnout among Rwandan perioperative care providers. METHODS: Semi-structured interviews were conducted with perioperative care providers (obstetricians, surgeons, anesthetists, midwives, nurses) in hospitals across all five provinces in Rwanda. Interviews were analyzed using both inductive and deductive coding following standard procedures of thematic analysis. RESULTS: Interviews were completed with 61 participants from all levels of public hospitals (37% teaching, 6% referral, 52% district, and 5% unknown level). The participants identified solutions at multiple levels fitting within the multilevel model of burnout. At the individual level, many drew on internal values and self-developed coping mechanisms to manage occupational stress, emphasizing the importance of fulfilling basic needs such as sleep and nutrition, and stress-relief activities such as exercise and music. At the interpersonal level, support networks involving family, friends, religious communities, and colleagues played a significant role in sustaining resilience. At the hospital level , participants found motivation through positive patient outcomes. They underscored the impact of hospital organization on workload and recommended reducing inefficiencies. Regarding the healthcare system, concerns were raised about insufficient financial resources affecting staff salaries and access to essential medicines and equipment. Participants emphasized that increasing staffing levels would improve scheduling flexibility and reduce burnout. Finally, cultural factors such as recognition, appreciation, and respectful workplace interactions were deemed essential for morale. CONCLUSIONS: This study illustrates that resilience among healthcare professionals is shaped by a complex interplay of individual, interpersonal, institutional, and systemic factors. While many rely on personal values and coping strategies to manage the demands of clinical work, their resilience is often strained by unmet basic needs, geographic isolation, organizational inefficiencies, and broader systemic limitations such as inadequate staffing and financing. Cultural dynamics, including recognition, respect, and workplace relationships, further influence the capacity to cope with stress. To address burnout effectively, solutions must be adapted to the Rwandan context and implemented at all levels, ranging from promoting self-care and peer support to improving hospital management and resource allocation, and to promoting innovative and evidence-based interventions.

Chronic Opioid Exposure Modifies the Association Between Preoperative Serum Albumin and 30-Day Readmission After Inpatient Surgery: A Cohort Study in the All of Us Research Program
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Preoperative serum albumin is widely used to stratify surgical risk and is often reduced to a single threshold, yet it is a negative acute-phase reactant that reports on inflammation, illness burden, and physiologic reserve rather than nutritional intake. The same value therefore need not carry the same prognostic meaning in every patient. Chronic preoperative opioid exposure defines one such context, but risk models treat albumin and opioid exposure as independent predictors and have not tested whether opioid exposure changes what an albumin value indicates. METHODS: We analyzed the All of Us Research Program Controlled Tier Curated Data Repository v9. Adults aged 18 years or older with a first inpatient surgical procedure and a serum albumin in the 90 days before surgery were eligible. Opioid exposure in the preceding year was classified as chronic (at least three fills or at least 90 cumulative days’ supply), some (one to two fills with fewer than 90 days’ supply), or naive. The outcome was 30-day all-cause inpatient readmission, anchored to the index discharge date. Logistic regression modeled readmission on albumin centered at 4.0 g/dL, chronic opioid exposure, and their interaction, adjusted for age, female sex, and Elixhauser comorbidity count. The albumin window was varied from 30 to 365 days. RESULTS: The cohort comprised 42,239 adults (23,032 opioid-naive, 6811 some-opioid exposure, 12,396 chronic), of whom 7798 of 42,239 (18.5%) were readmitted within 30 days. Albumin was not associated with readmission among nonchronic participants (odds ratio, 1.03 per 1 g/dL; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.98–1.09), nor was chronic opioid exposure at an albumin of 4.0 g/dL (odds ratio, 1.03; 95% CI, 0.97–1.09). The albumin × chronic-opioid interaction odds ratio was 0.738 (95% CI, 0.681–0.800), P < 0.001, indicating that higher albumin was associated with lower readmission odds specifically among chronic opioid users. On the harm scale, hypoalbuminemia (below 3.5 g/dL) interacted with chronic exposure in the same direction (odds ratio, 1.27; 95% CI, 1.13–1.43). The interaction held across all five albumin windows. CONCLUSIONS: Chronic preoperative opioid exposure modified the association between preoperative serum albumin and 30-day readmission, such that low albumin marked elevated readmission risk in chronic opioid users but not in other patients. This is statistical effect modification in observational data, not evidence of causation. It supports reading albumin in the context of opioid exposure rather than adopting a new or opioid-specific albumin threshold, which this study does not propose.

US Anesthesia Workforce Adequacy Through 2037: National Projections for Anesthesiology Physicians and Nurse Anesthetists
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: The United States faces evolving anesthesia workforce challenges associated with population aging, rising surgical demand, and training pipeline constraints. Understanding projected supply and demand for anesthesiology physicians and certified registered nurse anesthetists (CRNAs) is essential for workforce planning, training policy, and team-based care models. METHODS: This study presents a secondary analysis of US Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA) workforce projections from 2022 to 2037, accessed in December 2025. Full-time-equivalent (FTE) supply and demand were extracted for anesthesiology physicians and CRNAs at three levels of aggregation: national totals, all 50 states and the District of Columbia, and urban–rural strata. The primary outcome was adequacy, defined as the ratio of FTE supply to FTE demand. Secondary outcomes were the absolute workforce gap (supply minus demand), state-level distributional inequality (unweighted Gini coefficient and coefficient of variation [CV]), urban–rural adequacy, and 2037 adequacy under four HRSA-specified alternative supply scenarios (fewer graduates, more graduates, earlier retirement, later retirement). Because the HRSA model is deterministic, all values are point estimates without confidence intervals, and no statistical hypothesis testing was performed. RESULTS: National anesthesiology physician adequacy declined from 1.00 in 2022 (55,330 vs 55,330 FTEs; a value fixed by model calibration rather than observed) to 0.86 in 2037 (52,310 vs 60,760 FTEs; shortfall: 8,450 FTEs). CRNA adequacy rose from 1.00 in 2022 (59,460 vs 59,460 FTEs) to 1.14 (74,680 vs 65,300 FTEs; supply exceeding modeled demand by 9,380 FTEs). State-level physician adequacy deteriorated (median: 0.94–0.79; Gini: 0.16–0.19), while CRNA adequacy improved (median: 0.79–0.98; Gini: 0.39–0.31). Nonmetropolitan physician adequacy reached 0.24 by 2037 compared with 0.96 in metropolitan areas, versus nonmetropolitan CRNA adequacy of 1.71. Physician shortfalls persisted under all modeled scenarios (range: 0.81–0.91); CRNA supply remained above modeled demand in every scenario (range: 1.09–1.20). CONCLUSIONS: From 2022 to 2037, anesthesiology physician and CRNA workforces are projected to follow divergent adequacy trajectories, with geographic maldistribution and severe rural physician deficits. These deterministic projections are hypothesis-generating and support further evaluation of targeted workforce strategies that account for geographic variation, the complementary roles of each profession, and the organizational models through which anesthesia care is delivered.

Chronic preoperative benzodiazepine use and perioperative outcomes: a scoping review
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Expert clinical guidelines discourage routine benzodiazepine premedication in older adults because of associations with adverse postoperative outcomes, including delirium and prolonged length of stay. However, these recommendations primarily address acute administration, whereas chronic preoperative benzodiazepine use for non-surgical indications remains incompletely understood, and the relevant evidence has not been comprehensively synthesised. This scoping review characterised the literature on chronic preoperative benzodiazepine use and perioperative outcomes by mapping study characteristics, definitions of chronic use, and associated outcome domains and trends. METHODS: Published and grey literature were searched across MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO, Scopus, and thesis databases. Screening and full-text review were performed independently in duplicate. Eligible studies included adults undergoing surgery with chronic preoperative benzodiazepine use and excluded studies in which benzodiazepines were administered exclusively within 24 h of surgery. This scoping review was preregistered with the Open Science Framework (10.17605/OSF.IO/573JG). RESULTS: A total of 130 studies were included. Most were observational cohorts (n=109, 83.8%) and examined benzodiazepines as a secondary variable (n=100, 77.0%). Definitions of chronic use were heterogeneous, ranging from 1 month to >1 yr before surgery; duration was not systematically defined in 62 studies (47.7%). Postoperative opioid use (n=53, 40.8%) and delirium or cognitive impairment (n=19, 14.6%) were the most frequently examined outcome domains, with most studies reporting adverse associations with chronic preoperative benzodiazepine use. CONCLUSIONS: Chronic preoperative benzodiazepine use is an inconsistently defined but clinically relevant perioperative exposure. As this scoping review did not include a risk-of-bias assessment, its findings map the evidence but cannot support causal inference. Standardised definitions and prospective studies are needed to inform perioperative medication optimisation.

items.title: Reference values and web-based tool for intraoperative heart rate and blood pressure in paediatric patients undergoing general anaesthesia for noncardiac procedures
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Heart rate (HR) and arterial blood pressure (BP) monitoring is standard of care during paediatric anaesthesia, yet evidence-based reference values for anaesthetised children remain limited. Existing BP reference values do not account for the combined effects of age, sex, weight, and height, and HR reference values in this population are lacking. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective multicentre study using data from the Multicenter Perioperative Outcomes Group anaesthesia registry (2016-22). Included patients were aged <18 yr, ASA physical status 1 or 2, and undergoing noncardiac procedures under general anaesthesia. We used quantile regression to model the 2.3rd, 16th, 50th, 84th, and 97.7th centiles for HR, mean arterial pressure (MAP), systolic BP, and diastolic BP at two time points: the preparation phase (end of induction) and surgical phase (15-35 min after procedure start). Model covariates included age, sex, weight, and height. We selected the best model for each outcome using cross-validation with pinball loss. RESULTS: A total of 284 385 patients from 57 institutions were analysed. Optimal model complexity varied by outcome: a two-way interaction model was selected as the best-performing model for preparation phase HR and surgical phase MAP. A three-way interaction model was selected as the best-performing model for the remaining outcomes. Comprehensive prediction tables and an interactive web-based tool were developed for all outcomes. CONCLUSIONS: This study provides integrated HR and BP reference values for healthy paediatric patients undergoing general anaesthesia, incorporating age, sex, weight, and height simultaneously. These reference values with an interactive website can support clinical decision-making and haemodynamic monitoring.

Patient-reported disability has insufficient clinical accuracy for predicting physical function in survivors of critical illness: a secondary analysis of a cluster-randomised trial
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Post-ICU care often misses patients unable to attend in-person clinic visits. Remote assessments of physical function might increase access to ICU aftercare. We investigated whether patient-reported disability predicts handgrip strength (HGS) and the 2-Minute Walk Test (2MWT) distance with sufficient clinical accuracy. METHODS: This secondary analysis of the stepped-wedge cluster-randomised Enhanced Recovery after Intensive Care trial included patients from 10 German ICU clusters who completed the WHO Disability Assessment Schedule (WHODAS) 2.0 plus either HGS, the 2MWT, or both, 6 months after ICU discharge. Relationships between WHODAS 2.0, HGS, and 2MWT were analysed using scatter plots, correlation coefficients, linear regressions, and Bland-Altman plots. Predictions of HGS and the 2MWT were compared with the minimal clinically important difference (MCID) for both measures. RESULTS: Of 1463 enrolled patients, 620 were analysed. The median WHODAS 2.0 sum score was 11 (Q1, Q3: 3, 22). The median HGS, expressed as a percentage of the expected value (%exp), was 70.6%exp (Q1, Q3: 54.4, 85.6), and the median 2MWT distance was 73.7%exp (Q1, Q3: 61.5, 85.8). The 2MWT was not completed by 59% of patients. Higher disability was moderately correlated with lower HGS (Spearman %exp: -0.41) and shorter 2MWT distance (Spearman %exp: -0.47). In multivariable regression models, the WHODAS 2.0 sum score predicted HGS in kg (β: -0.27 [95% CI: -0.33 to -0.22]; P<0.001) and 2MWT distance in m (β: -1.94 [95% CI: -2.37 to -1.51]; P<0.001), but the limits of agreement exceeded the MCIDs. CONCLUSIONS: With increasing disability, HGS and 2MWT performance declined, although correlations were moderate and uncertainty of predictions exceeded MCIDs of both instruments. Remote WHODAS 2.0 assessments cannot replace in-person physical function testing. CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: NCT03671447.

Differential effects of prone positioning and PEEP on ventilation/perfusion distribution across inflammatory ARDS subphenotypes: a porcine experimental study
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: ARDS comprises distinct inflammatory subphenotypes, including hyper- and hypo-inflammatory forms. Whether these differ in ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) mismatch and response to ventilatory strategies remains unclear. Dual-energy CT enables regional assessment of aeration and perfusion. This experimental study aimed to compare V/Q mismatch between hyper- and hypo-inflammatory subphenotypes, and respective responses to PEEP and prone positioning. METHODS: In 10 pigs, hypo-inflammatory ARDS was induced by lung lavage followed by injurious ventilation. Hyper-inflammatory ARDS was produced by i.v. endotoxin infusion and fluid loading. Pigs were randomised to hypo- or hyperinflammatory ARDS, with similar oxygenation impairment. Dual-energy CT scans were obtained at individualised low, optimal, and high PEEP settings, in supine and prone positions. V/Q was derived from regional gas and blood volume and classified as low (<0.5), normal, or high (>2). Linear mixed-effects models included injury group, PEEP, and posture as fixed effects, and subject as a random effect. RESULTS: Hyper-inflammatory injury showed more severe V/Q mismatch than hypo-inflammatory injury (normal V/Q: 35% [sd=10] vs 51% [8] at low PEEP, supine position; P<0.01). Both PEEP optimisation and prone positioning improved V/Q. Prone positioning reduced high V/Q and dead space in hypo-inflammatory injury (group×posture interaction: F1,50=4.32, P=0.04), whereas PEEP reduced low V/Q and shunt in the supine position independent of ARDS subphenotype. CONCLUSIONS: In porcine models of hyper- and hypo-inflammatory ARDS, hyper-inflammatory injury was associated with more severe V/Q mismatch despite similar oxygenation. Distinct responses to PEEP and prone positioning support a subphenotype-tailored approach to ventilatory management.

Electroencephalography-derived spectral edge frequency 95 targets in toddlers under propofol anaesthesia✰
items.abstract: Background Proprietary processed EEG indices are less accurate in young children. We evaluated spectral edge frequency 95 (SEF95), a nonproprietary EEG index representing the frequency below which 95% of total EEG power resides, to establish target thresholds for varying anaesthetic depths during propofol anaesthesia in toddlers. Secondary objectives were to assess the relationship between SEF95 and plasma propofol concentration, and to evaluate airway reactivity during laryngoscopy. Methods In this prospective study of toddlers aged 13 to 24 months, Dixon's up-and-down method and centred isotonic regression were used to determine the SEF95 targets for 50% (ED 50 ) and 90% (ED 90 ) probability of nonresponse to three clinical stimuli: pacifier placement (assessing consciousness), electrical nerve stimulation (nociception), and laryngoscopy (intubation readiness). Linear mixed-effects regression was used to analyse the association between plasma propofol concentration and SEF95. Results Among 51 toddlers, SEF95 ED 50 and ED 90 targets (Hz) were 21.8 (90% CI 20.8-23.4) and 20.3 (19.1-20.7) Hz for pacifier placement, 12.0 (10.8-18.3) and 10.4 (8.7-11.3) Hz for electrical stimulation, and 10.3 (4.6-11.8) and 4.4 (1.5-5.4) Hz for laryngoscopy. Each 1 Hz increase in SEF95 corresponded to a 0.21 μg ml -1 decrease in plasma propofol (r=0.46, P -1 )=5.80-0.21×SEF95 (Hz). Conclusions This study defined EEG SEF95 targets for loss of consciousness, response to noxious stimuli, and intubation readiness in toddlers aged 13 to 24 months. When combined with existing infant data, these age-specific SEF95 targets can optimise propofol titration and dosing accuracy during EEG-guided propofol anaesthesia in patients aged Clinical trial registration NCT05701748. Registered 17 January 2023; PI: Ian Yuan.

The effects of ephedrine, phenylephrine, and norepinephrine on pregnant human myometrial contractility: an ex vivo study✰
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: The choice of vasopressor during Caesarean delivery to prevent maternal hypotension remains debated. This study aimed to determine the concentration-dependent effects of vasopressors on pregnant myometrium, with and without oxytocin. METHODS: In this prospective ex vivo study, myometrial samples were obtained from full-term pregnant women during elective Caesarean delivery. Myometrial contractility to vasopressors was recorded in the absence/presence of oxytocin compared with controls. Concentration-response testing was done with ephedrine, phenylephrine, and norepinephrine. The primary outcome was the motility index (amplitude×frequency). Isolated primary myometrial cells were also used for calcium mobilisation assays. RESULTS: Myometrial samples were obtained from 32 females. The mean motility index increased with ephedrine (+39.9%; 95% CI 20.6-62.5; P<0.001) and phenylephrine (+36.2%; 95% CI 19.3-55.4; P<0.001), but norepinephrine had no effect (+12.0%; 95% CI -0.7 to 26.1; P=0.066) compared with control. Similar changes in motility index were observed in the presence of oxytocin. Calcium mobilisation recordings on primary myometrial cells supported the contractility findings, with increases in intracellular calcium ions after ephedrine and phenylephrine, but not with norepinephrine compared with control. CONCLUSIONS: Ephedrine and phenylephrine increased ex vivo human myometrial contractility, both independently and in combination with oxytocin, consistent with improving uterine tone during Caesarean delivery. Norepinephrine does not affect myometrial contractility, suggesting that it is safe to use before delivery.

General anaesthesia rates for Caesarean delivery: a quality metric or a marker of system capacity?
items.abstract: General anaesthesia for Caesarean delivery is increasingly used as a quality indicator, but general anaesthesia rates alone are not measures of quality. The multinational anaesthesia practice for Caesarean delivery snapshot study demonstrates variation in general anaesthesia use across European centres, emphasising the need to interpret these rates within the systems in which anaesthetic decisions occur. We propose an interpretation framework based on three domains: access to appropriate neuraxial care, reliability of neuraxial techniques and rescue pathways, and patient experience. The rates of general anaesthesia for Caesarean delivery should prompt investigation of system capacity rather than serve as verdicts on quality or safety.

items.title: A call for post-implementation evaluation of the 2025 UK neurological death criteria in practice
items.abstract: The 2025 UK Code of Practice revised adult death determination using neurological criteria, including requirements for temperature, apnoea testing, and other aspects of assessment. National audit data describe how often testing occurs and record reasons for non-testing, but do not establish the consistency, quality, or physiological consequences of individual assessments. Testing rates were declining before the revised Code, precluding simple attribution of that decline to its introduction. We propose prospective patient-level evaluation from a predefined clinical screening trigger through assessment to confirmation of death, identification of persisting brainstem function, circulatory death before completion or after withdrawal of life-sustaining treatment, or continued treatment. A proposed dataset combines assessment timelines, individual prerequisites, test results, successive barriers, physiological events, and clinician experience. These findings should distinguish inconsistent interpretation from difficulties arising despite correct implementation and identify priorities for clarification, training, or focused evidence review.

Association of preoperative vaping-related disorder versus cigarette nicotine dependence with postoperative respiratory complications: a multicentre matched cohort study
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Electronic cigarette aerosols may promote airway inflammation, bronchial hyperreactivity, and impaired mucociliary defence, but their perioperative respiratory safety remains uncertain. We examined whether preoperative vaping-related disorder was associated with a higher risk of postoperative respiratory complications than cigarette nicotine dependence. METHODS: We conducted a nationwide matched cohort study using the TriNetX US Collaborative Network database, comparing surgical patients with documented preoperative vaping-related disorder and cigarette nicotine dependence. The primary outcome was a 30-day composite of postoperative respiratory complications, including pneumonia, respiratory failure, bronchospasm, noninvasive ventilation, and mechanical ventilation. RESULTS: Among 3817 matched pairs, preoperative vaping-related disorder was associated with a higher risk of 30-day respiratory complications than cigarette nicotine dependence (10.7% vs 5.1%, relative risk [RR] 2.11, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.79-2.49). Vaping-related disorder was also associated with increased risks of pneumonia (RR 3.20, 95% CI 2.40-4.28), respiratory failure (RR 2.48, 95% CI 1.98-3.10), bronchospasm (RR 1.92, 95% CI, 1.38-2.68), and noninvasive ventilation (RR 2.56, 95% CI 1.64-3.98). Vaping-related disorder combined with cigarette nicotine dependence was associated with a higher risk of respiratory complications than cigarette nicotine dependence alone (RR 1.98, 95% CI 1.55-2.53), whereas vaping-related disorder alone showed a larger RR increase than neither diagnosis (RR 3.11, 95% CI 2.56-3.76). CONCLUSIONS: Among surgical patients, preoperative vaping-related disorder was associated with a higher risk of postoperative respiratory complications than cigarette nicotine dependence. These findings suggest that vaping history should be specifically assessed during preoperative evaluation and considered in perioperative respiratory risk stratification.

items.title: Beyond the binary: vaping and the changing face of perioperative pulmonary risk
items.abstract: Postoperative pulmonary complications remain common, and preoperative respiratory risk assessment continues to rely on conventional cigarette smoking status. A recent study in the British Journal of Anaesthesia identifies an association between vaping-related disorder and postoperative pulmonary complications, while showing a less pronounced association with cigarette nicotine dependence. These findings suggest that binary classifications such as smoker and nonsmoker no longer adequately describe inhalational exposure. Perioperative assessment must evolve towards a broader and more nuanced characterisation of inhalational exposure.

items.title: Preoperative roxadustat in major elective noncardiac surgery: a phase 2a randomised clinical trial
items.abstract: Background Postoperative complications remain a leading cause of mortality. Experimental data indicate that roxadustat, a first-in-class prolyl hydroxylase inhibitor, reduces ischaemia-reperfusion injury, accelerates wound healing, and enhances survival in sepsis. Therefore, preoperative administration of roxadustat might reduce perioperative organ injury. We examined the perioperative tolerability and the potential for adverse surgical interactions with roxadustat. Methods In this phase 2a, single-centre, double-blind, randomised-controlled pilot trial, 150 patients undergoing major elective noncardiac surgery were allocated to preoperative roxadustat 100 mg or placebo for three alternate-day doses, with the last dose on the operative morning. The co-primary outcomes were preoperative adverse events and postoperative complications meeting standardised endpoint definitions within 30 days. Results Among 148 participants (52 [35.1%] females; median age 65 [range 24-84] yr) receiving at least one drug dose, at least one preoperative adverse event occurred in 21 of 75 (28%) in the roxadustat group and 20 of 73 (27%) in the placebo group (odds ratio 1.03; 95% CI 0.50-2.12). No serious adverse reactions occurred. Among 143 participants who proceeded to surgery (52 [36.4%] females; median age 65 [range 26-84] yr), ≥1 complication occurred in 23 of 74 participants (31%) who received roxadustat compared with 21 of 69 participants (30%) who received placebo (odds ratio 1.03; 95% CI 0.51-2.10). Days alive out of hospital within 30 days was similar between the groups. The annualised enrolment rate was 90 per year, with high levels of drug compliance. Conclusions Preoperative roxadustat was feasible in patients having major surgery. Uncertainty remains regarding the safety and efficacy of this intervention. Clinical trial registration www.anzctr.org.au; ACTRN12624000188538.

items.title: Socioeconomic position and health: priorities for equitable research and policy
items.abstract: Socioeconomic deprivation is a key determinant of health inequity. In a recent UK-based observational study, more socioeconomically deprived elective patients undergoing surgery were reported to have poorer baseline health despite presenting for surgery at a younger age. This study highlights potentially modifiable demographic characteristics and health behaviours. However, before these observations can be used to inform clinical decision-making and policy change, the complex multifactorial nature of these exposure-outcome relationships must be delineated. This includes accounting for the duration of exposure to components that drive social and economic disadvantage, differences across nations and over time, intersectionality, and the low representation of highly deprived and minority ethnic groups.

items.title: Intraoperative peripheral perfusion index and mortality after noncardiac surgery: a retrospective cohort study
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Intraoperative haemodynamic monitoring primarily targets arterial pressure and flow but might not adequately reflect tissue perfusion. The peripheral perfusion index provides a continuous, noninvasive, and readily available indicator of peripheral perfusion, but its prognostic significance across surgical populations remains uncertain. We hypothesised that greater intraoperative exposure to low perfusion index would be associated with postoperative complications and mortality. METHODS: In this prespecified multicentre cohort study using electronic health record data, we included adults (≥18 yr) undergoing general anaesthesia for noncardiac surgery. The primary exposure was cumulative intraoperative area under a perfusion index of 1.5 expressed in PI⋅min. The primary outcome was 30-day all-cause mortality. The secondary outcome was a 30-day composite of postoperative intensive care unit admission, reoperation, acute kidney injury, or prolonged hospital stay. RESULTS: Among 399 842 patients undergoing 540 101 procedures, a total of 7066 (1.3%) deaths occurred within 30 days: 654 (0.5%) among procedures with no exposure, 1185 (0.6%) in the lower half of exposed procedures, and 5227 (2.6%) in the upper half (split at 3.8 PI⋅min). Compared with no exposure, the adjusted odds ratio for 30-day mortality was 2.18 (95% CI 1.98-2.40, overall association P<0.001) at the 95th percentile of exposure (42.5 PI⋅min), with similar patterns observed across the major surgical specialties. For the composite outcome, the corresponding odds ratio was 1.16 (95% CI 1.14-1.18; P<0.001). CONCLUSIONS: Greater intraoperative exposure to low perfusion index was associated with higher postoperative mortality and complications in adult patients undergoing general anaesthesia for noncardiac surgery. CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: NCT07164339.

items.title: Postoperative delirium is associated with accelerated brain ageing: an exploratory cohort study
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Advanced age is a major risk factor for both delirium and dementia. A potential early biomarker for dementia is the brain-predicted age difference (brainPAD). We hypothesised that brain ageing accelerates after postoperative delirium (POD), and that increased brainPAD is associated with cognitive decline. METHODS: Brain MRI scans were obtained in 287 older patients before and 3 months after major elective surgery, and two MRI scans at similar time intervals were obtained in 46 nonsurgical control participants. We computed grey matter brainPAD in patients with POD (POD+), patients without POD (POD-), and nonsurgical controls. The Trail Making Test (TMT) was administered at both time points to examine associations between changes in brainPAD and changes in attention/processing speed (TMT-A) and executive task switching (TMT-B and TMT B-A). RESULTS: Compared with the POD- group, brainPAD increased by an additional 6 (sd=3) months over time in the POD+ group (P=0.002). For each 1 year-over-year increase in brain age gap, patients took 2.3 s longer to complete the TMT-A (P=0.016), whereas no association was observed with TMT-B (P=0.254) or TMT B-A (P=0.91). CONCLUSIONS: Postoperativ edelirium is associated with accelerated brain ageing, which in turn is associated with decline in attention and processing speed. These findings help to understand the complex relationship between ageing, delirium, and dementia. CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: NCT02265263.

Hypothalamic orexin input to the medial amygdala promotes arousal from anaesthesia and modulates exploratory behaviour
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Emergence from general anaesthesia is often accompanied by agitation, suggesting that recovery of consciousness can engage neural circuits that regulate arousal and behavioural responsiveness. The amygdala influences social, defensive, and exploratory behaviours, but whether orexinergic input to the amygdala regulates anaesthetic state transitions together with behavioural responses remains unclear. METHODS: In male orexin-Cre mice, we combined viral tracing, electrophysiology, and RNAscope to define a lateral hypothalamic orexin (LHAOx) projection to the medial amygdala (MeA). Optogenetics, electroencephalography, electromyography, and fibre photometry were used to test how this circuit regulates arousal from isoflurane anaesthesia, as well as exploratory and place-preference behaviour. RESULTS: LHAOx neurones densely innervated the MeA, where orexin receptor 2 was more abundant than orexin receptor 1 (P<0.0001). Optogenetic activation of the LHAOx→MeA projection promoted arousal from 0.75 vol% isoflurane sedation (P<0.0001), delayed induction by 3 vol% isoflurane as measured by loss of the righting reflex (P=0.0074), and accelerated emergence from 2 vol% isoflurane as measured by return of the righting reflex (P=0.0098). In behavioural assays, activation of this projection suppressed open-field exploration, increased real-time place preference, and did not produce conditioned place preference. Activation of the LHAOx→MeA projection was accompanied by increased activity in MeA vesicular GABA transporter (MeAvGAT)-expressing neurones. Direct activation of MeAvGAT neurones replicated the arousal-promoting and reduced exploratory behaviour, whereas silencing their synaptic output eliminated the induction-delaying effect and shifted the real-time preference. CONCLUSIONS: The LHAOx projection to the MeA promotes anaesthetic arousal and acutely suppresses exploratory behaviour in male mice, with MeAvGAT serving as a key downstream target.

Prognostic value of early renal recovery after cardiac surgery–associated acute kidney injury: a retrospective cohort study
items.abstract: Background Cardiac surgery-associated acute kidney injury (CSA-AKI) is common and strongly associated with adverse outcomes. Whether the timing of renal recovery adds prognostic information beyond AKI severity remains uncertain. We examined the association between renal recovery status after CSA-AKI and long-term mortality. Methods In a retrospective cohort from a nationally representative US electronic health record platform (2016-25), we identified adults who developed CSA-AKI within 7 days of coronary artery bypass grafting, valve surgery, or thoracic aortic surgery. The primary exposure was renal recovery status at 7 (early recovery) and 90 days (transition to chronic kidney disease [CKD]) after CSA-AKI onset. Full renal recovery was defined as a return of serum creatinine to Results From 539 658 patients, 111 232 (20.6%) developed CSA-AKI (mean age 68 yr; range 19-94; 28% female). In the early-recovery analysis, 90 029 of 111 232 patients (80.9%) recovered within 7 days; in the CKD-transition analysis, 94 064 of 100 916 (93.2%) recovered within 90 days. Both early non-recovery (adjusted hazard ratio 1.20; 95% CI 1.15-1.25; P Conclusions Both delayed renal recovery and transition to CKD after CSA-AKI are associated with higher long-term all-cause mortality that is independent of CSA-AKI severity.

items.title: From population targets to personalised titration: translating within-patient electroencephalographic responses into clinical practice
items.abstract: Population-derived target ranges of drug concentrations or EEG indices are commonly used in clinical practice for the titration of anaesthesia. By definition, this inevitably results in a relative overdose for most patients and an underdose for a few. For accurate individualised titration of anaesthesia, suitable within-subject targets need to be established. To be reliable, these targets require a measurable EEG response to changes in the hypnotic drug concentration, an EEG endpoint that reliably indicates absence of consciousness, and stability in the EEG drug-dose response relationship so that it is not influenced by other factors that might change through the course of the operation.

Inflammasome–caspase-1 activation is associated with infections in systemic inflammatory response syndrome after cardiac surgery: a prospective translational study
items.abstract: Background Cardiac surgery triggers the systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS), characterised by a dysregulated immune response involving concurrent pro- and anti-inflammatory activation. Postoperative immunosuppression increases susceptibility to postoperative infections, prolonged hospitalisation, and mortality. After burns and stroke, circulating cell-free DNA (cfDNA) initiates immune dysregulation via inflammasome activation. Whether this mechanism similarly contributes to SIRS-associated immunosuppression after cardiac surgery is unknown. Methods A total of 104 participants undergoing elective cardiac surgery were enrolled. SIRS was defined by ≥2 SIRS criteria 24 h after ICU admission. Serial immune responsiveness was analysed using whole blood stimulation assays. Plasma concentrations of inflammasome-dependent and independent cytokines, cleaved caspase-1, and cfDNA were quantified before/after surgery. Results Overall, 57 of 104 participants (55%) fulfilled ≥2 SIRS criteria 24 h after ICU admission (mean age 63 yr; range 28–81; 28% female). SIRS was associated with more frequent infections (odds ratio 6.1; 95% CI 2.1–17.7). Within the SIRS cohort, participants who developed infections had impaired immune responsiveness to inflammatory ligands within the first 2 days after surgery. SIRS associated with infection displayed increased inflammasome activation, as indicated by higher interleukin-1β, interleukin-1 receptor antagonist, and caspase-1 concentrations. For every 1 ng ml −1 increase in plasma interleukin-1 receptor antagonist, there was a 52% higher risk of developing postoperative infection ( P =0.018). cfDNA plasma concentrations were increased in the SIRS and infection groups and correlated with inflammasome-associated markers. Conclusions A subgroup of individuals after cardiac surgery has early inflammasome activation and profound immunosuppression, potentially predisposing them to subsequent infections. cfDNA is a potential inflammasome activator in this setting.

items.title: Videolaryngoscopy vs. direct laryngoscopy for tracheal intubation by anaesthesia resident doctors ( VILARE ): a pragmatic multicentre randomised trial
items.abstract: Introduction Videolaryngoscopy has been associated with improved glottic visualisation and higher first‐attempt tracheal intubation success compared with direct laryngoscopy. However, multicentre evidence evaluating its effectiveness when tracheal intubation is performed by anaesthesia resident doctors in routine practice is limited. Methods Adult patients undergoing surgery requiring tracheal intubation were assigned to videolaryngoscopy or direct laryngoscopy for the initial attempt. All tracheal intubations were performed by anaesthesia residents under consultant supervision. The primary outcome was successful tracheal intubation on the first attempt. Secondary outcomes included glottic visualisation; number of tracheal intubation attempts; need for adjunct airway devices; procedural difficulty; and procedural complications. Results We enrolled 1001 patients and assigned 501 to videolaryngoscopy and 500 patients to direct laryngoscopy. Successful first‐attempt tracheal intubation was achieved in 397 (79.2%) patients allocated to the videolaryngoscopy group and 351 (70.2%) patients allocated to the direct laryngoscopy group (absolute risk difference 9.0%, 95%CI 3.7–14.4%, p < 0.001). Videolaryngoscopy improved glottic visualisation, with more patients having a modified Cormack–Lehane grade 2 or 2a view (467/501 (93.3%) vs. 404/500 (80.8%); p < 0.001); decreased operator‐reported tracheal intubation difficulty (168/501 (33.5%) vs. 236/500 (47.2%); p < 0.001) and reduced procedural complications (39/501 (7.7%) vs. 91/500 (18.2%); p < 0.001), without a clinically meaningful difference in tracheal intubation time or the need for adjunct airway devices. Discussion In adult patients undergoing tracheal intubation by anaesthesia resident doctors, videolaryngoscopy increased first‐attempt success and improved overall procedural performance compared with direct laryngoscopy.

items.title: Complications in neonates with difficult tracheal intubation: an analysis of the Pediatric Difficult Intubation Registry
items.abstract: Introduction Difficult tracheal intubation is associated with serious complications, including hypoxia, bradycardia and cardiac arrest. Neonates have increased physiologic vulnerability compared with older children, yet detailed data on management strategies and outcomes in neonates with difficult tracheal intubation remain limited. We hypothesised that clinicians have lower first‐attempt tracheal intubation success and higher complication rates for neonates compared with older children with difficult tracheal intubation. Methods We analysed the Pediatric Difficult Intubation Registry to determine tracheal intubation first attempt success and incidence of complications. We used logistic regression to identify variables associated with complications in neonates. Results During the study period, 6283 paediatric difficult tracheal intubations were recorded, including 420 neonates. First attempt success was lower for neonates (139/420, 33.1%) than older children (2394/4683, 51.1%). Complications occurred more frequently in neonates (123/420, 29.3%) than older children (637/4683, 13.6%). Hypoxia occurred in 92/420 (21.9%) neonates and 269/4683 (5.7%) older children. Severe complications were more frequent in neonates vs. older children (12/420, 2.9% vs. 30/4683, 0.6%, respectively), with cardiac arrests occurring in 4/420 (1.0%) neonates and 11/4683 (0.2%) older children. Difficult mask ventilation occurred more frequently in neonates (60/419, 14.3%) than older children (353/4681, 7.5%). In neonates, increased number of tracheal intubation attempts (aOR 1.61 per attempt, 95%CI 1.30–2.00, p < 0.001) and difficult facemask ventilation (aOR 3.17, 95%CI 1.38–7.30, p = 0.007) were associated with complications. Anticipated difficulty with airway management had a protective effect (aOR 0.37, 95%CI 0.16–0.88, p = 0.025). Discussion Neonates with difficult tracheal intubation experience a substantially higher rate of complications than older children. Early recognition of risk is critical in order to enable careful planning to minimise tracheal intubation attempts in this vulnerable population.

items.title: Incidence of pain, supplemental analgesia and conversion to general anaesthesia during intrapartum caesarean delivery using converted epidural anaesthesia: a meta‐analysis
items.abstract: Introduction It is common practice to convert an existing labour epidural into surgical anaesthesia for intrapartum caesarean delivery. However, this approach does not always provide adequate anaesthesia. This meta‐analysis aimed to determine the incidence of inadequate anaesthesia during epidural conversion for intrapartum caesarean delivery. Methods Databases were searched for observational studies and randomised controlled trials evaluating epidural conversion for intrapartum caesarean delivery. Using a random‐effects model and the Freeman–Tukey double arcsine transformation, we calculated the respective incidences of intra‐operative patient‐reported pain; use of supplemental analgesia; and conversion to general anaesthesia. Results A total of 43 studies, involving 11,904 patients, were included in the meta‐analysis. Pooled incidences of intra‐operative pain (eight studies), supplemental analgesia (34 studies) and conversion to general anaesthesia (33 studies) were 20.2% (95%CI 12.2–29.5%, I 2 = 93.1%), 17.7% (95%CI 13.3–22.7%, I 2 = 96.3%) and 1.3% (95%CI 0.7–2.1%, I 2 = 81.7%), respectively. These results were consistent in sensitivity analyses and appeared unaffected by publication year, study design, country type, local anaesthetic used or use of epidural fentanyl. However, substantial heterogeneity was observed due to variability in study methodologies, measurement methods, definitions, thresholds and local clinical practices. Discussion This meta‐analysis highlights the risk of inadequate anaesthesia and emphasises the importance of thorough pre‐operative informed consent when converting labour epidurals to surgical anaesthesia for intrapartum caesarean delivery. However, the considerable heterogeneity in the pooled estimates indicates that these incidences vary significantly across different settings, suggesting that local audit data would be more informative for individual practices.

items.title: Opioid‐free vs. opioid‐inclusive anaesthesia in laparoscopic cholecystectomy: a multicentre randomised controlled trial*
items.abstract: Background Laparoscopic cholecystectomy is the most common abdominal operation worldwide, yet whether opioid‐free anaesthesia improves the overall analgesic benefit remains uncertain. Methods In this multicentre randomised controlled trial, adults undergoing elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy were randomised 1:1 to receive opioid‐free anaesthesia (dexmedetomidine, esketamine and sevoflurane) or opioid‐inclusive anaesthesia (sufentanil and sevoflurane). Patients received prophylactic anti‐emetics and multimodal analgesia with flurbiprofen axetil and ropivacaine wound infiltration. The primary outcome was the overall benefit of analgesia score (0–28, lower scores indicate greater benefit) at 24 h postoperatively; a 3‐point difference was considered clinically relevant. Secondary outcomes included pain on movement at 24 h and chronic postsurgical pain at 90 days. Results Between March and September 2025, 315 patients completed this trial (158 opioid‐free, 157 opioid‐inclusive). The mean (SD) 24‐h overall benefit of analgesia score was 2.2 (2.4) after opioid‐free anaesthesia vs 3.4 (3.1) after opioid‐inclusive anaesthesia (adjusted mean difference ‐1.3; 95%CI ‐1.8 to ‐0.8, p < 0.001), without reaching the threshold for clinical importance. Incidence of pain on movement (adjusted mean difference ‐0.2; 95%CI ‐0.4–0) and chronic postsurgical pain (16.1% vs 15.5%; adjusted relative risk 1.03; 95%CI 0.55–1.91) did not differ between groups. Opioid‐free anaesthesia was associated with reduced intra‐operative hypotension (19.6% vs 35.7%; relative risk 0.55; 95%CI 0.37–0.80) and lower incidence of postoperative nausea and vomiting (23.4% vs 33.8%; relative risk 0.69; 95%CI 0.48–0.98). Discussion Opioid‐free anaesthesia did not achieve a clinically meaningful improvement in overall benefit of analgesia. These findings do not support its routine adoption in laparoscopic cholecystectomy. However, the observed reductions in intra‐operative hypotension and postoperative nausea and vomiting suggest that this regimen may warrant consideration in selected patients, pending validation in future trials.

items.title: Patient‐reported outcomes, postoperative pain and pain relief after day‐case surgery ( POPPY ): persistent postoperative opioid use prevalence and associations
items.abstract: Introduction An increasing proportion of complex surgical procedures are being performed in the UK as day‐cases, and NHS targets aim for these to encompass ≥ 75% of all surgeries. There has been limited outcome follow‐up for this group of patients, particularly considering the prevalence of persistent postoperative opioid use and factors associated with its occurrence. Methods Data from POPPY, a national, prospective, observational study exploring outcomes following day‐case surgery in the UK, were used to estimate the prevalence of persistent postoperative opioid use at day 97 following surgery. Patient, anaesthetic and surgical factors associated with increased persistent postoperative opioid use were explored using multivariable analysis. Results Of the 7839 initially recruited patients, 3488 (44.5%) provided details of their analgesic medication at day 97 following surgery. The prevalence of daily persistent postoperative opioid use was estimated to be 11.8% (95%CI 11.1–13.2%). Patient factors associated with daily persistent postoperative opioid use were pre‐operative opioid use; opioid use at day 7; and composite pain scores (day 1, day 3 and day 7). Compared with general surgery, ENT, breast and orthopaedic surgery carried a higher risk of persistent postoperative opioid use. Patient factors associated with a reduced odds ratio of persistent postoperative opioid use were: female sex; higher composite pain score at baseline; and Index of Multiple Deprivation quintile 4. Daily persistent postoperative opioid use at day 97 following surgery was associated with reduced quality of life scores. Discussion Daily persistent postoperative opioid use is common in the UK following day‐case surgery. Patient and surgical factors that are associated with an increased risk of this outcome could be used to drive improvement in identification of at‐risk patients pre‐operatively and optimise postoperative prescribing pathways.

items.title: Antimicrobial stewardship and resistance in intensive care units in the UK : a prospective national audit
items.abstract: Introduction Principles of effective antimicrobial stewardship include prescription of empiric therapy based on the most likely causative organism, with medication review within 72 h. Adherence to best practice in UK ICUs is unknown and the aim of this study was to evaluate patient‐ and unit‐level antimicrobial use in UK ICUs. Methods We conducted a prospective national audit of antimicrobial use in adults (aged ≥ 18 y) admitted to ICUs in the UK and Isle of Man with a point‐prevalence survey. Subsequently, we collected longitudinal data on review of therapy and antimicrobial resistance in a subset of patients who had commenced therapy within the previous 3 days. Results We studied 2626 patients from 154/292 (52.7%) ICUs. Antimicrobial therapy was prescribed in 1592 (60.6%) patients. Of 2116 empiric antimicrobial orders, 1592 (75.2%) were compliant with unit‐level guidelines. For non‐compliant orders, 253 (12.0% of all empiric orders) were discussed with infection specialists and 69 (3.3%) provided justification for off‐guidance therapy, but 202 (9.5%) were prescribed outside guidance without justification or discussion with infection specialists. Guideline‐compliant review within 72 h of prescription took place in 1488/1606 (92.7%) eligible medication orders. A pre‐specified stop or review date was strongly associated with antimicrobial review within 72 h (adjusted OR 9.3, 95%CI 5.4–16.2). Discussion We have benchmarked critical care antimicrobial stewardship and guideline compliance across the UK. We recommend that pre‐specified review dates are added to all prescriptions, as the most important determinant of review identified in our audit. Future work should include national stewardship audit cycles to benchmark practice and inform quality improvement initiatives.
