items.title: Evaluation of cranial–caudal block spread in children using MRI : a dosage comparison
items.abstract: Introduction Caudal blockade is used widely in paediatric analgesia, but empirical data on the local anaesthetic dose–spread relationship remain limited. This study quantified craniocaudal spread dynamics of three ropivacaine concentrations using real‐time magnetic resonance imaging. Methods This prospective, observer‐blinded trial allocated children undergoing elective surgery to receive caudal 0.2% ropivacaine at doses of 0.5 ml.kg ‐1 , 1.0 ml.kg ‐1 or 1.5 ml.kg ‐1 (based on surgical requirements). Cranial spread was quantified using respiratory‐gated 3 Tesla magnetic resonance imaging and assigned a vertebral level. Optic nerve sheath diameter was measured before and after block administration in children allocated to the high‐dose group. Dose–spread relationships were assessed using linear regression. Results In total, data from 45 children (aged 1–3 y) were analysed. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed dose‐dependent median (IQR [range]) spread was L2 (L2–L2 [L2–L1]) for 0.5 ml.kg ‐1 ; T12 (T12–T10 [L1–T10]) for 1.0 ml.kg ‐1 ; and T9 (T10–T9 [T10–T8]) for 1.5 ml.kg ‐1 (group differences H = 38.6, p < 0.001). Linear regression established that vertebral level = 5.8 + 5.3 × Dose (R 2 = 0.79). Each 0.5 ml.kg ‐1 increment advanced spread by 3.1 levels (95%CI 2.6–3.6 levels). Dose correlated strongly with spread (Spearman's ρ = 0.87, p < 0.001), but not with age; weight; height; or scan time. No significant optic nerve sheath diameter changes occurred following the block. Discussion The magnetic resonance imaging‐quantified dose–response model for caudal blockade showed a predictable linear cranial progression with a 0.2% ropivacaine dose of 1.5 ml.kg ‐1 safely achieving mid‐thoracic coverage with no evidence of intracranial pressure elevation. The derived regression equation enables precise, personalised targeting of surgical sensory levels in children.

items.title: Impact of ozone on paediatric peri‐operative adverse events in the context of the ‘Fremantle Doctor’: a prospective cohort study
items.abstract: Introduction Peri‐operative respiratory adverse events are a major cause of morbidity and mortality in paediatric anaesthesia. Gaseous pollutants (such as ozone) and fine particles have direct effects on airways, and so exposure to pollutants may influence the risk of peri‐operative respiratory adverse events. This prospective, observational cohort study aimed to examine how the incidence of peri‐operative respiratory adverse events in children is influenced by pre‐hospital exposure to air pollution. Methods Data were collected prospectively at a tertiary paediatric centre in Western Australia over three data collection periods. Details of respiratory risk factors, anaesthesia management and the incidence of peri‐operative respiratory adverse events (laryngospasm, bronchospasm, airway obstruction, severe coughing, desaturation, pulmonary aspiration and postoperative stridor) were recorded during anaesthesia induction, maintenance, emergence and recovery. Each patient's home suburb was used to determine exposure to air pollution in the 2 days before their procedure. This used data from the Department of Water and Environmental Regulation air quality monitoring stations across Western Australia. Results In this low‐pollution Western Australian cohort of 7051 anaesthetic episodes involving 6754 individual patients undergoing general anaesthesia, short‐term exposure to particulate and gaseous pollutants other than ozone was not associated with increased incidence of peri‐operative respiratory adverse events. However, ozone exposure showed a borderline association with peri‐operative respiratory adverse events, particularly in children with pre‐existing respiratory disease. Discussion Ozone pollution showed a signal for increased peri‐operative risk, despite generally low pollutant concentrations. The coastal meteorology of Perth, including the regular sea breeze known locally as the ‘Fremantle Doctor’, provides important context for the largely low pollutant concentrations observed even during times of significant wildfires. Regions with higher or more variable pollution may show stronger or clinically more important effects.

items.title: Subarachnoid administration of hyperbaric prilocaine compared with hyperbaric bupivacaine for cervical cerclage (PRILOCC) in pregnant women: a multicentre, double‐blind randomised controlled trial*
items.abstract: Introduction Intrathecal prilocaine is used commonly in ambulatory surgery due to its favourable recovery profile, but its use for cervical cerclage is not well established. We aimed to examine the recovery profiles of equipotent intrathecal injections of hyperbaric prilocaine 2% and bupivacaine 0.5% for transvaginal cervical cerclage. We hypothesised that hyperbaric prilocaine 2% would result in a faster recovery of motor function. Methods We recruited pregnant women undergoing transvaginal cervical cerclage. Patients were allocated randomly to intrathecal injections of either 2 ml hyperbaric prilocaine 2% with 15 μg fentanyl or 2 ml hyperbaric bupivacaine 0.5% with 15 μg fentanyl. The primary outcome was time from intrathecal injection to full movement of legs (Bromage score of 1). Secondary outcomes included times to: regression of sensory block; first micturition; first ambulation; and meeting hospital discharge criteria. Results We enrolled 135 women and omitted one due to incomplete data, leaving 67 patients in each group. Mean (SD) time to achieve a Bromage score of 1 for the prilocaine group was 88 (51) min compared with 129 (63) min for the bupivacaine group (mean difference 40 min, 95%CI 21–60, p < 0.001). Prilocaine was also superior to bupivacaine with respect to time to regression of sensory block (mean difference 54 min, 95%CI 42–66, p < 0.001); first spontaneous micturition (mean difference 113 min, 95%CI 61–164, p < 0.001); first ambulation (mean difference 59 min, 95%CI 34–83, p < 0.001); and meeting hospital discharge criteria (estimated between‐group difference 74 min, 95%CI 38–108, p < 0.001). Discussion Intrathecal prilocaine for cervical cerclage results in a faster recovery of motor and sensory function, with similar efficacy to bupivacaine, as well as a shorter time to ambulation and meeting discharge criteria.

items.title: Postoperative pulmonary function after video-assisted thoracic surgery using epidural analgesia or oral morphine for pain management
Pre-operative anaemia and complications
items.abstract: BACKGROUND Pre-operative anaemia is common in patients undergoing colorectal surgery and has been associated with adverse postoperative outcomes. However, its direct causal impact remains uncertain. OBJECTIVE To estimate the causal effect of pre-operative anaemia on 30-day postoperative complications after elective colorectal surgery, using targeted maximum likelihood estimation (TMLE). DESIGN Causal analysis of two prospective, multicentre observational cohorts: EuroPOWER ( n = 2826) and POWER ( n = 1185). The EuroPOWER cohort was used for primary estimation; POWER was used for replication and transportability analyses. SETTING One hundred and eighty-five hospitals across 21 European countries for EuroPOWER and 80 Spanish centres for POWER. PATIENTS Patients undergoing elective colorectal surgery. Anaemia was defined using WHO thresholds (Hb < 13 g dl -1 in men, <12 g dl -1 in women). MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES The primary outcome was any 30-day postoperative complication. TMLE with SuperLearner ensembles estimated the average treatment effect (ATE) of correcting anaemia. Logistic regression, generalised additive models and an external transportability analysis were used for comparison and validation. RESULTS In EuroPOWER, pre-operative anaemia was associated with an absolute increase in postoperative complications risk from 23.6 to 28.6% [ATE +5.05 percentage points (p.p); 95% CI, 1.20 to 8.91; P = 0.01]. The external replication cohort yielded a similar point estimate, although statistical uncertainty remained substantial. Application of the EuroPOWER-trained model to the POWER cohort yielded an estimated transported ATE of +6.05 p.p. Pooled fixed-effect meta-analysis yielded an overall ATE of +4.65 p.p. (95% CI, 1.69 to 7.60; P = 0.002; I 2 = 0%). CONCLUSIONS Pre-operative anaemia was associated with higher estimated rates of postoperative complications in elective colorectal surgery within a causal inference framework. Although effect estimates were directionally similar across cohorts, uncertainty remained in the external replication analysis. These findings support systematic pre-operative anaemia assessment and optimisation strategies, while acknowledging that current therapeutic interventions may not necessarily reproduce the estimated counterfactual effects.

items.title: Paratracheal air cysts and their associations with postoperative pulmonary complications in patients undergoing surgery under general anesthesia: a retrospective propensity-score-matched study
items.containerTitle: Canadian Journal of Anesthesia/Journal canadien d'anesthésie
items.abstract: Purpose Paratracheal air cysts are rare benign anatomical variants. Although case reports suggest that paratracheal air cysts may lead to complications such as difficult ventilation and pneumothorax in patients whose lungs are mechanically ventilated, their association with postoperative pulmonary complications (PPCs) remains unclear. We hypothesized that the presence of cysts is associated with an increased incidence of PPCs. Methods In the context of COVID-19, we conducted a retrospective study of all patients undergoing surgery under general anesthesia in 2020. On the basis of the presence of paratracheal air cysts, we divided patients into two groups: the paratracheal air cyst group and the paratracheal-air-cyst‑free group. The primary outcome was the incidence of PPCs. We used propensity score matching to adjust for confounding and performed multivariable logistic regression analysis in the matched cohort to assess the association. Results Among 7,208 patients, the prevalence of paratracheal air cysts was 2.0% (141/7,208). The incidence of PPCs was 22% (31/141) in the paratracheal air cyst group and 15% (43/280) in the paratracheal-air-cyst-free group. Multivariable regression analysis showed that, after adjusting for confounders, the presence of paratracheal air cysts was associated with an increased risk of PPCs (adjusted odds ratio, 1.85; 95% confidence interval, 1.03 to 3.33; P = 0.04). Conclusions The presence of paratracheal air cysts was associated with an increased risk of PPCs. Although this association warrants cautious interpretation due to possible residual confounding and lack of data on intraoperative ventilatory settings, anesthesiologists should consider the potential perioperative implications of this anatomical abnormality during preoperative assessment.

items.title: Development and implementation of an objective framework for measuring clinician faculty research contributions in a Canadian anesthesiology department
items.containerTitle: Canadian Journal of Anesthesia/Journal canadien d'anesthésie
items.abstract: Purpose Given the fiduciary responsibility of an academic clinical department to ensure appropriate use of funds to support research, the Department of Anesthesia, Pain Management and Perioperative Medicine at Dalhousie University (Halifax, NS, Canada) aimed to create a framework to support the allocation of remunerated protected research time to clinician faculty members within the department. Methods A departmental Research Accountability Project (RAP) was undertaken in the context of a quality improvement initiative. The RAP initially engaged clinician faculty members in the form of a survey, interviews, and a questionnaire to provide feedback regarding current practices for evaluating protected time for research. On the basis of this feedback, a working group created a list of 151 research outputs encompassing the breadth of research-related activities and assigned scores based on their relative merit. Clinicians with protected research time completed their academic profile, and individual point allocations were calculated. Scores were then weighted by different categories (e.g., publications, grant capture, presentations), and a RAP dashboard was developed to capture research outputs, assign scores, and generate a reporting/feedback mechanism for further analysis. Results Faculty members acknowledged the importance of clinicians having remunerated protected time to carry out research; nevertheless, there was scepticism with respect to how protected research time was managed. These data were then assessed by the working group, and using the RAP metric, individual researcher reports consisting of scores and recommendations were sent to the department head for final evaluation. These reports formed the basis of the researchers' annual academic performance review and consideration for continuance. Conclusions The RAP scoring system provides an objective measure of remunerated protected research time for clinicians to assist in researcher accountability.

items.title: Evaluation of deep learning for the modified Cormack–Lehane classification in videolaryngoscopic images: a prospective observational study
items.containerTitle: Canadian Journal of Anesthesia/Journal canadien d'anesthésie
items.abstract: Purpose Predicting difficult intubation is still challenging, even with videolaryngoscopy. Videolaryngoscopy (VL) shows the larynx during intubation. The modified Cormack-Lehane (CL) classification grades laryngeal visibility but can vary between observers. Deep learning uses neural networks for objective, real-time airway image evaluation. We aimed to evaluate a YOLOv8-based model for object detection to automate modified CL grade classification from VL images in patients undergoing elective surgery. Methods In this prospective observational study, we developed a deep learning model using 346 VL images from 151 patients undergoing elective surgery. Two anesthesiologists classified images according to the modified CL system, and interobserver agreement was analysed using Cohen's kappa and weighted kappa. We split the data into training (80%), validation (10%), and test (10%) sets, with imbalance corrected via Albumentations augmentation. We evaluated the model results using sensitivity, specificity, and mean average precision with a 95% confidence interval (CI) and validated the model on 60 images not included in the training set. Results Interobserver agreement ranged from moderate (Cohen's kappa = 0.59; 95% CI, 0.53 to 0.66) to good (weighted kappa = 0.79; 95% CI, 0.75 to 0.84). In the test set, the overall recall rate was 0.87, and the specificity was 0.83. In the difficult intubation grades, recall and specificity were observed to be 0.79 (95% CI, 0.52 to 0.92) and 0.93 (95% CI, 0.78 to 0.98), respectively, for CL grade 2b, and 0.60 and 1.00, respectively, for CL grade 3. In the external validation data set (n = 60), the model achieved an overall accuracy of 0.767 with a recognition rate of 0.925 for clinically relevant CL grades 2b and 3. Conclusions The YOLOv8-based model showed promising performance in classifying modified CL grades, particularly for clinically relevant difficult views (CL grades 2b-3). Nevertheless, wide CIs and limited external validation indicate uncertainty. The model may be considered an auxiliary tool rather than an independent decision system and requires further validation in larger, multicentre data sets.

items.title: Voluntariness of same-day versus advance consent in low-risk clinical research: a randomized controlled trial
items.containerTitle: Canadian Journal of Anesthesia/Journal canadien d'anesthésie
items.abstract: Purpose The solicitation of same-day consent for participation in clinical research is commonly prohibited by research ethics boards because of concerns about limited decision-making time and patient vulnerability. However, these concerns lack empirical support and restrict both research efforts and patient participation opportunities, particularly in medical specialties such as emergency medicine, critical care, and anesthesiology, in which clinicians and patients interact for the first time on the day of a procedure. We aimed to assess the voluntariness of research consent solicited on the day of surgery compared with consent obtained in advance. Methods We performed a prospective, noninferiority randomized controlled trial examining the voluntariness of informed consent to participate in a low-risk clinical research trial at Women's College Hospital in Toronto, Ontario, Canada. The trial design included active deception (invitation to participate in a fabricated research trial) to capture authentic measurements of participants' perceptions of any perceived coercion. Results We randomized 114 patients scheduled to undergo anterior cruciate ligament repair for recruitment into a fabricated low-risk perioperative research trial at one of two time points: at a virtual preanesthesia clinic appointment in advance of the day of surgery, or on the day of surgery. Regardless of their decision, all participants received the (same) standard of care. Overall, 71/114 patients (62%) either consented to participate in the fabricated trial or declined participation but consented to a feedback session during which perceptions of coercion were assessed. Greater participation was observed among patients approached on the day of surgery (fabricated trial, 26/58 [45%]; feedback session only, 18/58 [31%]) than in advance (fabricated trial, 17/56 [30%]; feedback session only, 10/56 [18%]). Perceived coercion, measured using two validated psychometric instruments, did not differ between patients recruited on the day of surgery and those recruited in advance. A subset of patients in each group reported modest perceptions of undue influence, but regardless of recruitment time point, these patients demonstrated their agency to decline participation. Conclusions Our findings suggest that restrictive same-day consent policies, when based on concerns regarding undue influence, may represent a structural barrier to participation in low-risk trials that lacks empirical justification. Study registrations 1) Open Science Framework ( 46twc ); first submitted 17 March 2023; 2) ClinicalTrials.gov ( NCT07380035 ); first submitted 16 January 2026.

items.title: Fellowship, research, and practice preferences: an updated survey of Canadian anesthesiology residents
items.containerTitle: Canadian Journal of Anesthesia/Journal canadien d'anesthésie
items.abstract: Purpose Canada faces mounting anesthesia workforce pressures, particularly in rural and smaller urban centres. Understanding residents' motivations regarding practice setting, research, and fellowship training is essential for workforce planning. We aimed to update a 2015 national survey to characterize current preferences and temporal shifts among Canadian anesthesiology residents. Methods We conducted an anonymous, cross-sectional survey of residents in accredited Canadian anesthesiology programs (November-December 2024) using Research Electronic Data Capture. Items addressed demographics, practice setting, research experience and intentions, and fellowship plans. Selected responses were compared with 2015 survey items using Chi square tests and odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals; all tests used an alpha of 0.05. Results Ninety-four residents responded (12% response rate). Most preferred academic practice (63%), and half preferred to remain at their training institution (49%). Interest in rural practice was reported by 49%. Although research participation was common during medical school (94%) and residency (83%), only 18% intended to pursue research after residency. Approximately 63% intended to pursue fellowship training. Compared with the 2015 survey, there were significant increases in intention to remain at the same institution (from 35% to 50%; P = 0.02) and residency research participation (from 69% to 83%; P Conclusions Canadian anesthesiology residents continue to favour academic practice and fellowship training, yet fewer plan to integrate research into future careers. These findings highlight opportunities for targeted mentorship, greater research autonomy, financial support, and expanded rural training pathways to align resident priorities with workforce needs.

items.title: Cardiovascular disturbances and ward hypotension after major vascular surgery: a single-centre prospective cohort study
items.containerTitle: Canadian Journal of Anesthesia/Journal canadien d'anesthésie
items.abstract: PURPOSE: Postoperative hypotension can be caused by vasodilation, myocardial dysfunction, severe hypovolemia, and obstruction. We sought to estimate the effects of these causes on the incidence of hypotension after major vascular surgery. METHODS: We conducted a single-centre prospective cohort study of male and female adult patients undergoing major vascular surgery. We conducted point-of-care ultrasound and sidestream darkfield microscopy imaging to detect vasodilation, myocardial dysfunction, severe hypovolemia, and obstruction. The primary outcome was hypotension (systolic blood pressure < 90 mm Hg or a vasopressor infusion) within 24 hr of surgery. RESULTS: We recruited 100 patients, of whom 89 had data available for analysis. Hypotension occurred in 20 participants (23%), vasodilation in 30 (34%), and myocardial dysfunction in 11 (12%). Severe hypovolemia and obstruction were not observed. The adjusted marginal risk difference of hypotension was 33% (95% confidence interval [CI], 14% to 53%; P < 0.001) for vasodilation and 41% (95% CI, 3% to 79%; P = 0.03) for myocardial dysfunction. Vasodilation increased the risk of intensive care unit admission by 27% (95% CI, 8% to 45%; P = 0.006) and of requiring a vasopressor infusion by 22% (95% CI, 4% to 39%; P = 0.02). CONCLUSIONS: Vasodilation and myocardial dysfunction increased the risk of postoperative hypotension, providing insight into the mechanistic development of postoperative hypotension. The absence of severe hypovolemia was surprising. Clinicians should assess for vasodilation and myocardial dysfunction as potential preludes to postoperative hypotension, potentially using point-of-care echocardiography and sidestream darkfield microscopy.

items.title: Genetics-first versus muscle biopsy-first approach to investigating malignant hyperthermia susceptibility: a retrospective cost-consequence analysis
items.containerTitle: Canadian Journal of Anesthesia/Journal canadien d'anesthésie
items.abstract: Purpose Malignant hyperthermia (MH) is a rare pharmacogenetic condition with substantial morbidity and mortality. The current gold standard for diagnosis, caffeine-halothane contracture testing (CHCT), is invasive, costly, and available only at a single centre in Canada. Genetic testing offers a less invasive alternative, but access remains inconsistent across Canadian provinces. We sought to evaluate the cost-consequences and diagnostic wait times of a genetics-first vs biopsy-first strategy for MH susceptibility. Methods We conducted a retrospective cost-consequence analysis of 1,208 patients referred to the Canadian Malignant Hyperthermia Investigation Unit (2015-2024) with a personal or family history suggestive of MH, and their first-degree relatives. We compared the direct, indirect, and societal costs of the Ontario genetics-first approach with those of a hypothetical biopsy-first approach used in other provinces. We analyzed diagnostic timelines using Kaplan-Meier survival analyses. Results In the genetics-first strategy, 7.2% of probands (88/1,208) had a diagnostic variant and did not require biopsy for contracture testing, resulting in modest societal cost reduction for probands compared with the biopsy-first strategy (CAD 23.5M vs CAD 24.3M, respectively; CAD 700 saved per proband tested). The costs of cascade testing of their first-degree relatives were three-fold lower for the genetics-first strategy (CAD 3.6M vs CAD 11.3M). The median [interquartile range] time to diagnosis was 2 [1-5] months for patients with diagnostic variants, compared with 39 [22-51] months for those requiring biopsy (log-rank P Conclusions Compared with a hypothetical biopsy-first approach, offering genetics testing as initial step to all individuals with clinical suspicion of MH susceptibility did not increase societal costs, and resulted in substantial cost savings for cascade testing of their relatives, markedly shortening time to diagnosis for individuals who harbour a diagnostic variant.

items.title: Effect of sex on the relationship between perioperative risk factors and postoperative pulmonary complications after noncardiothoracic surgery in patients classified American Society of Anesthesiologists Physical Status III: a secondary analysis of a prospective multicentre cohort study
items.containerTitle: Canadian Journal of Anesthesia/Journal canadien d'anesthésie
items.abstract: PURPOSE: Postoperative pulmonary complications (PPCs) importantly contribute to postoperative morbidity and mortality, particularly for patients classified American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) Physical Status III. Whether PPC risk factors depend on sex remains unclear. We hypothesize that sex modifies the relationship between perioperative risk factors and PPCs in patients assigned an ASA III status undergoing noncardiothoracic surgery with general anesthesia. METHODS: We performed a secondary analysis of prospective data from 1,202 patients undergoing noncardiothoracic surgery. We collected data on preoperative patient demographics, comorbidities, intraoperative physiology, medications, and procedure information. The primary outcome was a composite of PPCs by postoperative day 7. Mixed-effects linear models incorporated sex as main and interaction effect. RESULTS: Age, upper abdominal surgery, and surgical duration significantly increased the odds of ≥ 1 PPC by postoperative day 7. Male patients presented a higher rate of ≥ 3 PPCs, and female patients received higher tidal volumes per predicted body weight and driving pressures. Sex did not significantly modify the relationship between perioperative factors and the primary outcome (no P < 0.05 for the interaction with sex). In the secondary analysis, gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) affected atelectasis more strongly in male than in female patients (relative odds ratio for female vs male patients, 0.27; 95% confidence interval, 0.13 to 0.57). CONCLUSIONS: In patients classified ASA III undergoing noncardiothoracic surgery with general anesthesia, perioperative factors are predominantly not modified by sex in their relationship to PPCs. The association between GERD and atelectasis in male patients could be explored in future prospective studies as a target for reducing PPCs.

items.title: Risk factors associated with the development of a catheter-related thrombosis in patients with critical illness: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.containerTitle: Canadian Journal of Anesthesia/Journal canadien d'anesthésie
items.abstract: Purpose We sought to conduct a systematic review and meta-analysis with the primary objective to identify prognostic factors associated with developing a catheter-related thrombosis in the critical care setting. Our secondary objective was to report the incidence of this entity. Sources We searched, MEDLINE® and Embase® from inception through 4 May 2024 for all studies in patients with critical illness that reported catheter-related thrombosis, with an updated search performed on 23 October 2025. We included English-language studies that described prognostic factors for developing a catheter-related thrombosis or reported the incidence of this complication in the critical care setting. Two authors performed citation screening and data extraction. We pooled adjusted odds ratios (aORs) and adjusted hazard ratios (aHRs) separately for prognostic factors using a random-effects model and inverse variance weighting. Risk of bias for individual studies was evaluated using the Quality in Prognosis Studies tool. We assessed certainty of evidence using the Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluations approach. Principle findings We included 32 studies involving 11,943 patients. Identified prognostic variables with a moderate- or high-certainty association for developing a catheter-related thrombosis include increasing age (aOR per 10-yr increase, 1.16; 95% CI, 1.06 to 1.27; three studies; 1,594 patients; high certainty), trauma-related admission (aOR, 1.48; 95% CI, 0.93 to 2.34; three studies; 3,089 patients; high certainty), surgical-related admission (aOR, 2.50; 95% CI, 1.77 to 3.52; three studies; 2,208 patients; aHR, 1.35; 95% CI, 0.60 to 3.02; two studies; 297 patients; high certainty), internal jugular insertion site as compared with other insertion sites (aOR, 3.76; 95% CI, 2.82 to 5.01; four studies; 4,681 patients; high certainty), single/double-lumen as compared with more lumens (aOR, 1.61; 95% CI, 0.82 to 3.13; three studies; 1,594 patients; moderate certainty), and peripheral insertion site (aOR, 2.30; 95% CI, 0.74 to 7.08; two studies; 264 patients; moderate certainty). The median incidence of catheter-related thrombosis was 13.3% [interquartile range, 3.7%-31.3%]. Conclusions In this systematic review and meta-analysis, we found that increasing age, surgical type admissions, large catheters, and factors potentially related with catheter duration were associated with developing a catheter-related thrombosis in the critical care setting. Furthermore, we identified significant variation in the reported rates of catheter-related thrombosis, with an average rate of approximately 1 in every 8 patients. When these identified risk factors are present, clinicians may consider more aggressive thromboprophylaxis regimens to better tailor prevention strategies to individual patient risk profiles. Study registration Open Science Framework ( https://osf.io/5zvg2) ; first submitted 15 June 2024.

items.title: Effects of lowering inspired oxygen fraction during anesthesia emergence on immediate postoperative loss of lung aeration assessed by ultrasonography: a multicentre randomized controlled trial
items.containerTitle: Canadian Journal of Anesthesia/Journal canadien d'anesthésie
items.abstract: Purpose Controversy remains regarding the effect of inspired oxygen fraction (F I O 2 ) on postoperative lung aeration. We sought to evaluate whether lowering F I O 2 solely during emergence from anesthesia reduces immediate postoperative loss of lung aeration, assessed by lung ultrasonography. Methods In this double-blind multicentre randomized controlled trial, we allocated 102 patients undergoing laparoscopic gastrectomy to either a low- or high-F I O 2 group (F I O 2 = 0.5 vs 0.8 during emergence, respectively). The primary outcome was the lung ultrasonography score (LUS) measured in the postanesthesia care unit (PACU). Secondary outcomes were the Oxygen Reserve Index™ (ORi™) after extubation, atelectasis on chest radiography taken on postoperative day (POD) 2, and oxygen desaturation events in the PACU and within the first 48 postoperative hr. Results The median [interquartile range (IQR)] LUS did not significantly differ between the two groups (low-F I O 2 group, 3 [2-5] vs high-F I O 2 group, 3 [2-6]; P = 0.48). The median [IQR] ORi values after extubation were 0.42 [0.10-0.74] and 0.52 [0.30-0.83] in the low- and high-F I O 2 groups, respectively (adjusted P = 0.36). The incidence of atelectasis on chest radiography on POD 2 (low-F I O 2 group, 57% vs high-F I O 2 group, 49%; P = 0.43; adjusted P > 0.99) and other pulmonary complication rates were not different between the groups. Conclusions Lowering the F I O 2 from 0.8 to 0.5 during the anesthesia emergence period alone did not reduce immediate postoperative LUS after laparoscopic gastrectomy. Routine reduction of the F I O 2 Study registration CRIS.nih.go.kr (KCT0008594); first submitted 29 June 2023.

items.title: Anesthetic considerations for obstetric patients with an implanted spinal cord stimulator
items.containerTitle: Canadian Journal of Anesthesia/Journal canadien d'anesthésie
items.abstract: Purpose Implantable spinal cord stimulators (SCSs) for the treatment of refractory neuropathic pain are becoming increasingly common in patients presenting for surgery, and their presence has important implications for anesthetic care. This is particularly relevant in obstetric anesthesia, where neuraxial techniques are routinely employed for labour analgesia and anesthesia for Cesarean delivery. In this Continuing Professional Development module, we synthesize the available case experience from the literature and provide practical recommendations to guide anesthesiologists in the perioperative management of obstetric patients with an SCS. Principal findings Numerous case reports describe the safe use of both epidural and spinal anesthetic techniques in obstetric patients with an SCS. All obstetric patients with an SCS should undergo antenatal consultation with an anesthesiologist and neuromodulation specialist (usually a pain medicine physician or neurosurgeon) responsible for managing the device. Preprocedural planning, including review of relevant imaging and a focused physical examination, is essential to minimize the risk of device damage. Ultrasound can be used to assist the provider in identifying a safe neuraxial access point and may also help to improve first-pass success. The literature suggests that prior implantation of SCS components within the epidural space may be associated with a higher risk of SCS lead movement, potential for infection, and inadequate epidural labour analgesia and surgical anesthesia. In contrast, the success of spinal anesthesia for Cesarean delivery appears largely unaffected by the presence of neurostimulation leads. In patients undergoing Cesarean delivery, management considerations include temporary device inactivation, minimizing the use of monopolar cautery, and being familiar with the course of the device's leads from the impulse generator to the stimulating electrode to avoid inadvertent surgical damage. Conclusions Neuraxial anesthesia is feasible and generally safe for obstetric patients with an SCS but requires careful planning and awareness of unique risks. Antenatal anesthesiology and neuromodulation consultation, imaging review, ultrasound guidance, and patient counselling can help optimize outcomes and minimize complications.

items.title: Electrolyte deficiencies in adult patients admitted to the intensive care unit: a narrative review
items.containerTitle: Canadian Journal of Anesthesia/Journal canadien d'anesthésie
items.abstract: Purpose Electrolyte deficiencies and their treatment are ubiquitous in patients admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU). We sought to conduct a narrative review of hypocalcemia, hypomagnesemia, hypophosphatemia, and hypokalemia in critical care. Source We searched Ovid MEDLINE®, Embase®, Cochrane CENTRAL, and reference lists for information relevant to the physiology, epidemiology, and treatment of electrolyte deficiencies in adults with critical illness. We also looked for information about financial costs and environmental impact of treatment. Principal findings Electrolyte deficiencies are common in patients admitted to the ICU, with prevalences of 55-88% for hypocalcemia, 27-66% for hypomagnesemia, 15-53% for hypophosphatemia, and 17-50% for hypokalemia. Neuromuscular and cardiovascular symptoms are common to all four deficiencies, and the benefits and harms of routine or protocolized treatment are uncertain. Calcium replacement is potentially fraught, with possible harm in cardiac arrest data, lack of any randomized controlled trials (RCTs) investigating replacement, and difficulties diagnosing deficiency outside of ionized calcium measurement. Prophylactic magnesium administration may prevent postoperative atrial fibrillation in patients undergoing cardiac surgery, but whether protocolized replacement reduces atrial fibrillation or mortality in patients with critical illness without cardiac problems is uncertain. Phosphate replacement may be relevant to ventilator weaning and ICU-acquired weakness, owing to its physiologic role in cellular energy and available clinical data. Potassium replacement has been investigated in large observational studies and an RCT, indicating that higher thresholds are not superior to lower ones. Enteral replacement is associated with lower costs and less environmental impact compared with the intravenous route. Conclusions Electrolyte deficiencies and their treatment are common in adult patients admitted to the ICU. The impact of particular thresholds and dosing strategies for treatment on patient outcomes, resource use, and the environment remain important areas for future research.

items.title: Trained immunity maybe a novel preoperative strategy to prevent perioperative neurocognitive disorders
From prediction to impact: The next frontier of perioperative artificial intelligence
Interpreting the 30-min monitoring recommendation after external oblique intercostal plane block
Long- versus medium-chain triglycerides in lipid resuscitation therapy for local anesthetic systemic toxicity: Does the length matter? A narrative review
items.abstract: Intravenous lipid emulsion (ILE) is the recommended first-line treatment for local anesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST), particularly when cardiovascular compromise occurs. However, uncertainty persists regarding the optimal lipid formulation, specifically the comparative efficacy of ILEs containing 100% long-chain triglycerides (LCT) versus ILEs containing a 50/50 mixture of medium- and long-chain triglycerides (MCT/LCT), as well as ILEs with a 20% versus 30% lipid concentration. The primary aim of this narrative review was to compare the efficacy of 100% LCT-containing ILEs versus 50% MCT/LCT-containing ILEs by analyzing their respective mechanisms of action in experimental models of local anesthetic-induced cardiovascular toxicity, whereas the secondary objective was to compare ILEs with a 20% versus a 30% lipid concentration. The review also integrates the physiological rationale underlying lipid resuscitation and explores a mechanistically informed framework for interpreting formulation-specific effects of ILEs. A literature search of PubMed, Embase, and Google Scholar was conducted from January 1998 through January 2026. Twenty experimental studies were identified-nine in vitro, one ex vivo, and ten in vivo-and qualitatively synthesized according to their principal mechanisms of action, including lipid shuttle, cardiotonic, vascular, and metabolic effects. The available experimental evidence suggests that 100% LCT-containing ILEs provide greater overall cardiovascular recovery than 50% MCT/LCT-containing ILEs, particularly through more effective lipid-shuttle activity and sustained myocardial protection. Conversely, 50% MCT/LCT-containing ILEs demonstrated greater vascular effects in several experimental models. Evidence comparing lipid concentrations was limited to 100% LCT-containing formulations and generally showed greater pharmacokinetic, hemodynamic, and survival effects with a 30% versus a 20% lipid concentration when administered at the same volume. The available evidence is derived exclusively from heterogeneous preclinical experimental models and should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating rather than practice-informing. Triglyceride composition and lipid concentration may influence distinct mechanisms contributing to cardiovascular recovery during LAST. These findings provide a mechanistic basis for exploring formulation-phenotype associations but do not establish formulation-specific treatment recommendations. Further experimental and translational studies are needed to determine whether these mechanistic findings translate into clinically meaningful benefits in patients with LAST.

items.title: Inhaled anesthetics and severe neurologic complications in individuals with Venezuelan maternal ancestry carrying the mitochondrial MT-ND4 m.11232 T > C variant: a systematic review
items.abstract: Severe neurologic injury after uncomplicated general anesthesia in previously healthy patients is rare. Since 2021, reports from South America and later from North America and Europe have described catastrophic neurologic deterioration and death after routine general anesthesia in children and adults with Venezuelan maternal ancestry. A homoplasmic mitochondrial DNA variant, MT-ND4 m.11232 T > C (p.Leu158Pro), affecting complex I of the electron transport chain, has emerged as the leading candidate susceptibility factor. This systematic review identified, appraised, and synthesized available evidence linking inhaled anesthetics, in particular sevoflurane, with severe perioperative neurologic complications in carriers of this variant and in individuals with Venezuelan maternal ancestry. The protocol was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261471143), with searches of major biomedical databases, gray literature, and variant databases. The evidence describes a consistent but incompletely characterized syndrome defined by maternal Venezuelan ancestry, apparent preoperative health, predominant sevoflurane exposure, delayed emergence, and severe basal ganglia injury with frequent death. In patient-derived fibroblasts and cybrids, sevoflurane markedly suppressed complex I-dependent respiration, whereas propofol did not. Incidence, penetrance, and agent-specific risk remain uncertain. Cautious perioperative strategies that avoid volatile anesthetics appear justified.

items.title: Perioperative management of patients with recent concussion undergoing noncardiac extracranial surgery: A modified Delphi consensus study
items.abstract: Background Many patients present for surgery soon after concussion, when cerebral physiologic regulation may remain disturbed, and no evidence-based guideline or standardized consensus recommendations exist. We sought expert consensus for adults with recent concussion undergoing noncardiac extracranial surgery. Methods We conducted a two-round modified Delphi study (November 2025-March 2026). Round 1 items, drafted from a systematic literature search, included case vignettes. Experts identified by bibliographic screening, directories, and nomination rated items on a five-point Likert scale; "do not know" responses were excluded from the denominator. Consensus was defined a priori as 75% agreement or greater, and strong consensus as 85% or greater. Results Thirty-five experts (33 anesthesiologists) from 17 countries completed both rounds; 13 of 16 Round 2 statements reached consensus. Agreement was unanimous for preoperative screening for concussion symptoms and neurologic red flags, and for avoidance of hypoxemia, abnormal carbon dioxide tension, sustained hypotension, and marked hypertension. Strong consensus supported generally deferring elective surgery until concussion symptoms resolve (97%), preoperative counseling (97%), structured follow-up (94%), and extended postoperative monitoring in higher-risk patients (91%). Consensus was not reached for regional anesthesia or monitored anesthesia care over general anesthesia (74%), electroencephalography-based depth of anesthesia monitoring (73%), or cautious long-acting neuraxial opioid use (69%). The panel did not define symptom resolution and established no symptom-independent waiting interval or concussion-specific numeric physiologic threshold. Conclusions This anesthesiology-led consensus supports symptom-guided timing, physiologic stability, counseling, and structured follow-up; anesthetic technique, electroencephalographic monitoring, and neuraxial opioid use remain unresolved. The statements form an expert-informed framework, not an evidence-based practice guideline.

items.title: Single-operator, syringe-free wire-in-needle technique for internal jugular vein catheterization under long-axis, in-plane ultrasound guidance: a simulation-based technical note
Purinergic signaling in perioperative ischemia–reperfusion injury: Pharmacological strategies for organ protection
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Perioperative ischemia-reperfusion injury (IRI) remains a significant cause of postoperative organ dysfunction and mortality after cardiac, vascular, transplant, and high-risk noncardiac surgery. Despite advances in anesthetic and surgical techniques, practical strategies to prevent IRI are limited. Growing evidence indicates that purinergic signaling, mediated by extracellular ATP, ADP, adenosine, and their receptors, centrally regulates inflammation, microvascular function, and tissue recovery during perioperative ischemia and reperfusion. METHODS: This narrative review synthesizes preclinical, translational, and clinical evidence on purinergic mechanisms in perioperative IRI across major organ systems, including the heart, lungs, kidneys, liver, intestines, and brain, emphasizing pharmacological strategies and anesthetic interactions relevant to intraoperative and early postoperative management. RESULTS: During ischemia and early reperfusion, extracellular ATP released from injured cells activates P2 receptors, promoting inflammasome activation, endothelial dysfunction, and microcirculatory injury. Subsequent hydrolysis of ATP by ectonucleotidases CD39 and CD73 generates adenosine, which activates P1 receptors (Adora1, Adora2a, Adora2b, and Adora3) to suppress inflammation, improve perfusion, and enhance tissue protection. Hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF)-dependent upregulation of CD73 and A2B transcriptionally amplifies this ATP-to-adenosine transition, and miRNAs post-transcriptionally modulate it. Pharmacological approaches targeting these pathways represent promising strategies for perioperative organ protection, whereas clinical evidence supporting anesthetic regimen selection for purinergic modulation remains insufficient. The efficacy of conditioning strategies, including ischemic preconditioning and remote ischemic preconditioning (RIPC), remains controversial, with negative large-scale trials highlighting the translational gap between preclinical models and multimorbid surgical patients. CONCLUSIONS: Purinergic signaling provides a unifying mechanistic framework for perioperative ischemia-reperfusion injury and represents a promising target for pharmacological organ protection. Prioritize pharmacological strategies that enhance adenosine generation, activate protective adenosine receptors, or inhibit ATP-P2X7-driven inflammation in perioperative clinical trials. Understanding how comorbidities and concomitant medications modulate purinergic pathways is essential for successful clinical translation.

items.title: Perioperative diabetes management in ambulatory surgery settings: A survey of Society for Ambulatory Anesthesia (SAMBA) members
Perioperative noise isolation for postoperative delirium in older adults undergoing hip surgery: a randomized clinical trial
items.abstract: Background Postoperative delirium (POD) is common in older adults undergoing hip surgery. Noise exposure is associated with increased delirium risk. We hypothesized that perioperative noise isolation would reduce POD in these patients. Methods In this single-center, randomized, patient- and assessor-blind trial, 320 patients (aged ≥65 y) undergoing hip surgery under sevoflurane anesthesia were randomly assigned 1:1 using block randomization stratified by age, surgery type, and planned surgical ICU admission to noise isolation (earmuffs from anesthesia induction to tracheal extubation before awakening) or control (routine care). The primary outcome was the incidence of POD during the first 7 postoperative days or until hospital discharge. Results Among 316 patients (mean age 78 y; 71.8% female) who completed the study (158 per group), POD occurred in 19 (12.0%) patients in the noise isolation group vs. 36 (22.8%) in the control group (relative risk 0.53; 95% CI 0.32-0.88; P = 0.012). The absolute risk reduction was 10.8% (number needed to treat 9). The interventional effect remained significant after multivariable adjustment for stratification factors (adjusted odds ratio 0.42; 95% CI 0.23-0.80; P = 0.009) and after additional adjustment for Charlson Comorbidity Index (adjusted odds ratio 0.43; 95% CI 0.23-0.82; P = 0.010). Patients receiving noise isolation were less likely to experience moderate-to-severe pain and required less rescue analgesia. Conclusions Perioperative noise isolation reduced the incidence of POD in older adults undergoing hip surgery. This simple, nonpharmacological intervention represents an immediately implementable strategy to enhance perioperative care. Trial registration Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR2400082211).

items.title: Assessment and treatment of pain and sedation in mainland Chinese ICUs: a nationwide web-based survey
items.abstract: To investigate the current practice and perception of pain, sedation, consciousness, and delirium management in intensive care units (ICUs) in mainland China. The Chinese Analgesia and Sedation Education and Research (CASER) group performed a nationwide online survey. The questionnaire covered respondent demographics, perceived importance of analgesia and sedation, self-reported guideline familiarity, physician-nurse responsibilities, assessment frequency, medications, and real-world analgesia/sedation delivery on the survey day. In total, 4521 valid responses were collected, 2999 from general ICUs and 2926 from physicians. Most respondents regarded pain (88.72%), sedation (89.89%), and consciousness/delirium assessment (85.84%) as important and reported familiarity with relevant guidelines. There was discrepancy in respondent self-reported knowledge of guidelines and their objective performance on test questions. Respondents reported analgesia and sedation were provided routinely at 15.51% and on demand at 70.34%. Physicians dominated treatment decisions. Assessment frequency varied substantially, particularly for consciousness and delirium; 43.37% performed such evaluations only based on clinical status. Opioids were the primary analgesics (87.69%); midazolam (44.57%) and propofol (31.01%) were the leading sedatives. Fewer than half of ICU patients received combined analgesia and sedation on the survey day (48.28%). The perception and practice of pain, sedation, consciousness, and delirium assessment and management among ICU staff in mainland China are heterogeneous and insufficiently standardized. More accurate understanding and rigorous implementation of existing clinical guidelines are urgently needed.

items.title: Intraoperative desaturation: the anesthesiologist's routine, research's blind spot
Finding the right balance – not just papering over the cracks. A broader system change is required not quotas alone
Sugammadex versus Neostigmine–Glycopyrrolate for Reducing the Risk of Postoperative Urinary Retention in High-Risk Patients Undergoing Otolaryngologic Surgery: A Randomised Controlled Trial
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Postoperative urinary retention (POUR) is a clinically important postoperative complication, particularly in patients at high risk for voiding dysfunction. Sugammadex reverses aminosteroid neuromuscular blockade without requiring concomitant antimuscarinic administration and may therefore reduce the risk of POUR compared with neostigmine-glycopyrrolate. METHODS: In this prospective randomised trial, 124 adults at high risk for POUR undergoing elective otolaryngologic surgery were randomly assigned (1:1) to receive neostigmine-glycopyrrolate or sugammadex for neuromuscular block reversal. The primary outcome was confirmed POUR, defined as inability to void requiring urinary catheterisation with an ultrasound-confirmed bladder volume ≥400 mL. Secondary outcomes included postoperative nausea and vomiting, haemodynamic events, patient-reported thirst intensity, and hospital length of stay. RESULTS: Confirmed POUR occurred in 12 of 62 patients (19.4%) in the neostigmine-glycopyrrolate group and in none of the 62 patients (0%) in the sugammadex group (risk difference, 19.4%; 95% CI, 9.5%-30.9%; P < 0.001; NNT = 6). Exploratory analysis showed that symptomatic urinary retention was also more frequent with neostigmine-glycopyrrolate than with sugammadex (40.3% vs. 4.8%; P < 0.001). No statistically significant between-group differences were observed in postoperative nausea and vomiting, haemodynamic events, thirst intensity, or hospital length of stay; secondary-outcome comparisons were not powered to detect between-group differences. CONCLUSIONS: Among patients at high risk for POUR undergoing elective otolaryngologic surgery, sugammadex reduced the risk of confirmed POUR compared with neostigmine-glycopyrrolate. Comparisons of secondary outcomes were underpowered and should be interpreted cautiously. REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT06398899; principal investigator: Pei-Lin Lin; registered on 5 March 2024).

items.title: From Sellick To The Ramped Position: Completing The Triangle Of Neck Pressure In The Videolaryngoscopy Era
Acute postoperative pain in surgical patients with cognitive impairment: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.abstract: Background Acute pain in the postoperative period and pre-existing cognitive impairment (CI) are both independently associated with increased postoperative adverse outcomes. Pre-existing cognitive impairment may interfere with the reporting, recognition, and treatment of pain in this population. Methods This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the impact of pre-existing cognitive impairment on pain and analgesic consumption after surgery in adults. MEDLINE, Embase, Cochrane Central, and Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews were searched for randomized controlled trials and cohort studies for adults undergoing non-cardiac, emergency, or elective surgery until April 9, 2026. Surgical patients with pre-existing cognitive impairment were compared to cognitively intact peers. The primary outcomes assessed were subjective ratings of pain and analgesic consumption postoperatively. Risk of bias was assessed using ROBINS-I and certainty of evidence was rated by GRADE. Meta-analysis used standard mean differences (SMDs) with 95% confidence intervals. Results Thirteen studies (37,918 patients) were included. Approximately one third (33%; 95% CI 0.25-0.41) of adult surgical patients screened positive for preoperative cognitive impairment. Subjective pain scores did not differ significantly between patients with and without cognitive impairment (Hedge's g: 0.11 (SD -0.15-0.36, I 2 85.3%, T 2 0.073). Patients with cognitive impairment had significantly less analgesic consumption than their cognitively intact counterparts (Cohen's d: 0.53 (0.29-0.76, I 2 67.4%, T 2 0.028). Conclusions Despite comparable pain scores, those with cognitive impairment received significantly less postoperative analgesia, raising concern for systematic under-recognition and undertreatment of pain. Increased awareness of this discrepancy and the use of standardized analgesia protocols may improve postoperative outcomes. Registration International Registry of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO:1117357).

items.title: Impact of preoperative cardiology consultations on perioperative management in patients undergoing non-cardiac surgery: a prospective cohort study
items.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Cardiology consultations may be requested during preoperative anesthetic assessment before non-cardiac surgery. However, data regarding their impact on perioperative management are limited. This study aimed to evaluate the effect of preoperative cardiology consultations on perioperative patient management. METHODS: We conducted a prospective, observational, single-center study in the Department of Anesthesiology and Critical Care at Angers University Hospital from September 1st, 2024, to August 31st, 2025. All patients referred for cardiology assessment after the anesthetic consultation were included. The primary endpoint was any change in perioperative management, including specific preoperative cardiac treatment, postponement or cancellation of surgery, and modification of anesthetic or surgical protocols. The secondary endpoint was to assess adherence of preoperative cardiac evaluation to current guideline recommendations. RESULTS: Among 9,621 preoperative anesthetic consultations, 138 (1%) patients were referred for cardiology assessment by the anesthesiologist and included in the study. 59 (43%) patients experienced a change in perioperative management. Of them, surgery was postponed in 52 (38%) patients, with a median delay of 81 [47-145] days, whereas only 6 patients underwent an invasive cardiac intervention (angioplasty, valvuloplasty, or electrical cardioversion). A previously unknown cardiac condition was identified in 19 (15%) patients. 111 (80%) cardiology referrals were consistent with current recommendations. CONCLUSION: In our study, preoperative cardiology consultations requested by an anesthesiologist were rare but frequently responsible for modification of perioperative management. These consultations often resulted in postponement of surgery, while only a small proportion of patients underwent an invasive cardiac intervention.

items.title: Renal Replacement Therapy in Cardiogenic Shock supported by microAxial Flow Pumps: A European multicentre study
items.abstract: Background Microaxial flow pumps (mAFP) improve hemodynamics and outcomes in myocardial infarction-related cardiogenic shock (CS) but are associated with an increased risk of acute kidney injury (AKI) requiring renal replacement therapy (RRT). We aimed to determine the incidence and factors associated with RRT and evaluate its association with mortality in a real-world cohort of miscellaneous CS patients supported with mAFP. Methods We conducted a retrospective multicentre registry including CS patients supported with mAFP across 11 European centres. The association between RRT and the primary outcome of 180-day all-cause mortality (with survival censored at heart transplantation or durable left ventricular assist device implantation) was assessed using a 1:1 propensity score-matched cohort. Factors associated with RRT were identified using multivariable logistic regression. Results Among 1043 patients, 972 were included, of whom 340 (35.0%) required RRT. RRT was associated with higher 180-day all-cause mortality both before (Kaplan-Meier estimates, 59.7% vs. 35.2%; HR 2.04, 95% CI 1.67-2.49; p Conclusions In this large European registry of mAFP-supported CS, RRT was frequent and associated with increased 180-day mortality and greater shock severity.

items.title: Sugammadex Use In Severe Renal Dysfunction Despite Regulatory Recommendations: A Secondary Analysis Of The Prospective Multicentre DELPO Cohort
items.abstract: Background European product information does not recommend sugammadex in severe renal impairment, including dialysis, because renal elimination is markedly reduced. European data describing reversal practice in this population are limited. Objective To determine whether sugammadex was the predominant pharmacological reversal agent among patients in GFR categories G4-G5 or receiving dialysis. Methods This secondary analysis of the prospective DELPO cohort included adults who received general anaesthesia, neuromuscular blockade, and pharmacological reversal with sugammadex or neostigmine at 43 Spanish hospitals. Patients were classified as being in GFR categories G1-G3 (eGFR ≥30 mL min - ¹ 1.73 m - ²) or GFR categories G4-G5 or receiving dialysis (eGFR - ¹ 1.73 m - ² or dialysis). Reversal-agent use was described overall and according to renal function. Results The analysis included 1331 patients, of whom 35 were in GFR categories G4-G5 or receiving dialysis, including 20 receiving dialysis. Sugammadex was used in 1,278 of 1,331 patients overall (96.0%), in 1248 of 1,296 patients in GFR categories G1-G3 (96.3%), and in 30 of 35 patients in GFR categories G4-G5 or receiving dialysis (85.7%; 95% CI, 70.6-93.7%). Among the 20 patients receiving dialysis, sugammadex was administered to 16 (80.0%; 95% CI, 58.4-91.9%). Conclusions Among patients in GFR categories G4-G5 or receiving dialysis who received pharmacological reversal, sugammadex was used in 85.7% (30/35), including 80.0% (16/20) of patients receiving dialysis, despite current European product information not recommending its use in this population.

items.title: Imaging Subphenotypes in Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome: From Characterization to Treatment-Effect Modification
items.abstract: Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is defined by clinical and radiographic criteria, yet patients differ in underlying biology, physiological impairment, and regional lung injury. Such heterogeneity may influence treatment response. Current ventilatory strategies, however, are generally guided by physiological targets without fully accounting for the biological, structural, and functional diversity of ARDS. Computed tomography, lung ultrasound, and electrical impedance tomography offer complementary information on lung morphology, aeration, and regional ventilation, while selected approaches may inform recruitability assessment. Nevertheless, evidence that imaging-defined subphenotypes identify patients who derive differential clinical benefit from specific interventions remains limited. This review examines the contribution of lung imaging to individualized respiratory management in ARDS, separating descriptive and prognostic findings from evidence of treatment-effect modification. Limitations of categorical classification and the dynamic nature of lung injury are discussed alongside the potential integration of imaging, physiological, biological, and clinical data. Such multimodal approaches remain investigational but may support evaluation of heterogeneous responses to positive end-expiratory pressure, prone positioning, and other supportive strategies. Before these approaches can guide treatment selection, standardized image acquisition, reproducible classification, longitudinal assessment, independent validation, and prospective demonstration of clinical benefit are required.

items.title: Monitoring of Venous Excess Ultrasound Score (VExUS) During Continuous Renal Replacement Therapy in the ICU: the MAVERIC pilot study
items.abstract: Background Venous congestion is increasingly recognised as a key determinant of organ dysfunction during acute kidney injury requiring continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT). Although the Venous Excess Ultrasound (VExUS) score is a promising bedside marker of systemic venous congestion, its dynamic evolution during CRRT remains unknown. We aimed to describe serial changes in VExUS during CRRT and explore their association with ultrafiltration intensity and fluid balance. Methods MAVERIC was a prospective single-centre observational pilot study including adults undergoing CRRT for acute kidney injury. VExUS was assessed before CRRT initiation and after 24 and 48 hours. The primary objective was to describe temporal changes in VExUS using an alluvial plot. Patients were classified into three a priori-defined patterns of congestion evolution. Associations with net ultrafiltration (NUF) and cumulative fluid balance were explored. Results Forty-seven patients were included. Overall, VExUS grades decreased significantly during the first 48 hours of CRRT (p = 0.0048). Three a priori-defined patterns of congestion evolution were identified: persistently low congestion (45%, n = 21), resolving congestion (32%, n = 15), and persistent or worsening congestion (23%, n = 11). Patients with resolving congestion had the highest NUF rates (1.35 [0.85-1.66] mL/kg/h) and the most negative cumulative fluid balance (-36.7 [-74.6 to -21.1] mL/kg), with significant differences across groups (p = 0.003 and p Conclusions Serial VExUS assessment provides dynamic information on systemic venous congestion during CRRT. Three a priori-defined patterns of congestion evolution were associated with differences in net ultrafiltration and fluid balance. Serial VExUS monitoring may help identify patients with persistent or worsening congestion, raising the hypothesis that it could inform reassessment of decongestion strategies. Whether integrating serial VExUS assessment into individualised decongestive strategies improves renal outcomes should be evaluated in prospective interventional studies.

items.title: Accuracy and Precision of Acceleromyography and Electromyography at the Adductor Pollicis Muscle in Restricted Thumb Movement Positions: An Observational Study
items.abstract: Background Quantitative neuromuscular monitoring commonly uses acceleromyography (AMG) or electromyography (EMG). Acceleromyography requires unrestricted thumb movement, whereas EMG is independent of thumb motion. We compared the accuracy and precision of AMG and EMG responses after patients' arms were immobilized during routine surgical positioning. Methods Patients undergoing general anaesthesia without neuromuscular block were enrolled. EMG and AMG monitors were placed on contralateral arms, and both arms were tucked under surgical drapes. The monitors simultaneously recorded train-of-four ratio (TOFR) after ulnar nerve stimulation every minute. Accuracy was defined as TOFR variability from the expected baseline value (1.00), and precision as consistency of repeated measurements, quantified by the coefficient of repeatability (CR). Failed measurements were defined as the absence of valid quantitative TOFR values, displayed as "0" or "?". AMG TOFR values were normalized to patient-specific baseline TOFR measurements for secondary analyses. Results Forty patients provided 3,733 TOFR measurements (1,879 EMG and 1,854 AMG). EMG was more accurate than AMG (mean EMG-AMG difference in absolute deviation from 1.0, -0.108; 95% confidence interval [CI], -0.134 to -0.083; p Conclusion EMG provided more accurate and precise TOFR measurements than AMG, including normalized AMG, with fewer failures, supporting EMG-based monitoring when upper extremity mobility is restricted. Registration Clinical trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov Database (Registration Number: NCT06805032, Principal investigator: J.R.R., date of registration January 28, 2025).

items.title: Empiric Antifungal Therapy in Critically Ill Patients Undergoing Surgery for Severe Intra-Abdominal Infection: a Large Retrospective Single-Center Cohort Study
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Intra-abdominal candidiasis is frequent in critically ill surgical patients and is associated with high mortality. Whether empiric antifungal therapy improves outcomes after surgery for intra-abdominal infection (IAI) in critically ill patients remains uncertain. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective single-center data warehouse-based cohort study of 1,061 adults admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) after surgery for IAI between 2018 and 2024. Patients who received systemic antifungal therapy within 24 hours after surgery were compared with those who did not. The primary endpoint was 30-day all-cause mortality. Secondary endpoints were day-5 renal dysfunction, assessed by the renal SOFA component and the creatinine-based KDIGO stage, and the need for surgical reintervention. Adjusted analyses used propensity-score overlap weighting. Prespecified subgroup and sensitivity analyses used a Peritonitis Score ≥3, the identification of at least one organism in peritoneal samples, and a yeast-positive peritoneal sample. RESULTS: Empiric antifungal therapy was initiated in 46.0% of patients. Peritoneal sampling was available in 957 patients (90.2%); 21.4% had no organism identified and 25.2% had a yeast-positive sample. In adjusted analyses, empiric therapy was not associated with reduced 30-day mortality (OR 1.53, 95% CI 0.83-2.78), lower day-5 renal SOFA score, lower KDIGO stage, or fewer reinterventions. Findings were consistent in patients with Peritonitis Score ≥3, with at least one identified organism, and with a yeast-positive sample. ICU and hospital stays were longer in treated patients after weighting. CONCLUSIONS: Empiric antifungal therapy initiated within 24 hours after surgery for severe IAI was not associated with improved short-term outcomes. TRIAL REGISTRATION: NA.

items.title: Correspondence on “Opioid-free versus opioid-based anesthesia for quality of recovery following laparoscopic hysterectomy: a randomized controlled non-inferiority trial”
Sugammadex versus neostigmine in adults aged 60 years and older undergoing surgery: a systematic review and meta-analysis of postoperative recovery and clinical outcomes
items.abstract: Background Uncertainty remains regarding the clinical advantages of sugammadex over neostigmine in older adults, particularly for recovery efficiency and postoperative outcomes. Aim To compare the effects of sugammadex versus neostigmine on postoperative recovery and clinical outcomes in adults aged 60 years and older undergoing surgery. Methods This systematic review and meta-analysis included eight randomized controlled trials. The primary outcome was postoperative residual neuromuscular blockade (PRNB). Secondary outcomes included post-anesthesia care unit (PACU) length of stay, hospital length of stay, time to extubation, hypoxemia, pneumonia, and postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV). Effect measures were risk ratio and mean difference. Results A total of 851 participants were included, and 50.2% received sugammadex. Sugammadex was associated with a lower risk of PRNB (RR 0.34 [95% CI: 0.18; 0.64]; p 2 = 0%), hospital length of stay (MD -1.12 [95% CI: -2.01; -0.24], p 2 = 16%), and hypoxemia (RR = 0.61 [95% CI: 0.38; 0.97]; p = 0.04, I 2 = 0%). No statistically significant differences were observed for the remaining outcomes. Conclusion Sugammadex was associated with a lower risk of PRNB and shorter PACU stays compared with neostigmine. Although the primary analyses suggested reductions in hypoxemia and hospital length of stay, these associations were not statistically significant after the Hartung-Knapp adjustment. INTERNATIONAL PROSPECTIVE REGISTER OF SYSTEMATIC REVIEWS (PROSPERO): CRD420261376045.

Effects of pneumoperitoneum pressure on perioperative atelectasis assessed using lung ultrasonography in patients undergoing robotic-assisted laparoscopic gynaecological surgery: A prospective, randomised controlled trial
items.abstract: Background Robotic-assisted gynaecological surgery commonly requires prolonged pneumoperitoneum and steep Trendelenburg positioning, which promote perioperative atelectasis and may increase complication risk. We aimed to investigate the effect of low pneumoperitoneum pressure (LPP) on atelectasis following robotic-assisted gynaecological surgery. Methods We conducted a prospective, surgeon- and assessor-blind, randomised controlled trial in women undergoing elective robot-assisted laparoscopic gynaecological surgery. Participants were randomly allocated to the LPP (12 mmHg) or standard pneumoperitoneum pressure (SPP: 15 mmHg) group. Primary outcomes were modified lung ultrasound (mLUS) scores assessed after surgery and 30 min post-extubation. Secondary outcomes included incidence of atelectasis, percentage of desaturation in the post-anaesthesia care unit (PACU), lengths of PACU and hospital stay, surgeon satisfaction with the operative visual field, numeric rating scale pain score and modified clinical pulmonary infection score on postoperative day 1, and postoperative pulmonary complications 7 days postoperatively. Results Sixty patients were enrolled (30 per group). The mLUSs were significantly lower in the LPP group versus the SPP group postoperatively (P Conclusions A low pneumoperitoneum pressure during robotic-assisted gynaecological surgery reduced perioperative modified lung ultrasound scores and the incidence of early postoperative atelectasis. However, this imaging difference was not accompanied by significant improvements in oxygenation. Further studies powered for clinical pulmonary outcomes are needed. Trial registration Chinese Clinical Trial Registry, https://www.chictr.org.cn/; ChiCTR 2400085515.

items.title: Interpreting the POSSUM trial: The challenge of composite respiratory endpoints
Plasma mitochondrial-associated proteins overlap with the hyperinflammatory phenotype in acute respiratory failure
items.abstract: Background The hyperinflammatory phenotype of acute respiratory failure (ARF) identifies patients with high mortality, but its underlying pathophysiology remains incompletely understood. Mitochondrial dysfunction may contribute to inflammation, oxidative stress, and cell injury in critical illness. We investigated whether plasma mitochondrial-associated proteins characterize the hyperinflammatory phenotype and whether they contribute to its association with mortality. Methods We analyzed 285 emergency department patients with ARF and suspected or confirmed COVID-19. Inflammatory phenotypes were derived by latent class analysis using nine biomarkers and clinical indicators. A mitochondrial-protein score was calculated from 59 MitoCarta3.0-matched proteins, and mitochondrial clusters were derived by principal component analysis and k-means clustering. The primary outcome was 28-day mortality. Results Latent class analysis identified 185 hypoinflammatory (65%) and 100 hyperinflammatory (35%) patients, with a significant difference in 28-day mortality (14/185, 7.6% vs. 31/100, 31.0%; p Conclusions The hyperinflammatory phenotype of ARF is characterized by increased plasma mitochondrial-associated proteins, linking inflammation with mitochondrial biology and cellular injury. This mitochondrial signature did not account for mortality independently of inflammatory phenotype, suggesting that it represents a biological component of the hyperinflammatory state.

items.title: Association between early self-reported quality of recovery and postoperative complications after non-cardiac surgery: A secondary analysis of three prospective cohort studies
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: To determine the overall postoperative outcome and success, it is important to assess the occurrence of postoperative complications as well as patients' perception of their health outcomes. The aim of this study was to evaluate the association between self-reported quality of recovery and postoperative complications. METHODS: This secondary analysis included data from three prospective observational studies evaluating quality of recovery in patients undergoing elective non-cardiac surgery. Self-reported quality of recovery was assessed using the Quality of Recovery-15 questionnaire (QoR-15), which was completed by patients preoperatively and on the first postoperative day. Postoperative complications were recorded between surgery and hospital discharge according to the Clavien-Dindo classification (CDC) of surgical complications. Binary logistic regression models were used to assess the association between self-reported quality of recovery and postoperative complications. RESULTS: A total of 1,151 patients were included in this secondary analysis. Of these, 361 (31.4%) experienced postoperative complications. The median difference between preoperative and postoperative QoR-15 sum scores was higher in patients with postoperative complications compared to patients without complications (34 [IQR: 15-51] vs. 22 [IQR: 7-41]; p < 0.001). We found a relevant association between a greater decline in QoR-15 scores from preoperative to first postoperative day and postoperative complications after adjusting for potential confounders (OR 1.18 [95% CI: 1.14;1.23], p < 0.001). The association with no or minor complications was stronger in heterogeneous populations with various types of surgical procedures than in patients with radical prostatectomy. CONCLUSIONS: Early self-reported quality of recovery is associated with the occurrence of postoperative complications after elective non-cardiac surgery. Whether this association may aid in identifying patients at risk of developing postoperative complications warrants further investigation.
