Correspondence on “Efficacy of Standard Meropenem Dosing in Healthcare-Associated Meningitis: Is It Universal?”
Prognostic performance of the Simplified Acute Physiology Score models II and 3 in critical care: a systematic review and meta-analysis of external validation studies
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: The prognostic performance of the Simplified Acute Physiology Score (SAPS) models has not been thoroughly investigated. We systematically reviewed and meta-analysed SAPS mortality prediction metrics across diverse intensive care unit (ICU) populations worldwide. METHODS: PubMed and Scopus were queried for external validations of SAPS in ICU settings. The "CHARMS" and "PROBAST" tools were applied for data extraction and risk-of-bias assessment, respectively. C-statistics and observed-to-expected ratios were summarised using random-effects models. Heterogeneity sources were explored using meta-regression. Evidence certainty was evaluated using the "GRADE" approach. PROSPERO registration CRD42023446721. RESULTS: Ninety studies (89 articles) were reviewed, totalling 565,994 ICU patients across 87 countries, and validating the SAPS II (n = 35), SAPS 3 global (n = 37), and/or SAPS 3 region-specific (n = 28) models. Endpoints were in-hospital (n = 70), in-ICU (n = 16), and/or 28/30-day mortality (n = 12). Nine studies performed recalibrations of SAPS II and 7 of SAPS 3. The meta-analyses provided high-certainty evidence of excellent discriminatory ability across all SAPS models in predicting in-hospital mortality, whereas data on unsatisfactory overall calibration were graded as low certainty. Successful recalibration was graded as high certainty for SAPS II and moderate certainty for SAPS 3. For ICU and 28/30-day mortality, the evidence was low to very low certainty for all SAPS models. Five decision curve analyses were conducted in three studies, all yielding positive net benefit across meaningful risk thresholds. CONCLUSIONS: SAPS models remain reliable as mortality risk-ranking tools in critical care. With adequate sample sizes, local recalibrations and dynamic updating of in-hospital mortality predictions are essential to ensure clinical utility. REGISTRATION: PROSPERO CRD42023446721.

items.title: Scoping review on dosing of anaesthetic and perioperative drugs in patients with obesity: which body weight for which molecule
items.abstract: Background The prevalence of obesity is rising. Patients with obesity are increasingly exposed to anaesthesia, critical care, and perioperative pharmacotherapy. Obesity alters drug pharmacokinetics in a non-linear, drug-specific manner, so that simply scaling doses to total body weight (TBW) exposes patients to overdose or underdose. A recurring clinical question is therefore: which body weight descriptor should be used for which molecule? Methods This review was conducted in accordance with the PRISMA extension for Scoping Reviews. We synthesized pharmacokinetic evidence, recent meta-analyses, and French and European guidelines on dose adjustment in adults with obesity for five drug classes of anaesthesia and critical care: hypnotics, opioids, neuromuscular blocking agents (NMBA), perioperative antibiotics, and non-opioid analgesics. We summarised the recommended dosing weight for each molecule in a table and a figure. Results No single weight descriptor applies. Lipophilic induction agents (propofol), most opioids (alfentanil, fentanyl, sufentanil), and non-depolarising NMBA are best dosed on lean or ideal body weight, whereas succinylcholine, neuromuscular reversal, and aminoglycosides use total or adjusted body weight. Maintenance of hypnosis and pain management in the post-anaesthesia care unit are titrated to monitored effect. Cephalosporin-based antibiotic prophylaxis relies on fixed doses (e.g., cefazolin 2 g) up to high body mass index values due to their hydrophilic properties. Paracetamol and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs are given at standard doses and never scaled to TBW. Findings are consolidated in a single bedside reference table. Conclusion Dosing in obesity must be molecule-specific, guided by the relevant weight descriptor and by intraoperative monitoring rather than by TBW alone.

items.title: Prophylactic Intraoperative Norepinephrine Infusion during Major Noncardiac Surgery: A Systematic Review and GRADE assessed Meta-analysis
items.abstract: Introduction Prophylactic norepinephrine infusion has gained increasing attention to prevent intraoperative hypotension during major non-cardiac surgery, but its effect on haemodynamic stability, tissue perfusion, fluid administration, and postoperative outcomes remains uncertain. Methods PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane CENTRAL were searched through May 9, 2026 for randomised trials comparing prophylactic norepinephrine with standard reactive management. Outcomes included change in serum lactate, haemodynamic measures, fluid administration, and postoperative outcomes, including complications and mortality. Risk of bias and certainty of evidence were assessed using Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 (RoB 2) and the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) approach, respectively. Sensitivity analyses and trial sequential analysis (TSA) were performed. Results Eleven trials (1688 patients) were included. Prophylactic norepinephrine was associated with a lower rise in lactate (mean difference (MD) -0.13 mmol/L, 95% CI -0.25 to -0.01; P = 0.03; I²=67.2%), higher post-induction mean arterial pressure (MD 10.79 mmHg, 95% CI 5.53 to 16.04; P Conclusions Prophylactic norepinephrine was associated with a statistically significant but small reduction in intraoperative lactate rise, higher post-induction and post-operative mean arterial pressures. Postoperative complication findings remain exploratory and require confirmation in adequately powered randomised trials. Registration PROSPERO (CRD420261345140).

items.title: An absent or weak cough doubles the odds of extubation failure after acute brain injury: an updated systematic review and Bayesian meta-analysis
items.abstract: Purpose To update the evidence on neurological and respiratory predictors of extubation failure after acute brain injury and to compare the two families, as pre-specified. Methods Five databases were searched through July 2026 for studies relating a predictor measured at or near extubation to extubation failure in ventilated adults with acute brain injury. Screening and extraction were done in duplicate; risk of bias was assessed using QUIPS. Adjusted estimates were pooled after harmonising outcome framing and predictor coding, restricting each pool to one scale and instrument, with random-effects (REML, Hartung-Knapp) and Bayesian hierarchical models. Certainty was assessed using GRADE. Results 98 studies (24 505 patients) yielded 415 predictor-outcome estimates; 194 carried a confidence interval, and 6 studies contributed to pooled adjusted estimates. Absent or weak cough was associated with failure (4 studies; OR 2.47, 95% CI 1.46-4.19; posterior median 2.55, 95% CrI 1.54-4.71, P(OR > 1) = 0.999; I² = 0%; moderate certainty), in line with the previous synthesis; in an illustrative projection at a 19% failure rate, about 30% versus 15%. Below-threshold motor GCS was associated with failure in two concordant studies (posterior median OR 5.99, 2.42-16.1; very low certainty). The pre-specified comparison between families could not be validly estimated from published data. Conclusions An absent or weak cough at extubation is the best-supported single bedside predictor of failure after acute brain injury and should be assessed with secretions, swallowing and consciousness. Fewer than one in ten eligible studies are poolable, mainly for remediable reporting reasons; a minimum reporting set is proposed. Registration PROSPERO CRD420261442541 (submitted 6 July 2026; registered 2 September 2026). Protocol v2.3 was prepared before the searches; the PROSPERO amendment and all deviations are listed in Supplementary Table S1. Reporting guideline PRISMA 2020 [1].

items.title: Streamlining the Evidence‐to‐Practice Pathway With Computerised Decision Support in Anaesthesiology and Critical Care: A Qualitative Study of Clinician and System‐Level Interest Holder Perspectives Across Five Scandinavian Countries
items.abstract: Background Implementing evidence‐based recommendations in anaesthesiology and critical care remains challenging due to guideline, workflow and contextual barriers. Guideline‐based computerised clinical decision support systems (CDSS), embedded in structured pathways linking international guidelines to Scandinavian‐endorsed recommendations and delivered via electronic health records, may help strengthen the evidence‐to‐practice pathway. This study aimed to explore perceived barriers and facilitators to their use. Methods This qualitative study interviewed 10 clinicians (anaesthesiologists and intensivists; specialists and non‐specialists; < 40 and ≥ 40 years; male and female) and nine system‐level stakeholders (hospital and health authority representatives) from Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway and Sweden. We integrated endorsed international guidelines into a CDSS providing patient‐specific reminders linked to recommendations, as well as shared decision‐making tools and decision‐analytic components. Using a simulation application, participants explored the CDSS in a demo electronic health record. Through a framework analysis based on the GUIDES checklist, we categorised perspectives as barriers, facilitators or suggestions. Results Clinicians and system‐level interest holders expressed broad interest in this multifunctional CDSS to support evidence‐based, patient‐centred care and appreciated the collaborative international pathway facilitated by digital tools. Key themes included the challenges hospitals face in translating international guidelines into up‐to‐date, locally adapted guidance. Artificial intelligence (AI) was perceived as having the potential to both enhance and challenge traditional CDSS. Opportunities were identified to strengthen shared decision‐making for major decisions through the proposed system. Finally, participants highlighted the potential value of using a decision‐analytic tool to prioritise reminders, although the tool was considered conceptually challenging in its current form and would require clearer presentation before being applied in CDSS. Conclusions This prototype study indicates support for a multifunctional CDSS. Building on the barriers and facilitators identified in this study, interviewees advocated for real‐world evaluation with particular attention to sustainable implementation. Editorial Comment This study aimed to describe how ICU clinicians experience interaction in a simulated electronic health record where there were chosen elements of decision support based on international treatment guidelines incorporated into the simulation. Participants were interviewed for their perceptions of what types of decision support might be most helpful to support their clinical work in future patient information and management systems.

items.title: Biomarkers in Patients With Acute Ischaemic Stroke Undergoing Thrombectomy Compared With Controls: A Pilot Study
items.abstract: Background Detection of cerebral ischaemia is challenging in patients who are anaesthetised, sedated or have reduced levels of consciousness, as neurological examination is difficult or even impossible to assess. Furthermore, as some patients cannot be transported for radiology, for example during surgery, a reliable blood biomarker for detecting acute cerebral events would be of considerable clinical value. We aimed to compare levels of brain injury biomarkers glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), neurofilament light chain (NfL), and total tau (tau) in patients with acute ischaemic stroke (AIS) undergoing endovascular thrombectomy under general anaesthesia or sedation to controls undergoing non‐cerebral surgery under general anaesthesia. These biomarkers were chosen because previous studies have demonstrated their potential as blood biomarkers of acute cerebral injury and ischaemic stroke. Methods In this prospective, observational pilot study, conducted at the Sahlgrenska University Hospital, Gothenburg, Sweden, between 2021 and 2024, GFAP, NfL, and tau were analysed using the Simoa Neurology 4‐plex assay, before thrombectomy or surgery and at 2‐ and 24 h thereafter. Results Blood samples from 21 patients with AIS and 19 controls were analysed. GFAP concentrations in patients with AIS increased significantly from baseline to 24 h (median 301.0 → 1443.0 pg/mL; p = 0.001) and were higher than in controls at all time points ( p < 0.01). In the controls there was no significant increase in GFAP from baseline to 24 h ( p = 0.449). NfL and tau increased significantly in patients with AIS ( p = 0.001 and 0.002) but also in the controls ( p = 0.001 and 0.047). Conclusion GFAP and NfL concentrations were higher in patients with acute ischaemic stroke than in surgical controls at all sampling time points, whereas tau differed only after 24 h. Unlike NfL and tau, GFAP did not increase significantly in controls, suggesting that it may be less influenced by anaesthesia and surgery. These findings support further evaluation of GFAP as a potential biomarker of acute cerebral injury in perioperative and critical care settings. Editorial Comment A biomarker of ischaemic cerebral injury could be attractive to support treatments to protect brain health during anaesthesia and surgery. In a pilot study, glial fibrillary acidic protein emerged as a potential candidate as it was increased in patients undergoing endovascular thrombectomy for large‐vessel ischaemic stroke compared to anaesthetised patients undergoing non‐cerebral surgery. Trial Registration ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT03919370

items.title: Correction to “Ephedrine for Reducing Onset Time of Rocuronium in Elderly Patients: A Randomised Study”
Avoidance Versus Use of Neuromuscular Blocking Agents for Optimising Video Laryngoscopy‐Assisted Tracheal Intubation—A Systematic Review With Meta‐Analysis and Trial Sequential Analysis
items.abstract: Background Tracheal intubation during anaesthesia carries risks, and difficult intubation can lead to severe complications. Neuromuscular blocking agents (NMBAs) are widely recommended to improve intubation conditions, but they have potential adverse effects. Video laryngoscopy is widely used, yet evidence on the role of NMBAs in this setting is sparse. We aimed to assess whether avoidance versus use of NMBAs affects first‐pass success and intubation conditions during video laryngoscopy in adults. Method Randomised controlled trials ( RCTs ) comparing avoidance versus use of NMBAs for tracheal intubation in adults during video laryngoscopy were included. The primary outcome was failed first‐pass intubation, as defined by the individual trials. Secondary outcomes were failed intubation, adverse effects ( AEs ) and serious adverse effects ( SAEs ), and acceptable intubation conditions. Furthermore, trial sequential analysis ( TSA ) was undertaken. Results 9483 records were screened. Eight RCTs (744 participants) met the inclusion criteria. The primary outcome was extractable from seven trials (690 participants). Individual trial estimates showed either no clear effect or an increased risk of failed first‐pass intubation when NMBAs were avoided. We found a statistically non‐significant RR: 1.81 (95% CI: 0.93–3.55, p = 0.08, Cochran's Q = 12.0, p = 0.04, I 2 = 58%, D 2 = 74%, TSA adjusted RR: 1.77, TSA adjusted 95% CI: 0.48–6.50, GRADE = very low certainty of evidence) comparing avoidance versus use of NMBAs. TSA showed that the trial sequential monitoring boundaries were not crossed, and the required information size of 2334 was not achieved. Conclusion The effect of avoidance of NMBAs for facilitating video laryngoscopy‐assisted tracheal intubation in adult patients is uncertain (very low certainty), and the required information size was not reached. Editorial Comment This systematic review assessed trial evidence concerning whether or not muscle relaxant use is related to first pass failure in intubation attempts using video laryngoscopy. Evidence to date does not support a clear conclusion on whether avoidance of muscle relaxants in this context is beneficial or not, at least for first pass intubation success, though the evidence has very low certainty for this question.

items.title: Digital Versus in‐Person Pre‐Anaesthetic Assessment and Postoperative Outcomes in Low‐Risk Patients: An Observational Study
items.abstract: Background Pre‐anaesthetic assessment is essential for identifying perioperative risk and optimising patient safety. Digital alternatives, including video consultation and structured electronic health record ( EHR ) review, may improve efficiency, but comparative evidence regarding postoperative safety remains limited. This study aimed to evaluate postoperative outcomes across pre‐anaesthetic assessment through EHR review, video consultation, and in‐person assessment. We hypothesised that patients selected for digital pre‐anaesthetic assessment within a structured triage system would have similar low 30‐day rates of major postoperative complications compared with in‐person assessment. Methods We conducted a single‐centre cohort study at Copenhagen University Hospital—Rigshospitalet, Denmark, including adult patients undergoing elective otorhinolaryngologic, oral, or maxillofacial surgery. Patients underwent pre‐anaesthetic assessment by one of three modalities: in‐person consultation, EHR review, or video consultation. The primary outcome was a composite of major postoperative complications within 30 days, including all‐cause mortality, intensive care unit admission, bleeding requiring transfusion, infection requiring antibiotics, or hospital readmission. A multivariable generalised linear model with a log‐link function was used to estimate adjusted relative risks (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Results A total of 862 patients were included (in‐person n = 300; EHR review n = 300; video consultation n = 262). Patients in the in‐person group were older and had a higher comorbidity burden. Using in‐person as reference, neither video consultation nor EHR review showed a significantly different risk of major postoperative complications. Hospital readmission was lower in both digital groups in pairwise comparisons with the in‐person group. Results were consistent across sensitivity analyses, including inverse probability weighting and win ratio analysis. Conclusion Patients selected for digital pre‐anaesthetic assessment had low rates of major postoperative complications. However, substantial baseline differences between groups indicate that assessment modality was strongly linked to clinical triage and baseline patient risk, thereby limiting direct comparison between pathways. Thus, these findings should not be interpreted as evidence of equivalence or non‐inferiority between pathways. Editorial Comment Preoperative anesthesia assessment is managed in different ways, based on local preferences logistics and resource availability, and perceived perioperative risk for complications. This study assessed this process for planned surgery in section at a university hospital. Those during a number of recent years chosen for in‐person preoperative assessment (for any reason) were compared to those who had some form of digital assessment chosen by the anesthesia personnel. The selection process for in‐person preoperative assessment seemed to identify those who had a higher chance of a major postoperative complication.

items.title: Predicting Gastrointestinal Complications After Cardiac Surgery From Mean Arterial Blood Pressure Under a Data‐Driven Threshold for Hypotension: Protocol for an Advanced Database Study
items.abstract: Background Hypotension during cardiopulmonary bypass may increase the risk of gastrointestinal complications due to insufficient splanchnic autoregulatory capacity. We hypothesize that both duration and level of blood pressure below a data‐driven threshold during cardiopulmonary bypass are associated with the risk of gastrointestinal complications. Methods Patients who underwent cardiac surgery at Copenhagen University Hospital, Rigshospitalet, during 2018–2022 will be included if they underwent on‐pump valve surgery, coronary artery bypass grafting, and/or surgery on the ascending aorta. The primary outcome is major gastrointestinal complications within 30 days, defined as acute intestinal ischemia, abdominal surgery, bowel perforation, or gastrointestinal hemorrhage. Secondary endpoints are serious gastrointestinal complications, delayed recovery of bowel function, cholinesterase inhibitor administration, and 30‐day mortality. The exposure is the exposure to lower blood pressure, calculated as the product of the duration and level of blood pressure below a data‐driven threshold. To identify the optimal threshold, we split the population in a training (75%) and validation cohort (25%). In the training cohort we will identify the threshold with the highest area under the receiver operating curve for the primary outcome. The selected threshold will then be applied to quantify the exposure to lower blood pressure for each patient. Patients will be grouped using a modified Youden's index (weighing sensitivity 80%) as a cutoff for high versus low exposure to lower blood pressure, and association with the study endpoints will be determined in the validation cohort. Conclusion Under the assumption of pressure‐dependent perfusion outside of an autoregulatory plateau, the exposure to blood pressure below a threshold might reflect the risk of gastrointestinal complications more accurately than point measures or averages. The results from this study may lead to relevant hypotheses for prospective testing.

items.title: Paediatric Sedation With Intranasal Dexmedetomidine for Magnetic Resonance Imaging
items.abstract: Background Paediatric sedation for magnetic resonance imaging presents significant challenges. To facilitate this, our department decided to implement paediatric sedation with intranasal dexmedetomidine for children requiring a scan. We aim to summarise lessons learnt from implementation of intranasal dexmedetomidine, comparing time consumption and effectiveness. Methods We conducted a prospective observational study. Data from children sedated with intranasal dexmedetomidine 4 μg/kg ( n = 51) were collected prospectively and compared with historical controls ( n = 100) collected from children previously anaesthetized with either sevoflurane or propofol. Results Sedation with intranasal dexmedetomidine resulted in a longer hospital stay (214 min vs. 133 min [67.94–94.74]), longer time to sufficient sedation (60 min vs. 26 min [29.31, 38.68]) and longer time in the post‐operative unit (112 min vs. 64, 48 min [36.11, 60, 80]). Of children sedated with dexmedetomidine, 75% were cooperative with the intranasal administration of the medicine and 37% were successfully sedated with dexmedetomidine as the sole sedative. In the historical controls, 43% of patients required airway management compared to 1.9% in the dexmedetomidine group [0.00, 0.19]. In the control group, 20% had post‐sedation agitation compared to none in the dexmedetomidine group. No serious bradycardia or desaturation was registered in either group. Conclusion Paediatric sedation with intranasal dexmedetomidine as the sole medicament for magnetic resonance imaging is more time‐consuming compared to sevoflurane and propofol. Sedation with intranasal dexmedetomidine has a relatively low success rate but is without serious adverse events. Editorial Comment This single center case‐control study with prospective datacollection for the case group, intranasal dexmedetomidine and comparison with a historical non‐dexmedetomidine sedation group described multiple possible clinical advantages with intranasal dexmedetomidine administration as it was done here.

items.title: Postoperative Acute Kidney Injury in Children Undergoing Major Non‐Cardiac Surgery: Protocol for a Multicentre Study ( POAKIDS )
items.abstract: Background Acute kidney injury (AKI) is associated with increased mortality and adverse long‐term outcomes. Postoperative AKI is a common and recognised complication after surgery in adults. In children, AKI following paediatric cardiac surgery has been extensively studied. However, the incidence and characteristics of postoperative AKI after non‐cardiac surgery in children remain poorly defined, with existing evidence largely derived from retrospective and single‐centre studies. Methods POAKIDS is an international, multicentre, prospective observational study including hospitalised children aged 0–16 years undergoing major non‐cardiac surgery under general anaesthesia. Postoperative AKI will be defined according to the Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO). The primary outcome is the incidence of postoperative AKI. Secondary objectives include evaluation of established and novel urinary biomarkers as predictors of postoperative AKI and exploration of perioperative potential predictors of renal injury. The maximal follow‐up is seven postoperative days. Sample size is based on the incidence estimate, with a planned inclusion of 2000 patients. Data will be analysed using descriptive statistics, agreement analyses, and exploratory regression models. Discussion This study aims to provide robust prospective data on the incidence of postoperative AKI in children undergoing major non‐cardiac surgery and to improve understanding of perioperative renal injury in this population. By combining standardised AKI definitions with systematic biomarker assessment, the results are expected to inform future preventive strategies and guide the design of interventional studies targeting postoperative renal injury in paediatric perioperative care.

items.title: Effects of Iloprost on Nitric Oxide Biomarkers in Patients With Septic Shock and Severe Endotheliopathy
items.abstract: Background Septic shock is characterized by profound endothelial dysfunction, which may involve changes in the prostacyclin and nitric oxide (NO) pathways and contribute to immune dysregulation, coagulopathy, and vascular instability. Iloprost has shown potential to modulate NO biomarkers in non‐septic conditions. We investigated whether treatment with the prostacyclin analog iloprost affected plasma concentrations of the NO biomarkers ADMA, SDMA, arginine, and homoarginine in patients with septic shock and severe endotheliopathy. Methods This preplanned sub‐study of the randomized, blinded COMBAT‐SHINE trial enrolled 274 adult ICU patients with septic shock and severe endotheliopathy (defined as soluble thrombomodulin (sTM) > 10 ng/mL) who had consented to the use of data. Five participants from the full trial population withdrew consent. Participants were allocated to a 72‐h infusion of iloprost (1 ng/kg/min) versus placebo. Plasma concentrations of ADMA, SDMA, arginine, and homoarginine were measured at 0, 24, 48, and 72 h. Changes in biomarker concentrations were assessed using linear mixed models, with predefined subgroup analyses. All results were considered exploratory. Results In explorative analyses, iloprost treatment, compared with placebo, did not statistically significantly change plasma concentrations of ADMA and SDMA (estimated difference in means −4% (95% CI: −13%, 6%; p = 0.4) and−2% (95% CI: −14%, 10%; p = 0.7), respectively), or plasma concentrations of arginine and homoarginine (estimated difference in means 9% (95% CI: −6%, 27%; p = 0.2) and 17% (95% CI: −3%, 42%; p = 0.10), respectively). None of the NO biomarkers changes over time (0–24 h, 24–48 h, or 48–72 h) differed between the iloprost and placebo groups (all p > 0.3). Findings were consistent across predefined subgroups. Conclusions In this sub‐study of a randomized clinical trial of adults in the ICU with septic shock and severe endotheliopathy, infusion of iloprost 1 ng/kg/min for 72 h did not affect plasma concentrations of the NO biomarkers ADMA, SDMA, arginine, and homoarginine. Editorial Comment This substudy of a larger trial of iloprost versus placebo for sepsis outcomes (COMBAT‐SHINE trial) examined specifically nitric oxide markers in a septic shock and epithelial injury cohort. Iloprost treatment at the tested dose did not appear to affect markers of nitric oxide measured as ADMA, SDMA, arginine or homoarginine levels.

items.title: Work‐Related Fatigue Among N orwegian Anaesthesiologists With a Focus on Shift Work: A National Cross‐Sectional Survey
items.abstract: Background There is a growing focus on fatigue among anaesthesiologists; however, data on work‐related fatigue in Norway, including its impact on personal well‐being and the risks associated with driving home after night shifts, are limited. In this study, we aimed to assess working conditions, the perceived risk of driving home after night shifts, and the reported levels and effects of work‐related fatigue among specialist and trainee anaesthesiologists in Norway. Methods A cross‐sectional, anonymous digital survey of specialist and trainee anaesthesiologists was conducted. These specialist and trainee anaesthesiologists were members of the Norwegian Association of Anaesthesia. A 27‐item online survey was used to assess work‐related fatigue and its impact on specialists and trainee anaesthesiologists. Results Ninety‐five percent of the 408 specialist and trainee anaesthesiologists who responded reported having experienced work‐related fatigue. The response rate was 22.5%. The lack of rest during shifts and understaffing were perceived as the most important contributing factors. Negative effects on health, sleep, and broader aspects of personal and social functioning were reported. Seventy‐three percent of respondents have, at some point, been so fatigued at work that they considered it unsafe. Conclusion Work‐related fatigue is common among anaesthesiologists in Norway, with perceived impacts on patient safety and negative professional and personal consequences, including the risk of driving home. These findings warrant increased attention, and hospital management should implement fatigue risk management systems to address this issue. Editorial Comment The results of this national survey highlights perceived fatigue among Norwegian anaesthesiologists, with reported consequences for wellbeing, patient safety, and driving after shifts. The low response rate and reliance on self‐reported outcomes limit generalisability and causal interpretation. Nevertheless, these findings support greater organisational attention to staffing, rest opportunities, and fatigue management, alongside evaluation of interventions to improve clinician and patient safety.

items.title: Prevalence and Predictors of Dysphagia Following Prolonged Intubation in ICU Patients, and the Association With Voice Impairment and Laryngeal Injury
items.abstract: Background Post‐extubation Dysphagia (PED), voice impairment, and laryngeal injuries are commonly observed in patients with prolonged intubation in intensive care units (ICU). PED is associated with negative patient outcomes, both short and long term. This study investigated the prevalence of PED and its potential risk factors, as well as the prevalence of voice impairment and laryngeal injuries and their associations with dysphagia. Methods This is a prospective study of adult ICU patients intubated for more than 48 h. Flexible Endoscopic Evaluation of Swallowing (FEES) was conducted bedside on all patients, by nine trained speech and language pathologists (SLP), following a standard protocol assessing function and structure of the velopharynx, pharynx, larynx, voice, and swallowing function. Dysphagia evaluation and ratings coincided during FEES, while voice and laryngeal injuries were retrospectively rated from FEES recordings. Associations between dysphagia and potential risk factors were analyzed using univariable and multivariable models. Results Among 51 participants, 82% had dysphagia, ranging from mild to severe. Voice impairment was present in 79%, and 83% had laryngeal injuries, including asymmetry (34%) and edema (57%). Voice impairment (92% vs. 14%) and laryngeal edema (64% vs. 25%) were associated with dysphagia ( p < 0.05). In multivariable analysis, voice impairment remained independently associated with dysphagia (OR 86.6, 95% CI 3.28–2285.59; p = 0.008). No association between dysphagia and other potential risk factors, such as length of intubation, tube size, or gender, was found. Conclusion This study shows a high prevalence of dysphagia, voice impairment, and laryngeal injuries in a diverse ICU population, aligning with earlier research. Voice impairment emerged as an independent predictor, suggesting it may be a useful clinical indicator for dysphagia. These findings support routine dysphagia screening in patients undergoing prolonged intubation to improve clinical management and outcomes. Editorial Comment Endotracheal intubation periods in ICU patients is recognized to have later airway sequelae in some ICU survivors. This prospective study assessed post‐extubation pharyngeal and laryngeal function within 2 days after extubation. High proportions of cases with dypagia and laryngeal dysfunction, including voice impairment, were observed.

items.title: Risk Factors, Survival and Discharge After Cardiac Surgery Across Age Groups: A Multicenter Retrospective Cohort Study
items.abstract: Background Elderly cardiac surgery patients typically present with more comorbidities and reduced physiological reserves. Additionally, they are often evaluated for complex surgery. This study aimed to compare survival outcomes across age groups undergoing cardiac surgery with special emphasis on octogenarians. Specifically, we sought to evaluate index hospitalization and 1‐year survival across age groups, characterize discharge patterns and their association with long‐term outcomes, and assess whether established risk factors for mortality demonstrate age‐specific effects. Methods This retrospective cohort study analyzed all cardiac surgery patients at the Department of Cardiothoracic and Vascular Surgery, Odense University Hospital and the Department of Cardiothoracic and Vascular Surgery, Aarhus University Hospital. Perioperative clinical variables were retrieved from the Western Denmark Heart Registry. Survival was evaluated using the Kaplan–Meier estimator, with log‐rank tests for group comparisons, applying Bonferroni‐Holm correction for multiple comparisons. Multivariate survival analysis was performed using Cox proportional hazard regression. Results In total 27,311 cardiac surgery patients were analyzed. Multivariate Cox regression analysis identified emergency surgery (HR 3.83, p < 0.001), advanced age (HR 3.43, p < 0.001), preoperative kidney dysfunction (HR 2.29, p < 0.001), COPD (HR 1.84, p < 0.001), extracardiac arteriopathy (HR 1.99, p < 0.001), and erythrocyte transfusions (HR 1.08, p < 0.001) as significant predictors of increased 1‐year mortality. Octogenarians achieved 95% index hospitalization survival and 90% 1‐year survival, with similar outcomes for home discharge and transfer to another hospital. Conclusion This analysis found that emergency surgery, advanced age, and preoperative kidney dysfunction were the strongest mortality predictors, while the findings demonstrate favorable short‐ and intermediate‐term survival among carefully selected octogenarians undergoing cardiac surgery. Editorial Comment In this retrospective study including 27,311 cardiac cases, emergency surgery, advanced age, and preoperative kidney dysfunction were the strongest mortality predictors. Interestingly, the findings also demonstrated favorable short‐ and intermediate‐term survival among octogenarians. Taking into account the study design, caution is needed for interpreting possible causal effects of these factors.

items.title: The incidence of postoperative hypotension among non-cardiac surgical specialties: A single-centre retrospective cohort study
items.abstract: Postoperative hypotension is associated with increased risk of postoperative complications and mortality. There are limited studies quantifying the incidence of this potentially life-threatening condition among different surgical cohorts. We aimed to describe and compare the incidence of postoperative hypotension in the first 48 h after leaving the post-anaesthesia care unit (PACU) across different surgical specialties after non-cardiac surgery. We conducted a single-centre retrospective study at the Royal Melbourne Hospital. The primary outcome was postoperative hypotension (systolic blood pressure (SBP) <90 mmHg) within 48 h after surgery and discharge from PACU, noted on routine blood pressure monitoring or a requirement for postoperative vasopressor or inotropic support. We estimated odds ratios (OR) using mixed-effects logistic regression models to account for multiple surgical procedures within the same patient. We identified 11,634 surgeries from 17 specialties, of which 47.3% were emergency operations. The median age was 53 years (interquartile range 35–68), with 42.2% being female and 42.5% of patients on regular antihypertensive medication. The overall incidence of ward hypotension was 4.4%. Trauma had the highest rate of postoperative hypotension (27.3%), followed by thoracic surgery (11.6%). Surgical specialties that had a higher risk of hypotension included trauma surgery (OR 13.0, 95% confidence interval (CI) 3.7–46.0) and thoracic surgery (OR 3.6, 95% CI 2.3–5.5). Specialties with a lower risk of hypotension included breast and endocrine surgery (OR 0.4, 95% CI 0.2–0.7) and plastic surgery (OR 0.4, 95% CI 0.3–0.6). Postoperative hypotension is relatively common with substantial variation in incidence between surgical specialties. These findings highlight the need for heightened vigilance for hypotension in certain patients.

items.title: Translating evidence into practice: Deimplementation of routine chest radiography after cardiothoracic drain removal
A case of massive gamma-hydroxybutyrate overdose mimicking brain death
items.abstract: A 36-year-old female was brought into hospital following a massive overdose of 100 ml of gamma-hydroxybutyrate. Unlike prior case reports where ethanol was a co-ingestant with gamma-hydroxybutyrate or its precursor, gamma-hydroxybutyrate was believed to have been the only substance ingested in this case. The patient developed a severe and persistent high anion gap metabolic acidosis and required continuous renal replacement therapy. The patient developed fixed and dilated pupils early on in her clinical course and was found to have a transient loss of most brainstem reflexes on clinical examination, thus mimicking brain death. She also developed generalised tonic-clonic seizures and received midazolam and levetiracetam for seizure control. She was successfully extubated after 5 days on mechanical ventilation and was discharged home on day 11 with no neurological deficits.

items.title: Conference Proceedings of the Asia Pacific Intensive Care Symposium 2026
A sympathetic solution: Brachial plexus blockade for suspected adrenaline-induced vasospasm
items.abstract: Vasospasm threatens perfusion across recently reconstructed vessels. Systemic adrenaline, (epinephrine) the first-line treatment for anaphylaxis, is a potent vasoconstrictor, and therefore represents a potential, albeit necessary, threat to newly reconstructed vessels. Brachial plexus blockade may dampen localised vasoconstriction, allowing for improved vascular perfusion and reduced risk of vasospasm. An adult male sustained a workplace injury resulting in an open fracture-dislocation of the distal radius and fracture and accompanying radial and ulnar artery transections, requiring a vein graft repair to both vessels and external fixation of the radius and ulna. At 36 h post-operatively, the patient developed anaphylaxis to intravenous amoxicillin–clavulanic acid, requiring boluses and subsequent infusion of adrenaline for anaphylaxis management. Within minutes, the affected limb distal to the arterial repair became pale, cold, pulseless and painful. Adrenaline-induced vasospasm was presumed after multidisciplinary discussion. An ultrasound-guided supraclavicular brachial plexus block using 20 ml of 0.5% ropivacaine was performed as a salvage measure while surgical re-exploration was being considered. Perfusion and pain improved within minutes and had a sustained effect in the setting of adrenaline infusion. The infusion was ceased after 8 h, and the block resolved after approximately 12 h without recurrence of vasospasm. Re-exploration was not required, given the clinical suspicion and subsequent improvement post-block. Brachial plexus block performed for presumed adrenaline-induced vasospasm restored vascular perfusion, by presumed selective blockade of sympathetic ganglion that is responsible for local vasoconstriction, while not counteracting the systemic effects of IV adrenaline administration.

items.title: Association between prior epidural labour analgesia and increased incidence of hypotension after spinal anaesthesia for caesarean section: A retrospective propensity score-matched cohort study
items.abstract: The administration of spinal anaesthesia after epidural labour analgesia may increase the risk of block failure or high spinal block, particularly when the intrathecal local anaesthetic dose is reduced. This retrospective, propensity score-matched cohort study evaluated the feasibility of using a standard spinal dose in partients (i.e. women who are in labour) with epidural labour analgesia undergoing caesarean section. Women who underwent caesarean delivery between April 2016 and March 2020 were analysed. The primary outcome was the rate of conversion to general anaesthesia. After 161 patients had been matched in the epidural labour analgesia-to-spinal anaesthesia and spinal anaesthesia groups, general anaesthesia conversion rates were comparable (3.3% vs 2.5%, P = 0.544); all conversions resulted from block failure. However, the epidural labour analgesia-to-spinal anaesthesia group experienced significantly more frequent hypotension (55.9% vs 30.4%, P < 0.001) and required higher doses of ephedrine (mean 8.3, standard deviation 9.8 mg vs mean 5.9, standard deviation 11.1 mg, P = 0.036). Although epidural labour analgesia did not increase the rates of block failure or high spinal block when preventive strategies were utilised, it was associated with a higher incidence of hypotension and increased vasopressor requirements.

items.title: Perioperative methadone: Clinical use and knowledge among Australian anaesthetists
items.abstract: Intravenous methadone has re-emerged as a perioperative analgesic, yet uncertainty persists regarding its optimal use. Variation in clinician practice and interpretation of pharmacological principles may influence its safe and effective application. We conducted a mixed-methods survey-based study within a national anaesthesia educational programme (ADVANCE). A voluntary, anonymous pre-presentation clinician survey was distributed to predominantly Australian anaesthetists to characterise methadone use, dosing strategies, adjunct prescribing and patient selection. Real-time audience polling during the educational session assessed clinician responses to pharmacology-based and clinical decision-making scenarios. Survey and polling datasets were analysed independently using descriptive statistics. A total of 726 clinicians completed the survey. Overall, 50.6% ( n = 367) of respondents reported using methadone. Among users ( n = 367), practice varied widely across surgical contexts and dosing strategies, including weight-based, fixed and procedure-dependent approaches. Concurrent administration of additional opioids and central nervous system depressants was common (86.1%). Clinicians reported avoiding methadone in specific patient groups, most frequently frail patients, those with prolonged QT interval, or obstructive sleep apnoea. Polling responses demonstrated variability in clinician interpretation of pharmacological principles, particularly regarding timing of central effects. Perioperative methadone use is characterised by substantial variation in uptake, dosing and adjunct prescribing. Variability in clinician responses relative to pharmacological reference data, combined with frequent co-administration of additional opioids and sedatives, highlights potential areas for targeted education and institutional safeguards to support safe implementation.

items.title: Freshwater drowning with profound hypofibrinogenaemia and refractory vasoplegic shock
items.abstract: We present a challenging case of freshwater drowning complicated by profound hypofibrinogenaemia and refractory vasoplegic shock in a 39-year-old male admitted following an out-of-hospital cardiac arrest. The constellation of physiological and laboratory abnormalities initially precluded a unifying diagnosis. The haemolysis, hyper-fibrinolysis and disseminated intravascular coagulation observed in our patient were likely sequelae of freshwater drowning and cardiac arrest. The refractory vasoplegic shock necessitated rescue off-label administration of hydroxocobalamin, resulting in restoration of haemodynamic stability.

items.title: Audit of procedural sedation in a remote Australian hospital 2010 – 2021
items.abstract: Procedural sedation is commonly provided in rural hospitals; however, there is little published safety data. The authors conducted a retrospective audit of anaesthetic records from 2010 to 2021 of procedural sedation in a remote hospital in South Australia. The data were collected from 1912 cases, which were provided mainly for gastroenterology procedures in day case theatre and emergency department settings. Sedation was provided by a general practitioner anaesthetist giving boluses of fentanyl, midazolam and propofol. All patients were low risk (American Society of Anesthesiologists physical status 1–3). There were few anaesthetic problems and no mortality during sedation or in the recovery area. The most common problem was desaturation requiring airway support and oxygen, and occurred in 2% of cases. Procedural sedation was practiced safely in this remote setting.

items.title: Comment on: Postoperative management after oesophagectomy – An evidence-based approach
Sprint National Anaesthesia Project 3: A survey of perioperative medicine services for older surgical patients in Australia
items.abstract: Increasing numbers of older people with age-related conditions such as frailty and multimorbidity are presenting for surgical procedures, which is associated with an increased risk of postoperative complications. This study aimed to assess the provision of perioperative medicine services for older surgical patients across Australian hospitals participating in the third Sprint National Anaesthesia Project. An organisational survey was conducted involving 23 Australian hospitals, collecting data on hospital characteristics, clinical governance, preoperative assessments (including frailty, cognition, and risk of delirium), and postoperative care practices for high-risk older patients. Responses were analysed to evaluate the structure and function of perioperative services for older surgical patients. Twenty-one hospitals completed the survey. Preoperative assessments of older surgical patients were predominantly nurse- or anaesthetist-led, with limited geriatrician involvement. Routine preoperative screening of frailty and cognition was rare, and there was significant variability in approaches to the assessment of postoperative delirium. The survey highlights inconsistencies in perioperative care delivery for older surgical patients, revealing gaps in the implementation of established guidelines and recommendations. There is a need for a structured approach to integrate geriatric services into surgical pathways, with an emphasis on routine screening for frailty, cognitive impairment, multimorbidity, and delirium.

items.title: Letter to the Editor: A characterisation audit of cases of necrotising soft tissue infections requiring intensive care support in Regional North Queensland
Comment on ‘Large language model prompt engineering for medical education: A practical guide for the Australian and New Zealand College of Anaesthetists Final Examination’
Population pharmacokinetic models of doxapram for use in preterm neonates: An external evaluation
items.abstract: Population pharmacokinetic models can support dose selection. Doxapram, used for apnoea of prematurity, has a relatively narrow range of acceptable concentrations. Neonatal dosing is further complicated by rapidly maturing organs and body size increases. Two paediatric models for doxapram have been reported, but their applicability to external populations is unknown. Two published models (Flint et al. and Ogawa et al.) were re-coded in NONMEM and used to predict doxapram concentrations at steady state in 32 infants who received oral doxapram as either 48 mg/kg followed by 24 mg/kg/6 h, or 24 mg/kg followed by 12 mg/kg/6 h. The Ogawa model was for intravenous dosing only, so oral absorption parameters reported by Flint were assumed. Models were evaluated using median prediction error (PE), median absolute PE and root mean square error. Visual predictive checks (VPCs) were used to assess model misspecification. Fifty-seven concentrations each of doxapram and keto-doxapram, from 31 infants, were included. The Ogawa model performed best, with median PE of −3.4 (95% CI: −7.8, 0.3) %, meaning the median model prediction was just ~3% lower than observed concentrations; median absolute PE was 8.7 (7.6–12.4) %. VPCs stratified by weight and postmenstrual age showed no major misspecification. Simulations with the adapted Ogawa model were used to explore further dosing strategies. The Ogawa model performed well when adapted for oral dosing. Our simulations suggest that, within the assumptions of the adapted Ogawa model, 25 mg/kg oral doxapram, followed by 15 mg/kg/6 h, will achieve concentrations ranging 2–5 mg/L, within the target range.
