Central venous access device complications: A review of 163 incidents reported to webAIRS
items.abstract: Central venous access device insertion is a valuable intervention for the perioperative management of complex patients or surgeries. While most insertions are without complication, there are repeated and often preventable adverse events that can result in serious harm or death. Between 2009 and 2023, 163 incidents involving a central venous access device were reported by Australian and New Zealand anaesthetists to webAIRS, a web-based anaesthetic incident voluntary reporting system. Most incidents occurred in older patients (49.7% were older than 60 years of age) and in patients with greater clinical complexity (82.2% were classified as the American Society of Anesthesiologists status III or higher), involved experienced anaesthetists (81.6% were at Post Fellowship level or above), occurred during daylight hours (76.6%) and involved staff who had been on duty 10 hours or less (78.5%). Eighteen reports described potential allergic reactions during central venous access device insertion, with six confirmed cases of anaphylaxis. There were 29 reports of arterial injury, 19 of which occurred despite ultrasound guidance during insertion. On four occasions, respiratory arrest followed inadvertent injection of muscle relaxant remaining in peripherally inserted central catheter line dead space. While most incidents resulted in minor or no effect (63.1%), there was a 28% incidence of temporary disability, 3% incidence of death and a 1.2% incidence of permanent disability. The event was assessed as preventable in 68.7% of incidents. Strategies to enhance the standardisation of central venous access device insertion and maintenance protocols, and routine use of measures to prevent these complications are discussed.

items.title: To top-up or not to top-up? Anaesthesia for caesarean delivery in 5494 cases at a regional hospital in Australia
items.abstract: Albury Wodonga Health, a regional referral obstetric service in Australia, delivers around 1600 babies per year. Our anaesthesia department has an ongoing audit of anaesthesia techniques utilised for elective and emergency caesarean sections. Data from a retrospective audit including all caesarean sections performed ( n = 5494) over an 11 year period (2014–2024) were included. Rates of general anaesthesia (GA), and conversion of regional anaesthesia to GA, were established and compared to accepted standards. Our service is at or close to recommended thresholds on all measures, although we were unable to separate category 1 caesarean sections from emergencies of other urgency categories. The rate of conversion of regional to GA appeared similar for emergency caesarean sections performed on patients with in situ labour epidural catheters, whether the epidural was topped up (6.0%, 95% confidence interval (CI) 4.7%–7.6%), or removed and a de novo spinal anaesthetic attempted or performed (8.3%, 95% CI 4.9%–12.9%). Our regional service maintained an acceptable standard of primary and conversion GA. Anaesthetists should consider their strategy when faced with a patient for emergency caesarean section with an in situ epidural catheter and consider combined spinal-epidural anaesthesia in this situation.

items.title: Intensive care for post-surgical nonagenarian and centenarian patients in Australia and New Zealand, 2010–2023
items.abstract: Data regarding postoperative intensive care unit admissions for patients older than 90 years are limited. We determined the incidence of intensive care unit admission, in-hospital and long-term mortality, and risk factors for hospital mortality among surgical patients 90 years or older. This registry-based retrospective cohort study used the Australian and New Zealand Intensive Care Society Adult Patient Database (2010–2023). A total of 21,195 patients were admitted with a surgical diagnosis, received active treatment, and had known hospital mortality. A sub-cohort of 11,474 patients was used for logistic regression modelling, and 10,459 patients had long-term mortality data. Hospital mortality decreased from 12.6% in 2010 to 8.6% in 2023. The median long-term survival was 31.5 months (95% confidence interval 30.5 to 32.6) for 2018–2023 admissions. Among preoperative factors, male sex (odds ratio 1.58; 95% confidence interval 1.33 to 1.87; P < 0.001) and frailty (odds ratio 1.34 per 1-point increase in Clinical Frailty Scale score, 95% confidence interval 1.25 to 1.43; P < 0.001) correlated with elevated mortality. Elective surgery (odds ratio 0.47, 95% confidence interval 0.38 to 0.58; P < 0.001), planned admissions (odds ratio 0.63, 95% confidence interval 0.52 to 0.77; P < 0.001), interventional cardiology (odds ratio 0.39, 95% confidence interval 0.20 to 0.76; P = 0.006), and orthopaedic procedures (odds ratio 0.77, 95% confidence interval 0.61 to 0.98; P =0.033) correlated with diminished hospital mortality. This binational database study indicated improving mortality outcomes and reasonable long-term survival among nonagenarian and centenarian surgical intensive care unit patients. These findings suggest that clinicians are selecting appropriate surgical candidates, and patient outcomes are improving.

items.title: Utilising consensus guidelines to apply personalised medicine in performing percutaneous dilatational tracheostomy
High-frequency jet ventilation of the non-dependent lung during one-lung ventilation in metatropic skeletal dysplasia: A case report
items.abstract: One-lung ventilation is frequently required during thoracic surgery but may be poorly tolerated in patients with limited pulmonary reserve. High-frequency jet ventilation has been described as a means of supporting oxygenation while preserving surgical exposure, although its planned use as an intraoperative adjunct to one-lung ventilation remains sparsely described in the literature. We present the case of a 27-year-old woman with metatrophic skeletal dysplasia resulting in severe kyphoscoliosis, restrictive lung disease and complicated airway anatomy, who underwent thoracic spine operation (T9–10 costovertebrectomy and cage insertion) via a left thoracotomy. In light of her markedly reduced pulmonary reserve and prior anaesthetic difficulties, a dual-ventilation strategy was planned preoperatively in anticipation of intolerance to conventional one-lung ventilation alone; her dependent right lung was ventilated conventionally via a double-lumen tube, whereas high-frequency jet ventilation was delivered to the non-dependent left lung through the bronchial lumen. This technique maintained arterial oxygenation and normocapnia throughout a prolonged 7-h procedure, with serial arterial blood gas analyses confirming sustained gas exchange. Brief intraoperative trials of conventional one-lung ventilation alone resulted in rapid desaturation, reinforcing the physiological necessity of this approach. The patient remained haemodynamically stable throughout the case and was extubated uneventfully at the conclusion of surgery, with an uncomplicated immediate postoperative course. Our findings advocate for high-frequency jet ventilation as a valuable intraoperative adjunct to one-lung ventilation in select high-risk patients with restrictive thoracic physiology and illustrate its capacity to be sustained over a prolonged operative course. This case underscores a novel, proactive approach to a predictable intraoperative challenge.

items.title: Practice patterns of midazolam administration in patients undergoing cardiac-related non-operating room procedures: analysis of a US anaesthesia database
items.abstract: Background: Midazolam can be administered as an anxiolytic, a cardio-stable sedative, or an anaesthetic agent during non-operating room anaesthesia (NORA) procedures. Guidelines suggest avoidance in older or frail patients, and current practices are unknown. We hypothesised that there would be significant variation in midazolam administration for cardiac-related NORA procedures by attending and institutional characteristics, in addition to patient characteristics. Methods: This is a retrospective observational analysis of a multi-institution US-centric electronic health record dataset including all adult patients undergoing cardiac-related NORA procedures in the Multicenter Perioperative Outcomes Group database from 2015 to 2022. The primary aim of the study was to identify the proportion of total variance in midazolam administration attributable to patient-, attending-, and institutional-level factors. The secondary aim was to identify practice pattern variations in the dosage and timing of midazolam administration. The primary outcome was any midazolam administration ≤1 h before anaesthesia start to 1 h after anaesthesia end. Secondary outcomes included total dose and timing of midazolam administration. Variance in midazolam administration attributable to patient, attending, and institutional factors was calculated with intraclass correlation coefficients following multilevel mixed-effects generalised linear models, in which a three-level nesting structure was assumed: patients nested within attendings and attendings nested within institutions. For the primary outcome, a binomial distribution and logit link function was specified. For the secondary outcome of total midazolam, the same three-level nesting structure was used, and covariates were modelled using a multilevel mixed-effects model specifying a Gaussian distribution and identity link function. Results: A total of 246 918 cardiac-related NORA procedures with care provided by 5212 unique anaesthesia attendings across 63 institutions with a median case volume of 9 (inter-quartile range [IQR] 2-37) were included in the analysis. Midazolam was administered in 33.0% of patients (n=81 602), including 25.5% of patients aged ≥65 yr (n=40 469). Midazolam administration declined from 50.7% of patients in 2015 to 29.0% in 2022 (P<0.001). The median dose was 2 mg (IQR 2-2), with 89.9% administered before procedure start. For transoesophageal echocardiography procedures, it was estimated that 37.0% of midazolam administration (30.4-44.3) was attributable to attending variation and 26.4% (19.2-35.2) to the institution, assuming that 36.6% of the variation was attributable to known patient factors. For transcatheter/endovascular procedures, attending, institution, and patient factors accounted for 45.7% (39.0-52.6), 27.7% (19.7-37.4), and 26.6%, respectively. Conclusions: Although patient-level factors accounted for a meaningful proportion of variability, substantial variation in midazolam administration was also attributable to attending- and institution-level factors. Further studies on clinical outcomes and patient experience associated with this type of midazolam administration have the potential to inform future practice.

items.title: Daily debriefings, burnout, and impostor phenomenon in anaesthesiology trainees and supervisors: a controlled feasibility study
items.abstract: Burnout is a growing concern in anaesthesiology. In the UK, one in four consultants has considered leaving the National Health Service within 5 yr, citing mental health deterioration.1 Anaesthesiologists work under sustained time, legal, and economic pressure, which can drive the emotional exhaustion (EE), depersonalisation (DP), and reduced accomplishment that constitute burnout.2 In academic hospitals, board-certified anaesthesiologists fulfil their clinical duties while supervising and teaching trainees, who are themselves highly exposed: burnout symptoms affect 38–85% of trainees in published surveys.

items.title: Effects of propofol- or sevoflurane-containing anaesthesia on auditory brainstem responses in children: a systematic review
items.abstract: Background: Auditory brainstem response (ABR) provides objective hearing assessment in children who cannot undergo reliable behavioural audiometry. Sedation or general anaesthesia may facilitate recording but can alter electrophysiological measurements and potentially influence diagnostic interpretation. The primary aim of this systematic review was to explore electrophysiological and diagnostic outcomes of paediatric ABR testing when at least one study condition included propofol or sevoflurane. Methods: This Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses 2020 systematic review was prospectively registered in International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (CRD420261324873). PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were searched from inception, with searches updated on 17 August 2026. Two reviewers independently screened the original search; one reviewer screened the later update. Because of clinical and methodological heterogeneity, findings were synthesised narratively. Results: The database searches identified 2386 records and yielded six eligible studies. Citation checking identified one additional study, giving seven in total. Four studies reported longer wave V latency under anaesthesia than under their respective comparators, but co-administered agents and differing populations preclude drug-specific attribution. In a within-participant comparison, hearing-loss classification differed between sevoflurane and propofol; a later observational cohort found no significant adjusted association for its distinct exposure groups. Conclusions: Four of seven studies reported longer ABR electrophysiological wave V latency under anaesthesia, but five studies had a high risk of bias. A single study with within-participant comparison found different diagnostic classifications under sevoflurane and propofol. Heterogeneous designs and exposures do not establish which anaesthesia technique best preserves paediatric ABR findings.

items.title: Prognostic value of growth differentiation factor 15 in older patients undergoing emergency abdominal surgery: a prospective observational study at a tertiary hospital
items.abstract: Background Emergency abdominal surgery in frail older patients carries a high risk of mortality and cardiovascular complications. Growth differentiation factor 15 (GDF-15) is a strong prognostic marker across different patient populations and may improve perioperative risk stratification. We assessed associations between preoperative GDF-15 concentrations and postoperative outcomes in older patients undergoing emergency abdominal surgery. Methods This preplanned secondary biomarker substudy of the ProPEL cohort included 142 patients aged ≥75 yr undergoing emergency abdominal surgery between January 2020 and April 2021. The primary endpoint was 30-day all-cause mortality. Secondary endpoints were 90-day mortality and 30-day mortality or major adverse cardiac events (MACEs). Intraoperative blood transfusion was added as a post hoc exploratory analysis. Results Overall, 30-day all-cause mortality was 12% (17/142). Mortality was 31% (11/36) in the highest GDF-15 quartile compared with 6% (2/35 or 2/36) in each of the lower quartiles. Each doubling of GDF-15 was associated with increased 30-day mortality (hazard ratio: 1.75, 95% confidence interval: 1.15–2.66, P =0.009) independent of age, sex, and Clinical Frailty Scale, and in a model adjusted for high-sensitivity cardiac troponin T hazard ratio 1.65 (1.03–2.65), P=0.037. GDF-15 predicted 30-day death or MACE, adjusted for age, sex, and Clinical Frailty Scale, but not after adjusting for high-sensitivity cardiac troponin T. Associations with 90-day mortality were attenuated after adjustment. A doubling of GDF-15 concentrations was associated with an adjusted odds ratio of 1.90 (95% confidence interval 1.29–2.78, P =0.001) for intraoperative blood transfusion. Conclusions GDF-15 was associated with 30-day mortality and the need for blood transfusion in older adults undergoing acute abdominal surgery.

items.title: Glutamate infusion and the incidence of acute kidney injury after coronary artery bypass grafting in relation to preoperative risk and baseline kidney function
items.abstract: Background Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a common and serious complication after cardiac surgery, with limited preventive strategies. Glutamate supplementation may reduce AKI indirectly by enhancing recovery of post-ischaemic myocardial metabolism and function; however, its metabolic effects appear attenuated in diabetic hearts. We investigated the association between glutamate infusion and postoperative AKI in patients without diabetes mellitus undergoing coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG), according to preoperative risk and kidney function. Methods This post hoc analysis pooled data from two randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled GLUTAMICS trials. Patients without diabetes mellitus undergoing CABG with or without concomitant valve surgery were allocated to i.v. 0.125 M L-glutamic acid or saline. AKI was defined as a postoperative increase in plasma creatinine ≥50% from baseline (RIFLE risk stage or higher) and analysed according to European System for Cardiac Operative Risk Evaluation II (EuroSCORE II) quartiles and estimated creatinine clearance. Results Among 791 patients, 391 received glutamate and 400 received placebo. In the combined two highest EuroSCORE II quartiles, AKI incidence was lower with glutamate (8.0% vs 16.8%; relative risk [RR] 0.47; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.27–0.84; P =0.011). Among patients with an estimated creatinine clearance of ≥50 ml min −1 , AKI occurred in 2.7% vs 9.6% (RR 0.28; 95% CI 0.14–0.58; P <0.001). No benefit was observed with severe preoperative kidney dysfunction (estimated creatinine clearance <50 ml min −1 ). Significant interactions were observed between glutamate allocation and preoperative risk ( P =0.025) and severe preoperative kidney dysfunction ( P =0.027). Conclusions Glutamate infusion was associated with a lower incidence of AKI in higher-risk patients without diabetes mellitus, particularly those without severe preoperative kidney dysfunction. These exploratory findings require prospective confirmation. Trial registration number ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT00489827 and NCT02592824).

items.title: Potential impact of expanded insurance coverage for ondansetron on prophylactic antiemetic prescriptions given and postoperative antiemetics delivered among patients undergoing general anaesthesia in Japan: a retrospective observational study using interrupted time-series analysis of a nationwide claims database
items.abstract: Background The impact of expanding health insurance coverage for ondansetron on antiemetic prescription trends and postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV) in Japan remains unknown. This nationwide Japanese descriptive study evaluated the impact of the coverage expansion on clinical practice and patient outcomes. Methods This large-scale retrospective observational study using an interruped time-series analysis (ITSA) analysed a nationwide health insurance claims database from more than 500 institutions in Japan (February 2020 to March 2024). The primary outcome was prophylactic and rescue antiemetic prescriptions given, and the secondary outcome was PONV the estimated occurence of PONV based on antiemetic treatment. Prescriptions on surgery day and postoperative days 1–2 were used as surrogate measures of prophylactic antiemetic use and pharmacologically treated (rescue-medicated) PONV, respectively; these surrogates were not direct measures of clinically observed PONV. Results A total of 2 150 497 general anaesthesia cases (2 022 695 adults; 127 802 children) were analysed. After coverage expansion, prophylactic antiemetic prescriptions increased (total prescriptions, from 492 998 of 1 052 933 [46.8%] to 636 158 of 1 097 564 [58.0%]; ≥2 prescriptions, from 92 134 of 1 052 933 [8.8%] to 246 572 of 1 097 564 [22.5%]). ITSA showed that ondansetron prescriptions increased significantly after coverage expansion (β=0.33; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.23–0.43; P <0.001). The combined effect of guideline release and coverage expansion was associated with a significant downward trend in pharmacologically treated PONV (β=−0.050; 95% CI −0.093 to −0.0079; P =0.021). Conclusions Established clinical guidelines and expanded insurance coverage of ondansetron were associated with changes in perioperative antiemetic prescribing and a modest decline in pharmacologically treated PONV in Japan. As a retrospective observational study, causality cannot be confirmed, and further studies are needed to assess generalisability.

items.title: Perioperative factors associated with insurance superutilisation after outpatient surgery: a retrospective single-centre cohort study at a quaternary academic centre
items.abstract: Background A small minority of patients called ‘superutilisers' incur many touchpoints with the healthcare system, leading to a high cost burden. Although superutilisation has been studied in inpatient cohorts, data are limited for surgical populations. This study aimed to evaluate patient and perioperative factors associated with superutilisation after outpatient surgery. Methods This single quaternary academic US-centre retrospective cohort study included adult outpatient surgical cases for patients who did not meet the superutiliser criteria in the 6 months preoperatively. The primary outcome, superutilisation, was defined as having ≥2 emergency department (ED) visits or inpatient encounters, or a combination of the two, in the 6 months after surgery. Classification and regression tree (CART) modelling and multivariable logistic regression were used to evaluate predictors of postoperative superutilisation, adjusting for confounders. Results Among the 93 048 cases meeting inclusion criteria between March 2013 and October 2025, 23 120 (24.9%) met the criteria for superutilisation. Postoperative superutilisation was significantly associated with age, payor type, and preoperative comorbidities (all P <0.001) in univariable and multivariable analyses. The CART model demonstrated surgical service, procedure duration, and postoperative care unit recovery time to be significantly associated with postoperative superutilisation. Conclusions Even in an outpatient cohort, nearly a quarter of cases met the criteria for postoperative superutilisation by a combination of inpatient encounters and ED visits, whereas less than 2% met the criteria on ED visits alone. These analyses highlight the need for developing better clinical definitions of superutilisation to identify at-risk patients and enhance preoperative risk stratification.

items.title: Laparoscopic surgery and cerebral oxygen saturation in neonates and infants: a prospective observational study
items.abstract: Background Cerebral oxygenation during anaesthesia and surgery is particularly vulnerable in infants owing to immature autoregulation. This observational study investigated the effect of capnoperitoneum insufflation on cerebral regional oxygen saturation (crSO 2 ) in neonates and infants undergoing laparoscopic surgery. Methods The primary endpoint of this single-centre study was to evaluate whether crSO 2 after capnoperitoneum insufflation is lower (defined as a decrease of at least 8%) than crSO 2 before insufflation. Secondary endpoints included maximum crSO 2 decrease and duration of decreases during anaesthesia phases compared with post-insufflation crSO 2, and clinical predictors of severe desaturation. Results A total of 30 laparoscopic procedures with a median corrected age of 7.3 weeks and a median weight of 4.8 kg were analysed. No clinically relevant crSO 2 decrease was observed after capnoperitoneum insufflation (pre- vs post-insufflation crSO 2 , 72.8% vs 75.1%; Δ 2.3%; 95% confidence interval −1.1 to 5.7; P =0.184). Across the entire procedure, the median maximum decrease from pre-induction crSO 2 was −13.5% (inter-quartile range [IQR] −21.5 to −9.5), with the greatest decreases during surgery (median −10.5%; IQR −16 to −5.5). Overall, patients spent a median of 22.0 min below their pre-induction crSO 2 . Severe crSO 2 decreases (>20% relative decrease from pre-induction crSO 2 ) occurred in 30% of patients. Maximum crSO 2 decrease did not correlate with age, weight, or ASA physical status, but remifentanil use was associated with larger decreases during induction of anaesthesia. Conclusions Capnoperitoneum insufflation does not reduce crSO 2 in neonates and infants. Nonetheless, severe desaturations were observed throughout the entire procedure, supporting further investigation of routine cerebral near-infrared spectroscopy monitoring in high-risk infants.

items.title: Oral midodrine or atomoxetine to prevent hypotension after major noncardiac surgery: a randomised pilot feasibility study
items.abstract: Background Postoperative hypotension occurs frequently, with an uncertain role for oral vasopressor treatment. Methods We conducted a single-centre, blinded, parallel-group, prospectively registered (ACTRN12624000342516) randomised controlled pilot trial comparing placebo three times daily with midodrine 10 mg three times daily or atomoxetine 18 mg daily. Eligible patients were adults who underwent noncardiac surgery under general anaesthesia with a systolic BP of <90 mm Hg for at least 10 min in the PACU. The primary outcome was the mean patient recruitment per week (with a target of ≥4). Secondary outcomes included acceptability, withdrawal of consent, treatment course completion, hypotension, and clinical outcomes. Results Eighty-nine participants (mean age 58 [standard deviation (sd) 18]; 44 [49%] female) were recruited over 32 weeks (mean 2.8 [95% confidence interval >2.3] per week). The proportions of patients completing the intended doses were 84% (placebo), 83% (midodrine), and 100% (atomoxetine). Small numbers of participants declined to continue (3% placebo, 3% midodrine, and 0% atomoxetine). The mean (sd) acceptability of intervention measure score was 16 (3) for placebo, 15 (3) for midodrine, and 17 (3) for atomoxetine. Hypotension within 24 h of discharge from the PACU was observed with placebo in 6 (19%), midodrine in 11 (38%), and atomoxetine in 6 (21%). Conclusions Although the average weekly recruitment rate was lower than the target, most patients completed the treatment course, making a large-scale trial feasible with substantial adjustments. This pilot study suggested further evaluation of atomoxetine rather than midodrine to prevent postoperative hypotension.

items.title: Inflammatory proteins and postoperative complications after major surgery: a bidirectional two-sample Mendelian randomisation study
items.abstract: Background Observational studies have reported an association between inflammatory biomarkers and postoperative complications but it is unclear whether these associations are causal. It is also unknown whether postoperative outcomes share a causal architecture with chronic, all-cause disease. Methods We performed bidirectional two-sample Mendelian randomisation to investigate potential causal effects of chronic exposure to genetically proxied concentrations of 19 inflammatory proteins (and pathway signalling) on postoperative acute kidney injury, atrial fibrillation, delirium, myocardial infarction, stroke, and surgical-site infection and their all-cause equivalents. Genetic instruments for inflammatory markers were sourced from previous genome-wide association studies of European participants with outcome data derived from UK Biobank. Results The primary postoperative analysis showed a protective effect of downregulated interleukin-6 (IL-6) signalling on stroke risk (odds ratio 0.26; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.1–0.68; P =0.006). However, this was not replicated in the all-cause analysis (odds ratio 1.14; 95% CI 0.75–1.24; P =0.78), whereas a robust protective effect was seen for downregulated IL-6 with atrial fibrillation ( P <0.009). In postoperative and all-cause analyses, genome-wide variants for C-reactive protein (CRP) showed a protective effect on delirium that was not present in cis-restricted analyses. Conclusions We found evidence supporting a potential causal role for IL-6 signalling in perioperative stroke. However, the divergence in IL-6 effects between postoperative and all-cause outcomes suggests that the inflammatory architecture of acute postoperative complications may differ from chronic disease states. Furthermore, our findings suggest that previously reported associations between CRP and delirium likely represent horizontal pleiotropy or residual bias rather than direct causation. Future work should interrogate local tissue responses and the immediate perioperative period.

items.title: Implementation of the Anaesthesia-CERTification (A-CERT) perioperative certification framework in Swiss hospitals: a descriptive implementation study
items.abstract: Background The Swiss Anaesthesia CERTification programme (A-CERT), was developed by the Swiss Society for Anaesthesiology and Perioperative Medicine (SSAPM) as part of its national quality strategy. This study describes the development, organisation, and initial implementation of the A-CERT framework within participating Swiss institutions. Methods This multicentre descriptive implementation study included the first 10 Swiss anaesthesia departments that voluntarily participated in the A-CERT programme. The certification framework comprises a standardised catalogue of 133 criteria structured across perioperative phases and organisational domains. Certification involves iterative self-assessment, document review, and external audit by two independent auditors from the Swiss Association for Quality and Management Systems and SSAPM. Descriptive statistics were used to summarise fulfilment rates and process-related changes. Certification is granted if all mandatory criteria are met and an overall fulfilment rate of 80% is achieved. Results All 10 participating anaesthesia departments completed A-CERT (10/10; 100%). These departments ranged from large academic medical centres to smaller hospitals and office-based institutions. Mean overall criterion fulfilment was 98.6% (262.3/266.0 points; range 258.0–266.0 points), with institutional fulfilment ranging from 97.0% to 100.0%. All participating departments fulfilled all mandatory criteria (10/10; 100%). Three deviations were identified during external audits and were resolved before certification. Structural or procedural changes after certification were documented in eight of 10 institutions (80%), primarily related to documentation, governance, and quality management processes. Conclusions The A-CERT programme is feasible to implement across diverse institutional settings in Switzerland and provides a structured approach to quality assurance in anaesthesia. The observed changes primarily reflect implementation-related processes occurring during the certification pathway, rather than demonstrating programme effectiveness. Further evaluation is required to assess long-term effects and potential associations with clinical outcomes.

items.title: Beyond accreditation: specialty certification, clinical ownership, and quality improvement in anaesthesia care
items.abstract: Specialty-specific department certification promises to bring quality assurance closer to the clinical realities of anaesthesia care, but its value depends on more than documenting compliance. The inaugural evaluation of Anaesthesia Certification (A-CERT), the Swiss Society for Anaesthesiology and Perioperative Medicine's national certification framework, suggests that structured department self-assessment and peer review can identify clinically relevant gaps and stimulate improvement before external audit. Hospital boards reported positive feedback more often than anaesthesia teams, highlighting the risk that certification may gain managerial legitimacy without securing frontline ownership. Therefore, further evaluation of A-CERT should test whether improvements persist, translate into better patient outcomes, and remain meaningful across departments with different resources and organisational cultures.

items.title: Obstetric anaesthesia quality benchmarking and between-unit variation in a regional UK hospital network. The GOAL Process, Outcome and Structure Targets (GOALPOSTs) multicentre audit and feedback programme
items.abstract: Background No UK system allows obstetric anaesthesia units to compare themselves with other centres. We aimed to understand individual unit performance and variation across units in our hospital network. Methods We undertook a multicentre audit and feedback programme in London and South East UK. We selected the Royal College of Anaesthetists' suggested best-practice standards for the percentage of pregnant womenwith general anaesthesia and general anaesthesia conversion for Caesarean birth, labour epidural response within 30 min, accidental dural puncture, and labour epidural replacement. We provided units with monthly reports to benchmark against these standards and against other hospitals' performance. At the end of the programme, we aggregated each unit's data for analysis. The primary outcome was the percentage of units meeting the standards. Secondary outcomes were between-unit variation, assessed using the latent intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC), and units' experience of participation, assessed using an exit questionnaire. Results We report data from 22 units with 156 908 deliveries between 2022 and 2025. Units compliant with individual standards varied from 22 of 22 (100%, 95% confidence interval [CI] 85–100%) for category 1 Caesarean under general anaesthesia to 16 of 21 (76%, 95% CI 53–92%) for accidental dural puncture. All metrics demonstrated between-unit variation (latent ICC 0.06 [95% CI 0.03–0.12] to 0.22 [0.12–0.41], P <0.001); 19 of 20 responding units (95%) expressed interest in future UK national benchmarking but raised concerns about data accuracy and resourcing. Conclusions We found significant variation in real-life practice compared with Royal College of Anaesthetists standards. This may reflect case-mix differences, data quality issues, or true differences in care quality.

items.title: Comparison of the effects of sevoflurane versus propofol anaesthesia on lactate concentrations as a marker of microvascular oxygenation during porcine cardiopulmonary bypass
items.abstract: Background This animal study compared the effects of sevoflurane and propofol anaesthesia on blood lactate kinetics and systemic global tissue microvascular oxygenation in a standardised porcine cardiopulmonary bypass model. We hypothesised that volatile anaesthesia with sevoflurane provides superior systemic metabolic stability and tissue oxygenation balance during cardiopulmonary bypass compared with continuous propofol infusion, despite higher fluid requirements. Methods A total of 36 female pigs (45–55 kg) were randomised to the sevoflurane group ( n =18) or a propofol group ( n =18) between October 2022 and May 2025. During cardiopulmonary bypass, MAP and CO were maintained identically. Analysed parameters included fluid/vasopressor requirements, central venous oxygen saturation (S v o 2 ), lactate kinetics, inflammatory cytokines (tumour necrosis factor-α [TNF-α]), and molecular apoptosis markers in liver and kidney tissue (BAX/BCL-2 and cleaved/pro-caspase-3 ratios normalised to glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate). Results The sevoflurane group required a significantly higher fluid volume to maintain MAP during the cross-clamping phase than the propofol group (median [inter-quartile range]: sevoflurane 3.0 [2.3–3.7] L vs propofol 1.5 [0.9–2.2] L; P =0.006). Despite this, S v o 2 was significantly higher under sevoflurane than under propofol (mean sd: sevoflurane 78.4% [7.4%] vs propofol 71.4% [10.0%]; P =0.038). In the propofol group, lactate concentrations increased significantly during reperfusion compared with the sevoflurane group (mean [sd]: propofol 3.9 [1.8] mM vs sevoflurane 2.8 [1.1] mM; P =0.049). The difference in TNF-α protein between groups did not reach statistical significance (mean [sd]: sevoflurane 154 [112] pg ml −1 vs propofol 532 [254] pg ml −1 ; P =0.062). Molecular apoptosis markers showed no significant differences between groups in either liver tissue (BAX/BCL-2 ratio, P =0.859; cleaved/pro-caspase-3 ratio, P =0.931) or kidney tissue (BAX/BCL-2 ratio, P =0.298; cleaved/pro-caspase-3 ratio, P =0.613). Conclusions In this porcine cardiopulmonary bypass model, sevoflurane (1.0–1.5 vol%) may provide superior metabolic stability during cardiopulmonary bypass compared with propofol (8–12 mg kg −1 h −1 ), as reflected by higher S v o 2 and lower lactate accumulation, despite higher fluid requirements.

items.title: Methadone for enhanced postoperative analgesia in intermediate-risk noncardiac surgery: protocol for a multicentre randomised trial (the MELODY trial)
items.abstract: Background Acute postoperative pain remains inadequately controlled in many surgical patients and may impair recovery despite contemporary multimodal analgesia. Conventional intraoperative analgesic strategies commonly rely on short-acting opioids, requiring repeated administration to maintain analgesia. Methadone provides prolonged analgesic exposure after a single dose and may reduce postoperative pain and additional opioid requirements. However, previous randomised trials have generally been small and predominantly single-centre and focused on pain intensity and opioid consumption. Whether the sustained analgesic profile of methadone translates into improved multidimensional patient-centred recovery remains uncertain. Methods The MELODY trial is a multicentre, patient-blinded, randomised, parallel-group superiority trial enrolling 400 adults undergoing elective intermediate-risk minimally invasive urological, gynaecological, or abdominal surgery at three University of California hospitals. Patients will be randomised 1:1 to receive either i.v. methadone (0.25 mg kg −1 ideal body weight) at induction of anaesthesia or conventional intraoperative short-acting opioid administration with fentanyl, hydromorphone, or both. All patients will receive a standardised multimodal perioperative analgesic regimen. The primary outcome is quality of recovery on postoperative day 1, assessed using the 15-item Quality of Recovery (QoR-15) questionnaire. Secondary outcomes include QoR-15 on postoperative day 2, postoperative opioid consumption, pain scores, opioid-related adverse events, and health-related quality of life at 30 days. Conclusions The MELODY trial will determine whether a single intraoperative dose of methadone improves early patient-centred recovery compared with conventional short-acting opioid-based anaesthesia. By evaluating multidimensional recovery rather than analgesia or opioid consumption alone, this trial aims to clarify the clinical value of intraoperative methadone in contemporary perioperative care. Clinical trial registration NCT07565870. Protocol version Version 1.0.

items.title: Defining high-impact chronic postsurgical pain in adolescents undergoing spine or pectus surgery: a comparison of operational definitions
Intraoperative Diastolic Blood Pressure Variability and Myocardial Injury in Acute Ischemic Stroke after Endovascular Treatment: A Retrospective Cohort Study
items.abstract: Background: The association between intraoperative blood pressure variability and postoperative myocardial injury (PMI) after endovascular therapy (EVT) for acute ischemic stroke (AIS) is unknown. Methods: This retrospective cohort study enrolled AIS patients who underwent EVT between June 28th, 2016, and January 11th, 2021. PMI was assessed using cardiac troponin I measurement. Intraoperative diastolic blood pressure (DBP) variability was assessed using the coefficient of variation (CV). A population-level CV threshold was derived from the inflection point of the logistic regression curve. The primary outcome was PMI during hospitalization. To establish the association between DBP variability and PMI, multivariable logistic regression was used to adjust for possible confounders. Results: During the study period, 469 AIS patients were included. The median age was 63 years, and 142 (30.3%) were women. A total of 84 (17.9%) patients experienced PMI. An intraoperative diastolic CV of 16% was estimated as the threshold. After adjusting for confounders, with every 1% increase in diastolic CV above 16%, there was a 17% increase in the odds of experiencing PMI ( OR =1.17; 95% CI: 1.09-1.27; P ≤0.001). Conclusions: DBP variability is associated with PMI in AIS patients undergoing EVT. Future randomized clinical trials should evaluate whether stabilizing diastolic perfusion pressure reduces the incidence of PMI.

items.title: Comparing Heart Rate Variability Upon Admission to Intensive Care Unit Between Moderate-Severe Traumatic Brain Injury and Orthopedic Controls: A Prospective Observational Study
items.abstract: Background: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is associated with autonomic dysfunction measurable through heart rate variability (HRV). Although reduced HRV during prolonged monitoring has been associated with poor outcomes following TBI, comparisons with other forms of traumatic injury remain limited. Methods: We conducted an exploratory prospective cohort study of adults with moderate-severe TBI (msTBI) and isolated severe orthopedic trauma controls enrolled at a single institution from 2020 to 2024. Continuous cardiac telemetry was collected during the first 15 minutes of intensive care unit (ICU) admission. HRV metrics included standard deviation of normal-to-normal intervals (SDNN), root-mean square of successive differences (RMSSD), percentage of successive normal-to-normal intervals differing by >50 ms (pNN50), and low-frequency to high-frequency power ratio (LF/HF). Clinical outcomes including pneumonia, sepsis, infection, acute respiratory distress syndrome, and acute kidney injury were assessed during the first week of hospitalization. Results: Among 94 patients (51 msTBI; 43 orthopedic controls), time-domain HRV measures were significantly reduced in the majority of msTBI patients compared with published normative values. In adjusted analyses, SDNN was similar across groups (mean difference: 27.0, 95% CI: −3.8 to 57.9, P =0.086). RMSSD, pNN50, and LF/HF were also similar. Within the msTBI cohort, HRV metrics were not associated with first-week clinical outcomes or hospital mortality. Conclusions: In this exploratory study, early HRV abnormalities following trauma may reflect autonomic impairment, but measurements immediately upon ICU admission may not capture evolving msTBI-specific dysfunction. Larger longitudinal studies are needed to draw definitive conclusions regarding clinically meaningful autonomic changes and associations with msTBI outcomes.

items.title: Bilateral Pterygopalatine Fossa Blockade as an Adjunct to Scalp Nerve Blockade for Awake Craniotomy
Right- versus left-sided double-lumen tubes and hypoxemia during anesthesia in patients undergoing unilateral surgery for left-sided lung tumors
items.abstract: Purpose Right-sided double-lumen endobronchial tubes (DLTs) are often avoided because of technical difficulties and concerns about respiratory complications, although evidence that they increase hypoxemia during anesthesia remains limited and inconsistent. We evaluated the association between DLT side and hypoxemia during anesthesia in patients undergoing unilateral surgery for left-sided lung tumors. Methods This single-center retrospective cohort study included adult patients undergoing unilateral surgery for left-sided lung tumors between October 2008 and May 2023. The primary outcome was hypoxemia during anesthesia, defined as SpO 2 ≤ 90% for at least 3 consecutive min during the anesthetic period. Propensity score overlap weighting was used to adjust for measured differences between patients receiving right-sided and left-sided DLTs. Odds ratios (ORs) and absolute risk differences (RDs) were estimated. Results Among 1,280 patients, 842 received right-sided DLTs and 438 received left-sided DLTs. After overlap weighting, measured covariates were well balanced. The incidence of hypoxemia during anesthesia was 20.0% with right-sided DLTs and 18.5% with left-sided DLTs (OR, 1.10; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.68-1.79; P = 0.70). The RD was 1.51 percentage points (95% CI - 3.86-6.87). No clear between-group differences were observed in exploratory secondary respiratory outcomes. Conclusion We found no clear evidence that right-sided DLT use was associated with a higher incidence of hypoxemia during anesthesia than left-sided DLT use. However, equivalence between the two devices was not established, and further studies are needed to determine whether clinically important differences in hypoxemia risk exist.

items.title: Comment on "sugammadex versus no pharmacological reversal under quantitative neuromuscular monitoring: a propensity score-matched analysis of postoperative pulmonary complications" by Narasaki et al

Comment on “Postoperative pulmonary complications of desflurane-versus sevoflurane-based general anesthesia in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease or asthma undergoing gastrointestinal cancer surgery: a nationwide retrospective cohort study.” by Makito et al.
Comparison of gasping breaths induced by three commonly used volatile anesthetics in mice
items.abstract: Background Previous studies showed that administration of inhaled 2-MAC sevoflurane induces gasping in mice by activating a persistent sodium current in the brainstem, an effect blocked by riluzole. However, whether other commonly used volatile anesthetics elicit a similar gasping response in mice has not previously been investigated. This study compared respiratory responses to high doses of three volatile anesthetics. Methods Seven spontaneously breathing adult mice each inhaled one of three anesthetics (sevoflurane, isoflurane, and desflurane) on separate days, and eventually inhaled all three anesthetics. Each anesthetic concentration was increased from 1 MAC to inhaled 2-MAC, while breathing patterns and suprahyoid muscle electromyographic activity (EMG SH ) were measured. The effects of riluzole (18 mg/kg, i.p.) on gasping were also tested in five additional mice anesthetized with desflurane and/or isoflurane. Results All three inhaled anesthetics altered the respiratory pattern from eupnea in 1 MAC to gasping in inhaled 2-MAC in seven mice. However, the time course of ventilation and EMG SH responses to volatile anesthetics at inhaled 2-MAC differed significantly among the three agents: desflurane had the strongest inhibitory effect on inspiratory and EMG SH activities, isoflurane had the weakest inhibitory effects and promoted stable gasping, and sevoflurane showed an intermediate effect. In addition, riluzole administration eliminated isoflurane- and desflurane-induced gasping in five mice. Conclusion All three anesthetics produced a similar gasping response at inhaled 2-MAC; however, the response's time course and the mechanism by which stable gasping was maintained depend heavily on the volatile anesthetic used.

items.title: Perioperative factors associated with postoperative continuation of mechanical ventilation after initial burn surgery: a retrospective cohort study
items.abstract: Purpose Early surgical intervention, including debridement and grafting, is crucial in acute burn injury management. Although early extubation in operating rooms (ORs) reduces intensive care unit length of stay and ventilator-associated complications, extubation feasibility following initial burn surgery remains uncertain. We investigated perioperative factors associated with postoperative continuation of mechanical ventilation (MV) after initial burn surgery. Methods This retrospective study analyzed patients with burns who underwent acute-phase debridement between 2018 and 2024. Patients requiring postoperative MV were compared with those extubated in ORs. Factors independently associated with postoperative MV were identified using multivariate logistic regression analysis. Results Among 418 patients, 75 required postoperative MV. Age (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] = 1.03, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.00-1.06), percentage of total body surface area (%TBSA) burned (aOR = 1.08, 95% CI 1.03-1.12), preoperative intubation (aOR = 11.8, 95% CI 3.02-46.4), intraoperative fluid administration volume (ml/kg) (aOR = 1.04, 95% CI 1.01-1.06), and intraoperative maximum vasoactive-inotropic score (VIS) (aOR = 1.18, 95% CI 1.10-1.26) were independently associated with postoperative MV continuation. This association between the intraoperative maximum VIS and postoperative MV continuation was maintained in the sensitivity analysis excluding preoperatively intubated patients (aOR = 1.16, 95% CI 1.08-1.25). Conclusion Age, %TBSA burned, preoperative intubation, intraoperative fluid administration volume, and maximum intraoperative VIS were independently associated with postoperative continuation of MV after initial burn surgery. Maximum intraoperative VIS may provide additional information regarding the hemodynamic component of perioperative severity by quantifying the intensity of vasoactive and inotropic support required during surgery.

items.title: Intraoperative bedside lung-ultrasound use to optimize positive end-expiratory pressure for elective robotic-assisted radical prostatectomy or cystectomy: a randomized clinical trial
items.abstract: Purpose This study evaluated efficacy and safety of intraoperative individualized stepwise positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) titration guided by lung ultrasound (LUS) in reducing pulmonary atelectasis and complications in patients undergoing robotic-assisted radical prostatectomy or cystectomy (RARPC). Methods This randomized trial included 88 patients undergoing elective RARPC. Patients were assigned to either standard ventilation (PEEP 4 cmH₂O; group C) or LUS-guided stepwise PEEP titration up to 12 cmH₂O (group R). Patients, outcome assessors, and the data analyst were blinded. The primary outcome was analyzed using a linear mixed-effects model, estimating the between-group difference in LUS score at 2 h after surgery. Results Group R showed significantly lower total LUS scores at 2 h after surgery (adjusted difference: -1.68, 95%CI: -2.89 to -0.47; p = 0.007) compared to group C. Likewise, significantly lower LUS scores were observed in Group R from the end of surgery onward. PEEP titration progressively reduced post-pneumoperitoneum atelectasis rates from 50% to 9.1%, at a highest PEEP level of 12 cmH₂O. Dynamic lung compliance in group R was significantly greater at Top compared with the control group (58.93 ± 3.48 vs. 49.91 ± 5.74 mL/cmH₂O; p Conclusion Intraoperative LUS-guided individualized PEEP optimization significantly reduced the incidence of postoperative atelectasis and improved dynamic lung compliance without compromising hemodynamic stability in patients undergoing RARPC. Lung ultrasound offers a practical, effective, and non-invasive bedside tool for optimizing ventilation in high-risk surgical settings. Trial registration and protocol This study was registered in ClinicalTrials.gov in March 2024 (ID: NCT06307704). The trial protocol is available through the ClinicalTrials.gov registry at https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06307704 .
