Fresh frozen plasma administration during cardiopulmonary bypass was not associated with postoperative transfusion requirements after elective total aortic arch replacement: a retrospective cohort study
items.abstract: Purpose Cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) during total aortic arch replacement (TAR) is associated with coagulopathy. We investigated whether fresh frozen plasma (FFP) administration during CPB was associated with postoperative transfusion requirements and coagulation profiles after TAR. Methods This single-center retrospective cohort study included adult patients who underwent elective TAR. Patients were categorized according to whether FFP was administered during CPB. The primary outcome was postoperative FFP transfusion from CPB separation to 12 h after intensive care unit admission. Secondary outcomes included perioperative plasma-derived product use, postoperative bleeding, re-exploration for bleeding, and serial coagulation parameters. Multivariable regression analyses were performed to adjust for potential confounders. Results Data from 156 patients were analyzed, including 111 patients in the Pre-FFP group and 45 in the Control group. Baseline characteristics were generally comparable, although deep hypothermic circulatory arrest duration and CPB fluid management differed between the groups. The adjusted mean difference in total post-CPB FFP transfusion units between the Pre-FFP and Control groups was - 1.54 units (95% confidence interval, - 7.51 to 4.43). No significant differences were observed in perioperative plasma-derived product use or bleeding outcomes. Although fibrinogen concentrations were higher and activated partial thromboplastin time and prothrombin time-international normalized ratio were shorter at the end of CPB in the Pre-FFP group, these differences largely resolved after CPB. Conclusion FFP administration during CPB was associated with transient improvement in coagulation parameters but was not associated with postoperative transfusion requirements or bleeding outcomes in adult patients undergoing elective TAR. Larger studies are needed to confirm these findings.

items.title: Clinical implementation of official ASA physical status examples: a questionnaire survey and multifaceted educational pre-post intervention study
items.abstract: Purpose The American Society of Anesthesiologists Physical Status (ASA-PS) classification is widely used, but subjective interpretations cause evaluation variability. Although specific clinical examples were added in 2014 and 2020 to reduce ambiguity, their clinical adoption remains unclear. We evaluated awareness of these examples and whether a multifaceted educational intervention was associated with scoring consistency. Methods This two-phase study evaluated ASA-PS scoring consistency. In Study 1, 45 anesthesiologists at two institutions evaluated 20 simulated adult, pediatric, and obstetric cases to assess understanding of official ASA-PS examples. In Study 2, a pre- and post-intervention study in clinical practice included 414 cases. The intervention included survey feedback, re-dissemination of official examples, and implementation of a reference system in the electronic medical record. The primary outcome was the exact agreement rate between clinician-assigned and consensus scores based on official examples. Results In Study 1, the overall correct rate with the official reference classifications was 47.6% (Cohen's kappa = 0.321). Correct rate was particularly low in pediatric cases (kappa = 0.243). Highly experienced anesthesiologists demonstrated lower correct rates and a tendency toward underestimation. In Study 2, the exact agreement rate increased from 73.5% before the intervention to 82.4% (OR 1.68, 95% CI 1.01-2.78) after the intervention. Cohen's kappa improved from 0.553 to 0.712, and underestimation decreased from 21.1% - 14.8%. Conclusion Publishing clinical examples alone may be insufficient to standardize ASA-PS classification. A multifaceted intervention incorporating educational feedback and an electronic reference system was associated with improved scoring consistency.

items.title: Palmitoylethanolamide versus ibuprofen for acute postoperative pain after extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy: a randomized trial
items.abstract: Purpose Palmitoylethanolamide (PEA), an endogenous lipid mediator, exhibits anti-inflammatory and analgesic properties, its efficacy as a stand-alone treatment for acute postoperative pain remains uncertain. This study compared oral micronized PEA with ibuprofen in managing pain following extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy (ESWL). Methods In this prospective, randomized, double-blind investigation, 120 patients classified as ASA I-II undergoing elective ESWL were evaluated. They were randomly divided to take either 600 mg of oral micronized PEA or 600 mg of ibuprofen two hours prior to the procedure, continuing every 12 h for 72 h. The primary endpoint was postoperative pain intensity quantified by visual analogue scale (VAS) 2 h post-ESWL. Secondary endpoints included VAS scores at predefined intervals, rescue analgesia, adverse events, and patient satisfaction. Results VAS scores were comparable between groups during the early postoperative period, including at 2 h (PEA: 1 [0-2] vs. ibuprofen: 1 [0-2], P = 0.091). However, pain was significantly higher with PEA at 12 h, 24 h, and 48 h (P Conclusion In this active-comparator trial, oral micronized PEA was inferior to ibuprofen at 12-48 h after ESWL, with more rescue analgesia, but early pain scores were similar. The analgesic effect of PEA itself cannot be established. Fewer gastrointestinal adverse events warrant further study.

items.title: Remimazolam for intraoperative evoked potential monitoring: a scoping review
items.abstract: Remimazolam is an ultra-short-acting benzodiazepine increasingly used for general anesthesia, but its effects on intraoperative evoked potential monitoring remain incompletely defined. This scoping review mapped the available clinical evidence on remimazolam-based anesthesia for intraoperative evoked potential monitoring. PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, Scopus, Web of Science, and ProQuest were searched for studies reporting remimazolam use in surgical patients undergoing evoked potential monitoring. Seventeen studies were included, comprising randomized controlled trials, a dose-escalation study, an observational comparative study, a retrospective cohort study, case series, and case reports. Reported modalities included motor evoked potentials, somatosensory evoked potentials, and visual evoked potentials; no eligible study reported brainstem auditory evoked potentials. Overall, intraoperative evoked potential signals were successfully recorded under remimazolam-based anesthesia, with reproducible waveforms reported across modalities. Some comparative studies reported amplitudes or latencies comparable to, or more favorable than, those observed with propofol-based anesthesia. However, findings were inconsistent and limited by small sample sizes, heterogeneous designs, variable dosing regimens, concomitant anesthetic use, and limited data on intraoperative movement, warning criteria, and diagnostic performance. Current evidence indicates that intraoperative evoked potential signals can be obtained under remimazolam-based anesthesia. However, the available evidence remains insufficient to establish the feasibility and reliability of remimazolam for intraoperative evoked potential monitoring, determine optimal dosing or monitoring-specific warning criteria, or demonstrate superiority over established anesthetic regimens.

items.title: Direct visualization of nailfold capillary blood flow during capillary refill time assessment
Comment on “Effect of granisetron on the spinal anesthesia-induced hemodynamic changes: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials” by Koo et al
Acknowledgment to reviewers
Weight- and age-dependent bias in remimazolam pharmacokinetic–pharmacodynamic models during bispectral index-guided anesthesia: a retrospective analysis
items.abstract: Background: The Schüttler pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic (PKPD) model for remimazolam was derived from healthy male volunteers (20-38 years; 64-99 kg). This study examined how body weight and age modify the relationship between effect-site concentration (Ce) and bispectral index (BIS) in Korean surgical patients. Methods: This retrospective study analyzed Schüttler-predicted remimazolam Ce and observed BIS from 52 adult patients under remimazolam-remifentanil total intravenous anesthesia. A linear mixed-effects model examined demographic modifiers of the Ce-BIS relationship, including Ce × weight and Ce × age interaction terms. Patients were stratified by body weight (< 60 vs. ≥ 60 kg) and age (< 40 vs. ≥ 40 years), reflecting the Schüttler development cohort boundaries. Prediction accuracy was assessed using median performance error (MDPE), and compared with the Masui, Zhou, and Eleveld models. Results: Body weight significantly modified the Ce-BIS relationship (Ce × weight interaction, P = 0.029), with lower body weight and older age each independently associated with lower observed BIS than model-predicted values. In patients weighing < 60 kg and aged ≥ 40 years, the Schüttler model showed greater negative bias (MDPE: -20.4%) than the Masui and Zhou models (MDPE: -17.5% and -18.9%, respectively), whereas the Eleveld model exhibited a qualitatively distinct, age-driven bidirectional bias pattern. Conclusions: Body weight and age significantly modify the Ce-BIS relationship in remimazolam-based anesthesia, with negative bias observed across all four PKPD models in low-body-weight older patients. These findings warrant prospective validation in larger and more diverse cohorts and remimazolam PKPD model refinement that adequately incorporates body size and age.

items.title: Association between serial perioperative oxygen reserve index measurements and postoperative pulmonary complications in patients at increased pulmonary risk undergoing non-thoracic surgery
items.abstract: Background: We examined whether the previously observed association between preoxygenation (preoxy) oxygen reserve index (ORi) and postoperative pulmonary complications (PPCs) could be reproduced in an independent non-thoracic surgical cohort and whether later intraoperative ORi measurements provided additional information. Methods: We prospectively studied 155 patients aged ≥ 51 years undergoing elective non-thoracic surgery. ORi was measured at 1, 2, and 3 min of preoxy and at four intraoperative time points. The primary outcome was at least one PPC by postoperative day 30. Logistic regression and receiver operating characteristic analysis assessed associations and discrimination, respectively. Results: PPCs occurred in 57 patients (37%). ORi was lower at 2 and 3 min of preoxy in patients who developed PPCs, with no significant intraoperative differences. After adjustment for Assess Respiratory Risk in Surgical Patients in Catalonia (ARISCAT) score and other clinical covariates, 3-min ORi was inversely associated with PPCs (odds ratio, 0.06; 95%CI, 0.01-0.28; P < 0.001). The within-patient ORi-arterial partial pressure of oxygen correlation was 0.38 (95% CI, 0.27-0.47; P < 0.001). Area under the curve (AUCs) were 0.645 for ORi, 0.711 for ARISCAT, and 0.760 for the combined model. Adding ORi improved model fit (χ² = 10.82, P = 0.001), with ΔAUC 0.049 (95% bootstrap CI, -0.002 to 0.100). Conclusions: Preoxy ORi, particularly at 3 min, was associated with PPCs. Although adding ORi to ARISCAT improved model fit, the gain in discrimination was modest and imprecisely estimated, supporting ORi as a complementary physiological marker rather than an alternative to established risk assessment.

items.title: Decompensation of occult diaphragmatic vulnerability following transient hemidiaphragmatic paresis: a case of prolonged hypoxemia
Recurrent delayed emergence after propofol-based anesthesia with suspected pharmacogenetic contribution: a case report
items.abstract: Background: Delayed emergence after general anesthesia is multifactorial, prolongs recovery, and mandates urgent evaluation. When common causes are excluded, pharmacogenetic variability may be considered. Case: A 49-year-old female underwent breast-conserving surgery (70 min) under propofol-remifentanil total intravenous anesthesia (TIVA). Despite stable ventilation, hemodynamics, and the absence of metabolic derangement or acute structural brain lesions, she remained unarousable for about 8 h. Notably, she had previously experienced a nearly identical episode after propofol-remifentanil TIVA. Targeted pharmacogenetic testing identified heterozygous variants in CYP2B6 (c.516G>T, c.785A>G) and a heterozygous UGT1A9 I399-related intronic variant (c.855+399T>C). Conclusions: This case highlights recurrent, profound delayed emergence after propofol-based anesthesia. The identified variants likely exert only modest individual functional effects, and the clinical phenotype is best explained by a multifactorial interaction involving both pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic factors. Direct pharmacokinetic measurements and expanded pharmacogenetic testing may help clarify the underlying mechanism in similar cases.

items.title: A practical guide to oropharyngeal leak pressure for supraglottic airway devices
items.abstract: Supraglottic airway devices (SGAs) are routinely used for airway maintenance and are considered key rescue devices in difficult airway algorithms when tracheal intubation fails. The oropharyngeal leak pressure (OPLP) is the most practical bedside surrogate for assessing SGA sealing performance, as it approximates the upper limit of airway pressure during positive-pressure ventilation. In this narrative review, we summarize how OPLP should be interpreted and used in practice. We define OPLP, explain the clinical meaning of low and high OPLP for ventilation adequacy and gastric insufflation, present practical approaches to OPLP measurement, present sources of interstudy variability, and describe common pitfalls related to malpositioning and protocol differences. We summarize the comparative evidence for widely used SGAs, including the i-gel family, LMA Supreme, LMA ProSeal, Baska Mask, Air-Q, and Ambu AuraGain, and highlight scenarios in which device-level differences may become clinically important upon increased airway pressure (e.g., obesity, pneumoperitoneum, Trendelenburg positioning, or reduced lung compliance). We also review patient-, procedure-, and operator-related factors that modify the OPLP and propose a practical approach for troubleshooting borderline ventilation, including repositioning, adjusting cuff pressure, upsizing or switching devices, and escalating to tracheal intubation. Finally, we outline the priorities for standardized reporting and future directions for developing individualized airway strategies that integrate bedside seal metrics with patient-specific assessments.

items.title: Hypotension Prediction Index-guided care in the HYT trial: hemodynamics through slicer and dicer
More than a fluid: reframing the role of albumin in sepsis
Effect of fascial plane blocks providing postoperative analgesia on mechanical ventilation duration in the ıntensive care unit and early oxygenation after cardiac surgery
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: The primary objective of this study was to examine whether a combined pecto-intercostal fascial plane block (PIFB) and serratus anterior plane block (SAPB) influences the duration of mechanical ventilation in patients who underwent open cardiac surgery via median sternotomy with cardiopulmonary bypass. Secondary objectives included evaluating the effects of this analgesic approach on early postoperative oxygenation parameters, pain intensity scores, and overall opioid consumption. METHODS: This retrospective observational study enrolled 206 adult patients who underwent open cardiac surgery through median sternotomy between January and July 2025. Participants were allocated into two groups based on the postoperative analgesic strategy employed: the Block group (G1, N.=107), which received combined PIFB and SAPB, and the Control group (G0, N.=99), which was managed with conventional multimodal analgesia. To minimize selection bias, inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) was applied using seven clinical covariates. Mechanical ventilation duration was analyzed using Kaplan-Meier survival curves, Cox proportional hazards regression, and the restricted mean survival time (RMST) method. RESULTS: Patients in the Block group demonstrated a significantly shorter median duration of mechanical ventilation compared to controls (300 vs. 420 min; RMST difference: -65.8 min; 95% CI: -94.2 to -41.6; P<0.001). The incidence of prolonged intubation, defined as mechanical ventilation exceeding 480 minutes, was markedly lower in the Block group (G1=6.5% vs. G0=20.2%; Firth OR: 0.29; 95% CI: 0.11-0.75; P=0.011). Postoperative pain scores were significantly reduced across all assessment time points in the Block group (Benjamini-Hochberg corrected q<0.001), and total opioid requirements declined by approximately 28% (IRR: 0.719; P<0.001). No statistically significant between-group differences were detected with respect to the PaO2/FiO2 ratio or the length of intensive care unit stay. CONCLUSİONS: The combined application of PIFB and SAPB was associated with a shorter duration of mechanical ventilation and lower opioid consumption following cardiac surgery. Incorporating fascial plane blocks into multimodal analgesia protocols may confer meaningful clinical benefits, particularly in patients considered to be at elevated perioperative risk.

items.title: Volatile-free total intravenous anesthesia for elective circumcision in two school-age survivors of Crisponi/cold-induced sweating syndrome type 1
Successful use of ultrasound-guided quadroiliac plane block for postoperative analgesia in a child undergoing percutaneous nephrolithotomy
Interscalene block versus serratus posterior superior intercostal plane block for analgesia after shoulder arthroscopy: a randomized controlled trial
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: This study aimed to compare the postoperative analgesic efficacy of Interscalene brachial plexus block (ISB), serratus posterior superior intercostal plane block (SPSIPB), and multimodal systemic analgesia in patients undergoing shoulder arthroscopy. METHODS: In this prospective, randomized, assessor-blinded trial, 90 patients scheduled for elective shoulder arthroscopy were allocated to three groups: ISB, SPSIPB, or control (multimodal analgesia without regional block). Ultrasound-guided blocks were performed using 30 mL of 0.25% bupivacaine. Postoperative pain intensity at rest and during movement was assessed using a visual analog scale at predefined time points within 24 hours. Total opioid consumption, rescue analgesia requirements, hemodynamic parameters, postoperative nausea and vomiting, and patient satisfaction were recorded. RESULTS: Early postoperative pain scores were significantly lower in the ISB group compared with both the SPSIPB and control groups (P<0.001). SPSIPB also provided better analgesia than multimodal analgesia alone during the early postoperative period. Total 24-hour postoperative tramadol consumption was lowest in the ISB group (median 140 mg), followed by the SPSIPB group (230 mg) and the control group (290 mg) (P<0.001). Pain trajectories differed significantly among groups over time (group × time interaction, P<0.001). Patient satisfaction was higher in both regional anesthesia groups compared with the control group (P<0.001). Block-related complications were observed exclusively in the ISB group, where three patients (10%) developed Horner syndrome, which resolved spontaneously during follow-up. CONCLUSIONS: ISB provided superior early postoperative analgesia and the greatest opioid-sparing effect following shoulder arthroscopy. SPSIPB offered clinically meaningful analgesic benefit compared with multimodal systemic analgesia alone and demonstrated a more stable postoperative pain profile over time. SPSIPB may represent a reasonable alternative when ISB is contraindicated or undesirable.

items.title: Preventive postoperative delirium management in geriatric patients. A prospective real-world pre-post implementation study
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Postoperative delirium (POD) is a common and serious complication in older patients, associated with an increased risk of morbidity, mortality, and longer hospital stays. This study aims to determine the feasibility and effectiveness of the implementation of evidence-based POD screening and preventive measures in large university hospitals. METHODS: This study is a prospective, real-world, pre-post implementation study (ethics EA1/054/20; NCT04355195). Patients ≥70 years undergoing surgery requiring anesthesia were eligible. The study was divided into standard care and intervention periods with daily screening up to day 5 after surgery and daily structured evidence-based POD prevention measures. The primary outcome was intervention implementation (≥2/day on postoperative days 1-3). RESULTS: Among 5767 patients, the implementation rate of the primary outcome rose from 35% to consistently >80% during intervention periods, and prevention bundle (defined as provision of at least one prevention measure of each domain per day per patient) implementation from 3% to 48%, respectively. Each successive intervention period yielded a 40% relative reduction (OR 0.60; 95% CI: 0.51-0.70; P<0.001) in POD incidence. Among POD cases, 90-day mortality (ΔRMST90 5.92 days; 95% CI: 2.69-8.66) was higher and decrease in postoperative nursing care level more often compared to POD free patients (ORs 2.23; 95% CI: 1.49-3.33; P=0.001). CONCLUSIONS: we demonstrated an improved implementation rate of screening and prevention measures. A measurable reduction in the POD incidence has been observed in the study population over the time of intervention. These results reinforce a sustainable implementation of screening and prevention measures in all hospitals caring for geriatric patients.

items.title: Artificial intelligence and enhanced recovery after surgery: from protocol-driven pathways to adaptive perioperative care systems (cognitive ERAS)
items.abstract: Enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS) programs have transformed perioperative care through standardized, evidence-based pathways, improving outcomes across surgical specialties. However, increasing patient complexity and heterogeneity expose important limitations of protocol-driven approaches, which often fail to capture dynamic physiological variability and individualized recovery trajectories. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers a pathway to overcome these constraints by integrating longitudinal perioperative data and generating individualized risk predictions. However, prediction alone is insufficient for clinically meaningful personalization, which requires causal reasoning to estimate which interventions are most likely to improve outcomes for specific patients and at different stages of recovery. In this context, ERAS may evolve toward a data-informed, adaptive care system that integrates prediction, causal inference, and supervised workflow coordination. Emerging agentic AI systems may further extend ERAS beyond passive decision support toward structured care orchestration within defined clinical governance boundaries. This review examines how different AI methodologies, including supervised learning, deep learning, reinforcement learning, natural language processing, generative models, and causal inference, can be aligned with ERAS objectives across the perioperative continuum. We also critically evaluate current evidence and key barriers to implementation. Looking forward, the convergence of AI, digital health technologies, and continuous patient monitoring may enable the emergence of cognitive ERAS, a data-driven perioperative care model that integrates prediction, causal estimation, and continuous learning to deliver personalized and dynamically adaptive recovery pathways.

items.title: Continuous quadroiliac plane block for postoperative analgesia in pediatric pyeloplasty surgery
Intraoperative norepinephrine exposure is associated with reduced hepatic arterial inflow and early graft dysfunction after liver transplantation
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Norepinephrine (NE) is widely used during liver transplantation to maintain systemic perfusion pressure. However, its association with hepatic inflow distribution and early graft function during liver transplantation remains uncertain. METHODS: In this retrospective observational study, 429 liver transplant recipients underwent standardized intraoperative hepatic flow assessment. Patients were classified according to continuous NE infusion at the time of flow measurement. Hepatic arterial and portal venous flows were measured using transit-time Doppler. Indexed hepatic arterial flow (mL/min/100 g) was the primary endpoint. Linear regression models, multivariable adjustment, propensity score methods, inverse probability weighting, and matching were applied to reduce confounding. RESULTS: After propensity score matching, 88 well-balanced pairs were analyzed. NE exposure was associated with lower hepatic arterial flow both in absolute terms and when indexed to graft weight. Across all analytical approaches, NE exposure remained associated with approximately 25% lower indexed hepatic arterial Flow. Portal flow and total hepatic flow were similar between groups. Macro-hemodynamic parameters at the end of surgery were comparable between groups. NE exposure was also associated with markers of impaired early graft function according to MEAF and Toronto classifications. No independent association with death or re-transplantation within 4 weeks was observed. CONCLUSIONS: Intraoperative norepinephrine exposure during liver transplantation was consistently associated with lower hepatic arterial inflow and impaired early graft function across multiple analytical approaches. However, causality cannot be inferred from this observational design, and norepinephrine exposure may also reflect greater intraoperative hemodynamic stress and graft-related instability.

items.title: Effect of cardiac-index guided intraoperative haemodynamic therapy on postoperative outcome in non-cardiac surgery patients – a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.abstract: Background Optimal perioperative haemodynamic management is essential to reduce postoperative complications. While multiple technologies allow for advanced monitoring, clear evidence on the effectiveness of Cardiac Index-guided goal-directed therapy (CI-GDT) compared to standard care in non-cardiac surgery is lacking. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to investigate the impact of CI-GDT on postoperative outcome. Methods A systematic search using PubMed and Web of Science (2010–2025) identified randomised controlled trials (RCT) comparing CI-GDT to standard care in adult non-cardiac surgery. Study selection and data extraction were conducted according to PRISMA guidelines and registered under PROSPERO (CRD420251058399). Odds ratios (OR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) and 95% prediction intervals (PI) were calculated using a random-effects model. Risk of bias was assessed via the RoB 2 tool. Heterogeneity was quantified with I 2 , τ 2 , and Cochran’s Q. Reporting bias was evaluated by funnel plots, Egger’s test, and trim-and-fill method. Sensitivity was assessed by leave-one-out analysis. Results Twenty-one RCTs were included, of which 20 contributed data to the meta-analysis of postoperative complications. CI-GDT significantly reduced the incidence of postoperative complications (OR .59 [.45–.78]; PI .20–1.74; I 2 = 62.9%). Mortality did not differ significantly between groups (OR 0.77 [.57–1.05]; I 2 = 0%). Funnel plot and Egger’s test indicated no significant publication bias ( p =.15). Leave-one-out analysis confirmed robustness of findings. Trim-and-fill did not suggest missing studies. Certainty of evidence was graded high. Discussion/conclusion CI-GDT was associated with a lower incidence of patients experiencing at least one postoperative complication, whereas mortality did not differ significantly. However, substantial heterogeneity and a prediction interval crossing the null indicate that the benefit may not be consistent across clinical settings. These findings do not establish an independent advantage of CI targeting over other GDT strategies.
items.limitations: This review has several limitations. The included evidence was derived from multiple relatively small trials involving clinically heterogeneous patient populations undergoing a wide range of surgical procedures. The haemodynamic interventions also varied substantially with respect to the predefined CI thresholds, additional target variables, monitoring technologies, and protocol-specified use of fluids, vasopressors, and inotropic drugs. Furthermore, definitions and observation periods for postoperative complications and mortality were not uniform across studies. These sources of clinical and methodological heterogeneity probably contributed to the observed statistical heterogeneity and the wide prediction interval.

items.title: Intraoperative fluid infusion rate during major pulmonary resection within an Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) pathway: a retrospective cohort study
items.abstract: Background Intraoperative fluid management remains a debated component of Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) pathways in thoracic surgery, with current guidelines recommending intraoperative infusion rates of 2–6 mL/kg/h despite limited high-quality evidence. We assessed whether the intraoperative fluid infusion rate was associated with prolonged length of stay (LOS) after major pulmonary resection. Methods We retrospectively reviewed 540 consecutive patients undergoing lobectomy, bi-lobectomy, or segmentectomy within a structured ERAS pathway, stratified by intraoperative infusion rate: G1 <4 mL/kg/h ( n= 76), G2 4–8 mL/kg/h ( n= 328, reference), and G3 >8 mL/kg/h ( n= 136). Multivariable logistic regression was performed to identify risk factors for prolonged LOS (>3 nights), before we conducted a generalised (multinomial) propensity score matching on four covariates (FEV1, blood loss, operating time, open surgical approach), yielding 59 matched triplets (177 patients). Results Prolonged LOS occurred in 206 patients (38.1%) and was independently associated with high intraoperative infusion rate (OR 2.86 [1.70–4.81]; p< 0.001). Propensity score matching confirmed a statistically significant association between prolonged LOS and infusion rate with 62.7% of G3 patients experiencing prolonged LOS compared to 42.4% in G2 and 39.0% in G1 ( p= 0.020). Conclusions Within a structured ERAS programme, high intraoperative fluid infusion rates (>8 mL/kg/h) were independently associated with prolonged length of stay after major pulmonary resection, in both multivariable and propensity-matched analyses. These findings suggest that high fluid infusion rates may be associated with longer hospital stay. Future efforts should prioritise prospective evaluation of individualised fluid strategies.

items.title: Impact of liberalised preoperative water intake and intravenous-to-oral transition on patient experience and system efficiency in thoracic surgery: a before-and-after study
items.abstract: Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) protocols aim to improve perioperative care by enhancing patient experience, workflow efficiency, and cost-effectiveness; however, quantitative evidence for their system-level impact in thoracic surgery remains limited. We evaluated patient-reported experience and system efficiency following implementation of an ERAS-based perioperative hydration/medication protocol. We conducted a single-centre comparative before-and-after study and included consecutive patients undergoing pulmonary resection or thymectomy (January–September 2025). The protocol permitted water intake until 3 h before surgery, reduced routine preoperative intravenous hydration, and replaced routine intravenous medications with oral alternatives when appropriate. Primary outcomes were postimplementation patient-reported measures (fasting-related discomfort, satisfaction, and actual preoperative water intake). Secondary outcomes included nursing time for medication-related tasks, perioperative outcomes, and direct institutional costs. We included 461 patients. Protocol implementation was not associated with increased postoperative complications. Within the postimplementation period, reported preoperative water intake was higher after the educational refinement (55.0% vs. 74.7%; relative risk 1.36). Intake was less frequent in men (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 0.38; P = 0.002) and more frequent among patients scheduled later in operative order (aOR, 1.90; P = 0.044). Discomfort was higher after wedge resection (aOR, 2.13; P = 0.027) and thymectomy (aOR, 2.47; P = 0.011) than after lobectomy, while satisfaction remained high. Transitioning routine medications from IV to oral reduced nursing task time by 71.8% per patient (median, 2.4–8.5 min) and was associated with estimated direct savings of ~ USD 18,700 per 1,000 surgeries. This ERAS-based protocol was associated with high patient-reported satisfaction, improved nursing workflow efficiency, and reduced institutional costs, with no observed safety signal.

items.title: The impact of hypertension on hemodynamic response to prone positioning during spine surgery: a prospective controlled observational study
items.abstract: Prone positioning during spine surgery can cause significant cardiovascular changes, which may be more pronounced and clinically relevant in patients with hypertension. This study aimed to evaluate intraoperative hemodynamic changes during prone positioning and compare these responses between patients with hypertension and those without comorbidities. In this prospective observational study, patients aged 18–75 years scheduled for spine surgery under general anesthesia were divided into two groups: those with controlled hypertension who continued angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB) therapy on the morning of surgery (Group H) and those without comorbidities (Group N). Hemodynamic parameters, including cardiac index (CI), stroke volume index (SVI), systemic vascular resistance index (SVRI), and arterial elastance (Ea), were continuously monitored using the MostCare® system, with measurements recorded at six prespecified time points before and after the transition to the prone position. Seventy patients were analyzed. Significant group-by-time interactions were observed for both CI and SVI ( p < 0.001 and p = 0.002, respectively), with significant reductions over time observed in Group H but not in Group N. SVRI showed significant changes over time in both groups. Ea values also varied significantly over time in both groups, whereas between-group differences were significant only at certain measurement points. In this study, patients with hypertension receiving continued ARB therapy exhibited different hemodynamic responses to prone positioning compared with patients without comorbidities, particularly in CI and SVI. These findings suggest that careful hemodynamic assessment during prone positioning may be relevant in this patient population. ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT06649487. Registered on October 17, 2024.

items.title: Healthcare professionals' experiences of an intensive weight loss programme as prehabilitation before cancer surgery: a qualitative study
items.abstract: Background Healthcare professionals (HCPs) are gatekeepers to recruitment in cancer trials. We aimed to explore HCPs views on recruiting to and delivering a trial of an intensive weight loss programme with dietetic support as prehabilitation before cancer surgery. Methods This was a qualitative study using semi-structured interviews with dietitians, nurses, and surgeons delivering the trial. Data were analysed descriptively, followed by a framework approach to chart the findings against the RE-AIM framework (reach, effectiveness, adoption, implementation, maintenance) to evaluate the scalability of the intervention. Results We interviewed six research nurses, four nurse specialists, and two surgeons from eight NHS recruiting hospitals in England and the three dietitians delivering the intervention. HCPs reported approaching most eligible patients but did not approach those thought to be emotionally burdened by their diagnosis (Reach). HCPs also described the programme as a simple way for people to lose weight, potentially improving their postoperative outcomes and allowing them to take control during an uncertain time, though this view compromised equipoise (Effectiveness). While HCPs found it straightforward to deliver the trial and had limited safety concerns, some questioned if the minimum body mass index eligibility of 28 kg/m 2 was too low (Adoption). Dietitians experienced a positive feedback loop when participants adhered to the programme, supporting their perception that the intervention was effective and worthwhile (Implementation). HCPs viewed the programme as filling a gap in prehabilitation but raised concerns about scalability due to limited dietetic workforce capacity (Maintenance). Conclusions HCPs involved in delivering the programme mostly supported introducing it as prehabilitation before cancer surgery. Scaling the programme may require improvements, particularly to its reach and maintenance. This could include exploring how other trained individuals with appropriate clinical and dietetic oversight could support the delivery of behavioural support. Trial Registration ISRCTN39207707, prospectively registered 13/03/2023.

items.title: Effect of buccal acupuncture combined with fascia iliaca compartment block on early postoperative pain and perioperative hemodynamic responses in total knee arthroplasty: a randomized controlled trial
items.abstract: Total knee arthroplasty (TKA) causes substantial postoperative pain that can hinder early mobilization. Fascia iliaca compartment block (FICB) is widely used, but non-pharmacological adjuncts may enhance its efficacy. This randomized trial evaluated whether adding buccal acupuncture to FICB improves early postoperative pain control and perioperative hemodynamic responses compared with FICB alone. Eighty patients undergoing elective TKA were randomly assigned to buccal acupuncture plus FICB (BA group, n = 40) or FICB alone (IF group, n = 40). Buccal acupuncture was performed after anesthesia induction at the ipsilateral knee-related acupoint, and patients were blinded. The primary outcome was postoperative pain intensity (Numerical Rating Scale, NRS) 5 min after extubation (T1) and at PACU discharge (T10). Secondary outcomes included heart rate (HR) and mean arterial pressure (MAP). Generalized estimating equations (GEE) analyzed repeated-measures data. Baseline characteristics were comparable (all standardized mean differences < 0.2, except height, − 0.37). NRS scores were lower with BA than with IF at 5 min after extubation (2.5 (0.8) vs. 3.4 (1.2); mean difference [MD] − 0.90, 95% CI − 1.35 to − 0.45; P < 0.001) and at PACU discharge (2.3 (0.7) vs. 3.2 (1.1); MD − 0.90, 95% CI − 1.31 to − 0.49; P < 0.001), although both differences were below the prespecified minimal clinically important difference (MCID, 1.0 point). GEE showed a significant group effect for NRS (beta = − 0.90, 95% CI − 1.34 to − 0.46; P < 0.001) and group-by-time interactions for HR and MAP (both P < 0.001). PACU stay was shorter with BA (57.3 (8.5) vs. 62.4 (9.1) minutes; MD − 5.0, 95% CI − 8.9 to − 1.1; P = 0.013). Nausea and vomiting were less frequent with BA (22.5% vs. 32.5%; risk ratio 0.69, 95% CI 0.33–1.43; P = 0.453). In patients undergoing TKA, adding buccal acupuncture to FICB did not produce a clinically important reduction in early postoperative pain: the between-group difference in NRS scores (0.9 points) was statistically significant but remained below the prespecified MCID of 1.0 point. Lower HR and MAP values and a PACU stay approximately 5 min shorter in the BA group were consistent with a modest adjunctive effect, but these differences were small and of uncertain clinical importance. Neither analgesic strategy was superior to the other, and these data do not support routine use of buccal acupuncture as an adjunct to FICB; larger multicentre trials with clinically anchored endpoints are needed. Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR2500110196); registered on October 10, 2025.

items.title: Preoperative low free triiodothyronine and severe creatinine-defined acute kidney injury after cardiac surgery: a retrospective cohort study
items.abstract: Low free triiodothyronine (FT3) is common in cardiovascular disease. Whether preoperative low FT3 is independently associated with severe cardiac surgery-associated acute kidney injury (CSA-AKI) is uncertain. This retrospective single-center cohort study (Chengdu, China) included adults with a preoperative FT3 measurement who underwent cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass (2018–2023), excluding patients receiving maintenance dialysis. Low FT3 was defined as FT3 < 3.1 pmol/L; the primary outcome was severe creatinine-defined CSA-AKI (KDIGO stage ≥ 2 within 7 days). Covariates were multiply imputed 50 times; logistic regression estimates and their variances were pooled across imputations using Rubin's rules. The primary estimand was the odds ratio adjusted for 10 preoperative covariates; a perioperative explanatory model added cardiopulmonary bypass time. Inverse-probability-of-selection weighting was used as a sensitivity analysis for bias from selective FT3 testing, and FT3 was also analyzed continuously. In-hospital mortality was a secondary outcome. We assessed whether adding low FT3 to a preoperative prediction model improved discrimination. Of 2,224 eligible adults, 265 (11.9%) lacked preoperative FT3; after 6 dialysis-related exclusions, 1,953 were analyzed. Low FT3 was present in 110 (5.6%) and severe CSA-AKI in 214 (11.0%). The crude OR was 2.29 (95% CI 1.41–3.71). Low FT3 was not significantly associated with severe CSA-AKI in the preoperative model (OR 1.11, 95% CI 0.64–1.93, P = 0.71) or the perioperative model (OR 1.11, 0.63–1.94). The selection-weighted estimate was similar (OR 1.07, 0.59–1.91), although residual covariate imbalance persisted after weighting. No statistically significant association was detected with FT3 analyzed continuously. The point estimate suggested higher odds of in-hospital mortality (OR 1.87, 0.84–4.16, P = 0.13). Adding low FT3 to the preoperative model did not improve discrimination compared with the same model without FT3. No statistically significant association was detected between low preoperative FT3 and severe CSA-AKI, and adding low FT3 to the preoperative model did not improve discrimination compared with the same model without FT3. The imprecise mortality estimate remained compatible with both no association and a clinically important increase in the odds of death. Confidence intervals remain compatible with clinically important associations, and selective testing and incomplete KDIGO ascertainment limit certainty. Preoperative low free triiodothyronine was not significantly associated with severe creatinine-defined CSA-AKI after cardiac surgery and did not improve risk discrimination beyond the specified preoperative clinical model—but clinically important associations cannot be excluded.

items.title: Prophylactic vasopressor strategies for preventing post-induction hypotension in noncardiac surgery: a systematic review and network meta-analysis
items.abstract: Post-induction hypotension (PIH) is common following the induction of general anaesthesia and is associated with adverse perioperative outcomes. Prophylactic vasopressors are widely used, but the comparative effects of individual drugs and administration strategies remain uncertain. We searched nine databases from inception to July 20, 2026, for parallel-group randomised controlled trials evaluating prophylactic systemic vasopressors for PIH prevention in adults undergoing noncardiac surgery under general anaesthesia. The primary outcome was PIH from induction to skin incision or within a prespecified post-induction interval. Drug-level and drug-by-administration strategy networks were analysed using Bayesian random-effects models, reporting risk ratios (RRs) with 95% credible intervals (CrIs). Risk of bias was assessed using RoB 2, and certainty of evidence for principal drug comparisons was evaluated using GRADE. Fifty-six trials involving 5143 participants were included, of which 18 trials involving 1593 participants formed the conservative primary network. Compared with no prophylaxis, PIH risk was reduced with ephedrine, phenylephrine, norepinephrine, methoxamine, and metaraminol, with RRs (95% CrIs) of 0.41 (0.27–0.60), 0.41 (0.26–0.62), 0.27 (0.17–0.41), 0.20 (0.11–0.32), and 0.11 (0.004–0.68), respectively. Network estimates suggested lower PIH risk with methoxamine than with ephedrine or phenylephrine, although these indirect comparisons require confirmation in direct trials. Several prophylactic administration strategies reduced PIH compared with no prophylaxis, but safety and postoperative outcome data were insufficient for reliable comparative assessment. Overall, prophylactic vasopressors reduced PIH compared with no prophylaxis, whereas the available evidence does not establish a preferred drug or administration strategy.

items.title: Comparison of Arterial Pressure-based Cardiac Output and Thermodilution Cardiac Output Before and After Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement:Method Comparison Study
items.containerTitle: Journal of Cardiothoracic and Vascular Anesthesia
items.abstract: Objectives To evaluate the agreement between arterial pressure-based cardiac output (APCO) and thermodilution-derived cardiac output (TDCO) before and after transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) and to assess whether APCO reflects periprocedural changes in cardiac output relative to TDCO. Design Prospective single-center study. Setting A tertiary academic medical center. Participants Patients with aortic stenosis scheduled for TAVR under general anesthesia. Interventions Simultaneous APCO and TDCO measurements were obtained immediately before and after TAVR using the FloTrac system (Edwards Lifesciences, Irvine, CA, USA) and right heart catheterization, respectively. Measurements and main results Of 100 patients enrolled in the study, 96 with available paired measurements of APCO and TDCO were included, and 95 had paired post-TAVR measurements. APCO underestimated TDCO both before and after TAVR. Before TAVR, the mean bias (APCO - TDCO) was -1.21 ± 1.23 L/min, with limits of agreement (LoA) of -3.63 to 1.21 L/min and a percentage error of 47.3%. After TAVR, the mean bias was -1.89 ± 1.41 L/min with LoA of -4.65 to 0.87 L/min and a percentage error of 48.2%. Changes in APCO and TDCO from before to after TAVR were not correlated (Pearson r = -0.03, p = 0.74; Spearman ρ = 0.005, p = 0.97). Conclusions FloTrac-derived APCO showed substantial disagreement with TDCO before and after TAVR and did not reflect corresponding periprocedural changes in TDCO. APCO and TDCO should not be considered interchangeable for cardiac output assessment in this population.

items.title: Association Between Body Mass Index and Outcomes in Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement Patients: A Statewide Cohort Study
items.containerTitle: Journal of Cardiothoracic and Vascular Anesthesia
items.abstract: This study aimed to explore whether body mass index (BMI) was associated with major complications or 30-day mortality after transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR). Retrospective cohort study. Ten Virginia hospitals. Patients undergoing TAVR. None. BMI was modeled as an exposure, and the primary outcome was a composite of major complications or 30-day mortality. One-year mortality was a secondary outcome. Generalized linear mixed models were fit with hospital modeled as a random intercept. Overall, BMI had no association with major complications or 30-day mortality in 8,489 patients undergoing TAVR (omnibus p = 0.33). Patients who had a BMI of 30 to 34.9 kg/m2 (obesity class I) had slightly increased odds of major complications or 30-day mortality compared with patients with a normal BMI (odds ratio [OR], 1.27; 95% CI, 1.04-1.55; p = 0.02). However, patients with a BMI of 35 to 39.9 kg/m2 (obesity class II) and patients with a BMI >40 kg/m2 (obesity class III) did not have higher odds of major complications or 30-day mortality, with an OR of 1.16 (95% CI, 0.89-1.50; p = 0.27) and 1.20 (95% CI, 0.89-1.61; p = 0.24), respectively. For 1-year mortality, patients with a BMI of 25 to 29.9 kg/m2 (overweight), 30 to 34.9 kg/m2 (obesity class I), and 35 to 39.9 kg/m2 (obesity class II) had lower odds of mortality than patients with a normal BMI (all p < 0.05). The analysis suggests that obesity is not a significant risk factor for major complications or 30-day mortality after TAVR, while at 1 year, patients who were overweight or obesity class I or II had improved survival.

items.title: Correlation Between the Bispectral Index and Patient State Index at 36°C and 32°C During Cardiopulmonary Bypass: A Prospective Observational Study
items.containerTitle: Journal of Cardiothoracic and Vascular Anesthesia
items.abstract: To compare the correlation, numerical agreement, and manufacturer-threshold categorical concordance between the bispectral index (BIS) and patient state index (PSI) at 36°C and 32°C during cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB). Prospective, single-center observational cohort study. Tertiary-care training and research hospital. Sixty adults undergoing elective on-pump coronary artery bypass grafting; 54 reached a temperature of 32°C and comprised the primary analysis cohort. None. Clinicians were blinded to both displays, and anesthesia was not index guided. Paired BIS and PSI values were recorded at 14 protocol time points. The primary estimand was the difference in dependent Pearson correlations between the 36°C and 32°C CPB anchors among the same participants. The correlations were 0.800 and 0.559, respectively (36°C-minus-32°C difference, 0.241; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.095-0.432; p = 0.001). The standard deviation of PSI fell from 7.2 at 36°C to 4.7 at 32°C, whereas that of BIS was 7.2 at 36°C and 8.7 at 32°C. The mean BIS-PSI difference increased from 7.1 to 15.0 index units (within-participant increase, 7.8; 95% CI, 6.2-9.4). Linear weighted κ decreased from 0.402 to 0.051 (difference, 0.351; 95% CI, 0.043-0.657). During the observed CPB sequence, the 32°C anchor had weaker BIS-PSI correlation, greater numerical separation, and lower manufacturer-threshold concordance by weighted κ than the 36°C anchor. Much of the weaker correlation reflected a narrower spread of PSI values. Because temperature varied with anesthetic exposure and other intraoperative factors, these findings do not isolate a temperature effect or identify which monitor better reflected hypnotic state.

items.title: Proteomics, Metabolomics, and Transcriptomics in Cardiac Surgery: A Narrative Review
items.containerTitle: Journal of Cardiothoracic and Vascular Anesthesia
items.abstract: The objectives of this study were to examine how proteomics, metabolomics, and transcriptomics have changed the understanding of major complications of cardiac surgery, and to consider how these findings might inform future cardiothoracic anesthesia and perioperative critical care research. Across ischemia-reperfusion injury, cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB)-induced systemic inflammation and coagulopathy, postoperative atrial fibrillation (POAF), cardiac surgery-associated acute kidney injury (CSA-AKI), delirium, and acute respiratory distress syndrome, omics studies indicate that these clinically similar syndromes are molecularly heterogeneous. Transcriptomics describes CPB-induced inflammation as an organized gene regulatory program; proteomics resolves network-level stress, complement, and tubular injury responses; and metabolomics captures rapid, phenotype-dependent shifts in substrate use, including the succinate-hypoxia-inducible factor 1-alpha axis linking ischemia to inflammation. Several signals-preoperative lipid-transport and redox proteins in patients with POAF, intraoperative proteomic shifts preceding delirium, and tubular metabolic reprogramming in patients with CSA-AKI-appear before conventional clinical criteria are met. The current contribution of omics is conceptual rather than clinical. Several molecular signals precede conventional clinical criteria, but earlier detection has so far not been shown to be actionable: there has been no randomized trial to test whether acting on an omics-derived signal alters outcome after cardiac surgery. Most evidence is derived from small, single-center, exploratory cohorts with limited independent replication, and no current guideline incorporates omics-based phenotyping. The near-term value lies in trial design-selection of higher-risk patients, matching interventions to plausible mechanisms, and sampling early enough to detect modifiable injury-rather than routine bedside use. Prospective serial sampling, standardized multicenter biobanks, and externally validated clinical-omics models are required before molecular phenotyping can guide perioperative care.

items.title: Aortic Root Abscess in Infective Endocarditis: Prognostic Impact and Outcomes of Patch Repair
items.containerTitle: The Journal of Thoracic and Cardiovascular Surgery
items.abstract: Objective Due to discrepancies between guidelines and expert consensus, we examined the perioperative and mid-term outcomes of aortic root abscesses to determine their prognostic significance and optimal surgical management. Methods We completed a single-center retrospective study of patients surgically treated for aortic valve infective endocarditis (AV IE) from 2019 to 2024. We compared outcomes in patients with and without root abscess, and among abscess cases, between patch repair and extended surgery (root reconstruction or replacement). The primary outcome was major adverse cardiac and cerebrovascular events (MACCE, composite of all-cause death, heart failure (HF) readmission, and stroke). Outcomes were analyzed using Kaplan Meier estimators and Cox proportional hazards. Results Among 158 patients (57% with abscess) with a median follow-up of 1.22 years (IQR 0.13-2.53), root abscesses were associated with increased MACCE (adjusted HR 3.15 (1.51-6.59), p=0.002) and HF readmission (SHR 4.54 (1.55-13.30), p=0.006). In patients with aortic root abscess, 62 underwent patch repair and 21 underwent extended surgery. Patch repair was associated with decreased MACCE (adjusted HR 0.34 (0.15-0.74), p=0.006), all-cause mortality (p=0.002), and death at 30 days (13% vs 33%, p=0.035) compared to extended surgery. Conclusions Aortic root abscess was associated with increased MACCE and HF readmissions compared to AV IE without abscess, identifying root abscess as a marker of adverse prognosis and supporting prompt recognition and referral in aortic valve endocarditis. Patch repair for aortic root abscesses is a safe and reasonable approach in patients with suitable anatomy compared to more extensive surgery.

items.title: Early versus delayed surgery to prevent hemorrhagic transformation in patients with septic cerebral emboli from infective endocarditis
items.containerTitle: The Journal of Thoracic and Cardiovascular Surgery
items.abstract: OBJECTIVE: The optimal timing of cardiac surgery in patients with infective endocarditis and ischemic septic cerebral embolism remains uncertain, largely because of concern for perioperative hemorrhagic transformation. This study evaluates the association between surgical timing and outcomes in this population. METHODS: Patients with infective endocarditis and preoperative septic cerebral emboli who underwent cardiac surgery were identified from an institutional database (1999-2025). After excluding those with preoperative cerebral hemorrhage, 240 patients with ischemic stroke were stratified by interval from stroke to surgery: early (≤7 days, n=109) versus delayed (8-30 days, n=131). Propensity score matching was used to balance baseline confounders. The primary outcome was postoperative hemorrhagic transformation; secondary outcomes included new postoperative stroke, intensive care unit and hospital length of stay, four-year survival assessed by Kaplan-Meier analysis, and mortality assessed by Cox proportional hazards modeling. RESULTS: Matching yielded 194 patients. Postoperative hemorrhagic transformation occurred in 10 of 194 (5.2%) patients and did not differ by timing (6.2% early vs. 4.1% delayed, p=0.73). New postoperative stroke occurred in 19 of 194 patients (9.8%) and was similar (10.3% early vs. 9.3% delayed, p>0.99), as was 30-day mortality (6.2% early vs. 10.3% delayed, p=0.42). Four-year survival did not differ by timing (68.0% early vs. 57.4% delayed, p=0.07), and there was no significant association between surgical timing and mortality (HR 0.67 [0.44-1.03]; p=0.07). CONCLUSIONS: In patients with infective endocarditis and ischemic stroke, early surgery (≤7 days) was not associated with increased rates of postoperative hemorrhagic transformation, new stroke, or 30-day or long-term mortality compared with delayed surgery.
