Transcatheter Tricuspid Valve Replacement Versus Medical Therapy for Severe Secondary Tricuspid Regurgitation
items.abstract: Background Severe tricuspid regurgitation (TR) carries a poor prognosis, yet comparative real-world data on transcatheter tricuspid valve replacement (TTVR) versus medical therapy remain limited. Objectives The aim of this study was to compare clinical outcomes of TTVR versus medical therapy in patients with secondary TR. Methods This observational study included the TRIPLACE registry (NCT06033274; TTVR cohort, N = 395, 24 centers, 2017-2025) and the Bronx-Valve Registry (NCT05453526; medical therapy cohort, N = 784, single center, 2017-2019). A 30-covariate propensity score was used for overlap weighting, targeting the average treatment effect in the overlap population (ATO). The primary endpoint was the 2-year composite of all-cause mortality or heart failure (HF) hospitalization. Results TTVR achieved ≤ mild TR in 93.7% and ≤ moderate TR in 98.7%. In-hospital mortality was 0.8%. The most common 30-day adverse events were new permanent pacemaker implantation (14.8%) and severe bleeding (6.5%). Median follow-up was 363 days (Q1-Q3: 63-1,151 days). After ATO weighting, all covariates included in the propensity score model achieved exact mean balance (maximum standardized mean difference: 0.000). TTVR was associated with a lower 2-year primary endpoint (ATO-HR: 0.60 [95% CI: 0.40-0.89]; P = 0.012) and lower all-cause mortality (ATO-HR: 0.61 [95% CI: 0.38-0.99]; P = 0.044), whereas HF hospitalization did not differ significantly between groups (ATO-cause-specific HR: 0.69 [95% CI: 0.39-1.24]; P = 0.215). Conclusions In this observational comparison, TTVR was associated with a lower 2-year risk of all-cause mortality or HF hospitalization compared with medical therapy in patients with secondary TR. These findings should be interpreted in the context of procedure-related risks and the nonrandomized study design. Registration (Global Multicenter Registry on Transcatheter TRIcuspid Valve RePLACEment [TRIPLACE]; NCT06033274).

items.title: Shattering the 9-mm taboo: soft-contact percutaneous closure of a doubly committed subarterial ventricular septal defect with aortic valve prolapse and aortic regurgitation
ERC advanced grant: moving cardiovascular prevention upstream of conception
items.abstract: Current cardiovascular disease primary prevention strategies have limited effect on reduction of the disease burden, especially among socially disadvantaged populations. Results from studies from the last three decades increasingly suggest that effective prevention of cardiovascular disease should start in the earliest phases of life and continue across the life course.1–3 Children with a high blood pressure and obesity at school age have increased risks of hypertension, coronary heart disease, and premature cardiovascular mortality in adulthood.1–3 Also, adverse fetal exposures are associated with increased risks of cardiovascular disease in adulthood.1–3 Currently, we miss a great potential for effective cardiovascular disease prevention by ignoring the first phases of life. However, before targeted early-life prevention strategies can be developed, insight is urgently needed into the underlying modifiable exposures, critical periods, and causality of the associations. The period from gametogenesis to embryogenesis might be crucial for later-life cardiovascular health and provide clues for novel cardiovascular prevention strategies.4 The periconception period includes the completion of meiotic maturation of oocytes, differentiation of spermatozoa, fertilization, and resumption of mitotic cell cycles in the zygote, marking the transition from the parental to the embryonic genome, and the onset of embryonic development. This process takes a few weeks and is characterized by extensive changes in morphology, epigenetic reorganization, and changes in metabolism. Animal studies showed that the quality of the maternal diet and physiological status including hyperglycaemia or dyslipidaemia around conception affects embryonic development and offspring cardiovascular disease risk across the life course.4 Also, maternal smoking, malnutrition, and obesity at the very start of pregnancy are related to higher blood pressure and cholesterol concentrations and increased risks of obesity in the offspring.4 In line with these findings, dietary patterns and micronutrients in early pregnancy were related to offspring birth weight and cardiovascular outcomes.4 Although animal studies strongly suggest that paternal obesity, malnutrition, and hyperglycaemia from conception onwards adversely affect offspring cardiovascular health, not much is known about the role of the fathers from human studies. These findings strongly suggest that the periconception period is important for developmental programming of later-life health. Identification of risk factors in both women and men from the preconception period, that are robustly associated with cardiovascular complications in their offspring, is urgently needed to identify groups at risk. Placental vascular bed development is essential for fetal nutrient supply and directly affects fetal cardiac and vascular development. Placental blood flow is an important stimulus for fetal cardiovascular development. Doppler of the uterine, spiral, intra-placental, umbilical, and chorionic arteries enables direct assessment of placental haemodynamic development and the onset of the placental circulation at the end of the first trimester. Placental epigenetic changes may play a key role in placental adaptations leading to offspring cardiovascular reprogramming.5 Examination of placentas at birth or in animal models does not provide adequate insight into human epigenetic placental adaptations in the crucial early-pregnancy period. Placental microRNAs (miRNAs) are secreted into the maternal and fetal circulation throughout gestation and can offer a first-trimester snapshot of placental epigenetic adaptations and potential for studies on exposures and outcomes of interest.5 Animal and human studies among selected populations suggest that specific placental-miRNAs regulate feto-placental angiogenesis, trophoblast invasion, fetal growth, and embryonic cardiovascular development. Placental miRNAs enable exciting new possibilities for innovative studies to identify biological mechanisms leading from preconception health-related factors in women and men to placental and embryonic adaptations and subsequent programming of cardiovascular diseases. Recent studies suggest that first-trimester developmental variation has consequences for cardiovascular health in later life.6,7 First-trimester fetal growth, measured by crown-to-rump length, was influenced by maternal age, blood pressure, haematocrit levels, smoking, and use of folic acid supplements.6 Compared to normal first-trimester fetal growth, impaired first-trimester fetal growth was associated with increased risks of preterm birth and small size at birth.6 Impaired first-trimester fetal growth was also associated with an adverse body fat distribution, higher blood pressure, and an adverse cholesterol profile in childhood.7 The main hypothesis for European Research Council-granted project PreconceptionOrigins is that suboptimal preconception lifestyle, nutrition, and health in women and men lead to adaptations in gametogenesis, which predispose individuals to early placental and embryonic programming of cardiovascular disease across the life course. This leads to an intergenerational and vicious circle of cardiovascular disease within families, especially among socially disadvantaged, ethnic minority, and healthcare-avoiding groups. The conceptional framework is given in Figure 1. The project includes the following: Observational analyses in a FAIR and sustainable European Preconception Cohort Network, based on the LifeCycle—EU Child Cohort Network, including data of 54 000 women, men, and their offspring followed until young adulthood focused on life course studies from the preconception period onwards and intergenerational causal inference approaches.8 This network includes cohorts with socially disadvantaged, ethnic minority, and healthcare-avoiding subgroups. Deep-phenotype population-based cohort study that combines prospectively collected data of preconception exposures in women and men with markers for their gametogenesis and subsequent placental, embryo, and childhood outcomes. This study will be embedded as subgroup in the ongoing Generation R Next Study.9 The methods will be aligned with the European Research Council project OBESE-EMBRYO.10 Population-based studies on the roles of oocyte and sperm quality in embryonic development of cardiovascular health and disease, with a specific focus on the role of fathers in the preconception period and programming by sperm cells and seminal plasma. Translation of results into novel prediction models for childhood birth and cardiovascular complications, which will be specifically designed for socially disadvantaged, ethnic minority, or healthcare-avoiding subgroups. ERC Project PreconceptionOrigins Conceptional Framework. This project aims to provide novel horizons for the preconception and embryonic origins of cardiovascular disease and lead to a paradigm shift for cardiovascular prevention strategies towards the earliest phases of life. The project combines observational studies for robust identification of modifiable exposures, risk modification by childhood factors, and causal inference, with population-based pathway studies on gametogenesis, early placentation and embryogenesis, and subsequent development of personalized preventive strategies for women and men, taking account of socially disadvantaged, ethnic minority, and healthcare-avoiding subgroups. Customized strategies for different subgroups will contribute to better understanding and addressing cardiovascular health-related inequities from the earliest phases of life onwards. All authors declare no disclosure of interest for this contribution. Funded by the European Union and European Research Council (PreconceptionOrgins(ERC-2025-ADG-10126594), OBESE-EMBRYO (ERC-2024-STG-101161004), EMBRYOandLATERHEALTH (ERC-2014-CoG-648916), and LifeCycle Project (Horizon 2020,733206). Views and opinions expressed are those of the authors only and do not necessarily reflect those of the European Union or the European Research Council. Neither the European Union nor the granting authority can be held responsible for them.

items.title: Highlights from the MICS congress 2026: minimally invasive and catheter solutions
items.abstract: The ninth MICS—Minimally Invasive and Catheter Solutions congress took place at the Hotel Excelsior in Naples from 11 to 13 June 2026. Organized by the Mitral Academy with GVM Care & Research and the European University of Rome, and endorsed by the European Association of Cardiovascular Imaging, it brought together more than 650 participants from 10 countries and over 120 faculty members.1 Cardiac surgeons, interventional and clinical cardiologists, imagers, electrophysiologists and perfusionists shared the same room, and anaesthesiologists joined the programme as well. The format favoured discussion over lectures: recorded procedures commented on by the operators (‘live in the box’), Heart Team case debates, and sessions in which an invited challenger questioned the speaker’s position. The main themes are summarized in Table 1. Main themes of MICS 2026 and the evidence that framed the discussion 3D TOE, three-dimensional transoesophageal echocardiography; AI, artificial intelligence; EACVI, European Association of Cardiovascular Imaging; TEER, transcatheter edge-to-edge repair. Minimally invasive cardiac surgery has evolved substantially since its introduction in the 1990s. Right mini-thoracotomy, totally endoscopic procedures and robotic surgery are now established components of the surgical armamentarium, particularly for mitral valve repair. These approaches are also increasingly used for aortic valve surgery, coronary revascularization, and combined procedures. In the UK Mini Mitral trial, right mini-thoracotomy did not accelerate recovery of physical function at 12 weeks compared with sternotomy, but repair rates (∼96%), residual regurgitation, and 1-year safety were equivalent.2 However, ‘minimally invasive’ should not be interpreted simply as a smaller incision. The true objective is to reduce the overall burden of treatment, including ventilation, intensive-care requirements, hospital stay, and time to functional recovery. Expansion of these techniques must proceed together with rigorous training, institutional expertise, appropriate patient selection, and long-term outcome assessment. For primary mitral regurgitation, surgical repair in experienced centres remains the reference, and transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (TEER) is an option for patients at high surgical risk with suitable anatomy, as reaffirmed by the 2025 ESC/EACTS guidelines.3 Secondary regurgitation is a different disease with a different evidence base. COAPT (cardiovascular outcomes assessment of the mitraclip percutaneous therapy) showed that TEER reduced heart-failure hospitalization and mortality in patients who remained symptomatic despite maximally tolerated medical therapy.4 The practical lesson is that this benefit belongs to the population that was actually studied: severe regurgitation, a left ventricle that is not excessively dilated, and medical therapy that has genuinely been optimized before referral. A dedicated tricuspid session covered the whole spectrum, from surgical repair to treatment algorithms for recurrent regurgitation. Two randomized trials now anchor the transcatheter field. TRILUMINATE Pivotal showed that tricuspid TEER reduced regurgitation and improved quality of life, without a detectable effect on death, surgery, or heart-failure hospitalization at 1 year.5 TRISCEND II reported a similar pattern for transcatheter replacement, with larger gains in symptoms but more severe bleeding and new pacemakers.6 Treatment selection requires detailed assessment of tricuspid anatomy, right-ventricular function, pulmonary hypertension, atrial fibrillation, comorbidities, and the presence of cardiac-device leads. Current consensus emphasizes multidisciplinary review, multimodality imaging, and shared decision-making. The aortic sessions moved beyond the transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI)-vs-surgery dichotomy towards the lifetime management of patients who will outlive their first prosthesis. Bicuspid anatomy, coronary access after TAVI, and the feasibility of future valve-in-valve procedures were discussed alongside the new guidelines3 and the position paper of the Italian Society of Cardiac Surgery. Native aortic regurgitation, long considered unsuitable for TAVI because of the lack of annular calcium, now has a dedicated device: in ALIGN-AR, a valve that anchors by clipping the native leaflets met its 30-day safety and 1-year efficacy endpoints in high-risk patients, albeit with a 24% pacemaker rate and no long-term durability data.7 For most patients with aortic regurgitation, and certainly for younger ones, surgery remains the default. Intraoperative three-dimensional transoesophageal echocardiography and multimodality imaging ran through almost every session. In patients with more than one diseased valve, an increasingly frequent scenario, imaging must establish the mechanism, severity, and interaction of each lesion before any procedure is planned.8 Artificial intelligence, discussed in the closing ‘Care Revolution’ session together with digital health and team organization, is likely to arrive first in image quantification and procedural planning; its value for individual treatment decisions remains to be proven. Rhythm control was addressed as both a catheter and a surgical problem, from pulsed-field ablation to appendage closure. In LAAOS III, surgical occlusion of the left atrial appendage during cardiac surgery performed for another indication reduced stroke or systemic embolism by about one third.9 A smaller incision is no reason to leave the appendage behind. The most useful debates in Naples concerned patient selection rather than devices: which patient, which lesion, which moment, and which team. Minimally invasive surgery and transcatheter therapy sit at two ends of the same continuum, and the distance between them is shrinking. The centres that will serve patients best are those where surgeons and interventional cardiologists train together, read the same images, and decide together—and where the physician recommending a procedure is able to offer its alternative. All authors declare no disclosure of interest for this contribution.

items.title: Acute pulmonary embolism: long-term cause-specific mortality in a Chinese nationwide registry
items.abstract: Background and Aims Long-term cause-specific mortality after acute pulmonary embolism (PE) remains poorly characterized. This study investigated cumulative mortality, temporal changes in causes of death, and associated factors in a national registry. Methods This registry-based cohort study consecutively enrolled 66 192 acute PE patients from 3223 Chest Pain Centres across China (2018-2023) (ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT04014972). Mortality was ascertained through national registry linkage. Cumulative incidence functions estimated temporal mortality patterns, while Fine-Gray models exploratorily examined factors associated with cause-specific mortality. Results At 60 months, cumulative all-cause mortality was 22.41% (95% confidence interval [CI] 21.92-22.91), comprising cardiovascular (CV) (11.84%, 95% CI 11.46-12.23) and non-CV mortality (10.57%, 95% CI 10.22-10.92). Causes of death varied over time: acute PE and ischaemic heart disease (IHD) predominated initially, malignancy peaked at 1-3 months, and IHD was the largest named cause in each interval beyond 12 months. Among CV deaths, IHD was the predominant cause (35.7%); malignancy (43.3%) and chronic pulmonary disease (24.6%) predominated among non-CV deaths. Men had higher cumulative CV and non-CV mortality than women; while women only had a higher proportion of CV causes among deaths. All-cause mortality increased with age (from 11.52% at <55 to 38.51% at ≥75 years); acute PE/malignancy dominated in younger patients, while CV/pulmonary disease prevailed in older ones. Exploratory analyses identified age, Western China residence, and vital signs as factors associated with mortality. Conclusions Among patients hospitalised with acute PE, 5-year cumulative mortality was 22.4%, and nearly half of deaths were from non-CV causes. Shifting mortality patterns highlight the need to evaluate risk-adapted long-term follow-up strategies.

items.title: The beautiful collateralization hypothesis is alive: coronary bypass surgery and infarct prevention
items.abstract: Schematic illustration of the mechanisms of bypass grafting for coronary artery disease. Grafts are placed distal to significant coronary disease (i.e. distal to significant and non-significant lesions and possibly also to complete total occlusions). The infarct-protective mechanism is likely to be activated by the prevention of an infarction in case one of the proximal lesions (which in most cases arise from non-flow-limiting lesions) causes flow obstruction.2 Importantly, this protection is therefore not limited to the lesion that initiated grafting: it applies to every plaque situated between that lesion and the distal anastomosis, most of which are not flow-limiting at the time of surgery, so that an acute rupture with complete vessel occlusion, which would otherwise cause an ST-elevation myocardial infarction, is rendered clinically inconsequential. If natural collaterals additionally exist, they may increase the protective potential of a graft. For instance, if a collateral from the left anterior descending artery (LAD) supplies the territory of an occluded right coronary artery (RCA), the LAD graft would also prevent an infarction occurring to the right coronary territory by preventing a distal LAD occlusion. Placing a patent graft to the distal RCA would have similar treatment potential ‘from the other side’. In practice, these mechanisms likely overlap and the latter may also be exploited by percutaneous coronary intervention.6 PDA, patent ductus arteriosus; LCx, left circumflex artery.

Reshaping lead–leaflet interaction: annuloplasty-enabled TEER for complex CIED-related tricuspid regurgitation
items.abstract: A 89-year-old male with a cardiac implantable electronic device (CIED) presented with symptomatic massive tricuspid regurgitation (TR). Previous major anticoagulation-related gastrointestinal bleeding made transcatheter tricuspid valve replacement unfavourable. Transoesophageal echocardiography demonstrated marked annular dilatation (mean diameter 42.3 mm), leaflet tethering and a 13-mm anteroseptal coaptation gap (Panel A). The pacing lead coursed near the posteroseptal commissure and impinged on the septal leaflet, contributing to a broad, multijetic regurgitation (Panel A). Rather than lead extraction or attempting edge-to-edge repair across the large coaptation defect, K-Clip annuloplasty was performed to modify the annular substrate around the lead. Annular remodelling reduced the septolateral diameter to 32.2 mm and the anteroseptal coaptation gap to 2 mm, improved leaflet coaptation and reduced TR from massive to moderate (Panel B). Importantly, remodelling reshaped the lead–septal leaflet interaction and transformed the broad regurgitant defect into a predominantly localized anteroseptal jet. This newly defined target enabled subsequent TriClip G5 implantation, further reducing TR to mild without lead extraction or repositioning (Panel C). The total device insertion-to-removal time was assessed as 75 min. This case highlights a staged, anatomy-guided strategy in which annuloplasty served as anatomical preconditioning, transforming unfavourable anatomy into a target amenable to transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (TEER) while preserving the functional transvalvular lead.1–3 More broadly, this sequential substrate remodelling followed by targeted repair may also provide a treatment framework for selected multi-mechanistic TR poorly suited to isolated TEER beyond CIED-related disease. Its procedural and long-term value warrants further prospective evaluation. Supplementary data are not available at European Heart Journal online. Authors have no conflicts of interest to disclose. No data were generated or analysed for or in support of this paper. This study was funded by National Natural Science Foundation of China (82470377, 8240021011).

items.title: Highlights from ESH 2026
items.abstract: The 35th European Meeting on Hypertension and Cardiovascular Protection was held in Gdańsk, Poland, from 28 to 31 May 2026, bringing together 2830 participants from more than 100 countries. Over 4 days, the programme comprised 112 scientific sessions, including 20 oral abstract sessions and two e-poster evenings, with a faculty of nearly 300 international experts. The congress theme, ‘Innovations in Cardiometabolic Management’, deliberately moved beyond blood pressure alone and placed hypertension within a wider cardiovascular, renal, and metabolic continuum.1,2 The programme combined emerging science with clinical implementation. Basic and translational science featured prominently, while practical formats included clinical cases, pro–con debates, hands-on workshops, Patient Journey sessions, and Meet-the-Expert discussions. New blood pressure technologies, resistant hypertension, obesity, chronic kidney disease (CKD), vascular ageing, sleep, inflammation, and women’s cardiovascular health appeared repeatedly across the programme, often with contributions from the active ESH Working Groups. A defining feature of ESH 2026 was its dialogue with other cardiovascular and medical communities. Joint sessions were organized with the European Society of Cardiology (ESC), European Renal Association (ERA), European Association for the Study of Obesity (EASO), European Federation of Internal Medicine, European Geriatric Medicine Society, International Society of Hypertension, and national societies.1 The Sunday ESH–ESC session, ‘From Early Coronary Events to Lifelong Risk: Rethinking Cardiovascular Disease in Young Women’, connected acute coronary syndromes and vascular disease in younger women with long-term cardiovascular risk after pregnancy complications. The ESH–ERA session addressed practical questions in hypertension and CKD, including ambulatory monitoring, renin–angiotensin system inhibition in advanced CKD, and diuretic strategies. Earlier joint sessions with EASO and internal medicine similarly explored obesity-related hypertension and the cardiovascular consequences of sleep disruption.1,2 Two Hot Line Clinical Trial sessions were among the scientific focal points of the meeting, together presenting eight late-breaking studies. Friday featured ERSHAM, exploring renal denervation in patients with hypertension and anxiety; OPTIMAL-HT, evaluating a streamlined triple single-pill combination strategy; new renal data on aprocitentan; and mechanistic findings from the baxdrostat programme. Saturday brought an individual participant data meta-analysis of blood pressure lowering across the CKD spectrum, the randomized RDN-ADPKD study, KARDIA-3 with the long-acting RNA-interference therapy zilebesiran, and new CKD data from LAUNCH-HTN with lorundrostat.1,2 Several presentations extended trial programmes already published in major journals. BaxHTN established the efficacy of aldosterone synthase inhibition with baxdrostat in uncontrolled and resistant hypertension,3 while LAUNCH-HTN provided phase 3 evidence for lorundrostat.4 The large Blood Pressure Lowering Treatment Trialists’ Collaboration analysis, published shortly before the congress, showed cardiovascular benefit from blood pressure lowering across the full spectrum of CKD.5 Other Hot Line contributions were published in the Journal of Hypertension congress supplement, allowing the Gdańsk meeting to combine genuinely late-breaking analyses with rapid translation of new evidence into clinical discussion.6–9 The keynote programme perhaps best illustrated how far the scientific scope of ESH has expanded. Lotte Bjerre Knudsen revisited the development of GLP-1-based medicines and their transition from glucose-lowering drugs to therapies affecting obesity and cardiovascular, renal, and metabolic outcomes. Jocelyne Bloch and Grégoire Courtine presented neuroprosthetic approaches to cardiovascular instability after spinal cord injury, building on recently published work showing that targeted epidural spinal cord stimulation can restore haemodynamic stability.10 Daniela Carnevale’s Björn Folkow Award Lecture explored the sympathetic–immune interface in hypertension.1,2 These lectures were complemented by sessions on obesity, the microbiome, vascular ageing, inflammation, cardiorenal disease, and cerebrovascular protection. The recurring message was that optimal blood pressure control remains central, but hypertension increasingly needs to be considered within a broader cardiometabolic framework. Artificial intelligence, cuffless and wearable blood pressure monitoring, remote monitoring, digital twins, and polygenic risk scores were highly visible throughout the meeting. Yet technology was consistently discussed together with its limitations: validation, equity, privacy, implementation, and the need to preserve clinical judgement. At the same time, the highly interactive ‘Doctor, Can I…?’ sessions addressed questions patients actually ask from medication timing and the treatment of erectile dysfunction to coffee, supplements, exercise, pregnancy, and sauna use. This balance between innovation and practical medicine became one of the distinctive characteristics of the Gdańsk meeting.1,2 Young investigators were given unusually prominent roles. The Young Investigators Group session ‘Hypertension in 2036’ explored digital twins, artificial intelligence, wearables, precision medicine, and future therapeutic strategies, with Giuseppe Mancia providing a senior perspective on future successes and disappointments. Activities extended beyond conventional sessions to the Under Pressure Quiz, a Young Investigators Social Evening, the Congress Run, networking initiatives, and a newly established Young Investigator Award.1,2 The city itself became part of the congress narrative (Figure 1). Gdańsk, closely associated with Solidarity and democratic transformation in Europe, provided a symbolic setting for a meeting focused on change and innovation. The Opening Ceremony captured this connection: former Polish President and Nobel Peace Prize laureate Lech Wałęsa was welcomed with a standing ovation, while Anna Dominiczak’s lecture, ‘Medicine, science, politics and politicians’, linked scientific progress with leadership and public responsibility.2 Highlights of ESH 2026 in Gdańsk. (A) Gdańsk, host city of the 35th European Meeting on Hypertension and Cardiovascular Protection; (B) a meeting with former Polish President and Nobel Peace Prize laureate Lech Wałęsa; (C) delegates during the Opening Ceremony of ESH 2026; (D) science in action during the scientific programme; (E) networking and interaction across the ESH community; and (F) the Sunrise Session on the Baltic coast in Sopot The congress also moved beyond conventional lecture halls. The Sunrise Session on the Baltic coast in Sopot brought science, physical activity, and circadian cardiometabolic health together at 05:00—an unconventional format that became one of the visual signatures of ESH 2026. ESH 2026 showed a specialty in transition. Hypertension remains at its core, but its future is increasingly connected to cardiology, nephrology, obesity medicine, neuroscience, digital health, and prevention. The strongest impression from Gdańsk was therefore not of one dominant drug, device, or technology, but of convergence—between disciplines, generations, science, and clinical implementation. That conversation will continue at ESH 2027 in Basel. All authors declare no disclosure of interest for this contribution.

Macrophage CD40 signalling inhibition improves cardiac function after myocardial infarction by limiting fibroblast activation
items.abstract: Background and Aims Myocardial infarction (MI) triggers a dynamic immune response transitioning through inflammatory, reparative, and fibrotic phases. While CD40L-CD40 signalling is central to immune activation, its role in macrophage-driven fibrosis post-MI remains poorly understood. Methods Plasma soluble (s)CD40L was determined in patients with ST-segment elevation MI (STEMI; n = 360). Left ventricular (LV) function was quantified by cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMR) at 5 days and 6 months post-MI. In a murine model of reperfused MI, CD40–TRAF6 signalling was inhibited using TRAF-STOP. LV function was assessed by echocardiography. Cardiac fibrosis was analysed histologically and by qPCR. Cardiac cells were profiled by scRNA-/CITE-seq, flow cytometry, and spatial transcriptomics. Predicted key cell–cell interactions were recapitulated in vitro. Results In STEMI patients, sCD40L peaked 5 days post-admission and was associated with scar size, LV remodelling, and re-hospitalization at 6 months. In mice, a CD40+SPP1+ macrophage population with pro-fibrotic marker expression (e.g. Fn1, Nampt, Spp1) emerged transiently at Day 5 post-MI and co-localized with activated fibroblasts. TRAF-STOP treatment initiated 5 days post-MI reduced CD40+SPP1+ macrophage abundance, attenuated fibrotic gene expression, limited scar formation, and improved LV function. In co-culture experiments, TRAF-STOP ameliorated pro-fibrotic macrophage signalling and macrophage-mediated fibroblast activation. Conclusions In STEMI patients, elevated plasma sCD40L at Day 5 post-MI is associated with larger scar size, impaired LV function, adverse remodelling, and an increased rate of re-hospitalization at 6 months. Mechanistically, this is driven by a transient CD40+SPP1+ macrophage population emerging during the reparative phase of MI that is targetable by CD40–TRAF6 inhibition to limit fibrosis and preserve LV function.

items.title: Correction to: Implementation of cardiac computed tomography in everyday practice: A clinical consensus statement of the European Association of Cardiovascular Imaging (EACVI) of the ESC and the ESC Council for Cardiology Practice
On generative artificial intelligence in scientific writing
items.containerTitle: The Journal of Heart and Lung Transplantation
items.abstract: Scientific communication-the dissemination of ideas, hypotheses, and discoveries-is fundamental to advancing human knowledge and to ensuring public access to new knowledge as it is generated. Growth in the use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in scientific communication has been explosive, likely driven by high uptake among an adept userbase with demanding schedules, making the efficiency gains attractive. The rapid uptake of AI is creating disruptive changes in the way scientific communication happens, affecting the methods by which abstracts, manuscripts, figures, presentations, and funding proposals are generated, and in many cases, impacting the final product. In this perspective piece, we reflect on the rapidly changing landscape of AI use in scientific communication with attention to the potential immediate and long-term risks. The inherent unauthorized secondary use of the data used to train AI models raises questions about credit and plagiarism in academia. Fabricated references have proliferated in the scientific literature resulting from "hallucinations" by AI models. Meanwhile, each use of an AI model comes with an incremental risk to the environment at an already perilous time. More abstractly, AI use in scientific communication risks the process itself becoming iterative, prioritizing summation while diminishing insights that fuel the scientific engine. Finally, the friction that AI models remove from writing may risk removing an essential part of the process of scientific thinking, particularly for the next generation of scientists. While we acknowledge that AI is here to stay, we feel an element of caution is warranted in its implementation to help preserve science and its dissemination as a fundamentally human endeavor.

items.title: Harnessing lung-kidney crosstalk: A novel ex vivo platform for donor lung rehabilitation
items.containerTitle: The Journal of Heart and Lung Transplantation
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: The lack of perfusate metabolic homeostasis during ex vivo lung perfusion (EVLP) may impair lung physiology or stability and limit the application of advanced donor lung therapies. There is evidence that additional organ support during EVLP can improve graft preservation and transplant outcomes. We hypothesized that incorporation of a kidney into an EVLP circuit would maintain perfusate homeostasis and improve lung preservation and metabolic activity. METHODS: A novel circuit was developed to allow simultaneous normothermic perfusion of lungs and kidney in parallel. Donor pig lungs underwent 12 hours of cellular EVLP (EVLP, n=5) or combined cellular ex vivo lung-kidney perfusion (EVLKP, n=5). Lung function was assessed hourly and inflammatory cytokines, edema formation, hemolysis, histologic injury, and kidney performance were evaluated. RESULTS: Simultaneous lung and kidney perfusion achieved target pulmonary and renal perfusion parameters with stable hemodynamics. EVLKP demonstrated trends of higher compliance, lower inspiratory pressure and pulmonary vascular resistance. Perfusate lactate concentration in EVLKP was markedly lower (P<0.0001), glucose concentrations were higher (P=0.0102), and pH shifted towards physiologic levels (P=0.0009) compared to EVLP. Oxygenation capacity was comparable between groups. Kidney perfusion remained stable throughout EVLKP. CONCLUSIONS: Combined ex vivo lung-kidney perfusion is safe and feasible in a large-animal model for prolonged lung perfusion. EVLKP improved perfusate homeostasis compared with EVLP alone, which is associated with trends of improvement in lung physiologic parameters. These findings suggest that kidney-derived metabolic and biological support may provide benefits beyond perfusate filtration and highlight the potential importance of organ-organ crosstalk during ex vivo perfusion.

items.title: Treatment of children and young adults with a Fontan circulation and cardiovascular dysfunction. 2026 Consensus Statement from the European Pediatric Pulmonary Vascular Disease Network (EPPVDN), endorsed by AHA, AEPC, EACTS, ISACHD, ISHLT and PICS
items.containerTitle: The Journal of Heart and Lung Transplantation
items.abstract: The Fontan operation enables long term survival for many individuals born with single ventricle heart disease, but the resulting circulation imposes a lifelong hemodynamic burden and predisposes to cardiovascular dysfunction and multisystem morbidity. Evidence based guidance for assessment and management of Fontan specific cardiac and vascular dysfunction, however, remains limited. The European Pediatric Pulmonary Vascular Disease Network (EPPVDN) convened an international, multidisciplinary executive writing group to review the available literature and develop consensus recommendations addressing cardiovascular dysfunction in children and young adults with a Fontan circulation. Recommendations were graded using established Class of Recommendation and Level of Evidence criteria adapted to the Fontan specific evidence base. The statement addresses cardiovascular assessment, pulmonary vascular disease and use of pulmonary vasodilator therapy, Fontan pathway obstruction, systemic venous and arterial abnormalities and collateral vessels, lymphatic dysfunction and intervention, myocardial dysfunction and heart failure therapy, and thromboembolic risk and antithrombotic therapy. The focus is on phenotype-guided management, hemodynamically informed treatment decisions, and medical, transcatheter, and surgical approaches tailored to Fontan circulation. Seven graded recommendation tables as well as a flowchart for considerations regarding pulmonary vasodilator therapy are provided to support clinical decision making. Fontan-specific evidence remains limited, so many recommendations necessarily represent expert opinion. This EPPVDN consensus statement, therefore, discusses knowledge gaps and priorities for collaborative research to improve outcomes for individuals living with a Fontan circulation.

items.title: Treatment of pulmonary hypertension in infants, children and young adults. 2026 consensus statement from the European Pediatric Pulmonary Vascular Disease Network (EPPVDN), endorsed by AHA, AEPC, EACTS, ESPR, PASCAR, PCS, and PICS
items.containerTitle: The Journal of Heart and Lung Transplantation
items.abstract: The European Pediatric Pulmonary Vascular Disease Network (EPPVDN) is a registered, non-profit organization dedicated to advancing innovative diagnostic methods and treatment options for all forms of pediatric pulmonary vascular disease, including pulmonary hypertension (PH) related to congenital heart disease (CHD), PH associated with developmental lung disease (DEVLD-PH), persistent PH of the newborn (PPHN), postcapillary PH in left heart disease (PH-LHD), and associated cardiac dysfunction/heart failure. In the past, the EPPVDN has published consensus statements on the diagnosis and treatment of pediatric PH (2016, 2019), which have been endorsed by multiple societies. The executive writing group conducted comprehensive searches of the PubMed/MEDLINE bibliographic database (2000 to 2025) and engaged in multiple web-based and in-person meetings. Thirteen section task forces discussed and created consented recommendations. Prospective clinical studies, clinical trials, meta-analyses, expert consensus guidelines, and other articles with pediatric data were included in the search, using the terms 'pulmonary hypertension' and related keywords. Classes of recommendation (COR) and levels of evidence (LOE) were assigned based on AHA/ESC definitions, pediatric PH studies, adult studies including a minimum N number of 15 children, or studies involving adults with CHD. Classifications and definitions from the 7th World Symposium on Pulmonary Hypertension (WSPH) in 2024 were incorporated and discussed. We produced 6 graded recommendation tables (COR, LOE) and 3 algorithms for the treatment of pulmonary hypertension in infants, children, and young adults. A total of 16 main and 17 supplemental display items cover a range of topics, including risk assessment, pharmacological therapy, transcatheter interventions and surgery, recommendations specific to PH subgroups/special populations and clinical settings. Adaptation of management recommendations for middle-to-low-income regions is provided. Together, these up-to-date guidelines provide a comprehensive, detailed, and practical framework for the treatment of pulmonary hypertension in infants, children and young adults, aiming to improve outcomes and quality of life for affected patients.

items.title: Disruptions in US heart transplantation: When innovation outpaces evidence
items.containerTitle: The Journal of Heart and Lung Transplantation
items.abstract: For nearly 4 decades, heart transplantation was defined by a stable, predictable paradigm: brain-dead donors, ice-cooler transport, uniform 3-drug immunosuppression, and biopsy-based surveillance. Within a few years, that paradigm has been upended. In this perspective, we examine the disruptions now reshaping heart transplantation in the United States. Some are desirable: new preservation platforms and the rapid growth of donation after circulatory death, which now accounts for nearly a quarter of US heart transplants, have expanded the donor pool, and cardiac xenotransplantation has reached clinical testing. Others remain controversial: the 2018 allocation policy has altered listing and support practices, normothermic regional perfusion raises unresolved questions about the determination of death, and inconsistent definitions of ischemic intervals undermine comparisons across donation after circulatory death (DCD) studies. Still others are troubling: organ procurement and transplantation network restructuring, uneven organ procurement organization (OPO) performance, outsourced procurement, rising costs, and press reports of donors showing signs of life have strained public trust. Underlying all of these is a data gap: national registries capture few DCD procurement and preservation variables, and little about recipients' long-term health beyond survival. Innovation has outpaced our ability to evaluate its consequences. We propose a shared DCD clock built on fixed timestamps, national ethical standards for normothermic regional perfusion, transparency in procurement and its costs, longitudinal outcome reporting, and accountability shared by OPOs and transplant centers. The challenge facing the field is no longer simply how to transplant more hearts, but how to ensure that more transplantation becomes better transplantation.

items.title: Net prolongation of life with ventricular assist device support in teenagers: Are we there yet?
items.containerTitle: The Journal of Heart and Lung Transplantation
items.abstract: Heart transplantation prolongs survival in children with end-stage heart disease, yet a single donor heart does not provide a normal lifespan. Contemporary graft survival for teenagers is approximately 15 years, the shortest of any pediatric age group, and re-transplantation remains uncommon. For most patients, the first allograft is the only allograft. Recent adult data demonstrating survival with durable mechanical circulatory support comparable to transplantation raise an important question for adolescents: could intentionally extending ventricular assist device (VAD) support through the teenage years, with transplantation deferred to adulthood, increase total life-years? This perspective examines that hypothesis for adolescents with dilated cardiomyopathy. We review the heightened risks of rejection, graft loss, and treatment nonadherence during adolescence; contemporary outcomes with dischargeable durable VADs in children; the potential for myocardial recovery during extended support; and organ allocation policies that may unintentionally discourage a prolonged-support strategy. We also examine patient and family perspectives and discuss unresolved questions regarding stroke risk, allosensitization, long-term quality of life, and optimal timing of transplantation. No prospective data currently support intentional long-term VAD support as a bridge to transplantation in teenagers, and this concept should be viewed as a hypothesis rather than a practice recommendation. However, for carefully selected adolescents who are clinically stable on durable VAD support, delayed transplantation may be a reasonable topic for shared decision-making discussions while acknowledging the substantial uncertainties that remain. As durable device technology continues to improve, evaluating whether prolonged VAD support can achieve net prolongation of life in teenagers warrants prospective investigation.

items.title: Measured left ventricular mass ratio for size-matching identifies graft failure risk in obese heart transplantation
items.containerTitle: The Journal of Heart and Lung Transplantation
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Optimal donor-recipient size-matching in heart transplantation with obese donors and/or recipients remains uncertain. We sought to validate the measured left ventricular mass (mLVM) ratio using local donor hospital echocardiograms, determine whether obesity modifies the association with 1-year graft failure compared to the predicted heart mass (PHM), and assess the clinical implications of discordance. METHODS: The Donor Heart Study prospectively collected echocardiograms from donation-after-brain-death donors. The associations of local mLVM ratio (donor measured LVM/recipient predicted LVM) and PHM ratio with 1-year graft failure (death or retransplantation) were assessed by adjusted Cox proportional hazards models and restricted cubic splines with obesity interaction terms. RESULTS: Among 2,036 heart transplants, size-matching ratios differed significantly by metric within and across obesity groups (all p < 0.001). Obesity significantly modified the association between mLVM ratio and 1-year graft failure (interaction: p = 0.009), but not PHM ratio. In obese transplants, the mLVM ratio demonstrated a U-shaped (nonlinear interaction: p = 0.011) association with 1-year graft failure, with significant adjusted risk at low and high mLVM ratios; where the mLVM ratio captured a unique phenotype associated with graft failure when oversized (>1.20, aHR: 2.50 [95% CI: 1.30-4.82]). Reclassification from PHM to mLVM ratio improved risk classification by 10.4% and concordantly abnormal PHM and mLVM ratios more than doubled the risk of graft failure (aHR: 2.15 [95% CI: 1.10-4.22]) in obese transplantation. CONCLUSION: In obese transplants, locally derived mLVM ratio may identify high-risk donor-recipient mismatches not captured by the PHM ratio, with increased graft failure risk at both low and high mLVM ratios.

items.title: Statement from the International Society for Heart and Lung Transplantation (ISHLT) Consensus Conference on the Evolving Role of Nursing Professionals in Thoracic Transplantation
items.containerTitle: The Journal of Heart and Lung Transplantation
items.abstract: Thoracic transplantation has become increasingly complex, with new donor technologies, higher-acuity candidates and recipients resulting in expanding clinical demands and placing significant pressure on transplant coordinators (TCs) and Advanced Practice Registered Nurses (APRNs), including Advanced Nurse Practitioners (ANPs) in some international centers. The International Society for Heart and Lung Transplantation (ISHLT) convened its second Transplant Nursing Consensus Conference on April 26, 2025, in Boston, to address these pressures and develop actionable recommendations. A multi-method approach integrated 3 sources: a pre-conference international survey of transplant nursing professionals, 2 virtual international roundtables with nurses from 8 countries, and 4 facilitated in-person breakout sessions. Findings converged across sources, identifying incremental accumulation of duties without resource relief, administrative and after-hours burden, role ambiguity between TCs and APRNs, and absent career structures as dominant threats to workforce sustainability. International input revealed wide variation in roles, prescribing rights, and care models, while affirming shared priorities around retention, role clarity, work-life balance, and recognition. Seven overarching themes guided recommendations: staffing models and workload; work environment and retention; workforce roles and qualifications; professional development and impact measurement; clinical processes and protocols; technology and innovation; and patient education access. The panel endorsed acuity-driven staffing ratios, hybrid call structures with protected recovery, offloading non-clinical tasks to dedicated personnel, competency-based career ladders linked to certification and compensation, standardized nurse-led protocols with clear escalation, digital tools that reduce documentation duplication, and a universal modular patient education curriculum. These consensus statements provide an internationally informed blueprint for sustaining the thoracic transplant nursing workforce.

items.title: Evaluating the Feasibility and Clinical Utility of Pre-Transplant Pharmacogenomic Testing in Adult Heart Transplant Recipients - A Pilot Study
items.containerTitle: The Journal of Heart and Lung Transplantation
items.abstract: Background Pharmacogenomic (PGx) testing identifies genetic variations that influence individual responses to medications. These genetically determined differences in drug metabolism necessitate personalized medication selection and dosage adjustments. Adult heart transplant recipients frequently receive multiple high-risk medications. Actionable findings from a priori screening of established PGx variants can optimize medication decisions, minimize toxicity, and reduce suboptimal therapeutic responses. Methods This single-center pilot study retrospectively assessed the feasibility of implementing CLIA-certified PGx testing, including 36 pharmacogenes in 79 adult heart transplant recipients. Patient phenotypes were interpreted as per the Clinical Pharmacogenetics Implementation Consortium (CPIC) guidelines. Actionable gene-drug interactions and dosage recommendations were summarized for each patient by extracting clinical phenotypes, medication history, and PGx-guided prescription recommendations from the electronic health record (EHR). Results The study identified clinically relevant gene-drug interactions including CYP3A5-tacrolimus, CYP2C19-voriconazole, and SLCO1B1-statin metabolism. 57% of the recipients were poor metabolizers/non-expressers of CYP3A5, while 43% were intermediate and extensive metabolizers/expressers. CYP3A5 expressers had higher tacrolimus dose requirements and modestly longer time to therapeutic trough concentrations compared with non-expressers. Genotype-guided changes to tacrolimus doses were made for 23 individuals. CYP2C19 phenotypes affecting voriconazole intake and SLCO1B1 phenotypes affecting statin dosing were also identified, with recommended dosage changes in 11 and 8 patients, respectively. Conclusions Pre-transplant PGx screening revealed a substantial burden of actionable drug-gene findings relevant to heart transplant pharmacotherapy. These preliminary results support the feasibility of pre-transplant PGx testing and may help inform larger studies aimed at PGx-guided care in transplantation.

items.title: Age-Specific Disparities in Pediatric Lung Transplant Waitlist Outcomes Across the LAS and CAS Eras
items.containerTitle: The Journal of Heart and Lung Transplantation
items.abstract: Pediatric lung transplant waitlist outcomes diverge markedly by age group as US allocation policy evolves. Among 980 children listed from 2010-2024, 62.9% were successfully transplanted. Across allocation eras, adolescents achieved sustained improvement in waitlist time, while infants experienced prolonged waitlist times and school-age children remained persistently disadvantaged. Infants had the highest 1-year cumulative waitlist mortality, followed by school-age children, preschool children, and adolescents. These divergent trajectories highlight age-related inequities in pediatric lung allocation and support consideration of age-informed policy refinements.

items.title: Innovations in Temporary Mechanical Circulatory Support in Cardiogenic Shock
items.containerTitle: The Journal of Heart and Lung Transplantation
items.abstract: Temporary mechanical circulatory support (tMCS) can provide rapid hemodynamic stabilization in cardiogenic shock (CS), creating a bridge to myocardial recovery, durable MCS or heart transplantation. Contemporary platforms remain constrained by risk of vascular and hemocompatability-related adverse events, restricted patient mobility and support duration. These limitations have become increasingly relevant as tMCS use expands beyond acute myocardial infarction-related CS to the highly heterogeneous heart failure-related and postcardiotomy shock states. Next generation tMCS technologies seek to address these issues through lower-profile access, improved hemocompatibility, dedicated right- and biventricular support, extended support duration with greater support capabilities, enhanced patient mobility, and integrated physiologic monitoring. This State-of-the-Art Review examines the design rationale, technological maturity, and emerging clinical evidence for these platforms, while highlighting clinical, data-related, engineering and regulatory gaps in the field. Ultimately, the challenge for next-generation tMCS is not simply to deliver greater flow, but to provide appropriate, phenotype-directed circulatory support while minimizing the biological, vascular, and operational costs.

items.title: Ex Situ Echocardiography During Normothermic Perfusion: Serial Physiologic Full Cardiac-Output Assessments for Transplant Suitability
items.containerTitle: The Journal of Heart and Lung Transplantation
items.abstract: Background Clinical normothermic ex situ donor-heart perfusion (NEHP) uses retrograde aortic infusion which prevents hemodynamic assessment. We sought to optimize and validate guideline-directed ex situ echocardiography (ESE) for assessment of transplant suitability using a novel full-cardiac output (FCO) circuit. Methods Following transthoracic echocardiography (TTE), porcine hearts were procured and maintained on NEHP for 24 hours. At hours 1, 12, and 24, maintenance NEHP was transitioned to low-preload working-heart mode (LPWH). Although not physiologic, LPWH ensured optimal coronary perfusion and allowed ESE. Hearts were transitioned to physiologic FCO mode and ESE was repeated. NEHP was returned to maintenance. LPWH-ESE and FCO-ESE parameters were compared to determine their ability to stratify function. Results Forty-two echocardiograms (6 TTE, 36 ESE) were performed (n=6; 55±8 kg; female 50%; hearts 311±40gm). When compared to FCO-ESE, LPWH-ESE at hour 1 underestimated function (cardiac output (CO) 0.78±0.38 vs 3.26±1.70L/min, p=0.012; cardiac index (CI) 0.0024±0.0010 vs 0.0102±0.0048L/m/gm, p=0.009; stroke volume (SV) 8.0±3.5 vs 30.0±8.2mL, p=0.001; stroke work (SW) 279±102 vs 1683±1134mL/mmHg, p=0.026) and correlation was poor (R 2 0.22-0.36). FCO-ESE successfully stratified function between hours 1 and 12 (LVEF 54.6±13.0 vs 33.6±6.0%, p=0.011; CO 3.26±1.70 vs 1.37±0.86L/min, p=0.003; CI 0.0102±0.0048 vs 0.0053±0.0027L/m/gm, p=0.016; SV 30.0±8.2 vs 15.3±6.6mL, p=0.001; SW 1683±1134 vs 686±472mL/mmHg, p=0.029), hours 12 and 24 (LVEF 33.6±6.0 vs 53.0±8.2%, p=0.036, and hours 1 and 24 (SV 30.0±8.2 vs 23.1±6.6mL, p=0.032). LPWH-ESE could not. Conclusion Physiologic FCO guideline-directed ESE should facilitate determination of transplant suitability in currently discarded donor hearts and thereby increase the number available for transplantation. Social media Guideline-directed Ex Situ Echocardiography during physiologic full cardiac output normothermic ex situ perfusion can reproducibly assess donor heart suitability for transplantation #EchoFirst @ASE360 @DHDrake.

items.title: Pushing the boundaries in extending cardiac graft preservation: Hypothermic, oxygenated perfusion (HOPE) versus enhanced normothermic perfusion in a porcine model of donation after circulatory death (DCD)
items.containerTitle: The Journal of Heart and Lung Transplantation
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Excellent outcomes have been reported for heart transplantation with donation after circulatory death (DCD) using graft preservation/evaluation protocols with normothermic ex situ heart perfusion (ESHP); however, little information is available for hypothermic oxygenated perfusion (HOPE). We investigated extending heart preservation with HOPE versus normothermic perfusion (NP) enhanced with plasma exchange using a porcine DCD model. METHODS: Healthy male adult pigs underwent simulated DCD with 15 minutes of warm ischemia. Two ESHP groups were included: enhanced NP (continued as long as ventricular contraction/coronary perfusion was maintained) versus HOPE (20 hours pre-defined duration). Cardiac recovery was evaluated in all hearts under normothermic conditions with ex situ left-ventricular loading. RESULTS: ESHP was significantly longer in HOPE versus NP hearts (23.5 versus 10.5 hours, p<0.05), while ventricular, vascular and metabolic recovery remained similar. Markers of oxidative stress and myocardial cell death, as well as cytokine release, were significantly reduced with HOPE compared to NP, but increased upon rewarming to levels similar to NP hearts. CONCLUSION: Both enhanced NP and HOPE enable extended ESHP of DCD hearts. Although HOPE preservation provides several benefits, such as ESHP times beyond 20 hours and cardioprotection by lowering oxidative stress and inflammation, the transition from HOPE to normothermic conditions poses a risk of rewarming-related damage, and graft evaluation methods during HOPE remain to be developed. Further research towards the optimization of HOPE for DCD hearts is required.

items.title: Integrating Donor Cardiovascular Risk to Guide Coronary Evaluation Strategies in DCD and DBD Heart Transplantation
items.containerTitle: The Journal of Heart and Lung Transplantation
items.abstract: Donor coronary artery disease (CAD) may affect heart transplant outcomes, yet coronary angiography is less common in donation after circulatory death (DCD) than donation after brain death (DBD) donors. We evaluated angiography use, developed a donor CAD risk score, and assessed its association with post-transplant coronary disease. Adult heart transplants in the United Network for Organ Sharing registry from January 2020 through June 2025 were analyzed. Predictors of abnormal donor angiography were selected using least absolute shrinkage and selection operator regression with bootstrap resampling and donor CAD risk score was derived. Post-transplant outcomes were evaluated using Kaplan-Meier and multivariable Cox analyses. Among 17,130 heart transplants, 1,868 (10.9%) used DCD donors. Coronary angiography was performed less frequently in DCD than DBD donors (20.8% vs 49.3%, p<0.001). Of 7,906 donors undergoing angiography, 829 (10.5%) had coronary artery disease. Predictors of abnormal donor coronary angiography included older age, male sex, higher BMI, reduced LVEF, smoking, inotrope use, and vasodilator use. Among recipients whose donors had no pre-donation angiography, each one-point increase in donor CAD risk score was associated with greater post-transplant CAV risk (hazard ratio, 1.10; 95% confidence interval, 1.04-1.16; p<0.001). DCD status was not independently associated with post-transplant coronary disease after adjustment for the risk score. Coronary angiography was less frequently performed in DCD than DBD donors. Although the donor CAD risk score had modest discrimination for donor CAD, higher scores were associated with increased post-transplant coronary disease risk. The score may help identify donor hearts warranting further coronary evaluation, supporting risk-based donor assessment.

items.title: Surgical reentry and evolving post-transplant risk among durable LVAD recipients
items.containerTitle: The Journal of Heart and Lung Transplantation

items.title: Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation in Patients With Pulmonary Hemorrhage
items.abstract: Severe pulmonary hemorrhage may lead to refractory hypoxemia and/or hemodynamic collapse and cause high mortality. However, the use of extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) in this patient population is rare. The aim of this study is to better define and understand this patient population by exploring the baseline characteristics, complications, and outcomes of patients who receive ECMO support due to pulmonary hemorrhage, based on data extracted from the extracorporeal life support organization (ELSO) registry. Between 2003 and 2023, 96 patients received ECMO due to pulmonary hemorrhage. Complications occurred in 54% of the patients, mainly acute kidney injury (AKI) with need for renal replacement therapy (RRT; 28%) and bleeding (pulmonary, gastrointestinal) (15%). Respiratory infections occurred in 37.1% of the patients. The most common diagnostic/therapeutic procedures were computed tomography scans in 9%, bronchoscopy in 41%, surgery in 8%, and apheresis in 6% of the patients. Interventional radiology procedures were performed in only 2% of the patients. Interpretation of these data should be performed cautiously, as underreporting is a known limitation of the ELSO Registry. Forty-seven patients (49%) were weaned from ECMO, and 46 (48%) survived until discharge. Survival and complication rates are comparable to the overall ECMO cohort in the ELSO Registry, which makes ECMO a feasible strategy in this patient population.

items.title: Learning to Live With a Ventricular Assist Device: Patient, Caregiver, and Clinician Concerns Following Implantation and Hospital Discharge
items.abstract: Patients undergoing ventricular assist device (VAD) implantation and their caregivers must attain knowledge and skills to perform VAD self-care safely. Little is known about the similarities and differences among patients, caregivers, and VAD clinicians related to VAD self-care training and management. This study explored the perspectives of 15 VAD patients, 12 VAD caregivers, and 18 VAD clinicians through individual semi-structured interviews focused on understanding barriers related to VAD self-care training and concerns about VAD self-care post-discharge. We identified four major themes (training related, care transitions, fear and uncertainty, clinical consequences). All participant groups discussed concerns related to daily VAD self-care and the transition home after implantation. Caregivers and clinicians discussed the steep VAD self-care learning curve. Caregivers and patients discussed fears in general ( eg , constant fear) and specific terms ( eg , VAD malfunction), whereas clinicians who discussed fear/uncertainty identified strategies for dealing with emergent situations. Concerns regarding adverse events and non-adherence arose primarily from clinicians. Although some alignment was found, concerns varied among stakeholders. A common understanding of these nuanced concerns may improve VAD self-care training and the preparation of patients and caregivers.

items.title: External Validation of a Risk Score Assessment for Pediatric Ventricular Assist Device Mortality
items.abstract: The ACTION score was internally validated to predict mortality after pediatric ventricular assist device (VAD) placement. This study aims to externally validate the ACTION score and compare its performance to the INTERMACS profile for prediction of mortality in pediatric VAD candidates. The publicly available Pedimacs dataset (531 patients) was used for external validation. The Pedimacs dataset as well as a contemporary ACTION dataset (1,304 patients) were used to compare the performance of the ACTION score and INTERMACS profile. A statistically significant linear trend in the proportion of death across increasing ACTION scores ( p < 0.0001) was observed in the Pedimacs dataset, with a receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve demonstrating an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.71. Both the ACTION score and the INTERMACS profile demonstrated a significant linear trend in the proportion of death across scores in the ACTION dataset. Receiver operating characteristic analysis demonstrated an AUC of 0.71 and 0.58 for the ACTION score and INTERMACS profile, respectively. The ACTION score is externally validated with the Pedimacs dataset and is a fair predictor of mortality. The ACTION score performed better than the INTERMACS profile in predicting mortality using both historical Pedimacs data and contemporary ACTION data.

items.title: Serologic Guidance for Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation Selection and Survival Using the Cosmos Dataset
items.abstract: Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) is a life-support therapy for patients with severe cardiac or respiratory failure. Despite its growing use, evidence-based guidelines for ECMO candidacy remain limited due to small, single-center studies and heterogeneous designs. This study leveraged Epic Cosmos, an electronic health record dataset encompassing over 300 million patient records, to analyze outcomes among 42,210 adults treated with ECMO between January 1, 2019, and February 15, 2026, involving 23,116 (54.8%) venoarterial (VA), 14,632 (34.7%) venovenous (VV), and 4,462 (10.6%) hybrid (VA and VV) cases. Hospital mortality varied from 37% (VV) to 50% (VA). Poisson models by ECMO type for in-hospital mortality adjusted for key demographic and clinical variables showed the admitting diagnosis group had the strongest association with subsequent mortality. Several blood chemistry markers measured within the 24 hours before ECMO initiation were also associated with increased mortality, including elevated lactate, elevated creatinine, and lower pH, though strength of association varied by ECMO type. Our findings support the use of large electronic health record (EHR) datasets for ECMO outcomes research and identify exploratory associations between preinitiation biomarkers and in-hospital mortality that require further validation.

items.title: Left Ventricular Unloading With Self-Expanding Pump During Venoarterial Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation in Acute Myocardial Infarction
items.abstract: Increased left ventricular (LV) afterload and distension during venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) support may impede myocardial perfusion in acute myocardial infarction (AMI). Active LV unloading has been associated with improved outcomes. We report the first clinical use of a self-expanding percutaneous ventricular assist device (NyokAssist; magAssist, Suzhou, China) for LV unloading during VA-ECMO in a 56 year old man with AMI-related cardiogenic shock (CS). Successful coronary angiography and percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) of the culprit left circumflex (LCx) lesion were performed with NyokAssist + VA-ECMO support. The patient was successfully weaned from VA-ECMO on post-procedure day 5 and remained on NyokAssist support alone for an additional 7 days before being transferred on VA-ECMO to a heart transplant center for consideration of advanced heart failure therapies due to limited myocardial recovery. No device-related complications were observed. This case demonstrates the technical feasibility of early implementation of a combined VA-ECMO and NyokAssist support strategy, enabling LV unloading, temporary hemodynamic stabilization, end-organ improvement, and VA-ECMO decannulation in a patient with AMI-related CS. As this report describes a single-patient experience, further clinical studies are warranted to define the safety, efficacy, and potential role of the use of NyokAssist in combination with VA-ECMO in the management of AMI-related CS.

items.title: Preoperative Six-Minute Walk Distance Predicts Mortality After Durable Left Ventricular Assist Device Implantation
items.abstract: Accurate preoperative risk stratification remains a challenge in advanced heart failure before durable left ventricular assist device (LVAD) implantation. We assessed whether preoperative six-minute walk distance (6MWD) was associated with all-cause mortality and compared its discrimination with peak oxygen uptake (pVO 2 ). In this retrospective single-center cohort (January 2016–May 2025), 136 of 206 implanted patients had an eligible preoperative 6MWD. Deaths through May 29, 2026, were ascertained from recorded death dates. During follow-up, 85 patients died; median observed follow-up was 871.5 days. The area under the receiver operating characteristic curve was 0.712 for 6MWD (n = 136) and 0.639 for pVO 2 (n = 127); paired comparison in 127 patients showed no significant difference (DeLong p = 0.212). Each 50 m increase in 6MWD was associated with lower mortality (hazard ratio [HR]: 0.88, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.79–0.98). Patients walking less than 350 m had worse survival (log-rank p = 0.002; HR: 1.98, 95% CI: 1.27–3.11). The association persisted after adjustment for age, INTERMACS profile, and device type (HR: 2.12, 95% CI: 1.27–3.54). Preoperative 6MWD may contribute to risk stratification before durable LVAD implantation; the threshold requires external validation.

items.title: Ventricular Assist Devices Effectively Bridge Pediatric Patients to Heart Retransplantation: An ACTION Registry Study
items.abstract: The use of ventricular assist devices (VAD) in pediatric patients as a bridge to heart transplantation has increased over the past two decades. However, the use of VAD to bridge pediatric transplant recipients to retransplantation is rare and under-studied. We performed a retrospective study using the Advanced Cardiac Therapies Improving Outcomes Network (ACTION) registry to evaluate patient characteristics and clinical outcomes in patients bridged to retransplant with VAD. A total of 24 patients were identified and supported for a median duration of 64 days (interquartile range [IQR]: 15.0–101.25). Of these, 54% (n = 13) were implanted as a bridge to retransplant candidacy (BTC) and 46% (n = 11) as a bridge to retransplant (BTT). We found a high prevalence of major adverse events, including infection in 75% (n = 18), bleeding in 42% (n = 10), renal dysfunction requiring dialysis in 33% (n = 8), and stroke in 8% (n = 2). Despite this, 71% (n = 17) survived to retransplant, with an 88% 1 year survival following retransplant. Device mortality was higher in BTC compared to BTT (46% vs . 9%; p = 0.046). Our study is the first multicenter study evaluating the use of VAD as a BTT. We exhibit a high prevalence of adverse events on VAD, but a favorable waitlist and post-retransplant survival.

items.title: ASAIO 2026 Annual Conference Summary
Extracorporeal Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation and Mortality in Pediatric Medical Venoarterial Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation
items.abstract: Extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) using extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) is increasingly used in pediatric refractory cardiac arrest. This study investigated the association between ECPR and mortality in pediatric patients receiving venoarterial ECMO (VA-ECMO) for medical indications. We conducted a retrospective cohort study of patients aged 28 days to <18 years who received VA-ECMO at a tertiary referral children’s hospital between January 2010 and May 2025. The primary outcome was pediatric intensive care unit (PICU) mortality. Among 73 patients (non-ECPR, n = 58; ECPR, n = 15), ECPR was associated with increased mortality in unadjusted analysis (odds ratio [OR], 5.23; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.47–18.53; p = 0.010). After adjustment for pre-ECMO physiologic variables, the association between ECPR and mortality was no longer significant (adjusted OR, 1.74; 95% CI, 0.37–8.08; p = 0.483). Lower pre-ECMO arterial pH remained associated with higher mortality (adjusted OR, 1.87 per 0.1 decrease; 95% CI, 1.20–2.92; p = 0.006). In a sensitivity analysis, underlying cardiac disease was associated with lower mortality than noncardiac disease (adjusted OR, 0.23; 95% CI, 0.07–0.79; p = 0.020). These findings highlight the associations of pre-ECMO physiologic status and underlying disease category with PICU mortality.

items.title: Precannulation Risk Factors Associated With Hemorrhagic Events During Respiratory Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation in Children: A Multicenter Retrospective Study
items.abstract: Hemorrhagic complications are frequent and clinically significant during pediatric extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO), yet associated precannulation factors remain poorly defined. We evaluated these factors in a multicenter retrospective cohort of children receiving respiratory ECMO at four Colombian centers during 2018–2022. A total of 106 children were included; 53 (50.0%) developed at least one hemorrhagic complication during ECMO support, and 83% of events occurred within the first 7 days after cannulation. Cannulation-site bleeding was most frequent (41.5%), followed by intracranial hemorrhage (22.6%) and pulmonary hemorrhage (17.0%). In bias-reduced adjusted analyses, higher precannulation lactate concentrations, lower bicarbonate levels, previous severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) infection, adenovirus infection at admission, and longer mechanical ventilation and vasoactive support before ECMO remained associated with bleeding. Patients who developed hemorrhagic complications had higher 28 day mortality than those without bleeding (39.6% vs . 13.2%; p = 0.002). When bleeding was modeled as a time-dependent exposure, hemorrhagic events were associated with a higher subsequent hazard of 28 day mortality (hazard ratio [HR], 4.93; 95% confidence interval [CI], 2.09–11.64). Hemorrhagic complications affected half of children receiving respiratory ECMO, occurred predominantly during the first week, and were associated with increased mortality. Several precannulation characteristics remained associated with bleeding in bias-reduced adjusted analyses. These hypothesis-generating findings require prospective validation.

items.title: Interpreting Hemodynamic Superiority of Direct Cardiac Compression: The Importance of Experimental Independence and Biventricular Balance
Development and Validation of a Reproducible Cross-Species Liver Machine Perfusion Platform in Rats and Mice
items.abstract: Ex vivo liver machine perfusion is increasingly used for graft assessment and reconditioning, but reproducible small-animal platforms remain limited. We developed a modular rat-mouse liver machine perfusion platform built around a shared extracorporeal circuit backbone with interchangeable cannulation interfaces, continuous inflow pressure monitoring, and a compact dry thermal-bead bath supporting benchtop subnormothermic and normothermic studies as well as cold-room hypothermic deployment. Performance was assessed by methylene blue perfusion mapping with pixel-based quantification and by blinded Suzuki histologic injury scoring. In mice, the portal cannulation site within the superior mesenteric vein-portal segment determined the completeness of whole-organ perfusion; positioning the cannula distal to the gastric/splenic/pancreatic tributary and proximal to the inferior pancreaticoduodenal vein ensured homogeneous lobar perfusion. In rats, single portal inflow left peripheral lobar regions relatively underperfused, whereas dual portal venous plus hepatic arterial inflow produced the most uniform perfusion (perfused surface area 58–75% vs. 100%). Histology showed preserved architecture on liver biopsies, with total Suzuki scores of 0–1 of 12 across procurement baseline, immediate perfusion, and cold storage plus reperfusion groups. Reproducible whole-organ perfusion demonstrated depends on species-specific vascular access. The current platform was validated for perfusion adequacy and short-term structural preservation; metabolically sustained support and functional viability remain to be demonstrated.

items.title: Automated Blood Conditioning for Artificial Lung Evaluation: A Feasibility Study
items.abstract: Artificial organs and Extracorporeal Life Support (ECLS) systems require extensive in vitro evaluation before in vivo preclinical and human trials are conducted. Current methodologies require large volumes of blood, extensive manual labor, and lengthy conditioning periods. To remedy these shortcomings, an “Automated Blood Conditioning (ABC) platform” was developed. Automated blood conditioning is a closed-loop perfusion circuit, control algorithm, and protocol that rapidly conditions and continuously maintains blood conditions for artificial lung and ECLS system evaluation, permitting efficient testing of ECLS devices with minimal blood volume, and showing potential for long-term use. The platform includes a hemoconcentrator, Terumo CDI 500 blood parameter monitor (CDI 500), custom gas mixer, and computer-based controller. A proportional-integral-derivative (PID) algorithm automatically adjusts sweep gas concentrations to maintain target inlet blood conditions despite disturbances from the test device. From arterial conditions, oxygen saturation (sO 2 %) settles at the venous target of 65% in approximately 5 minutes, and partial pressure of carbon dioxide (pCO 2 ) at 45 mm Hg in approximately 6 minutes. In this feasibility study, four independent runs on separate blood batches (48.5 hours) held sO 2 % within ±5% of target for 99.2% of steady-state samples (error 1.2%); the primary evaluation run maintained physiologic conditions for its first 10 closed-loop hours, and device flows up to 0.6 L/min using 1.1 L of blood.

items.title: Reply to Letter to the Editor: Interpreting Hemodynamic Superiority of Direct Cardiac Compression
Hemodynamic Effects of Three Different Mechanical Circulatory Support Strategies in Isolated Acute Right Heart Failure
items.abstract: Although acute right ventricular failure (aRVF) is commonly treated with venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA ECMO), this approach may increase complications. We compared femoro-femoral VA ECMO, single-lumen cannula femoro-pulmonary artery (V-Pa), and double-lumen cannula right atrium-to-pulmonary artery (RA-Pa) support configurations in a swine model of ischemic aRVF-induced cardiogenic shock. Twenty-six adult German Landrasse swine were randomly assigned to the three study groups. Systemic oxygen delivery was the primary end-point; secondary end-points included hemodynamic parameters and complications. Systemic oxygen delivery remained stable during support without intergroup differences.
