Conclusions and Relevance This study found that SBHC access was associated with improved mental health among high school students. There are nearly 4000 SBHCs in the United States, and they are primarily in schools with a high share of students from low-income families. Expanding access to SBHCs may help reduce mental health disparities.

items.title: Error in Article Information
Outcome Ascertainment in Circumcision and Autism Analyses—Reply
Outcome Ascertainment in Circumcision and Autism Analyses
Short-Form Videos and Adolescent Mental Health
Prescription Opioid Misuse Among Youths
items.abstract: Importance Despite reductions in prescription opioid prescribing, adolescents and young adults (youths) in the US continue to experience prescription opioid–related harm. Contemporary national estimates are needed to characterize current patterns of prescription opioid use, misuse, sources of access, and additional substance use. Objective To examine the prevalence of prescription opioid misuse among youths in the context of evolving opioid prescribing practices and the changing opioid epidemic. Design, Setting, and Participants A cross-sectional analysis in adolescents aged 12 to 17 years and young adults aged 18 to 25 years of the 2023 and 2024 National Survey on Drug Use and Health (NSDUH), a nationally representative survey of noninstitutionalized individuals aged 12 years and older related to drugs of misuse and substance use disorders. Data were analyzed from September to December 2025. Exposure Prescription opioid use. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcome was past-year prescription opioid use (defined as both medical and nonmedical use), misuse, and use disorder, along with sources of prescription opioids and concurrent substance use. Survey-weighted prevalence estimates with 95% CIs were calculated and group differences were assessed using χ 2 tests. Results The 2023 and 2024 NSDUH included 22 906 adolescents (aged 12-17 years) and 27 723 young adults (aged 18-25 years), among whom 24 831 (49.1%) were males, 13 256 (26.2%) were Hispanic, 6923 (13.7%) were non-Hispanic Black, 23 114 (45.6%) were non-Hispanic White, and 7336 (14.5%) were non-Hispanic all other races. Past-year prescription opioid use was reported by 13.0% (95% CI, 12.3%-13.7%) of adolescents and 16.2% (95% CI, 15.6%-16.8%) of young adults. Among those with reported prescription opioid use, 11.3% (95% CI, 10.3%-12.3%) reported misuse without use disorder and 7.5% (95% CI, 6.6%-8.3%) misuse with use disorder. Adolescents most commonly obtained prescription opioids from the health care system (42.6%; 95% CI, 32.0%-53.3%), whereas young adults more often sourced them from friends or relatives (44.8%; 95% CI, 39.2%-50.4%). Youths with prescription opioid misuse had substantially higher past-month use of additional substances, including stimulants (5.5% [95% CI, 3.2%-7.8%] vs 0.6% [95% CI, 0.2%-1.0%]; P &lt; .001) and tranquilizers (6.3% [95% CI, 4.8%-8.5%] vs 0.2% [95% CI, 0.1%-0.3%]; P &lt; .001) compared with those without misuse. Conclusions and Relevance This study found that prescription opioid use among youths has declined, reflecting the impact of opioid-prescribing reduction efforts. However, prescription opioid use disorder and concurrent substance use remain prevalent and concentrated among a smaller, high-risk group. As the opioid epidemic continues to evolve, prevention and treatment strategies should address both continued prescribing stewardship with targeted screening, harm reduction, and treatment efforts for adolescents and young adults at greatest risk.

items.title: Short-Form Video Use and Adolescent Suicidality, Nonsuicidal Self-Injury, and Mental Health
items.abstract: Importance Short-form video (SFV) use is widespread among adolescents, but measures that capture only viewing time or only addictive use may miss high-risk subgroups. Objective To examine whether SFV viewing time and addictive use are incompletely overlapping and whether transitions and cumulative exposure to a joint high-risk state are associated with suicidal ideation (SI), suicide attempts (SAs), nonsuicidal self-injury (NSSI), internalizing problems (IPs), and externalizing problems (EPs). Design, Setting, and Participants This 3-wave prospective cohort study (2022-2024) followed adolescents annually in Southern China. Data were analyzed from November 2025 to April 2026. Exposures SFV viewing time and addictive use were jointly classified into 4 use states: low viewing time–low addictive use, high viewing time–low addictive use, low viewing time–high addictive use, and high viewing time–high addictive use. Main Outcomes and Measures At year 3, adolescents reported SI, SAs, and NSSI and completed the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire for IPs and EPs. For each binary outcome at year 3, modified Poisson regression with robust variance was used to estimate adjusted risk ratios (aRRs) and 95% CIs. Results The analytic sample included 10 048 adolescents (mean [SD] age at year 1, 13.9 [1.3] years; 5431 female [54.1%]). At year 1, 1025 (10.2%) reported both high viewing time and high addictive use, and 2592 (25.8%) reported either high addictive use or high viewing time. Compared with adolescents who reported neither high addictive use nor high viewing time, changing to the high state on both dimensions was associated with higher risks across all 5 outcomes, whereas remission from the both high state to the neither high state was not associated with significantly higher risks of SI, SAs, or NSSI but remained associated with higher risks of IPs (aRR, 1.63; 95% CI, 1.31-2.04) and EPs (aRR, 2.20; 95% CI, 1.74-2.79). Cumulative exposure to both high addictive use and high viewing time showed graded associations across outcomes. Each additional year of reporting the high state on both dimensions was associated with aRRs of 1.26 (95% CI, 1.20-1.32) for SI, 1.63 (95% CI, 1.47-1.81) for SAs, 1.33 (95% CI, 1.22-1.46) for NSSI, 1.47 (95% CI, 1.39-1.55) for IPs, and 1.66 (95% CI, 1.58-1.76) for EPs. Conclusions and Relevance Entering, persisting in, or accumulating exposure to the both high viewing time and high addictive use state was associated with higher risks of suicidality, NSSI, and mental health problems. These findings suggest that joint longitudinal assessment of SFV viewing time and addictive use may improve risk stratification among adolescents.

items.title: Father-Inclusive Perinatal Obesity Prevention: A Randomized Clinical Trial
items.abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES Although fathers influence early child feeding, growth, and health behaviors, they are rarely included in early life obesity prevention interventions. We hypothesized that the father-inclusive First Heroes program would reduce rapid infant weight gain and improve parental weight-related and health behavior outcomes. METHODS We conducted a randomized controlled trial (2020-2023) in a Massachusetts health care system, enrolling 227 English- or Spanish-speaking mother-father dyads during the second trimester. Dyads were randomized to the First Heroes intervention—three virtual health coaching sessions plus multimedia content from pregnancy through 12 months postpartum—vs safety education control group. Primary outcomes were odds of rapid infant weight gain from birth to 6 and 12 months and infant overweight at 12 months. Secondary outcomes included maternal postpartum weight retention, paternal body mass index (BMI) change, and parent health care and infant-care behaviors. RESULTS Among 194 infants, intervention participants had lower odds of rapid infant weight gain vs control participants at 6 months (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 0.42; 95% CI, 0.19–0.93) and 12 months (aOR, 0.49; 95% CI, 0.25–0.99); however, there was no difference in odds of infant overweight between groups. Fathers in the intervention vs control group had greater BMI reduction at 6 months postpartum (adjusted difference, −1.08; 95% CI, −2.06 to −0.11). Maternal weight outcomes were not significantly different by randomization group. CONCLUSIONS The First Heroes trial was associated with improvements in rapid infant weight gain, although other primary infant growth outcomes were not significantly different between groups. Future studies should examine strategies to sustain family-based obesity prevention across infancy.

items.title: Engaging Fathers and Mothers to Promote Responsive Feeding and Healthy Infant Growth
items.abstract: Rapid weight gain during infancy, usually defined as change in weight-for-age z score of at least 0.67 during the first 4 to 24 months of life, has a strong association with obesity in childhood and adolescence.1 Despite recognition of modifiable risk factors that contribute to rapid weight gain, identifying practical interventions has remained challenging. In this issue of Pediatrics, Whooten et al2 intentionally engaged fathers in addition to mothers, the traditionally engaged caregiver, in an intervention called First Heroes to provide education and coaching on obesity prevention starting in late pregnancy and continuing through the first year. Compared with the control arm, which received similarly timed education on safety, infants in the intervention group had about half the rate of rapid weight gain.One potential contributor to this effect was a difference in the fathers’ reported feeding practices. Specifically, fathers in the intervention group were less likely to report encouraging their infant to finish a bottle when not hungry, a sign of responsive feeding. Fathers, but not mothers, also reported lower odds feeding infants to sleep or providing juice to their infant. Notably, there were no differences in other factors previously associated with rapid weight gain or pediatric obesity, including duration of exclusive breastfeeding, early introduction of solid complementary foods, or screen time. Behaviors were self-reported rather than observed measures, and thus were vulnerable to social desirability biases. However, the findings reinforce the importance of measuring maternal and paternal outcomes separately rather than assuming a uniform response.3Responsive feeding, as defined by Black and Aboud, consists of 4 processes that include routine and structure, attending to children’s cues, responding promptly to those cues, and creating a predictable feeding environment.4 Together, these processes encourage development of self-regulation in eating prompted by the child’s own psychological and developmental needs. Importantly, responsive feeding practices do not restrict infant intake or prescribe a particular growth trajectory but instead aim to support infants’ developing ability to regulate intake in response to hunger and satiety. Multiple clinical trials have demonstrated that responsive parenting, including a focus on responsive feeding, has positive associations with infant weight gain trajectories.5 Therefore, interventions that increase responsive feeding practices are likely to have beneficial effects for preventing childhood obesity.Here, Whooten et al report on the impact of the First Heroes intervention on 1 specific aspect of responsive parenting (collected via a single questionnaire item), whether the caregiver encouraged their infant to finish a bottle when not hungry. Significantly more fathers in the intervention group reported rarely or never doing this (42% vs 22% in the control group). This question reflects an important component of responsive feeding, which is recognizing and responding appropriately to infant satiety cues. However, as noted previously, responsive parenting is a multidimensional construct that encompasses additional behaviors that were not fully captured by this single questionnaire item. Thus, while the findings suggest that the intervention may have influenced a key feeding behavior, whether First Heroes targeted or changed additional components of the responsive parenting framework is not reported in this article. Future studies testing whether other aspects of responsive parenting can be changed would be interesting and potentially novel information, especially focused on fathers.Nonetheless, the intentional inclusion of fathers is an important evolution from earlier research in this area, which has traditionally focused on mothers. Over the last several decades, fathers have become more active in caregiving responsibilities, including grocery shopping, meal preparation, and feeding their children. Furthermore, feeding practices are known to differ between mothers and fathers, with fathers more likely to use coercive feeding practices that appear to decrease as mealtime involvement increased.6 Thus, interventions that engage both parents from the start may be better aligned with the realities of contemporary families, resulting in strengthened household support for responsive feeding.The intervention was also innovative compared with prior infant feeding interventions by spanning a critical developmental window across the first 1000 days, beginning during pregnancy and continuing through the first year, with tapered frequency and intensity. This longitudinal approach recognizes both the potential influence of prenatal nutrition and that parenting behaviors and family routines evolve rapidly during infancy. The attenuation of parental behavioral effects by 12 months mirrors prior behavioral intervention trials that have similarly reported that outcomes were not sustained long term,5 suggesting that on-going intensive educational efforts are necessary to maintain behavior change.Several characteristics of the study population should be considered when interpreting findings. The relatively low prevalence of overweight in the study sample may have limited the ability to detect differences at the upper extremes of the weight-for-length z score distribution. This may partly explain why differences were observed for odds of weight-for-length z score greater than the 85th percentile at 12 months, but not at the more stringent 95th-percentile threshold. Participants were predominantly well educated, with low rates of food or housing insecurity, and most were first-time parents, which together may have contributed to high engagement during the intervention. Whether similar effects can be achieved among populations at greatest risk for childhood obesity, including those from more socioeconomically disadvantaged backgrounds, warrants further research. Similarly, fewer fathers than mothers participated in the intervention, aligning with prior work showing that father-focused research faces recruitment challenges related to sociocultural expectations surrounding feeding practices and low paternal confidence in their knowledge of their child’s eating behaviors.3 Future studies should prioritize strategies to recruit and retain diverse populations of fathers.Another key next step will be determining how to sustain the positive effects of dual-parent responsive feeding interventions in a manner that is both scalable and cost-effective. Primary care and early childhood care programs may be important resources to reinforce these messages without creating entirely new infrastructure. Personalized digital supports including mobile phone applications, text messages, videos, or virtual coaching may also prove beneficial, but additional research is needed to identify the most effective components to influence outcomes.7The findings from Whooten et al move the field beyond risk identification, providing encouraging evidence that a family-centered intervention beginning prenatally can reduce rapid infant weight gain, a well-established risk factor for later childhood obesity. Although additional work is needed to determine how best to sustain these behavioral changes and extend their benefits to diverse populations, engaging both parents in responsive feeding education represents a promising strategy for early obesity prevention. Integrating responsive feeding education into existing systems that routinely support families during pregnancy and infancy may provide a scalable opportunity to promote healthy growth from the very beginning.ChatGPT Edu (OpenAI) through the University of Colorado was used for refining the outline, for minor grammar editing and for the title.

items.title: Supporting the Health and Well-Being of Youth Aging Out of Foster Care: Policy Statement
items.abstract: This policy statement examines disparities and structural barriers affecting youth aging out of foster care and evaluates existing policy efforts, such as extended foster care and Medicaid expansion, that have expanded access to care but remain constrained by administrative complexity, workforce shortages, and fragmented systems of care. This statement provides policy recommendations to improve outcomes for this population, including centering lived experience in policy development, strengthening collaboration between pediatricians and child welfare systems, expanding access to extended foster care, and enhancing transition planning for health care. Pediatricians play a key role in advocacy and trauma-informed care to support successful transitions to adulthood.

items.title: Advancing Pediatric Workforce Diversity and Culturally Effective Health Care for a Changing US Child Population: Policy Recommendations for Change: Policy Statement
items.abstract: This policy statement provides recommendations on enhancing pediatrician workforce diversity and providing culturally effective health care (CEHC). It highlights the barriers that racism and other biases create in providing culturally effective pediatric care and achieving child health equity. There are 3 interconnected areas needing greater attention: 1) expanding the underrepresented in medicine (URiM) candidate pool through fostering health career aspirations among diverse youth; 2) enhancing recruitment, retention, and leadership development of URiM pediatricians through facilitating health care system change; and 3) advancing CEHC delivery through synergistic efforts addressing care during clinical encounters, ability to access care, and ongoing improvement processes.

items.title: A Community-Engaged Research Partnership to Address Behavioral Health Inequities in ADHD Care
Weight Estimation and Dose Calculation in Resuscitation: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.abstract: CONTEXT The accuracy of instruments to estimate weight and calculate drug doses in children requiring medications during resuscitation is a critical patient safety issue. OBJECTIVE To determine if length-based tapes were superior to other instruments for drug dose calculation or improved the accuracy of weight estimation, time to drug administration, drug dose accuracy, or clinical outcomes during resuscitation. METHODS We systematically reviewed Embase, PubMed, and the Cochrane Library from inception to December 19, 2025. Systematic reviews, randomized controlled trials, nonrandomized studies were included. Country, sample size, study design, and results were extracted. RESULTS In the 250 included studies, 9 enrolled children requiring resuscitation. Compared with the Broselow tape, the PAWPER tape (a length-based tape with habitus correction) was superior for time to drug administration, drug dose accuracy, and weight estimation accuracy in all analyses. In direct paired meta-comparison for the proportions of estimates within 10% (P10), the PAWPER tape was superior to the Broselow tape (odds ratio, 2.48; 95% CI, 2.04–3.02]). All age-based formulas were consistently inaccurate (P10 < 50%). Findings were consistent across countries classified by income levels. There were no patient outcomes data. Children exceeding the length of the tape and children with skeletal deformities and growth restrictions were excluded from many source studies. CONCLUSIONS There were no studies of patient outcomes for instruments calculating drug dosing during resuscitation. Time to drug administration, drug dose, and weight estimation accuracy were superior with a length-based tape with body habitus correction compared with tapes without habitus correction in all populations.

items.title: Adolescent Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy Can Be the First Clue to Multisystem Mitochondrial Disease
items.abstract: Up to 40% of children with mitochondrial disease develop hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) during their disease course, but HCM is almost never the first presenting manifestation. When it is, the underlying mitochondrial disorder is easily missed: the cardiomyopathy is managed in isolation, and extracardiac findings that emerge later may be dismissed as unrelated. We describe an adolescent whose severe HCM was the first major manifestation of clinicopathologically confirmed multisystem mitochondrial disease with a phenotype consistent with Leber hereditary optic neuropathy. Her cardiomyopathy was managed in isolation for over a year before optic atrophy, primary ovarian insufficiency, osteopenia, and exercise intolerance were ultimately recognized as part of a single mitochondrial process. Endomyocardial and skeletal muscle biopsy confirmed mitochondrial pathology. The diagnosis directly changed management: cofactor supplementation was initiated, her visual acuity stabilized on idebenone, and perioperative planning for transplantation was adapted to prevent catabolic decompensation. Her cardiac disease progressed to heart failure requiring transplantation at age 16 years, but she remains clinically stable with preserved graft function more than 15 years later. This case challenges the assumption that mitochondrial disease should enter the differential only after neurologic dysfunction appears. General pediatricians, who see the whole child longitudinally, are uniquely positioned to recognize when dysfunction in other high-energy tissues points toward a unifying mitochondrial diagnosis in a child with cardiomyopathy.

items.title: To Test or Not to Test? A Dilemma in Prenatal Testing for an Adult-Onset Genetic Condition
items.abstract: Pediatric genetic testing for adult-onset genetic conditions is controversial and generally not recommended because of concerns about protecting a future child’s autonomy to decide as an adult whether to know their genetic status. Yet, preimplantation genetic testing of embryos and prenatal diagnosis of fetuses for adult-onset genetic conditions are routinely offered to at-risk prospective parents when parents intend to select unaffected embryos or terminate an affected pregnancy to avoid having a child with the condition. These commentaries consider a case in which expecting parents (1 of whom is at risk) request prenatal testing for Huntington disease (HD), a genetic, progressive, adult-onset neurological condition, but do not intend to terminate the pregnancy if affected. Such situations highlight the tension between protecting a potential child’s interest in an open future and honoring prospective parents’ reproductive autonomy and ability to make decisions that they determine to be in the best interests of their family and future child. The first commentary highlights ethical distinctions in the case from obstetric and pediatric perspectives. The second commentary considers the role of parental reason-giving in shifting ethical reasoning and deliberation between prenatal and pediatric frames of reference. The third commentary, from the perspective of an HD community member, offers reflections on the breadth of personal and family experiences of HD that may inform choices about prenatal testing. The fourth commentary considers clinicians’ process-related obligations while counseling families about prenatal testing for adult-onset conditions to argue for a shared decision-making model.

items.title: Primary Care Spending as a Proportion of Total Spending for Children vs Adults
items.abstract: BACKGROUND A crisis in primary care access for adults has led to calls to increase primary care spending to specific targets. It is unknown whether the same targets for primary care spending should be used in pediatrics since total and primary care spending patterns differ between adults and children. METHODS We determined percent of total spending devoted to primary care and average expenditures, along with trends over 20 years, by payer type (commercial vs. Medicaid) and age group, using the Medical Expenditure Panel Survey. RESULTS Primary care share averaged 8% during this period across all ages without significant change over time. Pediatrics (0-18 years) averaged 17.0%, partly reflecting lower total spending in pediatrics (fewer hospitalizations, expensive surgeries, and medications). Average expenditures ranged from $2,767 for 0-18 y.o. to $14,429 for elder adults. Primary care share was lower for children insured by Medicaid (11.7%), likely reflecting higher rates of chronic and complex conditions. Among all children, per capita primary care spend was $470, but varied from $276 for those on Medicaid to $494 for commercially-insured children. CONCLUSIONS Lower total pediatric expenditures partly reflect less high-cost need, but also high rates of Medicaid coverage with low payment. Pediatric primary care will benefit from increasing primary care percent spend and improvements in financing pediatric care. As percent expenditure on primary care for children is already higher than for older populations, simply raising it to a specific target (e.g., 15%) will benefit pediatrics less than other strategies (e.g., doubling primary care spend).

items.title: Bringing Children Into the Primary Care Investment Debate
items.abstract: The work of pediatrician Barbara Starfield established that primary care is unique. Defined by first-contact access, continuity, comprehensiveness, and coordination—and delivered through enduring relationships with patients and families—primary care provides the essential foundation for any high-performing health care system. Yet the United States has persistently underinvested in that foundation, leaving primary care practices chronically under resourced.1 Recognizing this crisis for the overall population, states and national organizations are measuring primary care spending, setting explicit investment targets, and pressing to rebalance the health care dollar toward primary care. Although these approaches differ in payer scope, definitions, and enforcement, they share a central premise: within a constrained health care budget, greater investment in primary care must be intentional rather than left to market forces. One recent expression of this movement, the Triple Double campaign, calls for doubling primary care investment from 5% to 10% of health care spending, while also doubling its reach and the proportion of the next generation choosing primary care.2 In this issue of Pediatrics, Perrin et al ask an essential question that this movement has largely left unanswered: What should primary care investment policy mean for children?3

items.title: Are They Flourishing? Enhancing Learner Well-Being in the Clinical Learning Environment
Gestational Age–Associated Pathogen Distributions in Very Preterm Infants With Sepsis
items.abstract: Early-onset sepsis (EOS) and late-onset sepsis (LOS) contribute substantially to morbidity and mortality among very preterm infants.1,2 Prior national evaluations described sepsis incidence and pathogens among US very preterm infants but did not characterize gestational age (GA) distribution in detail.3–5 GA-associated pathogen variation informs empirical therapy and prevention, particularly among infants born at the lowest GAs, who experience profound immunologic immaturity, prolonged hospitalization, and intensive invasive support that may alter microbial exposures and colonization patterns.6,7 The objective of this study was to define GA-associated distributions of EOS and LOS pathogens.Vermont Oxford Network (VON) is a global quality improvement and research collaborative.8 This observational study included all infants born weighing 1500 g or less and/or at 29 weeks, 6 days gestation or younger in 795 centers across 49 states between January 1, 2021, and December 31, 2024. Infants who died in the delivery room were excluded.EOS was a culture-confirmed bacterial infection of blood or cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) within 3 days of birth.5 LOS was a culture-confirmed bacterial or fungal infection of blood or CSF occurring beyond 3 days after birth, through discharge, death, or first birthday.9 Episodes were classified as EOS or LOS by day of first positive culture for an episode. EOS incidence was calculated per 1000 eligible infants and LOS incidence per 1000 infants hospitalized beyond 3 days, overall and by GA strata. Pathogens defined by the VON manual of operations10 were summarized as proportions of cases representing either 3% or higher in any GA group or as established pathogens of clinical relevance. The data set does not distinguish polymicrobial from repeat infections. Coagulase-negative staphylococcal (CONS) infections were classified as LOS only with clinical signs of infection and at least 5 days of antibiotics. Because these criteria apply to all organisms, CONS cannot be classified as pathogen or contaminant in polymicrobial bacteremia. For incidence, each infant could be counted once for EOS and once for LOS. For pathogen distributions, each organism was included and tabulated separately. Missing data were not imputed; characteristics were summarized among infants with nonmissing values, with the denominator reported for each variable.As a post hoc analysis, we compared incidence and pathogen proportions between infants born at 23 weeks’ gestation or earlier and those born at 24 weeks’ gestation or later, reporting absolute differences with 99% CIs. Incidence differences were expressed per 1000, and pathogen differences, calculated at the organism level, in percentage points. Analyses were performed using SAS 9.4.The VON Research Repository is a deidentified, HIPAA-compliant data set with WCG Institutional Review Board (https://www.wcgclinical.com) approval for queries.There were 168 235 infants eligible for inclusion; demographic and clinical characteristics are shown in Supplemental Table 1.Overall, 2151 infants (1.3%; 12.8 per 1000) had EOS; incidence decreased with advancing GA (Table 1). Escherichia coli was the most common pathogen across all GA groups (44% to 50%), whereas group B Streptococcus (GBS) accounted for 16% to 19%. Compared with infants born at 24 weeks or later, those born at 23 weeks or earlier had higher proportions of non-GBS streptococci and Klebsiella species (Supplemental Table 2).Among 161 338 infants (96%) who remained hospitalized beyond 3 days and were therefore at risk for LOS, 16 140 (10.0%; 100.0 per 1000) developed at least one episode of LOS; incidence decreased with advancing GA (Table 2). CONS proportions were stable across GA strata, and together, CONS and Staphylococcus aureus represented half of cases. E coli was the third most common pathogen. GBS infections increased with advancing GA (3.1% at ≤23 weeks to 5.9% at >29 weeks), whereas fungal infections declined (8.2% at ≤23 weeks, 4.8% at 24–25 weeks, and 2.6% at >29 weeks). Compared with infants born at 24 weeks or later, those born at 23 weeks or earlier had higher proportions of fungi, Enterococcus species, and Pseudomonas species and lower proportions of S aureus and GBS (Supplemental Table 3).Overall incidence and leading pathogens of EOS and LOS were similar to prior VON reports.3,4 Pathogen distributions were largely similar across GA strata, with modest differences observed among the most immature infants. Recognizing these differences may help clinicians identify gaps in coverage when infants deteriorate despite initial empirical antibiotic therapy.For EOS, E coli was the predominant pathogen across GAs, and infants born at 23 weeks’ gestation or earlier had modestly higher proportions of some less common organisms. For LOS, staphylococcal infections accounted for half of cases. Fungal infections were more common at lower GA and declined with maturity, whereas GBS increased with GA. These gradients likely reflect GA-dependent differences in immune maturation and care exposures.Strengths include a large national sample with standardized definitions. Limitations include the absence of antimicrobial susceptibility data, incomplete fungal speciation, no fungal infection data for EOS, and lack of antibiotic and antifungal exposure data, including antifungal prophylaxis. In addition, the data set cannot distinguish a single polymicrobial episode from separate sequential infections for EOS or LOS. Differential survival and time at risk across GA strata may influence LOS incidence and pathogen distribution.The modest GA-associated differences do not by themselves justify broader empirical coverage. Whether the higher proportion of fungal LOS among infants born at 23 weeks or earlier, a group with LOS incidence exceeding 30%, warrants GA-targeted antifungal prophylaxis merits further investigation. These data provide contemporary GA-stratified benchmarks for this growing population of survivors. Ongoing surveillance of antimicrobial susceptibility is needed to optimize empirical regimens.We are indebted to our colleagues who submit data to Vermont Oxford Network on behalf of infants and their families. The list of centers contributing data to this study is in the Supplemental Appendix.

items.title: Beyond Croup: A Phenotype-Based Perspective on Parainfluenza Virus Types in Children
items.abstract: Human parainfluenza viruses (PIVs) caused an estimated 18.8 million acute lower respiratory infection episodes, 725 000 hospitalizations, and 34 400 deaths among children under 5 in 2018, ranking second only to respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). Despite this burden, clinical attention has historically focused on croup, leading to the common perception that parainfluenza is a single disease entity. However, the 4 types differ substantially in taxonomy, tropism, clinical syndrome, and severity. PIV-1, the most common cause of croup, drives biennial epidemics in toddlers, whereas PIV-2 is less frequent but can cause severe disease, particularly in children with underlying conditions. PIV-3 predominates in young infants, causing bronchiolitis and pneumonia clinically like RSV infection, reflecting its early postnatal susceptibility, which may relate to earlier and more frequent viral exposure. PIV-4, historically underrecognized due to culture limitations, usually does not cause croup but is linked to lower respiratory tract disease, hypoxemia, and occasional neurologic complications. PIV infections are most severe in infants, immunocompromised children, and those in low-resource settings. Seasonal patterns vary by type and geography. Advances in multiplex molecular diagnostics now allow rapid type-specific detection, improving clinical interpretation and management. No vaccine or antiviral is licensed. Emerging therapeutics include sialidase-based antivirals with Food and Drug Administration Breakthrough designation; monoclonal antibodies capable of cross-neutralizing PIV-1, PIV-3, RSV, and human metapneumovirus; and messenger RNA vaccines showing early immunogenicity in children. Recognizing the distinct epidemiology, clinical features, and immune responses of each type is critical for informed pediatric care and the development of targeted preventive and therapeutic strategies.

items.title: Mental Health Diagnoses Among Children With and Without Complex and Chronic Conditions
items.abstract: OBJECTIVES Mental health (MH) diagnoses can complicate outcomes of underlying medical conditions. However, prevalence of MH diagnoses across the spectrum of complex and/or chronic conditions is poorly understood. We aimed to (1) compare prevalence of MH diagnoses across categories of complex and chronic conditions and (2) identify factors associated with MH diagnoses among children with noncomplex chronic conditions (NCCCs) and complex chronic conditions (CCCs). METHODS Retrospective cross-sectional study of 2.9 million children aged 5 to 17 years from MarketScan Medicaid Database representing 12 US states in 2022. The primary exposure was mutually exclusive categories of complex and chronic conditions: noncomplex nonchronic (NCNC) conditions, NCCCs, and CCCs. The outcome was presence of a mood or anxiety MH diagnosis (anxiety, depression, bipolar disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorders, trauma-related disorders, and suicide/self-injury) coded at 1 inpatient/emergency department or 2 outpatient encounters. RESULTS Prevalence of MH diagnoses increased with increasing medical complexity and chronicity: 7.6% in NCNC, 16.0% in NCCCs, and 20.0% in CCCs (P < .001). Among children with a CCC, categories with the greatest adjusted odds of MH diagnoses were cardiac (odds ratio [OR] 1.49; 95% CI, 1.44–1.54), neurologic (OR 1.18; 95% CI, 1.14–1.23), and renal (OR 1.13; 95% CI, 1.06–1.21). Among youth with NCCCs or CCCs, Black and Hispanic children had lower odds of MH diagnoses compared to non-Hispanic white children. CONCLUSIONS MH prevalence increased significantly with increasing medical complexity and chronicity. Differences in MH diagnoses were identified across individual NCCC and CCC categories and sociodemographic characteristics. These results may inform future screening, intervention, and health equity efforts among medically vulnerable populations.

items.title: Recognizing and Responding to Medical Neglect: Clinical Report
items.abstract: Medical neglect occurs when a caregiver fails to provide or seek necessary medical care, resulting in harm or risk of harm to a child. This clinical report outlines key diagnostic criteria for medical neglect, emphasizing that medical nonadherence alone does not constitute neglect unless accompanied by (1) harm or risk of harm; (2) significant benefit from recommended care (when care is sought); (3) a favorable risk-benefit ratio; (4) demonstrated accessibility of care; and (5) clear communication of medical advice. Medical neglect disproportionately affects children with chronic conditions, mental health needs, or special health care requirements, while systemic inequities such as poverty, racial disparities, and limited access to care further exacerbate risks. Clinical presentations vary widely, from untreated dental caries to life-threatening exacerbations of chronic illness. A multidisciplinary, family-centered approach is critical to address modifiable barriers including health literacy, transportation needs, and implicit biases while prioritizing the child’s safety. Strategies include enhancing communication, leveraging community resources, and collaborating with child protective services when necessary. This report highlights the pediatrician’s role in advocating for equitable health care access and systemic reforms to reduce disparities. By distinguishing neglect from nonadherence and addressing root causes, providers can mitigate harm and improve outcomes for vulnerable children.

items.title: How Discrimination Shapes Care-Seeking for Black Caregivers of Children With Medical Complexity
items.abstract: OBJECTIVES Black children with medical complexity (CMC) experience a disproportionately high number of hospitalizations and emergency department (ED) visits. This disparity may reflect systemic and interpersonal racism and discrimination. Understanding Black caregivers’ experiences is essential to designing programs that reduce acute care use. This study described caregivers’ experiences of racism and discrimination and explored how these experiences influence care-seeking and communication among Black caregivers of CMC. METHODS In partnership with family advocacy organizations, we recruited Black caregivers of CMC via national advocacy groups, social media, and electronic health record messaging. Eligible caregivers had a child aged 0 to 21 years with a hospitalization or ED visit in the previous year and a score of 3 or more on the Children with Special Health Care Needs screener. Purposive sampling ensured that one-third of participants were from rural areas. Semistructured interviews, guided by Critical Race Theory, were recorded, transcribed, and analyzed thematically. RESULTS Thirty-one caregivers completed interviews. Caregivers described discrimination in health care based on race and other characteristics. Five themes emerged in caregivers’ experiences of racism: dismissal, stereotyping, fear of retaliation, dehumanization, and differential access to resources. These experiences contributed to distrust, caregiver burnout, and perceived negative health outcomes. Caregivers’ responses to discrimination included withholding concerns, advocating, documenting, selecting specific clinicians, managing perceptions, and staying informed. CONCLUSIONS Perceived racism and discrimination shaped how Black caregivers of CMC communicated with clinicians and navigated health care, underscoring the need for health care systems and clinicians to foster trusting partnerships, address structural inequities, and provide equitable, family-centered care.

items.title: Supporting Children, Adolescents, and Families Experiencing Separation and Divorce: Clinical Report
items.abstract: Parental separation and divorce are common and can be associated with a range of adverse outcomes for children and families. Pediatricians are well positioned to support children and families who are experiencing separation and divorce through providing anticipatory guidance and by helping parents support their children during this transition. Additionally, by promoting relational health with all families, pediatricians can support emotional well-being and resilience that may help in mitigating adversities, including separation and divorce.

items.title: Changes in Childhood Food Allergy Following Implementation of Infant Feeding Guidelines
items.abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES Since 2016, Australian infant feeding guidelines recommend introducing allergenic foods into the diet in the first year of life to prevent food allergy. Here, we evaluated whether the prevalence of food allergy in 6-year-old children changed following implementation of these guidelines. METHODS We conducted 2 population-based studies using the same methodology in Melbourne, Australia, before and after the guideline changes, recruiting 5276 12-month-old infants in 2007 to 2011 and 1933 infants in 2018 to 2019. Both studies followed up with children at age 6 years (2012–2016 and 2024–2025 respectively) with questionnaires, optional skin prick tests, and oral food challenges. Direct regression standardization compared prevalence estimates between cohorts, adjusting for demographic differences between the samples. Multiple imputation was used to handle missing data. RESULTS Participation at age 6 years in 2012 to 2016 was 84% and in 2024 to 2025 was 83%. After adjusting for temporal changes in food allergy risk factors, and applying multiple imputation, the prevalence of food allergy decreased: absolute reduction −2.0% (95% CI −3.4% to −0.6%, P = .005; n = 7209) and relative reduction −31% (95% CI −50% to −11%, P = .002). Findings were similar using complete cases (absolute reduction −2.9%, 95% CI −4.5% to −1.2%, P < .001; relative reduction −37%, 95% CI −57% to −18%, P < 0.001; n = 4173). This reduction was primarily driven by changes in cashew and peanut allergy; prevalence of milk and egg allergy did not change substantially in this age group. CONCLUSION These findings provide evidence that infant feeding guidelines recommending earlier allergen introduction may translate to measurable reductions in childhood food allergy at the population level.

items.title: Rethinking the “Best” NICU
Acute Neurologic Decline in a Child With Unexplained Syndromic Features
items.abstract: A 17-year-old female patient was admitted for expedited neurologic examination after multiple falls. She had a history of 34-week prematurity, cognitive impairment, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, and hypotonia without a unifying diagnosis. Over the past 2 months, she developed slurred speech, new extremity tremors, impaired concentration and memory, gait instability, and more frequent incontinence. Initial examination was notable for hypernasal, slurred speech, tremors, tongue fasciculations, and intrusion saccades. Imaging and laboratory analysis were inconclusive for a definitive diagnosis, and she was discharged with several genetic and metabolic panels pending. Five days later, she was readmitted with worsening headache, vomiting, and altered mental status. This case provides key insights into a rare pediatric neurologic disorder, as well as a potentially life-threatening complication early in the course of the disease.

items.title: Euglycemic DKA in an Adolescent Treated With a Sodium-Glucose Cotransporter-2 Inhibitor
items.abstract: Sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) are a class of glucose-lowering medications that were recently approved for pediatric type 2 diabetes (T2D). A serious adverse effect of SGLT2i is euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis (euDKA), a rare life-threatening metabolic emergency that was recognized after an increase in adult cases noted in postapproval safety surveillance programs. To our knowledge, SGLT2i-assoicated euDKA has not yet been described in youth with T2D since SGLT2i received pediatric approval in 2023. We report on a 17-year-old female patient with T2D on an SGLT2i who developed euDKA. She initially presented with vomiting that improved with antiemetics; however, she had persistent ketosis and developed significant acidosis, prompting diagnosis of euDKA. She was treated with intravenous insulin, dextrose-containing fluids, and electrolyte replacement with resolution of euDKA. This case highlights the challenges of recognizing SGLT2i-asosciated euDKA because of its rarity and the lack of hyperglycemia. As an increasing number of youth are started on SGLT2i, practitioners must be aware of the risk of SGLT2i-associated euDKA to allow for early recognition, adequate treatment, and prevention of serious complications.

items.title: Intermittent Theta-Burst Stimulation for Adolescent Depression: A Randomized Trial
items.abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES Intermittent theta-burst stimulation (iTBS) is effective for adult depression, but evidence in adolescents is limited. Anhedonia predicts poor outcomes and correlates with reduced nucleus accumbens–prefrontal connectivity. This trial aimed to determine whether connectivity-guided iTBS targeting this circuit could alleviate depressive symptoms and anhedonia in adolescents with major depressive disorder (MDD) and whether anhedonia improvement mediates the effect. METHODS This randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial enrolled adolescents aged 10 to 17 years with MDD who did not respond to at least 1 adequate antidepressant trial. Active iTBS (1800 pulses/session, 80% resting motor threshold, once daily for 10 weekdays) targeted the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex voxel with the strongest resting-state functional connectivity to the contralateral nucleus accumbens; sham group received identical procedures. Primary outcome was Beck Depression Inventory-II (BDI-II) score change (baseline to 1-month posttreatment). Secondary outcomes were Snaith-Hamilton Pleasure Scale scores, anxiety, and response/remission rates. Exploratory analyses used causal mediation models. RESULTS Of 60 screened participants, 56 were randomized (mean age, 14.7 years; 75% female). Active iTBS reduced BDI-II score more than sham (mean change, 9.46 vs 3.04; difference, 6.43; d = 0.87; P = .002), with significant treatment-by-time interaction (P = .03). Anhedonia improvement favored active iTBS at posttreatment (difference 4.50; d = 0.89; P = .002) and 1-month follow-up (difference 7.46; d = 1.22; P < .001). Mediation analysis showed anhedonia improvement mediated the 1-month effect (indirect −2.38 [95% CI, −5.55 to −0.45]; 42.1% mediation [95% CI, 19.1%-307.5%]). No serious adverse events occurred. CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE Connectivity-guided iTBS significantly reduced depressive symptoms and anhedonia in adolescents with MDD, with effects significantly mediated by anhedonia improvement. Further research into this approach as a precision intervention for adolescent depression is warranted.

items.title: Prehospital Trauma Compendium: Prehospital Management of Pediatric Traumatic Out-of-Hospital Circulatory Arrest – A Joint Position Statement and Resource Document of NAEMSP, ACS-COT, ACEP, and AAP
items.abstract: In 2014 the National Association of EMS Physicians (NAEMSP), American College of Surgeons Committee on Trauma (ACS-COT), American College of Emergency Physicians (ACEP), and American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) published the first joint position statement discussing withholding and discontinuing resuscitation attempts for pediatric traumatic out-of-hospital circulatory arrest (TOHCA). Since then, the body of literature addressing pediatric TOHCA has evolved and evidence has grown that demonstrates the nearly uniformly poor prognosis of children who suffer circulatory arrest in the prehospital setting as a result of trauma. To support emergency medical services (EMS) clinicians in their approach to these high-acuity, low-frequency, and challenging cases, this project aimed to update guidance regarding decisions to withhold or discontinue resuscitation efforts for pediatric traumatic circulatory arrest. NAEMSP, ACEP, ACS-COT, and AAP recommend: EMS resuscitation of pediatric TOHCA should: ○ Prioritize prompt identification of patients who may benefit from transport to definitive care at trauma centers when safe and appropriate. On-scene resuscitation should be balanced against the potential benefit of transfer to a proximate trauma center.○ Emphasize the identification of reversible causes of traumatic circulatory arrest and timely use of clinically indicated life-saving interventions (LSIs) within the EMS clinician’s scope of practice. These include: ▪ External hemorrhage control with direct pressure, wound packing, and tourniquets▪ Airway management using the least-invasive airway interventions required to achieve and maintain airway patency, oxygenation, and adequate ventilation.▪ Chest decompression if clinical concern for tension pneumothorax. Empirical bilateral decompression is not recommended in the absence of suspected thoracic trauma.▪ External chest compressions and ventilations have a larger role in pediatric TOHCA resuscitation than in adult TOHCA resuscitation, with children frequently having TOHCA secondary to head injury, hypoxia and other non-hemorrhagic mechanisms. Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) should be provided when the cause of circulatory arrest is unclear.▪ Epinephrine is of lower priority than other LSIs.○ Consider point of care ultrasound (POCUS) to guide decisions to withhold or discontinue resuscitation efforts.Resuscitation attempts may be withheld in pediatric TOHCA patients with: ○ Injuries that are incompatible with life (eg, decapitation, hemi-corpectomy, incineration).○ Evidence of prolonged circulatory arrest (eg, rigor mortis, dependent lividity, decomposition).○ Advanced care planning documents that indicate Do Not Resuscitate (DNR)/ Do Not Attempt Resuscitation (DNAR)/Allow Natural Death medical orders.

items.title: Bridging Treatment Gaps in Adolescent Depression With Neuromodulation Targeting Anhedonia
items.abstract: Psychotherapy and pharmacotherapy remain the foundations of treatment for adolescent depression. Neuromodulation, such as electroconvulsive therapy or transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), is a relatively new approach to pediatric care and historically has not been used much within the field of child psychiatry. Electroconvulsive therapy is an important and highly effective treatment for selected adolescents with severe depression and catatonia.1 Its use, however, requires anesthesia and specialized clinical infrastructure and remains uncommon in pediatric practice. TMS offers a different form of neuromodulation with fewer procedural requirements that may help patients with significant depression. Anhedonia, or loss of interest and pleasure, deserves particular attention because greater anhedonia is associated with more severe illness and suicidality and may predict poorer treatment response.2,3In this issue of Pediatrics, Duan et al4 report a randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial of individualized functional connectivity-guided intermittent theta-burst stimulation (iTBS) in adolescents with major depressive disorder who had not responded adequately to at least one antidepressant trial. Compared with sham stimulation, active iTBS produced greater improvement in depressive symptoms. Improvement in anhedonia was particularly notable. The authors also found that change in anhedonia statistically mediated a substantial proportion of the later antidepressant effect. This finding does not establish anhedonia as the mechanism of treatment response, but it raises an intriguing possibility that reward-related symptoms may be an important target for neuromodulation.The individualized targeting strategy is another important feature of this study. The investigators selected a left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex region based on its functional connectivity with the nucleus accumbens, an important component of reward circuitry. Dysfunction in this network may contribute to impaired reward processing, reduced motivation, and difficulty engaging in goal-directed behavior. The study therefore provides an example of how treatment may eventually move beyond diagnosis alone and incorporate clinically important symptoms and their underlying circuitry.iTBS also has practical advantages for adolescents. It is a form of TMS that is noninvasive, does not require anesthesia, and can be delivered in an outpatient setting. Individual iTBS stimulation sessions are considerably shorter than conventional repetitive TMS sessions. This may make a repeated treatment course easier to incorporate into school and family schedules.In 2024, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) first cleared a TMS system as an adjunct for treatment of major depressive disorder in patients aged 15 to 21 years.5 Unlike the adult indication that specifies inadequate improvement with prior antidepressant medication, the adolescent indication does not require failed antidepressant trials. This regulatory language should not be interpreted as a recommendation to use TMS immediately after one unsuccessful selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) trial. It does, however, raise an important question about when consultation should occur.For pediatricians, the distinction between consultation and treatment may be more useful than defining a specific treatment threshold. The participants studied by Duan et al4 had greater treatment complexity than many adolescents with depression managed in primary care, including psychiatric comorbidity and substantial concomitant psychotropic medication use. Many were receiving other psychotropic medications, including antipsychotics, benzodiazepines, and mood stabilizers. These findings therefore should not be interpreted as establishing iTBS as the next treatment for an otherwise uncomplicated adolescent who has had an inadequate response to one SSRI.At the same time, referral does not need to wait until treatment has become highly complex. For an adolescent with persistent depression despite adequate initial treatment, particularly when anhedonia and functional impairment remain substantial, consultation with a child psychiatrist may be reasonable. TMS centers are increasingly available across the United States, and many practices can provide treatment to adolescents aged 15 years and older. However, child psychiatrists with specific expertise in neuromodulation remain relatively scarce, and consultation with a pediatric neuromodulation specialist may require referral to a regional specialty or academic center. This consultation model may be particularly relevant to pediatric practice. Pediatricians increasingly care for adolescents with depression because access to specialty mental health care remains limited. Referral for neuromodulation consultation does not require pediatricians to determine TMS candidacy themselves. Rather, it provides another option when initial treatment has not produced sufficient recovery.Several questions remain before this approach can be incorporated more broadly into care. The interaction between neuromodulation and other treatments deserves particular study. Medications may alter response to stimulation, and concurrent psychotherapy may enhance or modify treatment effects. These questions are especially relevant given the medication complexity of participants in this trial. Development also matters. The participants ranged from 10 to 17 years, a period of substantial brain maturation. Larger studies and longer follow-up are needed to better understand developmental differences, durability of response, and cognitive safety.Duan et al4 offer an important view of how treatment for adolescent depression may evolve. Their study combines a clinically meaningful symptom, individualized neural targeting, and a noninvasive intervention. For pediatricians, the immediate implication is not that iTBS should become the next step after an antidepressant fails. It is that neuromodulation can become part of the treatment discussion when depression persists despite appropriate initial treatment. Future research should help define which patients are most likely to benefit, how neuromodulation should be combined with psychotherapy and medication, and when consultation and treatment should occur.

items.title: Interstitial Lung Disease in Term Born Neonates
items.abstract: Congenital panhypopituitarism, also referred to as combined pituitary hormone deficiency (CPHD), is a rare endocrine disorder characterized by deficiency of multiple pituitary hormones, including somatotropins, thyrotropins, lactotropins, gonadotropins, and corticotropins. Neonates with CPHD may initially be asymptomatic or present with nonspecific clinical features, frequently resulting in delayed diagnosis of this potentially life-threatening condition. This article presents 3 cases of term-born neonates in whom early diagnosis of CPHD was established during the investigation of atypical neonatal respiratory distress syndrome, presenting with radiological features suggestive of interstitial lung disease (ILD). All 3 infants exhibited persistent oxygen dependency. Etiological work-up of the ILD revealed central hypothyroidism and cortisol deficiency, consistent with CPHD. Brain magnetic resonance imaging in all cases confirmed ectopic posterior pituitary with pituitary stalk interruption syndrome. Initiation of hydrocortisone replacement therapy led to complete resolution of respiratory symptoms and successful weaning from oxygen. Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome with an ILD-like presentation in term infants may represent an early manifestation of CPHD. Further research into the prevalence of respiratory distress in affected neonates is warranted. A nationwide study across French reference centers for pituitary disorders is currently underway to explore this association.

items.title: A National Pediatric Primary Care Research Agenda
items.abstract: Pediatric primary care (PPC) promotes child wellbeing through health supervision, anticipatory guidance, screening, and intervention. Given an evolving PPC landscape, content experts collaborated with the American Academy of Pediatrics Pediatric Research in Office Settings network in an iterative, multiyear process to create a PPC research agenda to advance child health that reflects professional and family priorities. Using an adapted nominal group technique, we identified research areas of focus based on (1) what PPC clinicians said they frequently encounter in practice; (2) the extent of the problem for families nationally; (3) evidence gaps; and (4) areas in which research could have the highest impact on child health. From 2022 to 2024, we synthesized contributor feedback from 8 key content expert sessions. This process resulted in 6 interconnected domains of highest priority for PPC research: (1) child mental health, (2) obesity, (3) communicating science to support families, (4) pediatric workforce, (5) injury prevention, and (6) adolescent health. We identified cross-cutting themes that warrant research in connection with these 6 prioritized domains. Examples of such themes include removing barriers to access and ensuring quality services for all children; under-resourced communities; care coordination and linkages within and outside PPC; supporting parents/caregivers; and technology and social media, which can serve as tools to enhance practice and can be assets or threats to child wellbeing. This manuscript details a vision for a national, coordinated PPC research agenda to inform investigators’ and funders’ efforts to advance primary health care and the health of all children based on our results.

items.title: Correction to “Pneumococcal Pneumonia in Hospitalized Children: 2017-2023”
items.abstract: Errors occurred in the article by Engstrom EE et al, titled “Pneumococcal Pneumonia in Hospitalized Children: 2017-2023,” published in the May 2026 issue of Pediatrics (2026;157[5]: e2025073196; doi: 10.1542/peds.2025-073196).On page 1, in the Abstract, under Results, the text read: “PCV13 serotypes 3, 19A, and 19F constituted over half of isolates; new serotypes in PCV15 (22F and 33F) and PCV20 (8, 10A, 11A, 12F, 15B, 22F, and 33F) accounted for 14% and 22% of isolates, respectively.”This should have read: “PCV13 serotypes 3, 19A, and 19F constituted over half of isolates; new serotypes in PCV15 (22F and 33F) and PCV20 (8, 10A, 11A, 12F, 15B, 22F, and 33F) accounted for 14% and 23% of isolates, respectively.”On page 3, in the Results section, under Serotypes, the text read: “Serotypes 22F and 33F included in PCV15 and PCV20 but not in PCV13 accounted for 14% of the serotyped isolates, and serotypes included in PCV20 but not included in PCV13 or PCV15 (10A, 11A, 12F, 15B) accounted for 8% of the serotyped isolates. Serotypes not present in any currently licensed pediatric vaccine accounted for 24% of isolates.”This should have read: “Serotypes 22F and 33F included in PCV15 and PCV20 but not in PCV13 accounted for 14% of the serotyped isolates, and serotypes included in PCV20 but not included in PCV13 or PCV15 (8, 10A, 11A, 12F, 15B) accounted for 9% of the serotyped isolates. Serotypes not present in any currently licensed pediatric vaccine accounted for 23% of isolates.”Figures 1 through 3 have been replaced to reflect that 3 serotype 8 isolates originally included under “Non-vaccine serotypes” are now included under the correct category labeled “8/10A/11A/12F/15B.”The online article has been updated accordingly.

items.title: Ocular Screening in Children With Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis or Treated With Hydroxychloroquine: Clinical Report
items.abstract: Ophthalmic screening examinations are critical in children at risk for inflammatory ocular diseases or toxicity from medication use. Children with juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) who are at risk for or have had a diagnosis of uveitis require scheduled ophthalmic examinations. Hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) is a treatment for several pediatric diseases and has a risk for retinal toxicity. Guidance is needed on the frequency of ophthalmic screening and the critical tests to be performed in both settings. Clinicians are highly encouraged to follow adult HCQ dosing recommendations (<5 mg/kg actual weight) until there are more specific data for children. This clinical report addresses recommendations for ophthalmic examinations in children with JIA, children with JIA-associated uveitis, and children receiving HCQ treatment. Families should be counseled about the critical importance of regular screening examinations for reducing the risk of visual impairment from disease-associated complications or medication toxicity. They can be reassured about the relative safety of medical therapy for these conditions if screening guidelines are followed.

items.title: Parent Tobacco or E-Cigarette Use and Adolescent Substance Use
items.abstract: Parental tobacco use is associated with adolescent smoking initiation,1 and parent e-cigarette use is associated with adolescent e-cigarette use.2 However, whether household tobacco and e-cigarette use are associated with broader adolescent substance use risk is poorly understood,3 particularly at population scale.4,5 Using a parent self-report from an electronic health record (EHR)-linked tobacco treatment program6 and an adolescent self-report via a confidential adolescent health questionnaire (AHQ),7 we tested the hypothesis that household tobacco and e-cigarette exposure would be associated with adolescent tobacco, alcohol, marijuana, and other substance use, including high-risk use (defined subsequently).We conducted a cross-sectional analysis of adolescents aged 13 to 19 years with a completed AHQ who completed parent/caregiver tobacco screening questionnaires at their most recent encounters (January 2025-May 2026) within a large pediatric primary care network. Encounters in which both parent tobacco and e-cigarette screening questions were answered “prefer not to answer” or missing were excluded (1.5% of encounters). The AHQ is a confidential previsit questionnaire completed by adolescents that includes a 30-day tobacco/nicotine use item and the Car, Relax, Alone, Forget, Friends, Trouble (CRAFFT) 2.1, a validated 6-item screen for adolescent substance use, with a score of 2 or more indicating a high risk for a Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition substance use disorder.8 Household tobacco and e-cigarette use was categorized as tobacco and e-cigarettes, tobacco only, e-cigarettes only, or none (reference), based on any parent/caregiver’s report of use for themselves (respondent), another adult household member (excluding the adolescent), or both. Patient race and ethnicity, obtained from EHR registration data, were reported to characterize the cohort. Multivariable logistic regression estimated adjusted odds ratios (aOR) and 95% CIs for each adolescent outcome, adjusting for child age, sex, insurance, and Child Opportunity Index (COI).9 This study was determined to be exempt by the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia institutional review board.Of 60 069 adolescents, 57.5% were aged 13 to 15 years, 49.8% were female, 49.7% non-Hispanic white, 22.8% non-Hispanic Black, and 8.4% Hispanic/Latino; 30.6% had Medicaid/ Medicaid/Children’s Health Insurance Program and 17.8% had very low COI. Adolescent tobacco use was 23.5% among those with combined parent/caregiver and household tobacco and e-cigarette exposure, compared with 13.5% with parent/caregiver-only tobacco use, 11.8% with household-only tobacco use, and 2.0% with no reported tobacco product use (Table 1). Similar patterns were observed across alcohol, marijuana, other drug use, and CRAFFT scores of 2 or more. After adjustment for child age, sex, insurance, and COI, combined parent-and-household tobacco and e-cigarette exposure was associated with the largest odds of adolescent tobacco use (aOR 12.87; 95% CI 8.55–18.96) and high-risk substance use (CRAFFT ≥ 2: aOR 14.85; 95% CI 9.67–22.21); odds were lower for either exposure source alone; among parent-only exposures, e-cigarette use alone was associated with greater odds of adolescent tobacco use (aOR 5.64; 95% CI 3.98–7.79) than combustible tobacco use alone (aOR 2.58; 95% CI 2.03–3.24), a pattern that held across most outcomes (Table 2).In this cross-sectional study, household tobacco and e-cigarette exposure was consistently associated withadolescent substance use, with the strongest associations when both a parent/caregiver respondent and another household member reported use. Parent e-cigarette use was associated with higher rates of adolescent substance use across most outcomes compared with parent combustible tobacco alone, suggesting e-cigarettes represent a distinct household risk exposure; this warrants further study because e-cigarettes may serve as a cessation aid for some parents or be perceived as vaping. A dose-response pattern across exposure tiers was consistent with social modeling and household access as plausible mechanisms1,4 and persisted after adjustment for socioeconomic factors.EHR-linked parent tobacco treatment programs capture household tobacco and e-cigarette status, and our results suggest this information could identify adolescents at elevated substance use risk. This may enable pediatric settings to support parental cessation and deliver substance use prevention for at-risk adolescents.Limitations include the cross-sectional design limiting assessment of causality, self-report misclassification, and generalizability limited to a single health system. We lacked data on parental use of other substances (eg, alcohol, cannabis), which may confound or contribute to the observed associations. The household tobacco questions ask about other household members; the questionnaire emphasizes adult use, and no adolescents have been referred through our cessation pathway, suggesting misclassification is unlikely. Future work is needed to examine associations between household exposure and adolescent use trajectories and test whether parent interventions (eg, EHR-linked parent respondent and/or household referral treatment programs6,10) can reduce adolescent risk.

items.title: Handheld Ultrasound Confirmation of Pediatric Endotracheal Intubation in a Resource-Limited Country
items.abstract: Objectives: Chest radiograph (CXR) and colorimetric capnography for confirmation of endotracheal tube (ETT) placement may be costly and inaccessible in resource-limited countries. Point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) is considered a low-cost, fast alternative. We sought to study the accuracy of bedside POCUS as compared with CXR, using a pocket-sized handheld device, for confirmation of ETT placement in the neonatal ICU and PICU. Design: Prospective, observational study. Setting: PICU and neonatal ICU in a tertiary care center in Nepal between October 1, 2023, and April 30, 2024. Patients: Newborns to 14-year-old children. Interventions: POCUS using a handheld device at the bedside. Measurements and Main Results: POCUS was performed on 59 intubated children; 37 (62%) were males. Median age was 3 hours (interquartile range [IQR], 1–5 hr) in newborns ( n = 27) and 24 months (IQR, 12–84 mo) in children ( n = 32). POCUS demonstrated tracheal-confirmed ETT placement in 53 children (89.8%), suspected endobronchial in four, and indeterminate in two. CXR agreed with all 53 POCUS tracheal-confirmed intubations. There were three additional tracheal-confirmed cases on CXR and three endobronchial intubations. Sensitivity and specificity of POCUS for detection of ETT placement in the trachea, compared with CXR, were 94.6% (95% CI, 85.1–98.9%) and 100% (95% CI, 29.2–100%), respectively. Based on this, accuracy was calculated at 94.9%. Conclusions: Our study demonstrated good accuracy of POCUS using a handheld device to confirm ETT placement in neonates and children. It could be a reliable and effective method in a resource-limited country like Nepal.

items.title: Between the Dings
Postoperative Infection Mediates and Modifies the Effect of Risk Adjustment for Congenital Heart Surgery-1 Category on Hospital Stay in Pediatric Cardiac Surgery: A Retrospective Cohort Study
items.abstract: Objectives: To investigate whether postoperative infection mediates and/or modifies the effect of surgical complexity, as defined by the Risk Adjustment for Congenital Heart Surgery (RACHS-1) category, on hospital length of stay (LOS) in pediatric cardiac surgery patients. Design: Retrospective cohort study. Setting: Tertiary pediatric cardiac center at Xinhua Hospital, Shanghai Jiao Tong University. Patients: A total of 1244 children who underwent congenital heart surgery between October 2020 and July 2024. Interventions: None. Measurements and Main Results: Multivariable regression and causal-mediation analyses were performed to estimate the direct and infection-mediated effects of surgical complexity on LOS. Higher-RACHS-1 categories and postoperative infection were independently associated with prolonged LOS (all p < 0.001). In negative binomial mediation analysis, infection mediated 17.4% of the total RACHS–LOS association for RACHS-1 category greater than or equal to 5 vs. 1, corresponding to an infection-mediated increase of 3.87 expected LOS days (95% CI, 1.70–6.42). Infection also modified the association between surgical complexity and LOS, with infection-associated excess LOS increasing to +16.73 days in RACHS-1 category greater than or equal to 5 vs. 1. Mediation was strongest among infants less than or equal to 1 year (28% for RACHS-1 category 3 vs. 1). Conclusions: Postoperative infection both mediates and amplifies the impact of surgical complexity on hospital LOS, particularly in high-risk infants. Targeted infection-prevention strategies are essential to reduce postoperative morbidity in this population.

items.title: The Serum Proteomic Signatures Associated With Organ Dysfunction Based on Phoenix Criteria in Pediatric Sepsis: A Pilot Study
items.abstract: Objectives: To investigate the serum proteomic characteristics linked to sepsis-induced organ dysfunction, as defined by the Phoenix Pediatric Sepsis (PPS) criteria. Design and Setting: We conducted a serum proteomic study using data-independent acquisition mass spectrometry in pediatric patients with sepsis, admitted to the PICU at a tertiary, university-affiliated children’s hospital in China. Patients: Thirty-eight patients with sepsis and 19 healthy controls were included from November 2020 to June 2022. Interventions: None. Measurements and Main Results: A total of 403 differentially expressed proteins (DEPs) were identified in the serum of pediatric sepsis patients compared with healthy controls. Gene Set Enrichment Analysis revealed that DEPs across the four PPS-defined organ dysfunction were enriched in the antimicrobial humoral response, negative regulation of inflammation, plasminogen activation, and cytokine-mediated signaling pathways. Weighted Gene Co-Expression Network Analysis (WGCNA) showed that the MEgreen module was highly associated with the PPS score and was enriched in neutrophils. Further analysis identified seven hub proteins (tissue inhibitor of metalloproteinase-1 [TIMP1], cathepsin L peptidase 1, β-1,4-galactosyltransferase 1, carbonic anhydrase 3, interleukin 1 receptor like 1, olfactomedin 4, and cathepsin G [CATG]) as candidate serum proteomic markers of organ dysfunction risk. We used the expression of these seven hub proteins in a least absolute shrinkage and selection operator regression model to predict organ system dysfunction. It achieved an area under the curve of 0.857 for the coagulation system and 0.769 for the cardiovascular system. All seven hub proteins were significantly correlated with lactic acid and the international normalized ratio (all p < 0.05); CATG was positively correlated with mean arterial pressure ( p = 0.005), TIMP1 displayed a positive correlation with d- dimer ( p = 0.021) and a negative correlation with platelet ( p = 0.005). Conclusions: We identified seven hub proteins that constitute a novel proteomic signature for predicting sepsis-associated organ dysfunction based on the Phoenix criteria. It is particularly relevant to the coagulation and cardiovascular systems.

items.title: The Quiet Struggle: Parental Perspectives on Sibling Well-Being During PICU Admission
items.abstract: Objective: To identify the impact of PICU admission on parental perceptions of the well-being of patients’ child-aged siblings and understand how families use hospital resources to support siblings. Design: Qualitative study using semi-structured interviews of parents of PICU patients with siblings to characterize sibling socioemotional changes during PICU admission and how the sibling interacted with hospital resources. Interviews were transcribed and thematically analyzed. Setting: Quaternary-care PICU at a level 1 trauma center in St. Louis, MO. Subjects: Parents of a child admitted to the PICU with at least one additional child living at home between the ages of 5 and 19 years. Interventions: None. Measurements and Main Results: Fourteen biological parents and one legal guardian representing 15 households and 17 siblings of PICU patients were interviewed. Four themes were identified describing parental perspective on sibling psychosocial well-being: 1) routine is important, 2) parents consider multiple factors when evaluating the impact of sibling visits on child well-being, 3) hospitalizations impacts sibling well-being in many ways, and 4) few siblings’ physical well-being changed following hospitalization. Two themes were identified regarding parental perspective of hospital resources: 5) parents believed that hospital support was designed to cultivate a sense of normalcy, and 6) the provision and utilization of child life services was not uniform. Conclusions: It is critical to prioritize the emotional and social well-being of siblings of critically ill and injured children through the maintenance of routine, balancing the needs of both patient and sibling when considering visitation policies, and providing hospital supports tailored to sibling’s age and cognitive level.

items.title: Who Counts in Pediatric Sepsis? Lessons From Ibero-Latin America
Sepsis Point Prevalence Across Ibero-Latin America PICUs: The 2024 Sepsis Prevalence Assessment Database in Pediatrics (SPREAD PED IBERO-LATAM)
items.abstract: Objectives: To determine the prevalence and outcome of sepsis in PICUs across Ibero-Latin America; to identify patient- and institution-level factors associated with mortality; and to explore the prognostic performance of pediatric sepsis definitions. Design: Multinational, multicenter, prospective point prevalence study with follow-up to hospital discharge. Setting: One hundred sixty-eight PICUs in 21 countries across Latin America, Spain, and Portugal. Patients: Children of 28 days to 18 years with a clinical diagnosis of sepsis or septic shock admitted to participating PICUs between September 9 and September 13, 2024. Interventions: None Measurements and Main Results: Among 1318 screened PICU patients, 340 met criteria for clinical sepsis, yielding a point prevalence of 25.8% (95% CI, 23.5–28.2%). Complete outcome data were available for 324 patients. PICU mortality was 42 of 324 (13.0% [95% CI, 9.5–17.1%), and total in-hospital mortality was 49 of 324 (15.1% [95% CI, 11.4–19.4%]). Cardiovascular and respiratory dysfunction were most frequent, whereas multivariable logistic regression identified greater odds of PICU mortality associated with renal dysfunction (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 3.2 [95% CI, 1.5–7.5]) and immunologic dysfunction (aOR, 12.7 [95% CI, 4.6–37.5]).In multivariable analysis, abnormal nutritional status, lack of vaccination, renal dysfunction, and admission to PICUs with intermediate or low resource availability were associated with greater odds of PICU mortality.
