Pre-illness clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential is associated with increased morbidity and mortality in sepsis
items.abstract: Sepsis is a life-threatening syndrome causing significant morbidity and mortality, especially in older adults. Clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential (CHIP) is an age-related condition linked to chronic illness and all-cause mortality. Here, we evaluated the association of pre-illness CHIP with mortality and morbidity in patients admitted to the ICU with sepsis. We performed a retrospective study using a de-identified electronic health record linked with a DNA biorepository. We identified adult patients with sepsis who had DNA collected prior to ICU admission. We tested the association between CHIP status determined from whole-genome sequencing, and ICU mortality, organ support-free days, and long-term survival adjusting for age, sex, race and Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score on ICU admission. The cohort comprised 220 patients with pre-illness CHIP and 3,010 patients without. Pre-illness CHIP was associated with increased sepsis mortality (OR = 1.54, 95% CI 1.13 to 2.07, P = 0.005) and fewer days alive and free of vasopressors (OR = 0.76, 95% CI 0.58–0.98, P = 0.036), assisted ventilation (OR = 0.7, 95% CI 0.53–0.93, P = 0.013), and kidney replacement therapy (OR = 0.56, 95% CI 0.37–0.87, P = 0.009) after adjusting for age, sex, race, and SOFA score on ICU admission. In sepsis survivors, CHIP was also associated with increased long-term mortality after discharge (HR 1.40, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.93, P = 0.041). Pre-illness CHIP was independently associated with increased mortality and morbidity in critically-ill adults with sepsis. These findings suggest that CHIP is a risk factor for sepsis severity. Uncovering the mechanism behind this link could lead to new treatments for sepsis, especially for the aging population.
items.limitations: There are also some limitations. First, data collection from a single quaternary referral center inherently enriches the patient population for sicker individuals, which limits the generalizability of our results to broader populations. Second, since we relied on institutional EHR data, information on prior hospitalizations at other centers not linked to our EHR is unavailable. A third limitation is that while the DNA biospecimens used were not collected during the acute sepsis encounter, they could have been obtained during other periods of illness. While BioVU generally collects DNA from samples obtained during outpatient care encounters, it is not fully discernable if patients were at their true baseline health at the time of collection. Another limitation is that some patients could have developed CHIP in the time between their pre-illness DNA biospecimen and their ICU admission, which could result in misclassification bias if some of the non-CHIP patients did in fact have CHIP by the time of their ICU admission. Finally, assessment of CHIP in this cohort was based on approximately 35X sequencing depth rather than the “gold standard” 1000X coverage of deep sequencing (longitudinal CHIP sequencing data), which could lead to an underestimation of CHIP and effect sizes. In conclusion, pre-illness CHIP in critically ill adults with sepsis was associated with higher mortality, fewer organ support-free days, and worse long-term survival. Furthermore, CHIP was associated with altered hematologic profiles during sepsis, suggesting a maladaptive inflammatory response, and sepsis was associated with increased expansion of mutant CHIP clones in longitudinal follow up. As genomic data become more integrated into clinical care, detecting CHIP could improve risk stratification and long-term management for critically ill patients.

items.title: Reconsidering futility after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest due to aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage
items.limitations: These limitations constrain causal and predictive inference, but do not alter the primary descriptive findings of the study. In other words, our data were intended to describe what occurred, not to establish why it occurred. Second, the interpretation of functional recovery warrants clarification. Chardon and colleagues correctly note that only one patient reached mRS 0–1, but their figure describes this as the only patient who recovered independently. Our cohort included one patient with mRS 1, but also four with mRS 2, and three with mRS 3 at six months. We would therefore distinguish an important unanswered question from a limitation of the question actually addressed. Linking donor and recipient data would be a valuable extension of this work, particularly given the preceding cardiac arrest and potential ischemia-reperfusion injury. A recent ILCOR systematic review and meta-analysis found comparable graft outcomes among brain-dead donors with and without preceding cardiopulmonary resuscitation. This provides reassuring evidence at the population level, but cannot determine graft outcomes in our own cohort. We also acknowledge that our wording concerning ICU admission for all patients could be read as placing organ donation at the center of the initial therapeutic rationale. Finally, we share the author call for prospective, time-resolved data encompassing aneurysm treatment, rebleeding, neurological assessment, treatment limitation, and both donation pathways, together with graft and recipient outcomes. Our central finding remains that OHCA-aSAH carries an extremely poor prognosis while recovery is possible in a tiny minority. The cohort supports careful assessment for individual, and after that, collective benefit, without assuming universal futility; it does not establish treatment efficacy, a validated selection strategy, or a quantified transplantation benefit. aSAH aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage

items.title: Impact of early beta-lactam renal dosing on the clinical outcomes of septic critically ill patients having sepsis-related acute kidney injury: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.abstract: To perform a systematic review with meta-analysis for assessing the potential impact of beta-lactam renal dosing adjustment on the clinical outcomes of critically ill patients having sepsis-related acute kidney injury (AKI). Two authors independently searched PubMed-MEDLINE and Scopus database from inception to 21st April 2026 for retrieving studies assessing the impact of beta-lactams renal dosing adjustment compared to the administration of beta-lactams full-dosing on clinical outcomes in critically ill patients with AKI. Mortality rate was set as the primary outcome, whereas clinical failure, 28-day vasopressor-free days, 28-day ventilator-free days, and occurrence of adverse events to beta-lactams were selected as the secondary outcomes. Treatment effects were calculated as odds ratio (OR) with 95% confidence interval (CI) for dichotomous data, using a random-effect model with the inverse variance method. Continuous data were calculated as the mean difference (MD) with 95%CI. Risk of bias of the included studies was independently assessed according to the RoB 2.0 and the ROBINS-I tools. Among a total of 21,183 articles screened, five observational studies were included ( N = 1,215; 573 receiving beta-lactam renal dosing adjustment vs. 642 treated with full-dosing). Treatment with beta-lactams full-dosing was associated with a significantly lower mortality rate compared to beta-lactams renal dosing adjustment ( N = 5; OR 0.67; 95%CI 0.54–0.82; p < 0.001; I 2 = 22.3%) and trended toward a higher number of vasopressor-free days at 28-day ( N = 2; mean difference 2.72; 95%CI − 0.14–5.57; p = 0.06; I 2 = 0.0%). Our hypothesis-generating meta-analysis could suggest that administering early beta-lactam full-dose in critical patients with sepsis-related AKI could be associated with lower mortality rate. RCTs and/or well-design prospective multicenter studies would be warranted for supporting our hypothesis.

items.title: The role of a recovery navigator in supporting older survivors of critical illness after hospital discharge: evidence from critical illness and insights from older adult populations
items.abstract: Survivors of critical illness aged 65 years or older experience high mortality and hospital readmission rates, as well as long-term physical, cognitive, social and psychological impairments that impact their quality of life. Despite the complex recovery needs of older survivors of critical illness, current follow-up care remains fragmented, and no standardised model of care exists to support their long-term recovery after hospital discharge. The role of a recovery navigator presents a promising strategy to address this problem by providing coordinated, person-centred support, addressing barriers to care and empowering survivors to self-manage their recovery journey. This narrative review synthesised and critically analysed the existing literature on recovery navigator interventions from two distinct populations – adult survivors of critical illness and broader, more diverse older adult populations. It aimed to identify the key knowledge gaps, inconsistencies and opportunities for improvement within existing recovery navigator interventions. Electronic databases (MEDLINE, EMBASE and EMCARE) were searched to identify relevant studies. Data were extracted by two reviewers and findings were synthesised narratively. Evidence for recovery navigator interventions in adult survivors of critical illness was limited and characterised by substantial heterogeneity, making it challenging to identify optimal intervention components and delivery strategies or draw firm conclusions regarding effectiveness. However, recovery navigator interventions delivered to broader older adult populations highlighted several potentially transferable features, including nurse-led delivery, individualised intervention duration and components tailored to the needs of older adults. These interventions were successfully implemented following hospital discharge and may provide valuable insights for the design of future recovery navigator models. Overall, the findings of this review may inform the development of a new model of care to support long-term recovery in older survivors of critical illness.

items.title: Altered LCN2 expression is observed in human sepsis and LCN2 deletion aggravates lung injury and mortality through JAK2/STAT3 pathway in experimental murine sepsis
items.abstract: Sepsis is a life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection. Lipocalin-2 (Lcn2) is capable of regulating inflammation, yet its precise role in sepsis remains poorly understood. Serum LCN2 level was measured in 48 septic patients sampled on the day of intensive care unit (ICU) and emergency department admission, 25 septic patients with Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS), and 47 healthy volunteers. In addition, LCN2 −/− and LCN2 fl/fl ; Col1a2-2A Cre mice was utilized to explore the underlying mechanisms of polymicrobial sepsis induced by cecal ligation and puncture (CLP). Additionally, recombinant LCN2 and baricitinib were administered to investigate their potential therapeutic effects on sepsis-induced acute lung injury. On the day of ICU and emergency department admission, the septic patients with ARDS showed a significant increase in serum LCN2 level compared with sepsis patient controls and healthy volunteers. Knocking out LCN2 in fibroblasts significantly increased bacterial load and inflammatory response. Both in vivo and in vitro experiments confirmed that LCN2 knockout increased interleukin-6 (IL-6) level and enhanced endothelial permeability. Mechanistically, LCN2 knockout might affect IL-6 secretion in fibroblasts by modulating the JAK2/STAT3 signaling pathway. Treatment with JAK inhibitors and recombinant LCN2 reduced inflammatory response, and promoted lung injury recovery in septic mice. Septic patients with ARDS had elevated serum LCN2 levels. Lcn2 predominantly in fibroblasts is crucial for lung injury in the sepsis. Administering JAK inhibitors and recombinant LCN2 could serve as a novel and effective strategy to boost recovery during lung injury. Not applicable.

items.title: Considerations in the association between red blood cell transfusion and infection after trauma
Association between hydrocortisone initiation and in-hospital death by day 28 according to initial diastolic shock index in septic shock: a multicenter cohort study
items.abstract: The association between hydrocortisone initiation and mortality in septic shock may differ across hemodynamic phenotypes. We investigated whether initial diastolic shock index (DSI), calculated as heart rate divided by diastolic blood pressure, identifies heterogeneity in hydrocortisone-associated mortality. We analyzed prospectively collected data from a 15-hospital sepsis registry. Adults with emergency department-onset sepsis and hypotension requiring fluid resuscitation and vasopressor support were included. Follow-up began at first vasopressor initiation, with hydrocortisone exposure coded as 0 before actual initiation and 1 thereafter. The primary outcome was in-hospital death by day 28 during the index study-hospital admission. Center-stratified multivariable cause-specific Cox models evaluated interactions with initial DSI, diastolic blood pressure, and pulse pressure. Restricted cubic splines, a 24-hour landmark analysis, overlap-weighted competing-risk analyses, and sensitivity analyses were performed. Among 6,562 patients, 1,029 (15.7%) received hydrocortisone. The primary adjusted analysis included 5,978 patients with 1,892 deaths. Hydrocortisone initiation was associated with a higher mortality hazard overall (adjusted hazard ratio [HR], 1.25; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.10–1.42), and the association differed according to initial DSI (P for interaction < 0.001). The adjusted HR was 1.67 (95% CI, 1.37–2.02) for DSI < 2.0 and 1.05 (95% CI, 0.90–1.23) for DSI ≥ 2.0. The DSI interaction remained significant in landmark and sensitivity analyses. In the restricted overlap-weighted landmark cohort of 4,882 patients, the day-28 risk difference was + 12.3% points (95% CI, + 6.3 to + 18.3) for DSI < 2.0 and − 0.7% points (95% CI, − 5.1 to + 3.7) for DSI ≥ 2.0. In this observational cohort, the association between hydrocortisone initiation and in-hospital death by day 28 varied according to initial DSI. These associations should be interpreted in the context of potential residual confounding from unmeasured clinical deterioration before hydrocortisone initiation. Initial ED DSI warrants prospective evaluation as a candidate stratification variable.

items.title: Venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation provides flow, not afterload: reframing left ventricular afterload during peripheral VA ECMO
items.abstract: Venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA ECMO) restores systemic perfusion and oxygen delivery, most commonly through peripheral femoro-femoral cannulation with retrograde arterial return into the descending aorta. From this configuration emerged the concept that peripheral VA ECMO intrinsically increases left ventricular (LV) afterload [ 1 ] because retrograde flow opposes native LV ejection. This concept has strongly influenced routine LV unloading strategies during VA ECMO [ 2 , 3 , 4 ].

items.title: Obstructive sleep apnoea: an overlooked challenge in the current NHS Strategy
items.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) is common, frequently symptomatic, and closely associated with conditions already prioritised by the UK National Health Service (NHS), including obesity, hypertension, type 2 diabetes, atrial fibrillation, cardiovascular disease, and stroke. Previous estimates suggest that approximately 8 million UK adults aged 30-69 years could have OSA, although the proportion remaining undiagnosed is uncertain. Evidence supports treatment benefits for daytime sleepiness, symptom burden, quality of life, driving safety, and blood pressure in some patients, but not a consistent reduction in major cardiovascular events. UK data indicate long diagnostic waits, regional variation, and gaps in follow-up. A proportionate NHS response should prioritise targeted case-finding within existing chronic-disease pathways, access to validated home-based diagnostics, specialist capacity for complex disease, and sustained treatment support. Implementation should be phased and evaluated prospectively for clinical outcomes, equity, workforce requirements, affordability, and budget impact.

items.title: Laennec beyond the stethoscope
Defining residual lung disease with CFTR modulators
Ending the global neglect of pneumonia: from awareness to accountability
Longitudinal change in FEV1 in adults with cystic fibrosis treated with elexacaftor–tezacaftor–ivacaftor in France: a prospective observational study
items.abstract: Background Without cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) modulators, cystic fibrosis is associated with an accelerated decline in percent predicted FEV 1 (ppFEV 1 ) of approximately 1·5% per year. Although treatment with elexacaftor-tezacaftor-ivacaftor (ETI) initially increases ppFEV 1 , little is known about its subsequent effect on ppFEV 1 decline. Recent analyses of the extension phases of the phase 3 ETI pivotal studies found no evidence of ppFEV 1 decline over 4 years in patients aged 12 years and older who were treated with ETI. The objective of this study was to examine the decline in ppFEV 1 in a large, real-world cohort of adults with cystic fibrosis. Methods Data from adults (aged ≥18 years) with cystic fibrosis and at least one F508del CFTR variant who initiated treatment with ETI between Dec 24, 2019, and Dec 23, 2023, at 31 cystic fibrosis centres included in the French prospective national observational ETI study in adults were analysed over 3 years. Eligible participants were those with at least three measures of ppFEV 1 taken within 3 months following ETI initiation and the end of follow-up. The reference ppFEV 1 was the highest ppFEV 1 reached during the first 3 months of ETI treatment, after which subsequent decline in ppFEV 1 was analysed by use of a linear mixed-effects model with random effects to estimate each participant's variation from the population mean. Findings Data from 2321 adults with cystic fibrosis were included in this analysis. 1262 (54·4%) participants were male and 1059 (45·6%) were female. Median age was 29·2 years (IQR 23·1-36·7) and the pre-ETI initiation ppFEV 1 was 59·7% (IQR 39·8-79·1). Within the first 3 months following ETI initiation, ppFEV 1 increased by a median of 14·5 percentage points (IQR 7·9-22·7). The subsequent mean decline in ppFEV 1 was 0·70% (95% CI 0·57-0·83) per year. Importantly, the decline in ppFEV 1 was heterogeneous, with 1583 (68·2%) of 2321 participants showing no or limited decline (less than or equal to 1·5% per year). The remaining 738 (31·8%) participants showed a decline of greater than 1·5% per year, with 342 (46·3%) of these participants having a decline of greater than 3·0% per year. In multivariable analyses, the decline in ppFEV 1 was greater in participants with a higher ppFEV 1 at 3 months after ETI initiation. Treatment with oral azithromycin at 1 year after ETI initiation was associated with a lower risk of having a decline greater than 1·5% per year (relative risk 0·78 [95% CI 0·68-0·90]; p Interpretation These results suggest that approximately a third of adults with cystic fibrosis who are treated with ETI had a persistent decline in ppFEV 1 . These data emphasise the importance of regular ppFEV 1 monitoring and highlight the need to improve current therapeutic strategies to prevent ppFEV 1 decline. Proposed strategies could include use of newer CFTR modulators to restore CFTR function more effectively, as well as mucoactive, anti-infective, and anti-inflammatory therapies. Funding Association Vaincre la Mucoviscidose, Société Française de la Mucoviscidose, and Filière Maladies Rares MUCO-CFTR.

items.title: Consensus on the definition, components, and grading of composite postoperative pulmonary complication outcomes (PrECiSIOn): insights from an international Delphi expert panel
items.abstract: Postoperative pulmonary complications (PPCs) are common after surgery and contribute substantially to morbidity, mortality, and health-care burden, and are frequently used as endpoints in clinical studies. However, absence of standardised definitions and heterogeneity in component selection limit comparability across studies and might bias estimates of treatment effects. The Postoperative Pulmonary Complications-Evaluation for Consensus on Standardised Outcomes (PrECiSIOn) study was an international, mixed-method consensus study using a Delphi process to establish a standardised definition of PPCs, determine severity-based ranking of individual components, and define approaches for their assessment. A multidisciplinary panel of experts in PPCs was recruited and candidate PPC components were identified through a focused literature review, structured into domains, and evaluated across iterative Delphi rounds using a seven-point Likert scale, with consensus predefined as ≥75% agreement. Patient and patient care representative perspectives were incorporated through interviews and surveys, and panellists assigned severity weights to components reaching consensus. Input from 44 panellists and five patients and patient representatives informed the prioritisation of clinically meaningful outcomes. Consensus was achieved on a standardised PPC construct comprising components grouped into four domains: symptoms, diagnoses, therapies, and outcomes. Panellists supported the use of routinely collected clinical data and a standardised in-hospital monitoring approach but did not reach consensus on the optimal follow-up period or need for post-discharge surveillance. Severity-based rank ordering enabled hierarchical organisation of PPC components according to their clinical importance, supporting the development of ordinal composite outcomes that account for differences in severity between individual complications. This international consensus-based framework provides a standardised definition of PPCs incorporating severity-based rank ordering, addresses important limitations of existing composite outcomes, and might facilitate more consistent and clinically meaningful evaluation of perioperative interventions. Further work should focus on external validation, implementation in clinical trial analyses, and assessment of applicability across diverse patient populations and health-care settings.

items.title: RSV multidose vaccine puts Africa's RSV burden in focus
Children are not small adults: CAD for childhood tuberculosis
Closing the logic gap—expanding who we consider for tuberculosis treatment
2027 GOLD COPD report
Ringer's lactate versus saline in the fluids in septic shock (FISSH) trial: a multicentre, blinded, parallel-group, randomised controlled trial
items.abstract: Background Despite fluid therapy being a hallmark of treatment for patients with septic shock, the optimal crystalloid to use in this setting remains unclear. We aimed to compare the effect of two different, commonly used crystalloids in patients with septic shock. Methods In this multicentre, blinded, parallel-group, randomised controlled trial, adults (aged ≥16 years) at 30 academic and community hospitals across Canada and Saudi Arabia who were critically ill with septic shock were randomly assigned (1:1) via a web-based randomisation system to receive Ringer's lactate or 0·9% saline for all bolus and maintenance fluid throughout their intensive care unit (ICU) stay up to day 30, stratified by hospital. Randomisation used permuted blocks of undisclosed variable sizes. We included patients who had a systolic blood pressure lower than 90 mm Hg or a mean arterial pressure of less than 65 mm Hg after 1 L bolus or a serum lactate greater than 4 mmol/L, had a clinically suspected infection, and were within 6 h of emergency department presentation or ICU consultation. We excluded patients who had new raised intracranial pressure, had acute burn injury on more than 10% of the body surface area, were already receiving chronic or acute dialysis at the time of screening, or were admitted to ICU directly from the operating room, post-anaesthetic care unit, or another hospital or health-care facility. All bedside clinicians, patients, caregivers, research staff, and biostatisticians were masked to allocation. The primary endpoint was 30-day in-hospital mortality analysed on an intention-to-treat basis. The trial was registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT03677102). Findings Between Oct 6, 2018, and Feb 1, 2026, we screened 2457 patients and randomly assigned 1113, with a further ten excluded after randomisation (557 patients in the Ringer's lactate group and 546 in the saline group). 491 (44·5%) were female and 612 (55·5%) were male, the mean baseline APACHE II score was 24·7 (SD 8·8), and patients received a mean of 5844 mL (SD 4761) of study fluid. The mean baseline serum lactate was 4·8 mmol/L (SD 3·5) and the mean serum creatinine was 176·5 μmol/L (SD 126·4). 187 (33·6%) patients died in the Ringer's lactate group 180 (33·0%) died in the saline group (relative risk 1·02 [95% CI 0·86-1·21]; p=0·80). There were no serious adverse events. Interpretation In this trial of patients who were critically ill with septic shock, Ringer's lactate compared with saline had no effect on 30-day in-hospital mortality. Funding The Canadian Institutes of Health Research and the Physician Services Incorporated Foundation.

items.title: Weathering the STORM: treatment de-escalation in CF
Association of BMI with type 2 biomarkers, asthma burden, and severe asthma attack risk: an analysis of control groups of the ORACLE2 patient-level meta-analysis
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Obesity-related asthma is frequently described as a type 2-low phenotype, but data on type 2 biomarker distributions across BMI and their relationship with asthma attack risk are scarce. We aimed to examine the distribution of type 2 biomarkers across BMI categories in adolescents and adults with asthma and to investigate how BMI relates to risk of severe attacks. METHODS: We analysed data from the ORACLE2 patient-level meta-analysis of control groups of 22 randomised placebo-controlled asthma trials, previously identified through a systematic review of MEDLINE from Jan 1, 1993, to April 1, 2021. We estimated annualised severe asthma attack rate ratios using negative binomial models, adjusted for sex, age, blood eosinophil count (BEC), fractional exhaled nitric oxide (FeNO), percent predicted forced expiratory volume in 1 s (ppFEV1), percent predicted forced vital capacity, treatment step, previous severe attacks, and trial. FINDINGS: In the ORACLE2 patient-level meta-analysis (n=6513), 2393 (37%) of 6513 participants with asthma had overweight (BMI 25 kg/m2 to <30 kg/m2) and 2723 (42%) had obesity (BMI ≥30 kg/m2). Those with obesity had highest symptom burden, lowest baseline ppFEV1, and were most frequently on Global Initiative for Asthma step 5 treatment. Although the proportion of patients with dual type 2-high biomarkers (BEC ≥0·3 × 109 cells per L and FeNO ≥35 parts per billion) was lower in the obese versus normal BMI group (15% vs 26%; p<0·0001), the proportion of type 2-low asthma (BEC <0·15 × 109 cells per L and FeNO <20 ppb) was higher (18% vs 13%; p<0·0001), indicating that 82% of asthma patients with obesity still have some degree of type 2 inflammation. Compared with normal BMI, severe obesity (BMI ≥40 kg/m2) was associated with a significantly higher asthma attack risk (adjusted rate ratio 1·57, 95% CI 1·06-2·33). INTERPRETATION: Most patients with obesity-related asthma have evidence of type 2 inflammation despite a modest shift towards type 2-low disease. High BMI is associated with increased asthma burden and attack risk. These findings support a multidimensional view of obesity-associated asthma, in which type 2 inflammation frequently coexists with obesity-related mechanisms that independently contribute to disease burden and asthma attack risk. FUNDING: National Institute for Health and Care Research, Oxford Biomedical Research Centre, Association Pulmonaire du Québec, Fonds de Recherche du Québec-Santé, Academy of Medical Sciences, and Ghent University Special Research Fund.

items.title: Stopping versus continuing nebulised mucoactive therapy in people with cystic fibrosis established on elexacaftor–tezacaftor–ivacaftor (CF STORM): a multicentre, registry-based, randomised, controlled, non-inferiority trial
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Reducing treatment burden is a priority for people with cystic fibrosis and their families. Daily nebulised therapies are a substantial treatment burden. The CF STORM study aimed to assess whether cessation of daily nebulised mucoactive therapy (dornase alfa, hypertonic saline, or both) was non-inferior to continuing treatment in people with cystic fibrosis established on the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CTFR) modulator elexacaftor plus tezacaftor plus ivacaftor (ETI). METHODS: CF STORM was a multicentre, open-label, randomised, controlled, non-inferiority trial, done across 40 adult or paediatric specialist cystic fibrosis centres in the UK. Eligible participants were aged 6 years or older with cystic fibrosis who were established on ETI treatment for at least 3 months, with a percentage predicted FEV1 (ppFEV1) of at least 40%. Eligibility assessment, consent, randomisation, and data collection were all done within the UK Cystic Fibrosis Registry. Patients were randomly assigned (1:1; using computer-generated random permuted blocks stratified by site and current mucoactive treatment) to stop their prescribed therapy (STOP) or continue their prescribed daily nebulised mucoactive therapy (dornase alfa, hypertonic saline, or both; CONTINUE). The primary outcome was change in ppFEV1 from baseline to 52 weeks (prespecified visit windows 51-55 weeks) assessed in all participants with primary outcome data. A non-inferiority margin of -3 percentage points was established for the difference between groups in ppFEV1. Safety was assessed in all randomly assigned participants who received at least one day of allocated treatment. This study is registered with the ISRCTN registry, ISRCTN14081521. FINDINGS: Between July 8, 2021, and Aug 6, 2024, 1716 people were screened. Of 684 patients eligible for enrolment, 591 were randomly assigned to either the STOP group (n=297) or the CONTINUE group (n=294). Median age was 15·5 years (IQR 12·7-29·4) and mean baseline ppFEV1 was 89·4% (SD 18·2). Stopping mucoactive therapy was non-inferior to continuing treatment for change in ppFEV1 from baseline to 52 weeks in the primary analysis population (STOP n=195, CONTINUE n=195; unadjusted mean change 0·15 [SD 6·85] ppFEV1 in STOP vs -0·79 [SD 8·01] in CONTINUE; adjusted mean difference 0·97 percentage points, 95% CI -0·51 to 2·45). Pulmonary exacerbations were more frequent in the STOP group than the CONTINUE group (incidence 0·90 vs 0·67 per person-year; incidence rate ratio [IRR] 1·34, 95% CI 1·06 to 1·71), but no significant differences were identified between groups in pulmonary exacerbations leading to treatment with intravenous antibiotic therapy (incidence 0·12 vs 0·08 per person-year; IRR 1·55, 95% CI 0·78 to 3·08). No serious adverse reactions to dornase alfa or related serious adverse events associated with hypertonic saline were reported. One death, unrelated to the study intervention, occurred in the STOP group. INTERPRETATION: Stopping nebulised mucoactive therapy was non-inferior to continuing treatment. Registry-recorded pulmonary exacerbations were more common in the STOP group than the CONTINUE group. These data provide evidence that discontinuing nebulised mucoactive therapy is unlikely to result in worsening respiratory function for people with cystic fibrosis established on ETI aged 6 years and older with a baseline percent predicted FEV1 of at least 40%. A more cautious approach is recommended for people with ppFEV1 of 40-69%. FUNDING: National Institute for Health and Care Research Health Technology Assessment Programme, Cystic Fibrosis Trust, and UK Research and Innovation.

items.title: Obesity and asthma: rethinking the type 2 immune landscape
Multi-biomarker risk score for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis based on serum proteins by the Prognostic Lung Fibrosis Consortium (PROLIFIC): a risk score development and validation study
items.abstract: Background Despite decades of research, clinicians still do not have approved prognostic biomarkers that can help predict how quickly idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) will progress in individual patients. The Prognostic Lung Fibrosis Consortium (PROLIFIC) was formed to develop well-qualified assays suitable for use as prognostic biomarkers within the context of clinical trials for IPF. Methods For this risk score development and validation study, assays were developed for 12 peripheral blood biomarkers discovered in previous studies, representing epithelial damage (CYFRA 21-1, SP-D, CA-125, CA-19-9, and KL-6), fibrosis (MMP-7, TNC, and POSTN), inflammation (CCL18, CXCL13, and sICAM-1), and thrombosis (PAI-1), and used for IPF patient baseline serum measurements within the derivation dataset (Pulmonary Fibrosis Foundation [PFF] Patient Registry; n=657) and the validation dataset (placebo groups of the ISABELA studies; n=229). The PFF Patient Registry enrolled patients in the USA (start date March 29, 2016; data cutoff Nov 30, 2022). ISABELA 1 (NCT03711162) enrolled patients in Australia, Belgium, Brazil, Chile, Czechia, Denmark, Germany, Greece, Japan, Peru, Spain, Taiwan, Türkiye, the UK, and the USA (start date Nov 28, 2018; completed March 30, 2021). ISABELA 2 (NCT03733444) enrolled patients in Argentina, Canada, France, Germany, Hungary, Israel, Italy, Japan, Mexico, Netherlands, New Zealand, Poland, South Africa, South Korea, and the USA (start date Nov 5, 2018; completed March 30, 2021). Single and multi-marker statistical analyses were performed for transplant-free survival and forced vital capacity (FVC) decline at 1 year, adjusting for sex, age, BMI, antifibrotic medication, smoking pack-years, percent predicted FVC (ppFVC), and percent predicted diffusion capacity of the lung for carbon monoxide. Penalised logistic regression was used to select prognostic biomarkers using the least absolute shrinkage and selection operator method, and the resulting model was used to derive a multi-marker risk score. The performance of the PROLIFIC risk score was assessed using area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) and by the sensitivity and specificity of the Youden Index. Findings In 657 participants in the PFF Patient Registry IPF derivation cohort, the mean age was 70·69 years (SD 8·08), 168 (26%) were female, 489 (74%) were male, 617 (94%) were White, ten (2%) were Black, 14 (2%) were Asian, and 16 (2%) were other race. A 10% or higher absolute decline of ppFVC within 1 year occurred in 20 (3%) of 657 patients. Overall longitudinal FVC decline was significantly associated with baseline MMP-7, SP-D, KL-6, PAI-1, CA19-9, CYFRA 21-1, CXCL13, and sICAM-1. Death (62 [9%] of 657 patients) or lung transplant (37 [6%] of 657 patients) within 1 year was significantly associated with baseline SP-D, sICAM-1, TNC, and KL-6. A multi-marker prognostic model or PROLIFIC risk score for the composite outcome of death, lung transplant, or at least 10% absolute decline in ppFVC at 1 year was associated with baseline SP-D, CXCL13, sICAM-1, TNC, and CA-125 (derivation area under the curve [AUC] 0·809 [95% CI 0·763-0·855]; Youden Index sensitivity 0·643 and specificity 0·847). In 229 participants in the ISABELA study validation cohort, the mean age was 70·08 years (SD 6·79), 36 (16%) were female, 193 (84%) were male, 168 (73%) were White, one ( Interpretation A multi-marker algorithm confirmed the important serum proteins consistent with findings from previous analyses and yielded a patient-level prognostic risk score for transplant-free survival and FVC decline in IPF. The PROLIFIC risk score has been accepted into the US Food and Drug Administration Biomarker Qualification Program as a prognostic biomarker in patients with IPF to identify patients who are more likely to have clinical events or disease progression within 1 year and to be used as a stratification factor or as an eligibility criterion in clinical trials. Funding The Prognostic Lung Fibrosis Consortium.

items.title: Precision medicine in the prognostic evaluation of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis

From rescue to donation: embedding ethics into the ECPR outcomes framework
Beyond barriers: Understanding delays before bystander CPR as a dynamic process
Positive pressure ventilation in newborns at birth: a systematic review of recipient characteristics and temporal trends
items.abstract: AIM: To synthesise evidence on temporal trends, recipient characteristics and variation in the use of positive pressure ventilation (PPV) at birth. METHODS: This systematic review was registered (CRD42024487025) and followed a condition-context-population framework. Five electronic databases and grey literature were searched to 25 June 2026. Risk of bias was assessed using the JBI checklist, and reporting followed PRISMA 2020. RESULTS: Forty-two studies from 34 countries (27 from high-income countries), reporting 269-10,696,831 livebirths per study (1984-2024), were included. Heterogeneity in whether continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) was distinguished from PPV, interface definitions and eligibility criteria precluded meta-analysis. Fifteen studies included only preterm infants and 19 excluded congenital anomalies. Nine population-based or large multicentre studies that excluded CPAP without PPV and included all gestations reported PPV incidence ranging from 3.0% to 8.0%. Rates were much higher among very and extremely preterm infants. Temporal trends suggested increasing PPV incidence overall and via facemask, whereas tracheal-tube PPV was stable or declining. Lower PPV incidence was reported in low-resource and lower-level birthing centres. Few studies reported indications for or timing of PPV initiation, and reported data items were inconsistent. CONCLUSIONS: PPV remains common in neonatal resuscitation, with higher use at lower gestational ages and higher-level birthing services. Limited and heterogeneous reporting of indications and PPV timelines constrains interpretation and comparison. Standardised, Neonatal Utstein-aligned reporting, including PPV indications and time intervals and separate reporting of airway interfaces and CPAP, is needed. Further population-based studies, particularly in low- and middle-income countries, are warranted.

items.title: Coronary perfusion pressure during cardiopulmonary resuscitation is associated with outcomes from pediatric in-hospital cardiac arrest
items.abstract: Background Multiple animal studies and one adult study establish that coronary perfusion pressure (CoPP) during cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) is associated with survival outcomes, such as return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC). Yet, CoPP during pediatric in-hospital cardiac arrest (pIHCA) has not been investigated. We hypothesized that an average CoPP ≥20 mmHg during the first 10 min of CPR for pIHCA would be associated with higher rates of ROSC. Methods We performed a secondary analysis of the ICU-RESUScitation trial, a cluster randomized, step-wedged trial of a physiology-focused quality improvement bundle in pIHCA. Index CPR events among patients ≥37 weeks corrected gestational age and Results Among 111 included patients, median age was 0.2 years [0.0, 0.6]. Seventy-one (64%) achieved ROSC. Thirty (27%) had CoPP ≥20 mmHg. Patients with CoPP ≥20 mmHg were more frequently ≥1 year of age and less frequently had congenital heart disease. In adjusted models, average CoPP ≥20 mmHg was associated with higher rates of ROSC (aRR 1.48 [95%CI 1.12, 1.95]; p = 0.005). CoPP Conclusions In this first investigation of CoPP during CPR for pIHCA, CoPP ≥20 mmHg was associated with ROSC.

items.title: Cycle-to-cycle prediction of return of spontaneous circulation using end-tidal carbon dioxide dynamics in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest
items.abstract: Background Prognostication in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) commonly relies on static pre-resuscitation variables, although resuscitation is a rapidly evolving physiologic process. End-tidal carbon dioxide (EtCO 2 ) is continuously available during cardiopulmonary resuscitation, but its sequential information has not been fully used for real-time prediction. We aim to develop and internally validate a cycle-to-cycle time-updated prediction model using sequential EtCO 2 values to estimate the probability of return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) in the subsequent 2-min resuscitation cycle. Methods We conducted a multicenter retrospective study of adult OHCA patients from the NTUH-HYCARD database between 2016 and 2023. Event-level EtCO 2 sequences were extracted from resuscitation records and standardized into 2-min intervals for up to 30 min, consistent with Advanced Cardiac Life Support reassessment cycles. At each prediction time point, the model used EtCO 2 values available from event onset to the current time point, without using future values. A two-layer long short-term memory model estimated the probability of ROSC in the subsequent cycle. Performance was evaluated using 10-fold cross-validation at two levels: the event level (one prediction per event) and the cycle level (one prediction per 2-min cycle). Results The final analysis included 1651 event-level EtCO 2 sequences from 1480 patients; 583 events ended with ROSC. At the event level, the model achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.876 (95% CI, 0.863-0.890) and a Brier score of 0.140 (95% CI, 0.131-0.149). When applied to every 2-min cycle (17,029 prediction points; ROSC prevalence, 3.4%), the AUROC was 0.685 (95% CI, 0.664-0.706), and the model systematically overestimated ROSC probability (Brier score, 0.285; 95% CI, 0.268-0.303). Conclusion Sequential EtCO 2 dynamics showed good event-level discrimination for predicting ROSC in the subsequent cycle. When applied at each cycle, the model retained modest discrimination but overestimated ROSC probability, indicating that recalibration is required before cycle-to-cycle use.

items.title: Immediate postresuscitation ventilation
Sixty years after the café coronary: witnessed but untreated choking in restaurants
Reply to: Does critical care training explain higher survival after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest?
Trends in United States pediatric in-hospital cardiac arrest incidence and mortality in a nationally representative sample, 2009–2022
items.abstract: Aim National estimates of pediatric in-hospital cardiac arrest (IHCA) incidence in the United States rely on a voluntary registry that may underrepresent smaller and critical access hospitals. Administrative datasets offer a nationally representative alternative. We estimated nationally representative pediatric IHCA incidence and mortality trends from 2009 through 2022. Methods Serial cross-sectional analysis of five triennial editions of the Kids' Inpatient Database (2009–2022), identifying IHCA in children <18 years by ICD-9 (99.60, 99.63) and ICD-10 (5A12012) cardiopulmonary resuscitation procedure codes. Two hospitals with implausible CPR rates were excluded. Survey-weighted incidence per 1,000 hospitalizations and in-hospital mortality among resuscitated children were estimated overall and by neonatal status, complex chronic condition (CCC) status, ZIP-code income quartile, and US Census region. Trends were tested with survey-weighted quasi-Poisson regression across the full period and, as exploratory analyses, within the ICD-10 era (2016–2022). Results Observed IHCA incidence was 1.11/1,000 in 2009 and 1.22/1,000 in 2012, decreased to 1.11/1,000 at the ICD-10 transition and increased to 1.35/1,000 by 2022. IHCA incidence in children hospitalized with a CCC rose from 3.26 to 6.60/1,000 (6.2%/year, p<0.001), while incidence without CCC remained low. Incidence varied by socioeconomic status (lowest vs highest income quartile 1.78 vs 1.04/1,000 in 2022). In-hospital mortality ranged from 34.1% (2012) to 40.4% (2019), whereas IHCA deaths per 1,000 hospitalizations increased 1.7%/year (p<0.001), concentrated among children with a CCC. Conclusion The incidence of pediatric IHCA increased among hospitalizations involving children with CCC and was higher among children who live in lower income areas. In-hospital mortality after CPR was largely stable, whereas arrest-related deaths per 1,000 hospitalizations increased among children with CCC. A single hospital's coding practices can materially distort national administrative estimates. What is already known Pediatric in-hospital cardiac arrest affects approximately 15,200 children annually in the United States, with this national estimate derived primarily from a voluntary registry that may underrepresent smaller and critical access hospitals. Administrative databases offer nationally representative coverage but rely on procedure codes that are susceptible to misclassification. What this study adds In this nationally representative administrative database sample spanning 2009–2022, this study demonstrated that: 1) the incidence of IHCA among children with complex chronic conditions (CCC) rose steadily and accounted for the substantial majority of events, 2) the overall IHCA incidence was higher among children who live in lower income areas with the gradient worsening over the period evaluated, and 3) in-hospital mortality after CPR increased only slightly (34–40%), whereas arrest-related deaths per 1,000 hospitalizations increased more, driven mainly by rising incidence among children with CCC, and 4) CPR coding at a single hospital can substantially distort national administrative estimates.

items.title: Can the pulse oximeter tell us when the heart is back?
Does critical care training explain higher survival after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest?
Ventilation feedback during resuscitation: lessons learned and implications for the future
Out-of-hospital cardiac arrests due to foreign body airway obstruction: A CanROC registry, retrospective cohort study
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Foreign body airway obstruction (FBAO) is a treatable cause of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA), but North American data are limited. METHODS: Exploratory retrospective cohort study of EMS-treated OHCAs using the Canadian Resuscitation Outcomes Consortium (CanROC) registry (2005-2023), classified as obviously FBAO-related or of no obvious cause (presumed cardiac). Logistic regression compared Utstein characteristics between etiologies and identified factors associated with prehospital return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) and survival to acute care discharge. RESULTS: Among 105,178 EMS-treated OHCAs, 1,106(1.1%) were obviously FBAO-related. Compared with cases of no obvious cause, obviously FBAO-related cases were older (median 73 vs 68 years, p<0.001), more often witnessed (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 6.98[5.36-9.25]), more often attended by trained bystanders (aOR 3.30[2.41-4.41]), and less often had a shockable rhythm (aOR 0.11[0.07-0.15]). Obviously FBAO-related cases more often achieved prehospital ROSC (62.7% vs 37.8%; OR 2.77[2.44-3.13]), but survival did not differ (10.6% vs 9.0%,p=0.094). Within the obviously FBAO-related cohort, ROSC was associated with witnessed arrest (aOR 1.66[1.13-2.43]) and shorter EMS response time (aOR 0.95 per minute[0.92-0.99]). Survival was associated with younger age (aOR 0.76 per decade[0.61-0.93]), initial shockable rhythm (aOR 4.76[1.55-13.30]), and shorter EMS response time (aOR 0.81 per minute[0.66-0.98]). Survival was 18.1% and 0.8% among obviously FBAO-related OHCAs with and without prehospital ROSC, respectively. CONCLUSIONS: Obviously FBAO-related OHCAs are uncommon but clinically distinct. ROSC is frequent, yet survival remains low and is associated with early prehospital factors, supporting choking prevention initiatives, bystander training, and rapid EMS response.

items.title: Commercially available multimodal LLMs for EEG-based prognostication after cardiac arrest
items.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Machine-learning and deep-learning approaches have been successfully applied to EEG-based prognostication in comatose patients after cardiac arrest (CA), but typically rely on task-specific signal processing, feature extraction, and model development. Here, we investigated whether two commercially available multimodal large language models (LLMs) could predict neurological outcome directly from EEG images. METHODS: Thirty-three comatose patients on the first day after CA from a prospective cohort were included. For each patient, a single 10-second EEG segment displayed using a longitudinal bipolar montage was rendered as PNG image. ChatGPT 5.4. and Claude Opus 4.7 were instructed to estimate the probability for favorable outcome for each case based on the EEG and a generic information block describing conditions of recordings. Five different prompting strategies were used, including few-shot prompting where four exemplary EEGs (not from the 33 patients) were provided. Predictive performance was quantified using AUC and accuracy. RESULTS: Across prompting strategies, the AUC ranged from 0.86 to 0.99 for ChatGPT and from 0.74 to 1.00 for Claude. The highest accuracy achieved by both models was 93.9% using few-shot prompting. As reference, a previously published dedicated deep-learning model achieved 100% on the same cohort. CONCLUSION: In this exploratory study of a small cohort, multimodal LLMs showed variable but potentially promising discrimination for predicting favorable outcome from single EEG image in comatose patients after CA. Performance depended substantially on prompt design. These findings require confirmation in a larger cohort.

items.title: Survival after neonatal chest compressions at birth: Temporal trends and prognostic factors in a population-based cohort, Queensland, Australia
items.abstract: AIM: To examine temporal trends and prognostic factors for 28-day survival among infants receiving chest compressions (CC) in Queensland, Australia. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective population-based cohort study using the Queensland Perinatal Data Collection (2008-2024), including all liveborn CC recipients at birth. Temporal trends in crude 28-day survival were examined overall and by gestational age (GA) groups. Multivariable generalised estimating equations were used to identify factors independently associated with survival while accounting for clustering within birthing locations. RESULTS: Among 3,077 CC recipients, 70.5% established regular spontaneous breathing within 60 minutes of birth, and 89.0% survived to 28 days. Crude 28-day survival improved from 82% in 2008 to 89% in 2024 and was consistently higher in term (GA ≥37+0 weeks) than preterm infants. Compared with term infants, adjusted odds of survival declined with decreasing GA: 32+0 to 36+6 weeks (aOR 0.56, 95% CI 0.40-0.77), 28+0 to 31+6 weeks (aOR 0.35, 95% CI 0.23-0.54), and <28+0 weeks (aOR 0.17, 95% CI 0.12-0.23). However, after adjusting for cord pH or epinephrine administration, survival in infants born at 32+0 to 36+6 weeks did not differ significantly from term infants. CONCLUSION: Survival to 28 days among CC recipients was high and increased over time. Lower gestational age was the strongest independent prognostic factor for mortality, although the survival difference between term and moderate-to-late preterm infants was attenuated after adjustment for cord pH or epinephrine administration. Prospective studies assessing CC indications and measures of resuscitation quality are needed to optimise neonatal resuscitation and improve outcomes.

items.title: Early prehospital prediction of neurological outcome after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest
items.abstract: Introduction Out-of-hospital cardiac (OHCA) arrest is a frequent emergency, and few patients will survive with good neurological outcome. Identification of patients with a low likelihood of meaningful recovery represents a major clinical challenge. Numerous scores have been developed to guide decision-making after OHCA, with variable goals and targets, but most of them have been validated on small cohorts, integrates variables not available in the prehospital field, or do have low prediction values. MIRA-29 score aimed to only rely on simple clinical variables, available in the prehospital setting. We hypothetized that such score will provide incremental neurological prognosis value at an early-stage following OHCA. Methods MIRA-29 score was derived and internally validated over a five-year period on a prospective cohort of 1099 adult patients, including all OHCA treated by our territory dispatch center. Multivariate analysis identified independent variables within the database, that were used to optimize the prediction model using machine-learning and genetic algorithms. The score was subsequently validated externally on 82 696 patients extracted from the French national cardiac arrest registry (RéAC). Results Out from the 1099 patients, 85 patients (7.7%) had a favorable neurological outcome. Multivariate analysis identified five independent variables associated with neurological outcome: age, low-flow duration, number of external electric shock, epinephrine dose, and the OHCA site (street, public facility, home). After model optimization and machine-learning, age was not retained within the final model. External validation depicted a precision of 0.86 and a recall of 0.88 of the model. The F1-Score and accuracy are respectively 0.87 and 0.88, and specificity for a bad neurological prognosis is 0.99. Conclusion MIRA‑29 strength lies on its ability to reliably identify patients with extremely high probability of poor neurological outcome, while being based on four simple clinical variables. The prospective validation of MIRA-29 in the clinical setting may evaluate its impact on clinical decision making.

items.title: RescQ™: One-year implementation and feasibility results of a digitally enabled support pathway for bystanders of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest
items.abstract: Background Bystanders to out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) are at significant risk of psychological distress, yet no standardised support pathway exists for them in the UK. RescQ™ is a digital-first bystander support pathway embedded within regional prehospital and cardiac arrest care services. Aim To evaluate the feasibility of embedding RescQ™ into routine emergency medical services (EMS) practice leading to appropriate contact with bystanders involved in OHCA. Secondary aims were to describe digital access, demand for liaison officer (LO) support, identification of younger bystanders, and EMS clinician acceptability. Methods Prospective one-year regional service evaluation of RescQ™ across Essex, UK. Bystanders involved in eligible OHCA events were registered by EMS clinicians and provided with immediate access to secure digital resources. Bystanders could self-refer for additional support through LO. Results During the one-year evaluation, 220 of 432 eligible OHCA incidents had at least one bystander identified and the incident entered into the RescQ™ pathway, representing an incident-level capture rate of 50.9%. Across these incidents, 298 bystanders were identified, of whom 260 eligible adults were registered with RescQ™. Of registered adult bystanders, 96.2% accessed the digital resources at least once. Among all identified bystanders, 30/298 (10.1%) were aged under 18 years. Approximately 10% of registered bystanders self-referred for additional personalised LO support. Among 25 EMS clinician survey respondents who had used RescQ™ in clinical practice, ratings indicated acceptability. Conclusion RescQ™ demonstrated the feasibility of identifying and supporting bystanders following OHCA through a digitally enabled pathway, achieving incident-level capture above the pre-specified feasibility threshold and high website access among registered adults. These findings support further multi-region evaluation of implementation, sustainability and scalability across different EMS systems.

items.title: Survival after out of hospital cardiac arrest in relation to AED usage in a multi response system including AED equipped drones
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Early defibrillation is a key determinant of survival in out‑of‑hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA). In multi-response systems, it remains unclear which responders contribute most to early AED use and survival. This study compared first AED-attaching responders and their association with 30-day survival in a regional multi-response system. METHODS: This registry‑based cohort study included OHCA cases in Västra Götaland Region, Sweden, between January 1, 2015, and December 31, 2024. Data were obtained from EMS, dispatch, and registry databases. The primary outcome was 30‑day survival. RESULTS: Among 9413 OHCAs, EMS attached the first AED in 72% of cases, followed by on-duty first responders (ODFR) (18%), bystanders (6.0%), and community first responders (CFR) (4.5%). EMS attachment decreased from 77% to 67%, whereas CFR involvement increased from 1% to 13%. 30‑day survival was highest when AEDs were attached by bystanders (28%), compared with 9.0% for EMS, 8.7% for ODFR and 8.6% for CFR. Among witnessed OHCAs with an initial shockable rhythm, 30-day survival was highest in bystander-attached cases (62%), compared with 36% for CFR, 32% for ODFR, and 24% for EMS. In the multivariable analysis, bystander AED attachment was associated with higher odds of 30‑day survival compared with EMS (OR 2.25; 95% CI 1.77-2.85). CONCLUSION: In this multi-response system, survival was highest when AEDs were first attached by bystanders and remained higher after adjustment for known prognostic factors. This association likely reflects earlier access to defibrillation. These findings suggest that improving immediate access to defibrillation may have the greatest impact on OHCA outcomes.

items.title: Community first responder activation reduces the negative impact of AED distance on bystander defibrillation after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest
items.abstract: Introduction Early defibrillation is critical for survival after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA), yet bystander defibrillation remains uncommon despite the availability of automated external defibrillators (AEDs). We investigated whether HeartRunner community first responder activation increased the likelihood of bystander defibrillation and 30-day survival in relation to the distance to the nearest accessible AED. Methods Linking data from the Danish Cardiac Arrest Registry, Danish AED Network, and HeartRunner application, we identified patients with OHCA eligible for HeartRunner activation during 2017-2021. Using street-network distances to the nearest accessible AED, we examined associations between HeartRunner activation, bystander defibrillation, and 30-day survival using multivariable logistic regression with interaction terms and targeted maximum likelihood estimation (TMLE). Results Among 5,753 OHCAs (median age, 74 years; 64% male; 78% in private locations), HeartRunner activation (41%) was associated with higher bystander defibrillation across AED distances (p-interaction = 0.004), with no interaction for 30-day survival (p-interaction = 0.054). Predicted bystander defibrillation with versus without HeartRunner activation was 9.6% vs 5.5% at Q1 (389 m), 10.0% vs 4.3% at median (717 m), and 13.0% vs 4.8% at Q3 (1,183 m). TMLE estimated a 6.1-percentage-point higher probability of bystander defibrillation (95% CI, 4.5-7.8; p Conclusion HeartRunner activation attenuated the decline in bystander defibrillation with increasing AED distance following OHCA, without a corresponding distance interaction for 30-day survival. Overall, TMLE supported higher bystander defibrillation and suggested a modest increase in 30-day survival with HeartRunner activation.

Total gastric and intragastric air volumes in immediate post-resuscitation whole-body computed tomography after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest: Association with airway management, aspiration, diaphragmatic position and initial blood gas analysis
items.abstract: Background Gastric distension (GD) may occur during cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR), but quantitative human data after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) remain limited. We quantified gastric volumes after OHCA and explored associations with prehospital airway strategy, CT-defined aspiration, diaphragmatic position, and initial blood gases. Methods This retrospective single-center study included OHCA patients undergoing post-resuscitation whole-body computed tomography (CT) within 180 minutes of emergency department (ED) admission between January 1, 2020, and March 31, 2025. Total gastric volume (TGV) and intragastric air volume (GAV) were quantified by CT volumetry. Results Of 255 identified patients, 120 underwent CT within 180 minutes. Median TGV was 594 mL and correlated strongly with GAV (p 2 and both TGV (ρ = 0.16; one-tailed p = 0.037) and GAV (ρ = 0.19; one-tailed p = 0.018). Conclusion Gastric volumes were high in this selected post-OHCA immediate CT (< 180 minutes) cohort. No significant differences were detected according to recorded prehospital airway strategy, and gastric volume was not associated with CT-defined aspiration. Mechanisms and clinical consequences remain uncertain and require prospective studies before preventive/ therapeutic implications can be established.
