Improvement in Peak Oxygen Consumption Following Cardiac Rehabilitation in Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest (OHCA) Survivors: A Comparative Study with ST-elevation Myocardial Infarction (STEMI) Patients
items.abstract: Aim To investigate the impact of phase II cardiac rehabilitation (CR) on cardiopulmonary fitness in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) survivors and to compare outcomes with ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) patients categorized by Killip classification. Methods This retrospective study was conducted at a tertiary medical center in Taiwan. We included 31 OHCA survivors whose cardiac events occurred between February 1, 2012, and June 30, 2023, and who completed phase II CR with symptom-limited cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET) performed before and after CR. For comparison, 78 patients with STEMI were included, comprising 54 with Killip class I-II and 24 with Killip class III-IV. All participants underwent phase II CR, which was scheduled for 36 sessions and consisted of aerobic and resistance training. The primary outcomes were changes in CPET parameters after CR, including peak workload, peak oxygen consumption (V̇O 2 peak), and percent-predicted V̇O 2 peak. Paired t tests were used to evaluate within-group changes, and repeated-measures ANOVA was employed to compare between-group differences. Results OHCA survivors exhibited significant improvements in V̇O 2 peak (+3.9 mL/kg/min, p 2 peak after CR, with a mean improvement of 24.8% in V̇O 2 peak. These gains were comparable to those seen in STEMI patients across Killip classes. Although OHCA survivors had lower pre-CR V̇O 2 peak, they demonstrated similar trainability. Conclusions This study highlights that OHCA survivors can undergo CR and achieve meaningful improvements in cardiopulmonary fitness, comparable to patients with myocardial infarction. These findings support the implementation of structured CR programs in this high-risk population.

items.title: When AI gets CPR wrong: why clinicians must stay in the loop
Reversed airflow during asynchronous volume controlled mechanical ventilation in Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: a physiological observational study
items.abstract: Aim Chest compressions during the inspiratory phase of a ventilation can force air out of the lungs, so-called reversed airflow. Human data on this phenomenon during mechanical ventilation are lacking. We aimed to quantify its frequency and magnitude during asynchronous mechanical ventilation in intubated adult out-of-hospital cardiac arrest patients receiving continuous chest compressions. Methods This single-centre descriptive cross-sectional study used prospectively collected data from patients treated by a physician-staffed prehospital team. After tracheal intubation, patients were ventilated with an Oxylog 3000 transport ventilator in volume-controlled mode without positive end-expiratory pressure, during continuous manual chest compressions. Intratracheal pressures recorded via two catheters allowed calculation of airflow and ventilation parameters during the first minute after intubation. Reversed airflow was defined as expiratory airflow during the inspiratory phase of a mechanical breath. Continuous data are reported as median (first-third quartile). Results Twelve patients were included (median age 68 years [62-75]; 7 [58.3%] male), of whom 5 (41.7%) achieved sustained return of spontaneous circulation. Reversed airflow occurred in 10 (83.3%; 95% CI 55.2-95.3) patients and in 141 of 172 (82.0%; 95% CI 75.6-87.0) analysed ventilations. The median reversed-airflow volume was 61 mL [42-80] per episode. Median ventilation rate was 14 breaths/min [13-16], gross inspiratory tidal volume 324 mL [305-345], minute ventilation 4.8 L/min [3.8-5.9], and peak inspiratory pressure 46 cmH 2 O [40-52]. Conclusion Reversed airflow occurred frequently during asynchronous volume-controlled mechanical ventilation with the Oxylog 3000 in intubated out-of-hospital cardiac arrest patients receiving continuous manual chest compressions. Its physiological and clinical implications require further investigation.

items.title: MRI-Derived Spatial Patterns of Post-Cardiac Arrest Brain Injury Are Associated With Cerebral Oxygenation Dynamics
items.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Post-cardiac arrest brain injury (PCABI) varies substantially in severity and anatomical distribution between patients. We evaluated whether anatomically resolved diffusion-weighted MRI (DWI) lesion patterns are associated with cerebral oxygenation following cardiac arrest. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective study of 24 patients with PCABI who underwent brain MRI and intraparenchymal neuromonitoring. Ischemic lesion burden was quantified as the percentage of tissue with an apparent diffusion coefficient <650×10-6 mm2/s across 164 brain segments. Principal component analysis (PCA) and k-means clustering were used to identify MRI-derived injury patterns for downstream physiological analysis. Brain tissue oxygen tension (PbtO2), intracranial pressure (ICP), and jugular venous oxygen saturation (SjvO2) were analyzed during the first 72 hours after cardiac arrest. RESULTS: Three reproducible MRI-derived injury patterns (i.e., clusters) were identified (n=13, 6, and 5), with progressively greater whole-brain lesion burden from Cluster 1 (10.16% [9.00-11.68]) to Cluster 2 (22.14% [17.83-25.12]) and Cluster 3 (38.40% [30.92-41.45]; p<0.001). Greater whole-brain lesion burden was associated with lower PbtO2 (r=-0.44, p=0.031) and higher SjvO2 (r=0.53, p=0.009), but not ICP (r=0.11, p=0.623). PbtO2 was lower in Cluster 3 than Cluster 1 (16.0±10.6 vs 26.6±9.0 mmHg; p=0.027), whereas SjvO2 was higher in Clusters 2 and 3 than Cluster 1 (both p<0.05). DISCUSSION: MRI-derived injury patterns differed in global lesion burden, PbtO2, and SjvO2, but not ICP. Greater whole-brain lesion burden was associated with lower PbtO2 and higher SjvO2, whereas no association was observed with ICP. These findings show that the extent and distribution of diffusion-restricted brain injury are linked to distinct cerebral oxygenation profiles after cardiac arrest.

items.title: Opioid administration prior to in-hospital cardiac arrest
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Opioid administration is common in hospitalised patients. The opioid antagonist naloxone has been proposed as a potential adjunct during cardiopulmonary resuscitation. We aimed to describe opioid exposure within 24 hours before in-hospital cardiac arrest (IHCA) and explore associations with outcomes. METHODS: Retrospective observational study on all adult (≥18 years) IHCA during 2024 across nine hospitals in southernmost Sweden, registered in the Swedish Registry for Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation. Opioid administrations were collected from medical records. Exploratory logistic regressions assessed associations between opioid exposure (any administration and cumulative dose) and return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) and 30-day survival, adjusted for age, sex, witnessed IHCA and national early warning score. RESULTS: Opioids were administered within 24 hours preceding IHCA in 108/267 (40%) patients and in 43/267 (16%) patients within the last two hours. Median time from last opioid administration to IHCA was 2.7 hours (IQR 0.5-7.7). Median oral cumulative morphine milligram equivalent dose was 17 mg (IQR 9-30). Naloxone was administered in 6/267 (2%) of IHCA. Opioid administration within 24 hours prior to IHCA was not associated with ROSC (OR 1.03 [95%CI 0.59-1.78, p=0.93]) or 30-day survival (OR 0.98 [95%CI 0.55-1.73], p=0.94). Higher cumulative opioid doses were associated with lower odds of ROSC (OR 0.91 [95%CI 0.83-1.00], p=0.042), but not 30-day survival (OR 0.98 [95%CI 0.90-1.08], p=0.69). CONCLUSIONS: Opioid administration within 24 hours preceding IHCA is common, with frequent administrations shortly before cardiac arrest. Further research is warranted investigating a potential role of opioid reversal during IHCA.

items.title: Psychological outcomes of spouses of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest survivors according to witnessing and cardiopulmonary resuscitation performance: Results from the cross-sectional DANCAS study
items.abstract: Aim Spouses often witness out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) and perform cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR), but associations with psychological outcomes remain unclear. The aim was to describe the prevalence of symptoms of anxiety, depression and caregiver strain according to spouses' level of involvement and to investigate associations between involvement and these outcomes. Methods This cross-sectional study used data from spouses participating in the national DANCAS survey. Symptoms of anxiety and depression were assessed using the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale, and caregiver strain using the Modified Caregiver Strain Index. Associations between involvement and psychological outcomes were investigated using logistic regression models adjusted for sex, age and employment status. Results Of 461 spouses, 32% (n=148) reported symptoms of anxiety, 10% (n=44) symptoms of depression and 25% (n=115) caregiver strain. The prevalence of symptoms did not differ significantly across the levels of involvement. In adjusted analyses, witnessing OHCA without performing CPR was associated with higher odds of symptoms of depression compared with not witnessing OHCA (OR 3.18 95% CI 1.38-7.35). No statistically significant associations were observed for symptoms of anxiety or caregiver strain. Conclusion Symptoms of anxiety and caregiver strain were common across all levels of involvement. Witnessing OHCA without performing CPR was associated with higher odds of symptoms of depression, while no other associations were found. These findings suggest that level of involvement alone may be insufficient to identify spouses at risk of psychological distress.

items.title: Sex Differences in Neurological Outcomes After Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: Sequential Adjusted Analysis from the JAAM Registry
items.abstract: Introduction Sex differences in outcomes after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) remain controversial. We examined sex differences in neurological outcomes after OHCA and explored how the estimated association changed as measured patient, arrest, and treatment characteristics were sequentially included. Methods We conducted a retrospective cohort study using data from the Japan Association for Acute Medicine OHCA Registry (2014-2022). Adult non-traumatic OHCA patients (≥ 18) were included. The primary outcome was favorable neurological outcome (CPC 1-2) at 1 month, and the secondary outcome was 1-month survival. Sequential logistic regression models adjusted for age, arrest characteristics, bystander interventions, initial shockable rhythm, public-access automated external defibrillator (PAD/AED) use, and advanced treatments. Age-stratified post hoc analyses further evaluated PAD/AED use and initial rhythm. Results Among 65,346 patients (39,576 men and 25,770 women), women had lower crude 1-month favorable neurological outcomes (2.4% vs. 5.4%; p < 0.01) and 1-month survival (4.5% vs. 8.7%; p < 0.01). The crude odds ratio (OR) for 1-month favorable neurological outcome in women versus men was 0.44 (95% CI, 0.40–0.48), compared with 1.00 (95% CI, 0.89–1.12) in the fully adjusted model. Women aged 18-64 years had better neurological outcomes than men when PAD/AED was used (66.7% vs. 49.0%; p < 0.01) or when the initial rhythm was shockable (37.7% vs. 30.0%; p < 0.01), but these differences diminished with age. Conclusions Women have poorer crude neurological and survival outcomes after OHCA. However, the association between women and favorable neurological outcomes progressively attenuated with the sequential inclusion of measured factors. The causal contributions of individual factors cannot be determined from this exploratory sequential analysis.

items.title: Trends in Temperature Control after Cardiac Arrest in Cardiac Intensive Care Units: An Analysis from the Critical Care Cardiology Trials Network
items.abstract: Temperature control (TC) is recommended for comatose patients after cardiac arrest (CA). In the TTM2 trial, targeted normothermia (≤37.5°C) resulted in similar mortality and functional outcomes as targeted hypothermia (33°C). The Critical Care Cardiology Trials Network (CCCTN) is a multinational registry of cardiac intensive care units (CICU) coordinated by the TIMI Study Group (Boston, MA). Between 2018-2024, consecutive comatose CA admissions were classified as occurring before vs. after publication and initial assimilation of TTM2. We compared temporal trends in TC use, temperature targets, and outcomes between the pre- and post-TTM2 eras, including in subgroups with initial shockable (VT/VF) vs. non-shockable (PEA/asystole) rhythms. Multivariable logistic regression was used to adjust for baseline differences. Among 1,706 comatose CA admissions, 773 occurred in the pre-TTM2 era and 933 in the post-TTM2 era. TC use was similar pre- and post-TTM2 (74% vs. 78%; p=0.06), including in subgroups with shockable (84% vs. 85%; p=0.85) and non-shockable rhythms (64% vs. 68%; p=0.26). Post-TTM2, target temperatures shifted towards normothermia (target temperature ≥36°C: 38% [pre] vs. 71% [post]; p<0.001). Mortality was higher post-TTM2 vs. pre-TTM2 among CA admissions with shockable rhythms (50% vs. 42%; aOR 1.48, 95% CI 1.11-1.99), but not with non-shockable rhythms (76% vs. 75%; aOR 1.03 [0.71-1.49]). Comparing CA admissions with shockable rhythms to non-CA admissions, the difference in proportional increase in mortality between eras was not statistically significant (ROR 1.20 [0.91-1.58]). In a large CICU cohort of comatose CA patients, overall use of TC remained stable over the study period (2018-2024), but clinicians increasingly favored targeted normothermia. In-hospital mortality among patients with initial shockable rhythms was higher in the post-TTM2 era, which may be related to secular changes in CICU patients over time.

items.title: Prevalence and Patterns of Acute Cerebral Infarctions in Comatose Survivors of Cardiac Arrest
items.abstract: It is well-established that hypoxic-ischemic brain injury (HIBI) is the leading cause of death and disability after cardiac arrest. However, there is limited information about concurrent acute cerebral infarctions (ACI) and their association with clinical outcomes in comatose cardiac arrest survivors. This was a retrospective multicenter cohort study of adult patients after cardiac arrest. We included patients who had brain MRIs performed within 7 days of cardiac arrest and excluded patients with a diagnosis of acute traumatic brain injury, intracranial hemorrhage, and acute ischemic stroke on admission. Univariate and multivariable analyses were performed to identify factors associated with ACI and to evaluate the association between ACI and unfavorable outcomes at hospital discharge (i.e., Cerebral Performance Category of 3-5). Of 351 patients included, 106 (30.2%) had ACI on MRI. The most common ACI pattern was multifocal small embolic-appearing (38.7%), followed by punctate (33%), territorial (18.9%), watershed (14.2%), and lacunar (14.2%), with overlapping patterns in 17% of patients with ACI. The patients with ACI were older (64 [54-71] vs 56 [39-66] years). Chronic white matter lesions were associated with ACI (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 1.79 [1.04-3.1], p<0.05). On univariate and multivariable analyses, ACI was not associated with unfavorable outcomes. Older age (aOR 1.04 [1.02-1.07], p<0.001) and presence of HIBI on MRI (aOR 8.41 [3.95-17.88], p<0.001) were associated with unfavorable outcomes on multivariable analysis. ACI was present in nearly a third of patients with cardiac arrest. The most common pattern of ACI was multifocal embolic-appearing, and ACI was associated with chronic white matter lesions. The independent impact of ACI on cardiac arrest survivors' outcomes requires additional investigation in future prospective studies.

items.title: Coronary artery disease severity in patients with refractory out-of-hospital cardiac arrest: a secondary analysis of the INCEPTION trial
items.abstract: Background Extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) can restore circulation in patients with refractory out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA). Subsequent invasive coronary angiography (ICA) allows the treatment of reversible causes and enables the evaluation of the presence and severity of coronary artery disease, facilitating insights into the cause of refractory arrest. Methods This secondary analysis of the INCEPTION trial, which randomized refractory OHCA patients between ECPR or conventional CPR, included all patients who underwent ICA. Angiograms were reanalyzed following a standardized protocol by two cardiologists, on presence of significant stenoses (>50%), with calculation of the SYNTAX score as a proxy for coronary artery disease severity. Patients were grouped as having "ROSC" or "no-ROSC", irrespective of the original assignment. In addition, patients with "no-ROSC" who had persistent ventricular arrhythmias were compared with those who converted to non-shockable rhythms. Results We included 73 patients: 29 ROSC and 44 no-ROSC (persistent ventricular arrhythmia, n=10; non-shockable conversion, n=34). No-ROSC patients had more frequent obstructive coronary artery disease (84% versus 66%, p=0.037), were more likely to have at least one acute culprit lesion (52% versus 21%, p=0.009) than ROSC patients, and had a higher SYNTAX score (17 ± 11 versus 10± 9, p=0.002). Lesions were predominantly left-sided. Conclusion Patients who do not achieve ROSC after refractory OHCA have more complex CAD and present more frequently with obstructive disease and a culprit lesion than patients who achieve ROSC. This seems particularly evident in patients who rapidly convert to a non-shockable rhythm.

items.title: Interleukin-6 Inhibition with Ziltivekimab for Atherosclerotic Disease
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: The inflammatory cytokine interleukin-6 is hypothesized to be a therapeutic target for patients with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease and chronic kidney disease. Whether neutralizing interleukin-6 levels with ziltivekimab, a monoclonal antibody, reduces the risk of adverse cardiovascular events remains unknown. METHODS: We conducted a multinational, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial involving adults with established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, chronic kidney disease, and cardiovascular inflammation (defined by a high-sensitivity C-reactive protein [CRP] level of ≥2 mg per liter). Patients were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to receive subcutaneous ziltivekimab (15 mg once monthly) or placebo. The primary efficacy end point was a 3-point major adverse cardiovascular event (MACE). This composite end point included death from cardiovascular causes, nonfatal myocardial infarction, or nonfatal stroke. RESULTS: A total of 6376 patients were included in the full analysis population: 3184 were assigned to receive ziltivekimab and 3192 to receive placebo. The mean age of the patients was 69.4 years, and 27.5% were women. At 24 months, the between-group difference in the median percent change in the levels of inflammatory biomarkers among patients receiving ziltivekimab as compared with those receiving placebo was -76 percentage points for free interleukin-6 and -64 percentage points for high-sensitivity CRP. During a median follow-up of 33 months, a primary end-point event occurred in 561 patients (17.6%) in the ziltivekimab group and in 565 patients (17.7%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.99; 95% confidence interval, 0.88 to 1.11; P = 0.84). Serious adverse events occurred in 54.6% of the patients in the ziltivekimab group and in 54.8% of those in the placebo group; serious infections occurred in 20.4% and 17.9%, respectively. CONCLUSIONS: Among patients with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, chronic kidney disease, and cardiovascular inflammation, a strategy of lowering interleukin-6 levels with ziltivekimab did not result in a lower risk of cardiovascular events than placebo. (Funded by Novo Nordisk; ZEUS ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT05021835.).

items.title: Pelacarsen and Cardiovascular Outcomes in Patients with High Lipoprotein(a)
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Pelacarsen, an antisense oligonucleotide, reduces serum levels of lipoprotein(a). However, the effect of pelacarsen on cardiovascular outcomes remains uncertain. METHODS: We conducted an international, randomized, placebo-controlled trial involving patients with preexisting cardiovascular disease and a lipoprotein(a) level of at least 70 mg per deciliter. Patients were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to receive subcutaneous pelacarsen (80 mg) administered monthly or matching placebo. The primary end point was a major adverse cardiovascular event, defined as a composite of death from cardiovascular causes, nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, or urgent coronary revascularization. RESULTS: A total of 8350 patients underwent randomization, with 8322 included in the efficacy analysis; 4157 patients were assigned to receive pelacarsen, and 4165 to receive placebo. The mean age of the patients was 59.7 years, and 27.0% were women. The median lipoprotein(a) level at baseline was 236 nmol per liter. At 12 months, the lipoprotein(a) level was 64.4 nmol per liter in the pelacarsen group and 233.4 nmol per liter in the placebo group. The median follow-up was 4.7 years. A primary end-point event occurred in 511 patients (12.3%) in the pelacarsen group and in 503 (12.1%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 1.02, 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.90 to 1.15, P = 0.76). Among patients with a baseline lipoprotein(a) level of at least 90 mg per deciliter, a primary end-point event occurred in 402 of 3266 patients (12.3%) in the pelacarsen group and in 403 of 3274 (12.3%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 1.00; 95% CI, 0.87 to 1.15; P = 0.99). Serious adverse events occurred in 1553 of 4166 patients (37.3%) who received pelacarsen and in 1709 of 4154 (41.1%) who received placebo. CONCLUSIONS: Pelacarsen did not result in a lower risk of major adverse cardiovascular events than placebo at a median follow-up of 4.7 years. (Funded by Novartis; Lp[a]HORIZON ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT04023552.)See also in NEJM Evidence: Extended Analyses of Pelacarsen and Cardiovascular Outcomes in Patients with High Lipoprotein(a).

items.title: Bringing Rapid Reperfusion to More Patients with Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest
items.abstract: It has taken a long time to move extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) from a method used for late rescue of patients in cardiac arrest toward one used for earlier reperfusion. The priority for ECPR is not to replace high-quality cardiopulmonary resuscitation or rapid defibrillation but to serve as an alternative intervention while advanced cardiovascular life support efforts continue. When spontaneous circulation cannot be restored promptly, ECPR — using extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) to provide circulation and gas exchange — can buy time to treat the underlying cause of the arrest and support recovery. ECPR is a lifeline and therapeutic bridge, . . .

items.title: Prehospital Extracorporeal Life Support in Refractory Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: In patients with refractory out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) with the use of venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation can be performed to establish reperfusion. Data comparing prehospital ECPR with conventional care regarding survival until hospital discharge among patients who are 50 years of age or younger with refractory out-of-hospital cardiac arrest are limited. METHODS: In a nationwide, nonrandomized study conducted in the Netherlands, we evaluated the outcomes in young adults who were attended by Helicopter Emergency Medical Services (HEMS) that were equipped to deliver prehospital ECPR (intervention group) as compared with those attended by HEMS without ECPR capability (conventional group). The primary outcome was survival until hospital discharge. RESULTS: A total of 144 patients were included in the intervention group, and 87 were included in the conventional group. In the intervention group, 57 of 144 patients (40%) survived until hospital discharge, as compared with 17 of 87 patients (20%) in the conventional group (odds ratio, 2.72; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.59 to 4.66; P = 0.002). At 6 months, a favorable neurologic outcome was reported in 51 of 141 patients (36%) in the intervention group and in 11 of 85 patients (13%) in the conventional group (odds ratio, 4.22; 95% CI, 2.82 to 6.32). There were 32 adverse events in the intervention group and 11 in the conventional group. CONCLUSIONS: Among patients who were 50 years of age or younger with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, incorporating ECPR into HEMS was associated with improved survival until hospital discharge, as compared with conventional care. (Funded by the Dutch Ministry of Health; OnScene ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT04620070.).

items.title: Intensive Blood-Pressure Control in Patients with Previous Ischemic Stroke
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Whether intensive blood-pressure control reduces cardiovascular risk after cerebrovascular events remains uncertain. METHODS: In this multicenter, open-label, randomized trial conducted at 30 sites in Brazil, we assigned participants with elevated blood pressure and previous ischemic stroke or transient ischemic attack to receive intensive treatment targeting a systolic blood pressure of less than 120 mm Hg or to receive standard treatment targeting a systolic blood pressure of less than 140 mm Hg. The primary outcome was a composite of death from cardiovascular causes, nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, or hospitalization for unstable angina or heart failure. RESULTS: A total of 4368 participants were enrolled, with 2172 assigned to intensive treatment and 2196 to standard treatment. The mean (±SD) age of the participants was 63.9±11.2 years, and 2093 (47.9%) were women. During the follow-up period, excluding the first 3 months, the mean systolic blood pressure was 122.0±11.5 mm Hg (median, 119.6 mm Hg) in the intensive-treatment group and 135.2±9.7 mm Hg (median, 135.0 mm Hg) in the standard-treatment group, with a between-group mean difference of 13.1 mm Hg (95% confidence interval [CI], 12.5 to 13.8). Over a median follow-up of 3.9 years, a primary-outcome event occurred in 236 participants (10.9%; 3.25 events per 100 person-years) with intensive treatment and in 297 (13.5%; 4.11 events per 100 person-years) with standard treatment (hazard ratio, 0.79; 95% CI, 0.67 to 0.94; P = 0.007). The composite renal outcome (sustained reduction of ≥50% in the estimated glomerular filtration rate or progression to end-stage renal disease) was more common with intensive treatment. The overall incidence of serious adverse events was similar in the two groups. CONCLUSIONS: Among participants with previous ischemic stroke or transient ischemic attack, targeting a systolic blood pressure of less than 120 mm Hg resulted in a lower incidence of major cardiovascular events than targeting a systolic blood pressure of less than 140 mm Hg. (Funded by Hospital Israelita Albert Einstein and the Brazilian Ministry of Health; OPTIMAL-STROKE ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT04036409.).

items.title: Discontinuing Statins in Older Adults without Cardiovascular Disease
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Whether discontinuing statin therapy in older adults with at least two chronic conditions but no known cardiovascular disease affects the time to a first cardiovascular event is not well characterized. METHODS: We conducted an international, open-label, randomized, controlled trial that enrolled adults at least 70 years of age who were taking statins for primary prevention. Participants were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to either discontinue or continue statin therapy and other lipid-lowering therapies. The primary outcome was a composite of nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal ischemic stroke, or death from any cause, whichever occurred first. The primary analysis assessed noninferiority on the basis of the between-group difference in restricted mean event-free survival time at 2 years, with a noninferiority margin of -5.2 weeks. RESULTS: A total of 1880 participants underwent randomization: 938 were assigned to the discontinuation group and 942 to the continuation group. The mean age of the participants was 77.5 years, and 46.9% were women. The between-group difference in the restricted mean event-free survival time at 2 years was -2.0 weeks (95% confidence interval, -3.7 to -0.3; P<0.001 for noninferiority). Over a median follow-up of 103 weeks, 119 participants (12.7%) in the discontinuation group and 87 (9.2%) in the continuation group had a primary-outcome event. At least one serious adverse event occurred in 43.0% of the participants in the discontinuation group and in 39.8% in the continuation group. CONCLUSIONS: Among older adults with at least two chronic conditions but no known cardiovascular disease, discontinuation of statin therapy was noninferior to continuation with respect to major cardiovascular events or death from any cause at 2 years. (Funded by the Swiss National Science Foundation; STREAM ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT05178420.).

items.title: Intensive Blood-Pressure Lowering in Patients with Type 2 Diabetes
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Uncertainty persists regarding the effects of intensive blood-pressure lowering in patients with type 2 diabetes. METHODS: In this multicenter, open-label, randomized trial conducted in Brazil, patients with elevated blood pressure, type 2 diabetes, and high cardiovascular risk received intensive therapy targeting a systolic blood pressure of less than 120 mm Hg or standard therapy targeting a systolic blood pressure of less than 140 mm Hg. The primary end point was a composite of death from cardiovascular causes, nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, or hospitalization for unstable angina or heart failure. RESULTS: Of the 9476 ethnically diverse patients who were enrolled, 4745 were assigned to receive intensive therapy and 4731 to receive standard therapy. The mean (±SD) age was 64.7±8.2 years, and 5871 of the patients (62.0%) were women. The mean systolic blood pressure during follow-up (with exclusion of the first 3 months) was 121.8±10.8 mm Hg in the intensive-therapy group and 135.4±8.2 mm Hg in the standard-therapy group. During a median follow-up of 4.0 years (interquartile range, 3.9 to 4.0), a primary-outcome event occurred in 286 patients (6.0%; 1.65 events per 100 person-years) in the intensive-therapy group and in 315 patients (6.7%; 1.83 events per 100 person-years) in the standard-therapy group (hazard ratio, 0.90; 95% confidence interval, 0.77 to 1.06; P = 0.20). Serious adverse events occurred in 706 patients (14.9%) with intensive therapy and in 693 patients (14.6%) with standard therapy. CONCLUSIONS: Among patients with type 2 diabetes, targeting a systolic blood pressure of less than 120 mm Hg, as compared with less than 140 mm Hg, did not reduce the occurrence of major cardiovascular events. (Funded by Hospital Israelita Albert Einstein and the Brazilian Ministry of Health; OPTIMAL-DIABETES ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT04040634.).

items.title: Retatrutide Once Weekly in Adults with Knee Osteoarthritis Pain and Obesity
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Retatrutide, an investigational triple agonist of GIP, GLP-1, and glucagon receptors, may be useful for the treatment of painful knee osteoarthritis in persons with obesity. METHODS: In two phase 3 trials, adults without diabetes who had painful knee osteoarthritis and a body-mass index of at least 27 were randomly assigned to receive once-weekly subcutaneous retatrutide (9 or 12 mg in TRIUMPH-4 and 4, 9, or 12 mg in TRIUMPH-1-OA) or placebo. In TRIUMPH-4, the primary end points were the change in the WOMAC pain score (range, 0 to 10, with higher scores indicating worse pain) and the percent change in body weight at week 68. In TRIUMPH-1-OA, the primary end point was the change in the WOMAC pain score at week 80. For non-pain-related end points, intercurrent events were handled with a treatment-policy strategy. For pain-related end points, a hybrid-treatment estimand was applied, with a hypothetical strategy for intercurrent events that suggested treatment failure and a treatment-policy strategy elsewhere. We also report results for an intention-to-treat (ITT) estimand. RESULTS: A total of 445 participants underwent randomization in TRIUMPH-4 and 574 in TRIUMPH-1-OA. At 68 weeks, the mean changes in the WOMAC pain score (hybrid-treatment estimand) with retatrutide in TRIUMPH-4 were -3.96 (9 mg) and -3.74 (12 mg), versus -2.12 with placebo (difference vs. placebo, -1.83 [95% confidence interval {CI}, -2.37 to -1.30] and -1.61 [95% CI, -2.16 to -1.07], respectively). For the ITT estimand, the corresponding differences from placebo were -1.70 (95% CI, -2.19 to -1.22) and -1.38 (95% CI, -1.91 to -0.85) (P<0.001 for all comparisons). The mean percent changes in body weight with retatrutide were -20.0% (9 mg) and -23.7% (12 mg), versus -4.6% with placebo (difference vs. placebo, -15.4 percentage points [95% CI, -18.7 to -12.1] and -19.2 percentage points [95% CI, -22.4 to -15.9]; P<0.001 for both comparisons). At 80 weeks, the mean changes in the WOMAC pain score (hybrid-treatment estimand) with retatrutide in TRIUMPH-1-OA were -3.22 (4 mg), -3.48 (9 mg), and -3.64 (12 mg), versus -1.87 with placebo (difference vs. placebo, -1.35 [95% CI, -1.92 to -0.78], -1.61 [95% CI, -2.20 to -1.02], and -1.77 [95% CI, -2.34 to -1.20], respectively). For the ITT estimand, the corresponding differences from placebo were -0.96 (95% CI, -1.61 to -0.30), -1.41 (95% CI, -2.07 to -0.75), and -1.64 (95% CI, -2.26 to -1.02) (P≤0.005 for all comparisons). In both trials, serious adverse events were more common with retatrutide than with placebo, and the most common adverse events were gastrointestinal. CONCLUSIONS: In participants with painful knee osteoarthritis and obesity, treatment with retatrutide resulted in significantly greater reductions in both the WOMAC pain score and body weight than placebo. (Funded by Eli Lilly; TRIUMPH-4 and -1 ClinicalTrials.gov numbers, NCT05931367 and NCT05929066.).

items.title: A Liver-Targeted CIDEB siRNA in Adults with MASLD
items.abstract: A single dose of an siRNA targeting liver expression of CIDEB was associated with a reduction in liver fat of 58 to 80% at week 36 after treatment in persons with metabolic dysfunction–associated steatotic liver disease.

items.title: Left Bundle-Branch Pacing versus Right Ventricular Pacing for Atrioventricular Block
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Right ventricular pacing is associated with cardiac dyssynchrony and left ventricular systolic dysfunction. Left bundle-branch pacing preserves left ventricular electrical and mechanical synchrony, but its clinical benefits relative to right ventricular pacing in patients with atrioventricular block remain unclear. METHODS: In this investigator-initiated, international, open-label, randomized, controlled trial, we assigned patients with atrioventricular block in a 1:1 ratio to receive left bundle-branch pacing or right ventricular pacing. The primary outcome was a composite of death from any cause, hospitalization for heart failure, or pacing-induced cardiomyopathy. RESULTS: A total of 702 patients underwent randomization, with 348 assigned to receive left bundle-branch pacing and 354 to receive right ventricular pacing; 17 patients (6 in the left bundle-branch pacing group and 11 in the right ventricular pacing group) were excluded before device implantation. A total of 685 patients (342 in the left bundle-branch pacing group and 343 in the right ventricular pacing group) were included in the modified intention-to-treat analysis. The mean age of the patients was 68.4 years, and 57.5% were men. At the prespecified interim analysis, the data monitoring committee recommended early termination of the trial. At a median follow-up of 35.1 months (interquartile range, 23.6 to 40.7), a primary-outcome event had occurred in 16 patients in the left bundle-branch pacing group and in 35 patients in the right ventricular pacing group (Kaplan-Meier 4-year cumulative incidence, 8.5% and 19.2%, respectively; hazard ratio, 0.41; 95% confidence interval, 0.23 to 0.75; P = 0.003 by a stratified log-rank test). Serious adverse events unrelated to implantation procedures occurred in 39 patients (11.8%) who had received left bundle-branch pacing and in 33 patients (9.3%) who had received right ventricular pacing (P = 0.32). CONCLUSIONS: Among patients with atrioventricular block, left bundle-branch pacing was superior to right ventricular pacing in reducing the risk of a composite of death from any cause, hospitalization for heart failure, or pacing-induced cardiomyopathy. (Funded by Project on New Technology of Jiangsu Province and others; OptimPacing ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT04624763.).

items.title: Community and EMS Interventions to Improve Survival in Cardiac Arrest
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Early cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) and defibrillation improve survival after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, but evidence from randomized trials about whether community-based implementation strategies improve outcomes is lacking. METHODS: We conducted a registry-based, cluster-randomized trial involving adults with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest treated by emergency medical services (EMS) in North Carolina counties. The counties were grouped into clusters, which were then randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to implement a multifaceted intervention or administer usual care. The intervention included four components: training of 911 telecommunicators to improve rapid recognition of cardiac arrest, training of 911 telecommunicators to improve delivery of CPR instructions from telecommunicators to bystanders, community CPR training, and enhanced use of automated external defibrillators by first responders or bystanders before EMS arrival. Data were collected through the Cardiac Arrest Registry to Enhance Survival. The primary outcome was survival to hospital discharge with a good neurologic outcome (Cerebral Performance Category score of 1 or 2; range, 1 to 5, with higher scores indicating worse neurologic outcome). RESULTS: From July 1, 2022, to June 30, 2026, a total of 28 clusters comprising 11,615 patients were assigned to the intervention group, and 27 clusters comprising 10,844 patients were assigned to the usual-care group. The median age of the patients was 64.0 years, and 36.7% were women. The percentage of patients who survived to hospital discharge with a good neurologic outcome was 9.0% (1048 of 11,608 patients) in the intervention group and 9.4% (1017 of 10,839 patients) in the usual-care group (adjusted odds ratio, 0.97; 95% confidence interval, 0.75 to 1.26; P = 0.80). CONCLUSIONS: Among adults with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, implementation of a multifaceted strategy involving the community and EMS did not result in a greater percentage of patients who survived to hospital discharge with a favorable neurologic outcome than usual care. (Funded by the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute of the National Institutes of Health; RACE-CARS ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT04660526.).

items.title: ANGPTL4 Inhibition in Adults with Elevated Triglyceride Levels
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Angiopoietin-like protein 4 (ANGPTL4) inhibits lipoprotein lipase and regulates triglyceride-rich lipoprotein metabolism. MAR001 is a monoclonal antibody against ANGPTL4 that is being evaluated for lowering triglyceride levels. METHODS: We conducted a two-part, phase 2b, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial. In part A, the focus of this report, we enrolled adults who had a nonfasting triglyceride level of at least 175 mg per deciliter and a remnant cholesterol level of at least 35 mg per deciliter at initial screening, followed by a fasting triglyceride level of at least 150 mg per deciliter and a remnant cholesterol level of at least 30 mg per deciliter on confirmatory screening. Participants were randomly assigned in a 1:1:1:1 ratio to receive MAR001 at a dose of 300, 450, or 900 mg or matching placebo subcutaneously every 4 weeks for 24 weeks. The primary end point was the percent change from baseline in the fasting triglyceride level at week 12, reported as the difference between each MAR001 dose group and the placebo group (placebo-adjusted change). RESULTS: A total of 236 participants were enrolled in the trial, with 177 assigned to receive MAR001 and 59 to receive placebo; a total of 235 participants received at least one dose of MAR001 or placebo and were included in the primary efficacy analyses. The mean age of the participants was 60.4 years, and 39% were women. The median triglyceride level at baseline was 249.5 mg per deciliter (interquartile range, 210.0 to 313.0). At week 12, in an intention-to-treat analysis, the placebo-adjusted least-squares mean percent changes in the fasting triglyceride level were -39.1 percentage points, -40.5 percentage points, and -45.3 percentage points for the 300-mg, 450-mg, and 900-mg doses, respectively (P<0.001 for all comparisons). Adverse events occurred in 123 of 177 participants (69%) in the pooled MAR001 group and in 45 of 58 participants (78%) in the placebo group. CONCLUSIONS: Inhibition of ANGPTL4 with MAR001 significantly reduced fasting triglyceride levels at 12 weeks. (Funded by Marea Therapeutics; TYDAL-TIMI 78 ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT07028749.).

items.title: Cancer Vaccines — From Treatment to Prevention
items.abstract: Vaccines have been among the most transformative advances in modern medicine, dramatically reducing the global burden of infectious diseases. Vaccines against the hepatitis B virus (HBV) and human papillomavirus (HPV) also play an important role in reducing the incidence of certain virus-associated cancers. However, until now, efforts to develop vaccines that directly target established cancers have been largely unsuccessful. Yet despite decades of repeated clinical setbacks, research in the field of cancer vaccines has continued to stumble forward, buoyed by new mechanistic insights that have emerged from the era of immune checkpoint inhibitors. items.title: Interferon-γ Underlying Thymoma-Associated Immune Dysregulation
items.abstract: In an observational study, thymoma-associated immune dysregulation was characterized by interferon-γ pathway activation. Four patients with severe disease treated with Janus kinase 1/2 inhibitors had clinical and biomarker responses.

items.title: Autoantibodies against Type I Interferons and Death from H7N7 Avian Influenza
Subretinal Gene Therapy in X-Linked Retinoschisis
items.abstract: To the Editor: Liang et al. (June 11 issue) 1 report the results of a study involving 12 pediatric patients with X-linked retinoschisis. Complete closure of the macular schisis cavity was observed in the treated eye of each patient after subretinal injection of a self-complementary AAV8 vector containing a human RS1 transgene (scAAV8-hRS1). Although these results are encouraging, pars plana vitrectomy, posterior vitreous detachment, stripping of the internal limiting membrane, and air tamponade were performed in all the treated eyes before administration of scAAV8-hRS1 (see the Supplementary Appendix of the article). The effects of these surgical manipulations on schisis closure warrant . . .

items.title: Iptacopan in IgA Nephropathy — Final 24-Month Data
items.abstract: To the Editor: IgA nephropathy is the most common chronic glomerulonephritis in children, and its disease burden extends across decades. Barratt et al. (July 30 issue) 1 report final 24-month results from APPLAUSE-IgAN, a trial involving adults. The absence of dedicated data from children drives widespread off-label reliance on broad immunosuppression and its associated growth and metabolic toxic effects. 2 Enrollment of younger children across complement-targeted trials has been incomplete; although IgA nephropathy trials of iptacopan (ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT06994845 ) and ravulizumab ( NCT07024563 ) are enrolling children as young as 2 years of age, many trials exclude children. The proteinuria-based end points in the . . .

items.title: Perioperative Apalutamide in High-Risk Localized Prostate Cancer
items.abstract: To the Editor: In their report of the PROTEUS (Perioperative Treatment with Erleada United with Surgery) trial, Taplin et al. (Aug. 6 issue) 1 conclude that perioperative treatment with androgen-deprivation therapy (ADT) plus apalutamide improved the outcomes of radical prostatectomy in high-risk prostate cancer as compared with ADT plus placebo. Two concerns should temper this conclusion. First, the benefit with respect to metastasis-free survival was fragile. The hazard ratio of 0.80 for distant metastasis or death (P=0.02) was driven by metastasis events detected on prostate-specific membrane antigen positron-emission tomography (PSMA PET); the between-group difference in metastasis-free survival as assessed with conventional . . .

items.abstract: A 50-year-old man was admitted to the hospital for recurrent systolic heart failure. He had a history of obstructive sleep apnea, impaired libido, and intermittent erythrocytosis. A diagnosis was made.

items.title: Aspirin Therapy — Enough after Arthroplasty?
items.abstract: Choosing thromboprophylaxis after hip or knee arthroplasty requires balancing the prevention of venous thromboembolism (VTE) against the risks of bleeding and wound complications. Aspirin is inexpensive and convenient, but whether it can replace anticoagulants, particularly immediately after surgery, has remained uncertain. The Pulmonary Embolism Prevention trial, 1 which was completed more than 20 years ago, showed that aspirin led to a lower risk of VTE than placebo among patients undergoing major orthopedic surgery, predominantly surgery to repair hip fracture. Subsequent trials tested aspirin after initial anticoagulant prophylaxis: the EPCAT I (Extended Prophylaxis Comparing Low-Molecular-Weight Heparin to Aspirin in Total Hip Arthroplasty . . .

items.abstract: An 81-year-old man with a remote history of rib and lung resection was noted on examination to have a soft protrusion from the chest wall that moved inward during inspiration and outward during expiration (shown in a video).

items.title: Prevention of Venous Thromboembolism after Total Hip or Knee Replacement
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Studies comparing aspirin with anticoagulants for venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis after total hip or knee arthroplasty have had conflicting results. METHODS: In a comparative-effectiveness noninferiority trial, we randomly assigned patients undergoing elective hip or knee arthroplasty to receive aspirin (81 mg twice daily), warfarin (to a target international normalized ratio of 2.0), or rivaroxaban (10 mg daily) for 30 days. The composite primary effectiveness outcome (death from any cause or symptomatic VTE) and primary safety outcome (bleeding, reoperation for wound problems, or myocardial infarction) were evaluated through 6 months in a blinded fashion. The noninferiority margin for the risk difference was 0.69 percentage points. RESULTS: Among 18,883 participants who had undergone randomization, 15,317 (7214 with hip arthroplasty and 8103 with knee arthroplasty) were included in the primary per-protocol analysis. A primary effectiveness outcome event occurred in 77 of 6090 participants (1.26%) in the aspirin group, in 52 of 4231 (1.23%) in the warfarin group, and in 47 of 4996 (0.94%) in the rivaroxaban group; a primary safety outcome event occurred in 177 (2.91%), 142 (3.36%), and 174 (3.48%), respectively. In pairwise comparisons, 6-month risks of a primary effectiveness outcome event were 1.24% and 0.94% for aspirin versus rivaroxaban (difference, 0.30 percentage points; 95% confidence interval [CI], -0.20 to 0.81); 1.24% and 1.01% for aspirin versus warfarin (difference, 0.23 percentage points; 95% CI, -0.34 to 0.81); and 1.13% and 1.10% for warfarin versus rivaroxaban (difference, 0.03 percentage points; 95% CI, -0.57 to 0.63). Risks of a primary safety outcome event were 3.70% and 3.02% for rivaroxaban versus aspirin (difference, 0.68 percentage points; 95% CI, -0.04 to 1.41); 3.65% and 2.88% for warfarin versus aspirin (difference, 0.77 percentage points; 95% CI, -0.04 to 1.58); and 3.59% and 3.61% for rivaroxaban versus warfarin (difference, -0.02 percentage points; 95% CI, -0.89 to 0.85). Intention-to-treat analyses yielded similar results. CONCLUSIONS: Aspirin prophylaxis after total hip or knee arthroplasty was not noninferior to rivaroxaban or warfarin with respect to death or symptomatic VTE. Warfarin and rivaroxaban were not noninferior to aspirin for safety. (Funded by the Patient-Centered Outcomes Research Institute; PEPPER ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT02810704.).

items.title: Preventing Malaria Infections and Moving toward Malaria Elimination
items.abstract: Malaria continues to be a major health challenge worldwide, causing an estimated 282 million cases of illness and 610,000 deaths in 2024, predominantly among African children. Despite recent stagnation in the progress of malaria prevention, the landscape is undergoing rapid transformation. This review examines current and emerging approaches to preventing malaria infection and supporting malaria elimination, including vector control, transmission-blocking interventions, chemoprevention, monoclonal antibodies, and vaccines. Next-generation insecticide-treated nets, expanded use of seasonal malaria chemoprevention, and the introduction of RTS,S/AS01 and R21/Matrix-M vaccines are already reshaping control strategies. Looking ahead, long-acting injectable chemoprevention, transmission-blocking medicines and vaccines, and improved surveillance-driven deployment may further accelerate progress. As funding becomes constrained and decision making shifts increasingly to countries where malaria is endemic, effective malaria prevention will depend on locally tailored, integrated combinations of interventions supported by strong surveillance, regulatory capacity, and national leadership.

items.title: High-Flow Oxygen Therapy with Nasal Cannula
items.abstract: This video demonstrates high-flow oxygen delivery with a nasal cannula, a device widely used in perioperative medicine and critical care.

items.title: Intismeran Autogene plus Pembrolizumab for Resected Stage IIB to IV Melanoma
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Intismeran autogene (intismeran) is an individualized neoantigen therapy that is designed to induce new T-cell responses and expand preexisting T-cell responses against patient-specific tumor neoantigens, which may potentially improve the efficacy of adjuvant therapy in patients with melanoma. METHODS: In this phase 3, double-blind trial, we randomly assigned patients with completely resected stage IIB to IV cutaneous melanoma in a 2:1 ratio to receive intramuscular intismeran (at a dose of 1 mg) or placebo every 3 weeks for nine doses; all the patients received intravenous pembrolizumab (at a dose of 400 mg) every 6 weeks for nine cycles. The primary end point was investigator-determined recurrence-free survival, assessed in a time-to-event analysis. Key secondary end points included investigator-determined distant-metastasis-free survival (assessed in a time-to-event analysis) and safety. RESULTS: A total of 1137 patients underwent randomization: 757 to the intismeran-pembrolizumab group and 380 to the placebo-pembrolizumab group. The median follow-up was 24.6 months. Recurrence-free survival at 24 months was 82.2% in the intismeran-pembrolizumab group and 70.0% in the placebo-pembrolizumab group (two-sided P<0.001); the piecewise hazard ratio was 0.99 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.66 to 1.49) before 6 months and 0.42 (95% CI, 0.30 to 0.58) after 6 months. Distant-metastasis-free survival at 24 months was 88.5% with intismeran-pembrolizumab and 80.2% with placebo-pembrolizumab (two-sided P = 0.002); the piecewise hazard ratio was 1.01 (95% CI, 0.58 to 1.79) before 6 months and 0.50 (95% CI, 0.34 to 0.73) after 6 months. Adverse events of grade 3 or higher occurred in 23.6% of the patients in the intismeran-pembrolizumab group and 20.3% of the patients in the placebo-pembrolizumab group. Eight patients (1.1%) in the intismeran-pembrolizumab group died from an adverse event; five of the deaths occurred before intismeran was administered. CONCLUSIONS: Adjuvant therapy with intismeran plus pembrolizumab significantly prolonged recurrence-free survival and distant-metastasis-free survival as compared with pembrolizumab alone in patients with completely resected, high-risk cutaneous melanoma. (Funded by Merck Sharp and Dohme and Moderna; ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT05933577.).

items.title: Functional Fixed Dystonia of the Foot

items.title: Semaglutide for the Treatment of Obesity in Children 6 to <12 Years of Age
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Childhood obesity is a chronic, neurometabolic disease with limited options for medical treatments that are efficacious and durable. Once-weekly subcutaneous semaglutide is approved for the treatment of obesity in adolescents and adults, but data for its use in young children are lacking. METHODS: We conducted a phase 3, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial involving children (6 to <12 years of age) with obesity. Participants were randomly assigned in a 2:1 ratio to receive once-weekly subcutaneous semaglutide or placebo for a period of 104 weeks, after which participants stopped taking semaglutide or placebo for a 7-week washout period. Both groups received counseling for lifestyle modification. The primary end point was the percent change in the body-mass index (BMI; the weight in kilograms divided by the square of the height in meters) from baseline to week 68. The confirmatory secondary end point was a reduction in BMI category at week 68. RESULTS: Among 167 children who underwent randomization, 112 were assigned to receive semaglutide and 55 to receive placebo. At week 68, the mean percent change in BMI was -13.5% with semaglutide and 2.7% with placebo (estimated between-group difference, -16.2 percentage points; 95% confidence interval [CI], -19.4 to -12.9; P<0.001). The percent change in BMI at week 104 was -9.4% with semaglutide and 8.4% with placebo (between-group difference, -17.8 percentage points; 95% CI, -22.2 to -13.3). At week 68, a reduction in BMI category had occurred in 79% of the participants in the semaglutide group and in 23% of those in the placebo group (odds ratio, 7.8; 95% CI, 3.5 to 17.6; P<0.001), with the BMI below the threshold for obesity (the 95th percentile for age and sex) in 38% of the participants who received semaglutide and in 2% of those who received placebo. Adverse events occurred in 96% of the participants receiving semaglutide and in 93% of those receiving placebo. Gastrointestinal adverse events were the most common, occurred more frequently with semaglutide than with placebo, and led to discontinuation in 1 participant in the semaglutide group. CONCLUSIONS: Among children (6 to <12 years of age) with obesity, treatment with semaglutide for 68 weeks resulted in a significantly greater mean percent reduction in BMI than placebo. (Funded by Novo Nordisk; STEP Young ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT05726227.).

items.title: Closing the Gap
Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome
items.abstract: Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is a common cause of acute hypoxemic respiratory failure in patients with pneumonia, sepsis, aspiration of gastric contents, severe trauma, or other inciting triggers. Although the definition of the syndrome has evolved over the past several decades, the core elements (acute onset, hypoxemia, and bilateral radiographic opacities) remain consistent. Critical components of management include identification and treatment of the underlying cause of ARDS as well as avoidance of ventilator-induced lung injury and volume overload. Ongoing areas of controversy include the best strategy for supporting nonintubated patients, personalization of positive end-expiratory pressure, the role of innovative ventilatory strategies, and the use of glucocorticoids. New research suggests that precision medicine approaches to ARDS management that focus on discrete biologic, radiographic, or physiological subphenotypes may improve outcomes, and prospective trials of these approaches are ongoing.

items.title: Assessing Multiple Treatment Regimens for Tuberculosis
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Ganfeborole and BTZ-043 are new drugs that may improve tuberculosis treatment. METHODS: In this phase 2, randomized, controlled trial, we assigned participants with rifampin-susceptible pulmonary tuberculosis to receive the standard four-drug combination (isoniazid-rifampin-pyrazinamide-ethambutol; HRZE) for 24 weeks; bedaquiline-delamanid-moxifloxacin for 16 weeks; or one of 10 new four-drug combinations for 16 weeks. The new regimens contained ganfeborole, BTZ-043, or both, with combinations of bedaquiline, delamanid, moxifloxacin, pyrazinamide, pretomanid, and linezolid. The primary end point was the log10(time to positivity) slope (rate of change from baseline to week 12 in the time to Mycobacterium tuberculosis growth in a positive sputum culture). The treatment effect was assessed as the Bayesian posterior probability of superiority of each new regimen to HRZE with respect to the primary end point (results were used to select regimens for further evaluation, rather than for characterization of efficacy). RESULTS: A total of 401 participants underwent randomization; 371 were included in the modified intention-to-treat population and 400 in the safety population. We identified two promising regimens for further evaluation: ganfeborole-bedaquiline-pretomanid-moxifloxacin (BPMG) and BTZ-043-bedaquiline-delamanid-moxifloxacin (BDMT). The log10(time to positivity) slope was 0.129 log10(days) per week (95% Bayesian credible interval, 0.112 to 0.146) with BPMG and 0.142 log10(days) per week (95% Bayesian credible interval, 0.126 to 0.160) with BDMT, as compared with 0.118 log10(days) per week (95% Bayesian credible interval, 0.105 to 0.131) with HRZE, for a relative difference of 9.1% (95% Bayesian credible interval, -8.6 to 29.0) and 20.5% (95% Bayesian credible interval, 2.7 to 41.1), respectively, and a posterior probability of superiority of 0.83 and 0.99. The incidence of adverse events of grade 3 or higher was 38% in the BPMG group (none of the participants discontinued), 28% in the BDMT group (one discontinued because of a drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms), and 24% in the HRZE group (none discontinued). Bedaquiline-moxifloxacin-pyrazinamide-BTZ-043 was discontinued because of hepatotoxic effects. CONCLUSIONS: In this trial, two four-drug regimens, one with ganfeborole and one with BTZ-043, showed evidence of potential efficacy and a safety profile that did not preclude progression to further evaluation. (Funded by Innovative Medicines Initiative 2 Joint Undertaking and others; PARADIGM4TB ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT06114628.).

items.title: Giredestrant in the Treatment of ER-Positive, HER2-Negative Early Breast Cancer
items.abstract: BackgroundAdjuvant endocrine therapy remains the cornerstone of treatment for patients with estrogen receptor (ER)–positive early breast cancer. However, recurrence develops in up to one quarter of patients within 5 years after diagnosis, and a continuous risk persists for decades. MethodsIn this phase 3, multinational, open-label, randomized trial, we enrolled patients with ER-positive, human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2)–negative, stage I, II, or III, intermediate- or high-risk early breast cancer after surgery and chemotherapy (if administered). The patients were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to receive giredestrant (a new oral selective ER degrader and full ER antagonist) or standard endocrine therapy. The primary end point was invasive disease–free survival. We report results from the prespecified interim analysis of efficacy. ResultsA total of 2084 patients were randomly assigned to receive giredestrant and 2086 to receive standard endocrine therapy. The analysis was conducted when 336 events (invasive-disease recurrence or death) had occurred (median follow-up, 32.3 months). Invasive-disease recurrence or death was reported in 140 patients (6.7%) in the giredestrant group and in 196 (9.4%) in the standard endocrine therapy group (stratified hazard ratio, 0.70; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.57 to 0.87; P=0.001). In the first interim analysis of overall survival, 57 patients (2.7%) had died in the giredestrant group and 71 (3.4%) had died in the standard endocrine therapy group (stratified hazard ratio, 0.79; 95% CI, 0.56 to 1.12). Adverse events of any grade occurred in 94.9% of the patients receiving giredestrant and in 94.4% of those receiving standard endocrine therapy. Arthralgia occurred in 48.0% of patients receiving giredestrant, 50.1% of those receiving aromatase inhibitors, and 31.0% of those receiving tamoxifen. Bradycardia occurred in 11.3% of the patients in the giredestrant group and 3.2% of those in the standard endocrine therapy group. Adverse events leading to discontinuation of trial treatment occurred in 5.3% and 8.2%, respectively. ConclusionsIn this trial, giredestrant resulted in significantly better invasive disease–free survival outcomes than standard endocrine therapy. The incidence of adverse events was similar in the two groups. (Funded by F. Hoffmann–La Roche; lidERA Breast Cancer ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT04961996.)

items.title: Blood-Pressure–Lowering Treatment across the Cardiovascular Risk Spectrum
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Treatment for lowering blood pressure reduces the risk of cardiovascular events among persons at high risk. Whether this benefit extends to those at lower risk remains unclear. METHODS: We performed a meta-analysis of individual participant data from randomized trials comparing antihypertensive treatment (intervention) with placebo, an active comparator, or usual care (comparator). The primary outcome was the first occurrence of a major cardiovascular event (fatal or nonfatal stroke, fatal or nonfatal ischemic heart disease, or heart failure resulting in death or hospitalization; composite outcome). Safety was assessed in trials that compared antihypertensive treatment with placebo or usual care, according to three prespecified composite outcomes: cardiovascular or hemodynamic events (palpitations, bradycardia, or hypotension), adverse renal events, and neurovestibular or fall-associated events. Participants were grouped into deciles according to predicted 5-year risk of a major cardiovascular event (median, 12.3%; lowest decile, <4%; highest decile, >27%). RESULTS: We included data from 51 trials and 357,440 participants - 169,042 in the intervention group and 188,398 in the comparator group. Over a median follow-up of 4.2 years, a major cardiovascular event occurred in 19,202 participants (11.4%) in the intervention group and in 24,398 (13.0%) in the comparator group. The overall estimated hazard ratio for a major cardiovascular event per 5-mm Hg reduction in systolic blood pressure was 0.90 (95% confidence interval, 0.88 to 0.92), with no evidence of variation across deciles. The absolute reduction in the 5-year cumulative risk of a major cardiovascular event was greater in the highest decile than in the lowest decile (2.6 vs. 0.4 percentage points), and the number needed to treat to prevent one major cardiovascular event over 5 years was lower in the highest decile than in the lowest decile (38 vs. 255). The incidence of a cardiovascular or hemodynamic event was 12.0 per 1000 person-years in the intervention group and 6.5 per 1000 person-years in the comparator group; the incidence of an adverse renal event was 3.3 and 2.2 per 1000 person-years, respectively; and the incidence of a neurovestibular or fall-associated event was 19.1 and 16.6 per 1000 person-years. The relative increase in the risk of each safety-outcome event with antihypertensive treatment as compared with placebo or usual care did not appear to vary across deciles. CONCLUSIONS: Blood-pressure lowering was associated with a decreased risk of major cardiovascular events across the risk spectrum, including a predicted 5-year risk below 4%. (Funded by the British Heart Foundation; PROSPERO registry number, CRD42018099283.).

items.title: Giant-Cell Arteritis
items.abstract: Giant-cell arteritis is a granulomatous vasculitis of large and medium-sized arteries that occurs almost exclusively in older adults. Suspected giant-cell arteritis warrants urgent diagnostic evaluation and, when ischemic risk is high, immediate treatment before diagnostic confirmation. Although glucocorticoids remain the cornerstone of therapy, treatment is frequently prolonged, associated with substantial toxic effects, and complicated by relapses. Advances in vascular imaging and insights into disease immunopathogenesis have expanded our understanding of disease heterogeneity and enabled the development of targeted therapies, particularly interleukin-6-receptor and Janus kinase inhibitors. Here, we review current concepts in the pathogenesis, clinical presentation, diagnosis, and management of giant-cell arteritis and highlight areas of uncertainty that warrant further investigation.

Long-Term Survival After Initial Invasive or Conservative Management of Stable Coronary Disease in ISCHEMIA-EXTEND
Long-Term Survival After Initial Invasive or Conservative Management of Stable Coronary Disease in ISCHEMIA-EXTEND
items.abstract: Importance It is unknown whether routine invasive management of chronic coronary disease improves long-term survival when added to guideline-directed medical therapy. Objective To compare the effects of initial invasive and conservative strategies on long-term mortality in patients with chronic coronary disease. Design, Setting, and Participants In this long-term follow-up study of the International Study of Comparative Health Effectiveness with Medical and Invasive Approaches (ISCHEMIA), an international trial of patients with chronic coronary disease, moderate or severe ischemia, left ventricular ejection fraction of 35% or more, and no left main coronary artery disease, unacceptable angina, or recent acute coronary syndrome, participants were randomized at 320 sites in 37 countries beginning August 2012 and followed up through December 2025. Data were analyzed using the intention-to-treat principle. Intervention ISCHEMIA randomized patients to an initial invasive strategy of guideline-directed medical therapy plus coronary angiography and revascularization (when feasible) or an initial conservative strategy with guideline-directed medical therapy alone, with invasive management for failure of medical therapy. Main Outcomes and Measures All-cause, cardiovascular, and noncardiovascular mortality were analyzed using cumulative incidence estimates, Cox and Fine-Gray models, bayesian analysis, and restricted mean survival time. Results Among 5179 participants, median age was 64 (IQR, 58-70) years; 23% were female, 42% had diabetes, and median ejection fraction was 60% (IQR, 55%-65%). During 9-year median follow-up (range, 1 day to 13.4 years), 1071 deaths occurred (782 during extended follow-up): 672 cardiovascular, 359 noncardiovascular, and 40 unclassified. All-cause 11-year mortality was not significantly different between groups (25.8% invasive vs 26.9% conservative; estimated difference, −1.0 percentage point [95% CI, −4.2 to 2.1 percentage points]; adjusted hazard ratio [AHR], 0.97 [95% CI, 0.86-1.09]). By bayesian analysis, the posterior probability of more than 1 percentage-point survival benefit to invasive vs conservative was low (18%). Cardiovascular mortality at 11 years was 15.8% in the invasive group vs 17.1% in the conservative group (estimated difference, −1.4 percentage points [95% CI, −4.0 to 1.3 percentage points]; AHR, 0.88 [95% CI, 0.75-1.02]). Noncardiovascular mortality at 11 years was 9.1% in the invasive group vs 8.1% in the conservative group (estimated difference, 1.0 percentage point [95% CI, −0.9 to 2.9 percentage points]; AHR, 1.18 [95% CI, 0.96-1.45]). Eleven-year restricted mean survival was not significantly different (estimated difference, 14 days [95% CI, −41 to 70 days]). Conclusions and Relevance In this study, long-term all-cause mortality in patients with high-risk chronic coronary disease was not significantly different after routine invasive vs initial conservative management. Trial Registration ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT04894877

items.title: The ISCHEMIA Trial a Decade Later—What Have We Learned?
Implementation of Single-Pill Combination Therapy Through Team-Based Care for Hypertension Control in Resource-Constrained Settings
Implementation of Single-Pill Combination Therapy Through Team-Based Care for Hypertension Control in Resource-Constrained Settings
items.abstract: Importance Single-pill combination therapy improves medication adherence and hypertension control. However, limited evidence is available on its implementation in routine clinical practice. Objective To assess the long-term effectiveness, implementation, and sustainability of single-pill combination therapy through team-based care for blood pressure reduction among patients with uncontrolled hypertension in primary care settings in Colombia and Jamaica. Design, Setting, and Participants Multicountry, unblinded, pragmatic, cluster randomized clinical trial. Twenty primary care clinics in Jamaica and 20 in Colombia were randomly assigned to either the single-pill combination therapy group or the standard care group. A total of 1706 adults with uncontrolled hypertension were enrolled between February 23, 2023, and September 12, 2024. The final follow-up visit occurred on September 9, 2026. Interventions In the intervention group (n = 869), a team-based care approach that included physician and nurse training, health coaching, home blood pressure monitoring, and blood pressure audit and feedback was used to implement single-pill combination therapy. Single-pill combinations were purchased locally and provided to patients. In the standard care group (n = 837), patients received monotherapy or polytherapy with guideline-recommended medications covered by health insurance or government programs. The intervention lasted 18 months, with additional follow-up at 24 months. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcome was the between-group difference in change in systolic blood pressure from baseline to 18 months. Three blood pressure measurements were obtained at each of 2 visits at each time point using a standard protocol. Results Among the 1706 enrolled participants, at baseline, the mean age was 61.4 years, 69.9% of participants were female, and 98.2% were taking antihypertensive medications. Among the 1574 participants included in the primary analysis, systolic blood pressure decreased by 19.1 mm Hg, from 145.9 mm Hg at baseline to 126.8 mm Hg at 18 months, in the intervention group and by 9.0 mm Hg, from 145.0 mm Hg to 136.1 mm Hg, in the standard care group, with a between-group difference of −10.1 mm Hg (95% CI, −13.3 to −6.9 mm Hg; P &lt; .001). At 18 months, 69.5% of patients in the intervention group and 29.2% in the standard care group achieved systolic blood pressure less than 130 and diastolic blood pressure less than 80 mm Hg. Serious adverse events (death and hospitalization) occurred at similar frequencies in the intervention (7.9%) and standard care (9.9%) groups. Conclusions and Relevance Implementing single-pill combination therapy through team-based care significantly reduced blood pressure over 18 months among adults with uncontrolled hypertension in Colombia and Jamaica. This comprehensive strategy integrating single-pill combination therapy with team-based care could be widely adopted and scaled up for hypertension control, particularly in resource-constrained settings. Trial Registration ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT05405920

items.title: Low-Voltage Area Ablation for Persistent Atrial Fibrillation
items.abstract: Importance Pulmonary vein isolation (PVI) for persistent atrial fibrillation (AF) has demonstrated modest success rates. Ablation of atrial low-voltage areas (LVA) has shown potential results, but more data are required. Objective To determine whether PVI plus LVA ablation is superior to PVI alone in reducing atrial arrhythmia recurrence in patients with AF. Design, Setting, and Participants Single-blind randomized clinical trial in 14 AF ablation centers in Canada. Adults with persistent AF of more than 3 months were enrolled between August 2018 and September 2024 and followed up for 18 to 36 months through April 2026. Intervention Patients were randomized to PVI plus LVA ablation or PVI alone. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcome was atrial arrhythmia recurrence beyond 90 days after a single catheter ablation procedure. Secondary outcomes included repeat ablation for AF, atrial flutter, or atrial tachycardia, emergency visits or hospitalization, arrhythmia recurrence over 18 months, procedure duration, total ablation delivery time, AF burden, and safety outcomes. The primary efficacy analysis was based on the modified intention-to-treat principle for patients who received the intervention. Results Among 508 enrolled patients, 253 were randomized to PVI plus LVA ablation and 255 to PVI alone. Mean (SD) age was 65.2 (9.0) years, 386 (76%) were male and 268 (54%) had LVA. After a mean (SD) follow-up of 21 (15) months, 124 (49.4%) randomized to PVI plus LVA and 146 (57.5%) randomized to PVI reached the primary outcome (hazard ratio [HR], 0.82; 95% CI, 0.65-1.04; P = .11). In the prespecified principal subgroup analysis of 268 patients with LVA, arrhythmia recurrence occurred in 68 of 138 patients (49.3%) following PVI plus LVA ablation compared with 90 of 130 patients (69.2%) following PVI alone (HR, 0.77; 95% CI, 0.66-0.91; P = .002). Arrhythmia recurrence over 18 months (37.0% vs 56.2%; HR, 0.77; 95% CI, 0.64-0.92) and AF burden were lower after PVI plus LVA ablation in this group. Among patients without LVA, recurrence was similar between ablation groups (56 of 113 [49.6%] vs 51 of 113 [45.1%]; HR, 1.09; 95% CI, 0.90-1.32). Procedure duration and ablation delivery time were longer in the PVI plus LVA ablation group. Safety outcomes were similar between groups. Conclusions and Relevance In this study, among patients with persistent AF, adjunctive LVA ablation did not significantly reduce atrial arrhythmia recurrence in the overall population over a mean 21-month follow-up. A prespecified principal subgroup analysis of patients with LVA suggested that adjunctive LVA ablation was consistent with reduced recurrence of atrial arrhythmias in this group. Trial Registration ClinicalTrials.gov, Identifier: NCT03347227

items.title: Low-Voltage Area Ablation for Persistent Atrial Fibrillation
Orforglipron for Obstructive Sleep Apnea
items.abstract: Importance Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is a common disorder characterized by repeated upper airway collapse during sleep that is associated with reduced quality of life and increased incidence of cardiometabolic disease. Objective To assess the effects of orforglipron on moderate to severe OSA in adults with obesity or overweight, compared with placebo. Design, Setting, and Participants Two 52-week, phase 3, multicenter, double-blind, placebo-controlled randomized clinical trials were conducted at 66 sites in the US, Argentina, Brazil, China, Czech Republic, Germany, Japan, Mexico, and Taiwan. Adults with moderate to severe OSA and body mass index (BMI; calculated as weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared) of 27 or higher were enrolled between November 11, 2024, and July 23, 2025. Final follow-up occurred on July 30, 2026. Trial 1 included patients not receiving positive airway pressure treatment and trial 2 included patients receiving positive airway pressure treatment. Intervention Patients were randomized (1:1) to receive either once-daily orforglipron (maximum tolerated dose: equivalent to 9-, 14.5-, or 17.2-mg tablet dose) or placebo. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary end point was change in apnea-hypopnea index (AHI, events/h) from baseline to week 52. Seven key multiplicity-controlled secondary end points included change in sleep apnea–specific hypoxic burden, the Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System Short Form Sleep-Related Impairment T-score, and high-sensitivity C-reactive protein. Results A total of 363 patients were randomized in trial 1 (mean age, 48.4 years; BMI, 37.4; AHI, 50.7 events/h; 31.4% female) and 349 patients were randomized in trial 2 (mean age, 51.1 years; BMI, 38.6; AHI, 57.6 events/h; 26.9% female). For the treatment regimen estimand, in trial 1, the mean AHI change was −17.8 for orforglipron compared with −4.5 for placebo (difference, −13.2 [95% CI, −17.7 to −8.7]; P &lt; .001) at 52 weeks. In trial 2, the mean AHI change was −17.3 for orforglipron and −5.3 for placebo (difference, −12.0 [95% CI, −17.1 to −6.9]; P &lt; .001) at 52 weeks. Of 7 key secondary end points, 6 were statistically significant, favoring orforglipron. Gastrointestinal events were the most commonly reported adverse events, occurring in 123 (68.0%) participants randomized to receive orforglipron vs 68 (37.4%) randomized to receive placebo in trial 1 and in 125 (70.6%) participants randomized to receive orforglipron vs 63 (36.6%) randomized to receive placebo in trial 2. Conclusions and Relevance These results provide evidence for the potential use of oral orforglipron to improve sleep-disordered breathing in adults with moderate to severe OSA and obesity or overweight. Trial Registration ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT06649045
