HOPO 14-1, an Oral Actinide Chelator
items.abstract: Importance Current treatments approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for internal actinide contamination (pentetate calcium trisodium and pentetate zinc trisodium) require intravenous injection or nebulized inhalation under medical supervision and have limited radionuclide coverage. HOPO 14-1, an oral form of 3,4,3-LI(1,2-HOPO), is the first shelf-stable, broad-spectrum actinide chelator in clinical development that does not require intravenous access or trained personnel. In preclinical models, 3,4,3-LI(1,2-HOPO) removed a broad range of actinides, and its oral route supports scalable emergency medical use. Objective To evaluate the safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetic parameters, and excretion of a single dose of HOPO 14-1 in healthy adults. Design, Setting, and Participants This was a phase 1 nonrandomized clinical trial including 42 healthy adults (6 per dose level) with evaluations for 14 days after administration of a single dose and conducted at a single site in the US. Participants were recruited and screened between March 2023 and July 2025 and follow-up was completed in August 2025. Intervention Single oral dose of HOPO 14-1 administered at 1 of 7 dose levels (100 mg, 200 mg, 500 mg, 1200 mg, 2500 mg, 5000 mg, or 7500 mg) with follow-up through day 14 after dose administration. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcomes were the incidence and severity of adverse events, drug-related adverse events, and serious adverse events. The secondary outcomes were plasma pharmacokinetic parameters and cumulative urinary and fecal excretion. Results Of the 42 healthy adults enrolled (median age, 43 [IQR, 34-51] years; 64% female), all received a single dose of HOPO 14-1 (administered across all dose levels as assigned). There were no serious adverse events or dose-limiting toxic effects. The drug-related adverse events included diarrhea (31%), vomiting (14%), headache (12%), and fatigue (7%); all were mild to moderate in severity. Gastrointestinal adverse events were the principal tolerability findings and most evident at the highest doses. The plasma pharmacokinetic parameters demonstrated rapid absorption (median time of maximum plasma concentration, 0.86 [range, 0.53-1.60] hours to 1.90 [range, 1.40-2.90] hours) and dose-dependent increases in systemic exposure, with greater than proportional increases at higher doses. Fecal excretion was the primary route of elimination; urinary excretion was minimal. Conclusions and Relevance Single oral doses of HOPO 14-1 up to 7500 mg were administered without dose-limiting toxicity or serious adverse events in healthy adults. Gastrointestinal tolerability defined the practical single-dose ceiling. These findings establish the first human safety and pharmacokinetic profile of a novel, orally administered actinide chelator and support further clinical evaluation of HOPO 14-1 as a countermeasure for internal radionuclide and heavy metal contamination. Development of a deployable and population-level emergency intervention addresses a long-standing unmet need with important implications for public health preparedness. Trial Registration ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT05628961

Treatment of Acute Ischemic Stroke
items.abstract: Importance Acute ischemic stroke, caused by thrombotic or embolic occlusion of a cervical or cerebral artery, leads to neurologic injury due to sudden disruption of blood flow to the brain. Ischemic stroke is a leading cause of disability and death and accounts for about 85% of strokes in the US. Observations Symptoms of acute ischemic stroke vary based on the area of the affected brain. Common presentations include sudden arm or leg weakness, aphasia or slurred speech, sudden loss of balance or coordination, sudden visual difficulties, and/or facial drooping. Patients with suspected stroke should be transported to the nearest emergency department for urgent brain imaging, typically noncontrast computed tomography (CT). Based on 2026 American Heart Association/American Stroke Association (AHA/ASA) guidelines, first-line therapy for patients with acute ischemic stroke presenting within 4.5 hours from symptom onset with disabling symptoms (eg, affecting the ability to perform activities of daily living) is intravenous thrombolysis (tenecteplase or alteplase) in those without intracranial hemorrhage or other contraindications to thrombolysis. The treatment window can be extended to 9 hours—and up to 24 hours in patients with large vessel occlusion (eg, involving the internal carotid artery or proximal middle cerebral artery [M1 segment]) who are unable to receive thrombectomy—based on identification of salvageable tissue using perfusion imaging with CT perfusion or magnetic resonance imaging. In appropriately selected patients with acute ischemic stroke, pooled randomized trial data show an approximately 10% absolute increase in the probability of a better functional outcome with intravenous thrombolysis. Based on 2026 AHA/ASA guidelines, endovascular thrombectomy, which involves clot removal with an intra-arterial mechanical device, is recommended for patients with large vessel occlusion within 6 hours of stroke onset (class 1 recommendation) and is recommended in selected patients with large vessel occlusion within 24 hours of last known well (class 1 recommendation). Endovascular therapy should be performed after intravenous thrombolysis unless patients have contraindications to thrombolytic therapy. Compared with medical management, which includes intravenous thrombolysis when indicated, endovascular thrombectomy produces an approximately 20% absolute increase in functional independence. Conclusions and Relevance Acute ischemic stroke causes substantial disability and mortality. First-line therapy for patients with disabling acute stroke symptoms is intravenous thrombolysis (if no contraindications) within 4.5 hours of stroke onset and up to 24 hours in carefully selected patients not receiving mechanical thrombectomy; for large vessel occlusions, mechanical thrombectomy may be performed up to 24 hours after stroke onset in eligible patients.

items.title: A Review of Hip Fractures—Reply
Izalontamab Brengitecan in Recurrent or Metastatic Esophageal Squamous Cell Carcinoma
items.abstract: Importance Effective therapy remains lacking for patients with advanced esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) whose disease progressed after standard treatment. Izalontamab brengitecan, an epidermal growth factor receptor and human epidermal growth factor receptor 3 bispecific antibody-drug conjugate with a topoisomerase I inhibitor, Ed-04, has shown clinical activity in ESCC in a phase 1b study. Objective To evaluate the efficacy and safety of izalontamab brengitecan compared with chemotherapy in patients with advanced ESCC who progressed after first-line programmed cell death 1 protein (PD-1)/programmed cell death 1 ligand 1 (PD-L1) inhibitor plus platinum-containing chemotherapy. Design, Setting, and Participants This phase 3, open-label, randomized clinical trial was conducted across 80 hospitals in China. Patients with recurrent or metastatic ESCC that had progressed with first-line PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitor plus platinum-containing chemotherapy were enrolled. Between March 19, 2024, and August 1, 2025 (final follow-up, October 17, 2025), a total of 704 patients were screened, and 497 were enrolled and randomized. Interventions Patients were randomly assigned (1:1) to receive either izalontamab brengitecan (n = 249; 2.5 mg/kg on days 1 and 8 every 3 weeks) or physician-selected chemotherapy (n = 248; irinotecan, paclitaxel, or docetaxel) every 3 weeks. Main Outcomes and Measures The dual primary end points were progression-free survival (PFS) assessed by blinded independent central review according to Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors version 1.1 and overall survival (OS). Results Of 497 patients who underwent randomization (median age, 61.0 years [range, 34-76]; 448 male patients [90.1%]), 493 received study treatment. At this interim analysis, izalontamab brengitecan demonstrated statistically significant improvement in both PFS and OS. Median PFS by blinded independent central review was 4.17 months (95% CI, 3.61-4.53 months) with izalontamab brengitecan vs 1.97 months (95% CI, 1.61-2.73 months) with chemotherapy (hazard ratio, 0.50; 95% CI, 0.40-0.63; log-rank P &lt; .001). Median OS was 9.79 months (95% CI, 7.89-11.01 months) with izalontamab brengitecan vs 7.20 months (95% CI, 6.18-7.82 months) with chemotherapy (hazard ratio, 0.63; 95% CI, 0.48-0.82; log-rank P &lt; .001). Grade 3 or higher treatment-related adverse events occurred in 212 of 249 patients (85.1%) with izalontamab brengitecan and 147 of 248 patients (59.3%) with chemotherapy and were predominantly hematologic. Conclusions and Relevance Izalontamab brengitecan significantly improved PFS and OS vs chemotherapy in patients with recurrent or metastatic ESCC whose disease had progressed after first-line treatment. These findings support izalontamab brengitecan as a new second-line treatment for this population in China. Trial Registration ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT06304974

items.title: JAMA Editors' Summary Podcast
Fluid eMTBR-tau243 as a Biomarker of Mixed 3-Repeat and 4-Repeat Tau Pathology
items.abstract: Importance Neurodegenerative diseases with abnormal tau protein aggregation in the brain (ie, tauopathies) can be classified by the tau isoform that accumulates: 3-repeat (3R), 4-repeat (4R), or mixed 3R/4R tauopathies, which include chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), some forms of frontotemporal lobar degeneration, and Alzheimer disease (AD). The endogenously cleaved form of tau microtubule binding region containing the residue 243 (eMTBR-tau243) can be detected in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and blood and has been associated with AD tau pathology, but its specificity and biological interpretation in non-AD tauopathies remains unclear. Objective To evaluate biofluid eMTBR-tau243 in a range of tauopathies. Design, Setting, and Participants This case-control study included 4 biorepositories based in the US that contributed CSF and plasma samples from participants with and without tauopathies, many of whom had antemortem biofluid samples paired with autopsy or genetically defined neuropathology. Samples were analyzed between August 2023 and December 2025. Data analysis occurred from August 2024 to July 2026. Exposure CSF and plasma eMTBR-tau243 concentrations measured using a mass spectrometry–based assay. Main Outcomes and Measures Outcomes included mixed 3R/4R tauopathy (eg, AD and CTE) based on autopsy, frontotemporal lobar degeneration with MAPT variants (FTLD- MAPT ), and CTE stage. Differences in biomarker levels between groups were evaluated using analysis of variance or analysis of covariance, and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) was calculated to evaluate the discriminative performance of fluid eMTBR-tau243. Results Among the 229 participants (196 with CSF samples and 55 with plasma samples [22 with both]), mean (SD) age at fluid sample collection was 63 (13) years and 108 (47%) were female. Median (IQR) CSF eMTBR-tau243 was increased in 10 patients with AD (0.459 [0.246-0.801] fmol/mL) compared with 29 cognitively unimpaired controls (0.002 [0.001-0.005] fmol/mL) (adjusted P &lt; .001), but other autopsy-confirmed non-AD tauopathies (which included 52 individuals with conditions including progressive supranuclear palsy and corticobasal degeneration) did not demonstrate an increase (0.015 [0.008, 0.039] fmol/mL). Six symptomatic FTLD- MAPT variant carriers with mixed 3R/4R tauopathy (R406W, V337M, and G389R) had increased median (IQR) CSF eMTBR-tau243 (0.140 [0.055-0.174] fmol/mL) compared with 15 4R tauopathy variant carriers including N279K and P301L (0.004 [0.001-0.044] fmol/mL) ( P = .001). Median (IQR) plasma eMTBR-tau243 was increased in 11 patients with CTE (1.93 [0.42-3.68] fmol/L) compared with 20 cognitively unimpaired controls (0.29 [0.05-0.62] fmol/L) (adjusted P = .007), but did not increase as high as among 14 patients with AD (11.25 [2.29-19.38] fmol/L). Plasma eMTBR-tau243 distinguished CTE stage III and IV from controls (AUC, 0.97; 95% CI, 0.92-1.00), but not CTE stage I from controls (AUC, 0.64; 95% CI, 0.32-0.97). Conclusions and Relevance This study found that plasma and CSF eMTBR-tau243 were increased in mixed 3R/4R tauopathies including AD, high-stage CTE, and a subset of genetic FTLD- MAPT , compared with cognitively unimpaired controls. Further validation in larger cohorts is needed to determine the clinical utility of eMTBR-tau243 as a potential diagnostic biomarker for CTE and other tauopathies beyond AD.

items.title: Tale of Two Estimands
Pediatric Obesity Pharmacotherapy
Once-Weekly Ribupatide for Weight Loss in Adults in China With Overweight or Obesity
items.abstract: IMPORTANCE Obesity is a major health problem in China; more pharmacotherapy choices for long-term weight management are needed. OBJECTIVE To evaluate the efficacy and safety of once-weekly subcutaneous ribupatide, a dual glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide/glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist, for weight loss in adults in China with overweight or obesity without diabetes. DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS This multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 3 clinical trial was conducted at 55 sites in China. From May to June 2024, adults without diabetes who had a body mass index of 28 or greater or 24 or greater with at least 1 weight-related comorbidity were enrolled, with final follow-up on June 20, 2025. INTERVENTIONS Participants were randomized to receive once-weekly subcutaneous ribupatide (target doses of 2 mg, 4 mg, or 6 mg) or matching placebo for 48 weeks, with dose escalation for up to 20 weeks and concomitant lifestyle intervention. MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES The primary outcome was change in body weight from baseline to week 48, including percent change in body weight and the percentage of participants achieving at least 5% body weight reduction, analyzed under the treatment policy estimand. RESULTS Among 567 randomized participants (309 [54.5%] female; mean [SD] age was 34.4 [8.4] years, body weight was 93.0 [17.3] kg, and body mass index was 33.3 [4.5]), 514 (90.7%) completed the 48-week treatment period. Least-squares mean percentage changes in body weight at week 48 were −10.7%, −16.4%, and −17.7% with ribupatide 2, 4, and 6 mg, respectively, vs −1.4% with placebo. At week 48, the placebo-adjusted differences in percentage change in body weight were −9.3 (95% CI, −11.4 to −7.3) percentage points with ribupatide 2 mg, −15.0 (95% CI, −17.1 to −12.9) percentage points with ribupatide 4 mg, and −16.3 (95% CI, −18.4 to −14.2) percentage points with ribupatide 6 mg ( P &lt; .001 for all). For at least 5% body weight reduction at week 48, the multiply imputed response rates were 68.1% (95% CI, 59.9% to 75.3%) for ribupatide 2 mg (97 of 142), 88.0% (95% CI, 81.3% to 92.6%) for ribupatide 4 mg (124 of 141), 85.7% (95% CI, 78.6% to 90.7%) with ribupatide 6 mg (121 of 141), and 16.0% (95% CI, 10.8% to 23.1%) with placebo (23 of 143). Placebo-adjusted differences for ribupatide 2, 4, and 6 mg were 52.0 (95% CI, 42.2 to 61.9), 72.0 (95% CI, 63.7 to 80.2), and 69.7 (95% CI, 61.1 to 78.3) percentage points, respectively (all P &lt; .001). The most frequent treatment-emergent adverse events with ribupatide were gastrointestinal events, occurring in 47.9%, 58.2%, and 63.1% of participants receiving ribupatide 2 mg, 4 mg, and 6 mg, respectively, compared with 23.1% receiving placebo; most were mild to moderate in severity and few participants (0.7%) permanently discontinued study treatment because of adverse events. CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE Among adults in China with overweight or obesity without diabetes, once-weekly subcutaneous ribupatide resulted in significantly greater weight loss at 48 weeks. Gastrointestinal adverse events were the most frequent tolerability findings. TRIAL REGISTRATION ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT06396429

items.title: Tirzepatide in Adolescents With Obesity
items.abstract: Importance Information on the effects of tirzepatide, a once-weekly glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide and glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist approved for obesity management in adults with obesity, remains limited in adolescents. Objective To evaluate the efficacy and safety of once-weekly tirzepatide in adolescents with obesity or overweight with at least 1 obesity-related complication. Design, Setting, and Participants This phase 3, randomized, double-blind, 72-week clinical trial was conducted at 31 medical research centers and hospitals in Canada, the Czech Republic, Israel, Italy, Poland, and the US from October 16, 2023, to June 2, 2026, among adolescents aged 12 years to younger than 18 years with obesity or overweight with at least 1 obesity-related complication. Interventions Participants were randomized 2:1 to receive once-weekly subcutaneous tirzepatide, escalated to a maximum tolerated dose (5, 10, or 15 mg), or placebo for 72 weeks, in addition to healthy lifestyle intervention. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary end point was percent change in body mass index (BMI; calculated as weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared) from baseline to week 72. Key secondary end points included percentages of participants achieving BMI reductions of at least 5%, at least 10%, at least 15%, and at least 20%; changes in BMI SD score; BMI expressed as a percentage of the 95th percentile; and body weight, waist circumference, and physical functioning from baseline to week 72. Safety outcomes included treatment-emergent adverse events, serious adverse events, and discontinuations due to adverse events. Results A total of 160 participants were randomized to receive tirzepatide (n = 109) or placebo (n = 51). Mean (SD) age at baseline was 14.6 (1.6) years, 99 participants (61.9%) were female, mean body weight was 109.7 kg, and mean BMI was 38.6. At week 72, tirzepatide was associated with 18.5% reduction in BMI, compared with 0.5% increase in BMI with placebo, demonstrating superiority over placebo (estimated treatment difference, −19.0 [95% CI, −23.9 to −14.1] percentage points; P &lt; .001). Of 10 key secondary outcomes, all demonstrated statistically significant differences favoring tirzepatide compared with placebo. Overall, 79.6% of tirzepatide-treated participants achieved BMI reduction of at least 5% compared with 28.5% of participants in the placebo group (risk difference, 51.2 [95% CI, 36.3-66.1] percentage points; P &lt; .001). The most common adverse events with tirzepatide treatment were gastrointestinal (mostly mild to moderate). Conclusions and Relevance In adolescents with obesity or overweight with obesity-related complications, tirzepatide, in addition to healthy lifestyle intervention, led to significant reductions in percent change in BMI compared with placebo at 72 weeks. Trial Registration ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT06075667

A Plasma eMTBR-Tau Immunoassay for Detection of Advanced Insoluble Tau Pathology
items.abstract: Importance Blood biomarkers that reflect neurofibrillary tau burden, a defining hallmark of Alzheimer disease (AD), remain limited. Endogenously cleaved microtubule-binding region tau 243 (eMTBR-tau243) has shown promise when measured by mass spectrometry; a scalable immunoassay could broaden research access and support clinical evaluation. Objective To determine whether plasma levels of eMTBR-tau measured by a novel immunoassay are associated with tau neurofibrillary tangle pathology defined by neuropathology and tau positron emission tomography (PET). Design, Setting, and Participants This cross-sectional study included brain donors with antemortem plasma from 2 US autopsy cohorts, and individuals with plasma samples and tau PET from 2 imaging cohorts in Canada and Sweden, with visits between 2002 and 2025 depending on the cohort. Exposures Plasma eMTBR-tau measured with an immunoassay and eMTBR-tau243 measured with mass spectrometry. Main Outcomes and Measures Plasma eMTBR-tau levels across neuropathologic Braak neurofibrillary tangle stages (I-VI, ranging from tangles confined to the entorhinal region to widespread neocortical tangles) and tau-PET Braak stages (0-VI), expressed as fold changes. Correlations with regional tau-PET standardized uptake value ratios (SUVRs; higher values indicating more tau tangles), discrimination of regional tau-PET positivity (area under the curve [AUC]), and correlation with mass spectrometry–based eMTBR-tau243. Results The study included 728 participants in 4 cohorts (median age by cohort, 71.0-83.5 years; 41.3%-56.6% female). In the 2 autopsy cohorts (n = 241 and n = 240), eMTBR-tau age- and sex-adjusted geometric means were 0.0021 pg/mL and 0.0040 pg/mL, respectively, at Braak stages I-II vs 0.107 pg/mL and 0.101 pg/mL at Braak stage VI (50.5-fold [95% CI, 26.3-97.0] and 25.2-fold [95% CI, 15.8-40.3] higher for stage VI vs stages I-II; P &lt; .001 for both cohorts). In one imaging cohort (n = 99), compared with tau-PET Braak stage 0, eMTBR-tau levels were 11.0-fold (95% CI, 6.9-17.5) higher at stages III-IV and 59.9-fold (95% CI, 39.5-90.7) higher at stages V-VI. Among participants positive for amyloid-β (Aβ) in another imaging cohort (n = 50), the Spearman rank correlations for eMTBR-tau with tau-PET SUVRs were ρ = 0.52 (95% CI, 0.28-0.70) in Braak regions I-II, 0.76 (95% CI, 0.61-0.86) in regions III-IV, and 0.85 (95% CI, 0.75-0.91) in regions V-VI (all P &lt; .001). Immunoassay and mass spectrometry measurements were strongly correlated (Spearman rank correlation, ρ = 0.93 in all participants [n = 108] and ρ = 0.96 in Aβ-positive participants [n = 54]) and discriminated tau-PET positivity similarly (n = 102; AUC range, 0.96-0.99 for the immunoassay and 0.97-0.99 for mass spectrometry). Conclusions and Relevance A plasma eMTBR-tau immunoassay identified neocortical tau pathology in autopsy and tau-PET cohorts and correlated strongly with mass spectrometry measurements, a proof of principle that eMTBR-tau can be measured by immunoassay as a marker of advanced neurofibrillary tangle pathology.

items.title: Toward a Healthier Future Through Obesity Prevention and Care
items.abstract: Importance Obesity is one of the most difficult challenges of the modern era, affecting more than 1 billion people worldwide. Nearly half of US adults and 1 in 5 US children meet the medical definition of having obesity, with major consequences for cardiometabolic, kidney, hepatic, pulmonary, musculoskeletal, reproductive, oncologic, and mental health. Obesity also carries social and economic harms through stigma, discrimination, and bias. Observations Drivers of the obesity epidemic include changes in food production and consumption accompanied by social, economic, and technological shifts that reduce food preparation, disrupt sleep, and decrease physical activity. The burden of these changes is not equally distributed, with higher obesity prevalence among socioeconomically disadvantaged populations. Current prevention measures include nutrition standards, food and menu labeling, school meal policies, sugar-sweetened beverage taxes, community-based lifestyle programs, and public assistance efforts. The impact of these approaches has been inadequate. Contemporary clinical management recognizes obesity as a chronic disease characterized by genetic, biological, and behavioral susceptibilities. Access, affordability, tolerability, and the chronicity of use remain major challenges for all available obesity management strategies, including new glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist therapies. Potential solutions require a coordinated, multisector response and include efforts to prevent obesity at the societal level, improve care of individuals with obesity, and strengthen research and innovation. Priority areas include improving the food and physical activity environment; strengthening communication and education; strengthening childhood obesity prevention; addressing health inequities; reducing stigma and bias; modernizing obesity care delivery; expanding access to lifestyle, healthy food, medication, and surgical interventions; and supporting long-term treatment adherence and maintenance. Proposed actions include new government policies on food production, labeling, marketing, and school nutrition; modernization of drug evaluation; payment reform to support comprehensive obesity treatment; development of multidisciplinary care models; incentives to promote cross-sector partnerships; and research to advance personalized prevention and treatment strategies. Conclusions and Relevance The emergence of effective obesity management medications offers a significant opportunity to curb the prevalence of obesity. However, no single intervention will be enough. Sustained improvement will require addressing the underlying structural and environmental drivers of obesity, along with person-centered, multilevel strategies that simultaneously improve prevention, reduce stigma, and expand equitable access to evidence-based treatment. Coordinated action across government, health care systems, clinicians, payers, industry, schools, communities, and researchers will be essential to achieving long-term improvement.

Medical Imaging and Pediatric and Adolescent Brain Tumor Risk
items.abstract: Importance Ionizing radiation from medical imaging may increase brain tumor risk. Objective To quantify brain tumor risk associated with radiation exposure from medical imaging in children and adolescents. Design, Setting, and Participants Retrospective cohort study of children born from 1996 through 2016 who were enrolled from birth in 6 US health care systems or Ontario, Canada, and were alive and cancer-free at age 2 years, with follow-up through December 31, 2017 (US sites), and December 31, 2024 (Ontario). Exposures Cumulative radiation dose to the brain from medical imaging, lagged by 2 years. Main Outcomes and Measures Incident brain or other central nervous system tumors. Hazard ratios (HRs) were estimated using Cox proportional hazards models for categorical dose, and excess relative risks (ERRs) were estimated using linear dose-response models for continuous dose. Results Among 3 704 860 children (1 900 285 [51.3%] male) followed up for 45 671 641 person-years (mean follow-up, 12.3 years), 1536 brain tumors were diagnosed. Mean radiation dose from 1 head computed tomography (CT) examination was 66.2 mGy (SD, 22.2). Among children with cumulative dose of 1 mGy or greater, mean cumulative dose was 73 mGy (SD, 95) overall and 100 mGy (SD, 105) among those diagnosed with brain tumors. Compared with no exposure, brain tumor risk increased with cumulative dose (&gt;0 to &lt;1 mGy: HR, 1.12 [95% CI, 1.01-1.26]; 1 to &lt;5 mGy: HR, 1.71 [95% CI, 0.88-2.96]; 5 to &lt;50 mGy: HR, 1.86 [95% CI, 1.16-2.81]; 50 to &lt;75 mGy: HR, 2.30 [95% CI, 1.64-3.12]; 75 to &lt;100 mGy: HR, 2.02 [95% CI, 1.13-3.30]; 100 to &lt;150 mGy: HR, 2.81 [95% CI, 1.53-4.66]; ≥150 mGy: HR, 3.85 [95% CI, 2.43-5.75]). Cumulative dose was associated with brain tumor risk overall (ERR per 100 mGy, 1.27 [95% CI, 0.83-1.77]; P &lt; .001), with stronger associations for aggressive histologies (ERR per 100 mGy, 1.51 [95% CI, 1.00-2.11]; P &lt; .001). By age 21 years, exposure comparable to 1 head CT was associated with 7.9 excess brain tumors per 10 000 children, or approximately 1 excess tumor per 1266 head CT examinations. The estimated population-attributable fraction was 10.1% (95% CI, 5.8%-14.2%). Conclusions and Relevance Medical imaging in children and adolescents was associated with a dose-related increase in brain tumor risk. These findings support careful clinical justification and dose minimization when pediatric imaging using ionizing radiation is indicated.

Plasma eMTBR-tau as a Biomarker for Chronic Traumatic Encephalopathy Tau Tangle Neuropathology
items.abstract: Importance Chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) is a neurodegenerative disease that cannot accurately be diagnosed during life due to the absence of in vivo biomarkers for CTE neuropathology. Objective To evaluate plasma endogenously cleaved microtubule-binding region tau (eMTBR-tau) as a candidate biomarker for CTE tau tangle neuropathology. Design, Setting, and Participants This case series included 21 former American-style football players who completed a blood draw as part of participation in clinical research at Boston University beginning April 17, 2008, and who subsequently died, donated their brain, and had completed autopsy by October 9, 2026. Exposures Plasma eMTBR-tau nucleic acid–linked immunosandwich assay single-plex immunoassay and plasma phosphorylated tau 217 (p-tau217) (SP-X n = 20; Elecsys n = 1). Main Outcomes and Measures CTE status and stage. Cumulative neuropathologic tau burden scores ranged from 0 to 33 (higher scores indicate tau burden; 0, no tau burden). Results Among 21 male brain donors (median age at blood draw, CTE positive: 68 years [IQR, 61-77]; CTE negative: 49 years [IQR, 47-56]), 18 had a neuropathologic diagnosis of CTE. Of these participants, 16 had a diagnosis of high-stage CTE (stage IV = 8, stage III = 8); and 2, of low-stage CTE (stage II = 1, stage I = 1). Five CTE-positive participants had intermediate or high Alzheimer disease neuropathologic change (ADNC). Plasma eMTBR-tau concentration was significantly higher in CTE-positive participants (median, 0.019 pg/mL [IQR, 0.004-0.030]) compared with CTE-negative participants (0.001 pg/mL [IQR, 0.001-0.001]; β = 1.61 [95% CI, 0.51-2.70]). Plasma eMTBR-tau concentrations were highest among CTE-positive participants with comorbid ADNC (0.082 pg/mL [IQR, 0.059-0.131]) and intermediate among those with high-stage CTE without ADNC (n = 11; median, 0.009 pg/mL [IQR, 0.004-0.021]). Plasma eMTBR-tau concentration was significantly higher in high-stage CTE (median, 0.021 pg/mL [IQR, 0.006-0.038]) compared with low-stage CTE (median, 0.001 pg/mL [IQR, 0.001-0.002]; β = 1.79 [95% CI, 0.45-3.13]) or no CTE (median, 0.001 pg/mL [IQR, 0.001-0.001]; β = 1.78 [95% CI, 0.85-2.71]). Differences remained significant after exclusion of 5 cases with comorbid ADNC. Plasma eMTBR-tau concentration was associated with higher cumulative neuropathologic tau burden score across 11 brain regions (β = 0.71 [95% CI, 0.38-1.05]). Plasma p-tau217 concentration was positively associated with eMTBR-tau (β = 0.68 [95% CI, 0.32-1.04]) but was not associated with CTE. P-tau217 concentrations were in the negative range (n = 11) or intermediate range (n = 5) for participants without ADNC copathology. Four participants with ADNC had p-tau217 concentrations in the positive range; and 1, in the intermediate range. Conclusions and Relevance Participants with high-stage CTE had higher concentrations of plasma eMTBR-tau than those with low-stage or no CTE; concentrations were highest among those with CTE and comorbid ADNC. Plasma eMTBR-tau may represent a feasible biomarker candidate for high-stage CTE tau tangle neuropathology. Larger autopsy and clinical validation studies are needed to establish overall diagnostic accuracy and specificity of plasma eMTBR-tau for CTE neuropathology, in addition to the associated prognostic and clinical implications.

Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy
items.abstract: Importance Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is defined as left ventricular hypertrophy of greater than 15 mm in any part of the left ventricular wall in the absence of valvular disease, uncontrolled hypertension, or other chronic conditions causing severe left ventricular hypertrophy such as uncontrolled hypertension or cardiac amyloidosis. Most people with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy have a normal lifespan; however, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is associated with a 0.8% annual incidence of sudden cardiac death. Observations Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy affects an estimated 0.2% of people worldwide (including more than 600 000 people in the US) and is typically diagnosed with echocardiography. Approximately 35% to 40% of patients report effort-related dyspnea, chest pain or pressure, or lightheadedness. Approximately 30% to 40% of people with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy have a pathogenic gene variant that encodes for cardiac sarcomere proteins (predominantly myosin binding protein C, myosin heavy chain, and troponin). Other patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy may have a polygenic predisposition and/or nongenetic risk factors. The sarcomeric gene variants cause hypercontractility and delayed relaxation of the cardiac sarcomere, which characterizes the underlying pathophysiologic problem in people with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Approximately 60% to 70% of patients have obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, characterized by dynamic left ventricular outflow tract obstruction due to basal septal hypertrophy. The remainder do not have outflow tract obstruction and, therefore, have nonobstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy should participate in regular low- to moderate-intensity physical activity (such as brisk walking, jogging) as part of a healthy lifestyle. Medical therapies such as β-blockers (eg, metoprolol, bisoprolol, nadolol) and nondihydropyridine-class calcium channel blockers (eg, verapamil or diltiazem) are first-line medical therapy for patients with symptoms due to hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. If first-line therapies do not relieve symptoms, alternative treatments include disopyramide, which improves symptoms in approximately 60% of patients, cardiac myosin inhibitors (mavacamten or aficamten), which improve symptoms in approximately 70% to 80% of patients, or procedures to thin the septal wall of the left ventricle, including percutaneous alcohol septal ablation, which improves symptoms in approximately 75% to 80% of patients, or surgical septal myectomy, which improves symptoms in approximately 90% to 95% of patients. Guidelines recommend that first-degree relatives of patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy undergo screening for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with genetic testing or echocardiography. Conclusions Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is caused by a monogenetic pathogenic variant in approximately 30% to 40% of patients and can cause effort-related dyspnea, chest pain or pressure, or lightheadedness. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is associated with an incidence of sudden cardiac death of 0.8% per year. First-line therapies for symptomatic hypertrophic cardiomyopathy are β-blockers (eg, metoprolol, bisoprolol, nadolol) or nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (eg, verapamil, diltiazem).

items.title: Intramuscular Olanzapine or Droperidol for Acute Behavioral Disturbance in Children and Adolescents
items.abstract: Importance Acute behavioral disturbance is a high-risk emergency department presentation. There is limited evidence for the comparative effectiveness of intramuscular sedative medications in children and adolescents, which may be required when there is imminent risk of serious harm due to agitation. Objective To determine whether olanzapine is more effective than droperidol intramuscularly in achieving behavioral containment. Design, Setting, and Participants This investigator-initiated, open-label, multicenter, superiority, randomized clinical trial recruited children and adolescents aged 9 to 17 years presenting to 10 Australian emergency departments with acute behavioral disturbance clinically deemed to require intramuscular medication from November 8, 2021, to February 16, 2026. The last participant follow-up occurred on March 17, 2026. Data were analyzed from April 15 to 27, 2026. Interventions Participants were randomly assigned to a single weight-based dose of olanzapine or droperidol (&lt;40 kg, 5 mg; ≥40 kg, 10 mg). Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcome was successful sedation (Sedation Assessment Tool score ≤0) without the need for additional sedatives 1 hour after randomization. A range of secondary outcomes, including adverse events, were assessed. Results Of 348 recruited individuals (mean [IQR] age, 14.9 [13.6-16.1] years; 215 [62%] female; 75 Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander individuals), 176 were assigned to olanzapine and 172 to droperidol. Of those randomized, 117 individuals (66%) in the olanzapine group and 121 individuals (70%) in the droperidol group were administered their study medication within 30 minutes of randomization. Successful sedation without the requirement for additional sedatives occurred in 89 individuals (53%) in the olanzapine group and 104 individuals (62%) in the droperidol group. No evidence of superiority was observed (adjusted risk difference, −8.3% [95% CI, −18.6% to 2.1%]; P = .12). One serious adverse event (apnea) occurred in the olanzapine group. Conclusions and Relevance In this randomized clinical trial in children and adolescents presenting to the emergency department with behavioral disturbance, intramuscular olanzapine did not result in a clinically meaningfully greater proportion achieving successful sedation compared with droperidol. The limited effectiveness observed with both medications highlights the need for more effective pharmacological and nonpharmacological management strategies. Trial Registration anzctr.org.au Identifier: ACTRN12621001238864

Prehospital Fluid Resuscitation for Patients With Suspected Sepsis
items.abstract: Importance Early resuscitation with intravenous fluids is recommended for patients with sepsis. Objective To determine the effect of liberal vs more conservative fluid resuscitation strategies in the ambulance on mortality among patients with suspected sepsis. Design, Setting, and Participants Multicenter, 2 × 2 factorial randomized clinical trial conducted by 4 paramedic services and their destination hospitals in Ontario, Canada. Participants were adults with suspected sepsis, defined as suspected infection, fever (≥38.0 °C), and hypotension (systolic blood pressure [SBP] &lt;100 mm Hg), and obtainable intravenous access. Patients were enrolled between March 23, 2020, and August 20, 2025, with last follow-up in December 2025. Intervention Patients were randomized to receive liberal fluids (up to 2 L of normal saline regardless of subsequent SBP) or usual care (fluids only when SBP &lt;90 mm Hg and stopped when SBP ≥100 mm Hg) during prehospital care and until transfer of care in the emergency department. (Patients were additionally randomized to receive ceftriaxone vs placebo; analysis of which is reported separately.) Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcome was hospital mortality, defined as death prior to hospital discharge up to day 90. There were 17 secondary outcomes, including all-cause mortality at 90 days, hospitalization, intensive care unit admission, mechanical ventilation, vasopressor therapy, dialysis, and total fluids infused within 24 hours of hospital arrival. Results Among 1686 randomized patients, 1669 were eligible and 1646 were included in the primary outcome analysis (830 in the liberal fluids group and 816 in the usual fluids group). The median age of patients was 76 (IQR, 63-85) years and 938 (57.0%) were male. Most patients in both groups received a fluid bolus (826/848 [97.4%] in the liberal fluids group; 700/821 [85.3%] in the usual fluids group) during transport, but patients in the liberal fluids group received a larger volume (median, 1500 mL [IQR, 1000-2000 mL]) vs 500 mL [IQR, 175-800 mL] in the usual fluids group; difference, 910.1 mL [95% CI, 857.3-962.9 mL]). Hospital mortality was 149/830 (18.0%) in the liberal fluids group and 149/816 (18.3%) in the usual fluids group (risk ratio, 0.98 [95% CI, 0.80-1.20]; unadjusted risk difference, −0.3 [95% CI, −4.0 to 3.4]; P = .82). Among the 17 secondary outcomes, all were similar between groups. Adverse events, including pulmonary edema during transport, were infrequent in both groups. Conclusions and Relevance A more liberal fluid resuscitation strategy for the prehospital management of patients with suspected sepsis did not reduce mortality compared with more restrictive usual care. Trial Registration ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT03068741

items.title: Prehospital Antibiotics for Patients With Suspected Sepsis
items.abstract: Importance Early treatment with antibiotics is considered an important intervention to reduce mortality for patients with sepsis. Objective To determine the effect of earlier treatment with antibiotics in the ambulance on 90-day mortality compared with usual treatment in the emergency department. Design, Setting, and Participants This multicenter, 2 × 2 factorial randomized, placebo-controlled trial was conducted among 4 paramedic services and their destination hospitals in Ontario, Canada. Participants were adults with suspected sepsis, defined as suspected infection, fever (≥38.0 °C), and hypotension (systolic blood pressure &lt;100 mm Hg). Patients were enrolled between March 23, 2020, and August 20, 2025, with final follow-up in December 2025. Interventions Patients were randomized to receive 1 g of intramuscular ceftriaxone or placebo (and to receive liberal fluids vs usual fluids; reported separately) during prehospital care in the ambulance. All patients could receive open-label antibiotics in the emergency department. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcome was hospital mortality, defined as death prior to hospital discharge to day 90. There were 17 secondary outcomes, including all-cause mortality at 90 days, hospitalization, intensive care unit admission, use of mechanical ventilation, use of dialysis, positive culture results, and antibiotics within 24 hours of hospital arrival. Results Among 2091 randomized patients, 2048 were eligible for the primary analysis, with 1026 randomized to receive ceftriaxone and 1022 randomized to receive placebo. The median (IQR) age of patients was 75 (62-85) years and 1162 (56.7%) were males. The mean (SD) time from paramedic arrival at patient to administration of study drug was 37 (36) minutes in the ceftriaxone group and 39 (55) minutes in the placebo group. Most patients (735 of 795 [92.5%] in the ceftriaxone group and 730 of 792 [92.2%] in placebo group) were treated with antibiotics in the hospital after a mean (SD) of 247.3 (207.7) minutes after paramedic arrival among patients in the ceftriaxone group and 252.8 (218.0) minutes among the placebo group. The rate of hospital mortality was 182 of 1009 (18.0%) in the ceftriaxone group and 186 of 1011 (18.4%) in the placebo group (risk ratio, 0.97 [95% CI, 0.81-1.17]; P = .77). Of 17 secondary outcomes, all were similar between the groups. Conclusions and Relevance Among patients with suspected sepsis on evaluation by paramedics, earlier treatment with antibiotics in the ambulance did not reduce mortality compared with usual care provided in the emergency department. Trial Registration ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT03068741

Toward Zero Harm for Patients Receiving Mechanical Ventilation—What Is Expected vs What Is Optional
Telehealth to Support Coordinated Spontaneous Awakening and Breathing Trials in Invasive Ventilation
items.abstract: Importance Coordinated spontaneous awakening trials and spontaneous breathing trials (C-SAT/SBT) improve outcomes for patients receiving invasive mechanical ventilation, but implementation remains inadequate. Objective To evaluate whether a telehealth intervention added to a standard audit and feedback implementation of C-SAT/SBT increases adherence and improves outcomes compared with standard audit and feedback implementation alone (control). Design, Setting, and Participants A cluster randomized type 2 hybrid effectiveness-implementation clinical trial was conducted in 12 Intermountain Health hospitals in Utah and Idaho. Patients aged 16 years or older who were intubated and mechanically ventilated in the intensive care unit were enrolled from December 1, 2022, until July 31, 2025, with last follow-up on January 23, 2026. Intervention Telehealth hospitals received real-time oversight from telecritical care nurses and respiratory therapists for adherence to C-SAT/SBT and a standard audit and feedback implementation. Control hospitals received only standard audit and feedback. Main Outcomes and Measures Co–primary outcome measures were adherence to C-SAT/SBT and ventilator-free days to day 28. C-SAT/SBT was defined as any day that the SAT and SBT were separately adherent, and the SAT followed the SBT within 2 hours or both occurred before noon, or the patient was extubated. Change in adherence from baseline was compared between groups using a mixed-effects logistic model with prespecified 1-sided significance testing. Change in ventilator-free days was compared using a mixed-effects proportional odds model. Results There were 4544 patients at telehealth hospitals, 6438 patients at control hospitals, and 1789 preimplementation common baseline patients (median [IQR] age, 62 [47-71] years; 4826 [37.8%] female). The baseline C-SAT/SBT adherence rate of 43.9% increased to 90.3% at telehealth intervention hospitals and to 77.6% at control hospitals (odds ratio for change in telehealth vs change in control, 2.87; 1-sided 95% lower confidence limit, 2.44; P &lt; .001; absolute difference, 11.4%; 95% CI, 8.8%-14.3%). Median (IQR) ventilator-free days from a common baseline of 24 (0-26) increased to 25 (10-27) at telehealth intervention hospitals and 25 (1-27) at control hospitals (odds ratio for change in telehealth vs change in control, 1.21; 95% CI, 1.01-1.45, P = .04; absolute difference, 1.02 days; 95% CI, 0.05-1.96 days). Conclusions and Relevance Among adults intubated and mechanically ventilated in the intensive care unit, adding real-time telehealth support for C-SAT/SBT improved adherence and increased ventilator-free days more than a standard audit and feedback implementation alone. Trial Registration ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT05141396

Cangrelor versus crushed ticagrelor in acute myocardial infarction complicated by cardiogenic shock (DAPT-SHOCK-AMI): a randomised, double-blind trial
items.abstract: Background Acute myocardial infarction complicated by cardiogenic shock (AMI-CS) can compromise the administration and absorption of oral P2Y 12 inhibitors and carries high ischaemic and mortality risks. This trial assessed whether intravenous cangrelor was non-inferior to crushed oral ticagrelor for short-term clinical outcomes and whether it provided faster and more consistent platelet inhibition in patients with AMI-CS. Methods DAPT-SHOCK-AMI was a double-blind trial conducted at 29 hospitals across five European countries (Czech Republic, France, Germany, Poland, and Slovakia). Patients older than 18 years with AMI-CS were randomly assigned (1:1 ratio, stratified by centre, age, sex, presence or absence of ST-segment elevation, and mechanical ventilation) to cangrelor (30 μg/kg bolus followed by an infusion of 4 μg/kg per min for at least 2 h) or crushed ticagrelor (180 mg loading dose). The primary laboratory endpoint was a platelet reactivity index of less than 50% at the end of primary percutaneous coronary intervention. The primary clinical endpoint was death, myocardial infarction, or ischaemic stroke at 30 days. The primary clinical endpoint was analysed for non-inferiority with a prespecified margin of 1 percentage point among all randomly assigned patients who received study treatment. The study is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT03551964) and EudraCT (2018-002161-19); recruitment and 1-year follow-up are complete, and 5-year follow-up is ongoing. Findings Between Aug 1, 2018, and Jan 19, 2024, 605 patients (137 [23%] were female) were randomly assigned to cangrelor (n=298) or ticagrelor (n=307); no surviving patients were lost to the 1-year follow-up. The primary laboratory endpoint was analysed in 56 (19%) patients in the cangrelor group and 68 (22%) in the ticagrelor group, and was achieved in 56 (100%) of 56 patients receiving cangrelor and 15 (22%) of 68 receiving ticagrelor (p non-inferiority =0·13). Major bleeding at 30 days occurred in 19 (6%) of 298 patients receiving cangrelor and 16 (5%) of 307 receiving ticagrelor. Interpretation To our knowledge, this is the first randomised trial to compare P2Y 12 inhibitor strategies specifically in patients with AMI-CS. Cangrelor achieved effective platelet inhibition more frequently than crushed ticagrelor at the end of primary percutaneous coronary intervention. Non-inferiority of cangrelor versus crushed ticagrelor was not demonstrated for the primary 30-day clinical endpoint. These trial findings can inform future trials of P2Y 12 inhibition strategies in patients with AMI-CS. Funding Czech Republic Ministry of Health, Charles University (Czech Republic), and NextGenerationEU.

items.title: Cardiovascular outcomes with survodutide in adults with obesity at increased cardiovascular risk (SYNCHRONIZE-CVOT): a double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial
items.abstract: Background Survodutide, a glucagon receptor and GLP-1 receptor dual agonist, improved markers of cardiometabolic health in people with obesity, but cardiovascular safety for this new class remains to be established. Methods SYNCHRONIZE-CVOT was a global, phase 3, randomised, double-blind, parallel-group, placebo-controlled, multicentre, event-driven, cardiovascular safety trial conducted at 524 clinical sites in 34 countries. We included participants aged 18 years or older with a BMI of 27 kg/m 2 or greater and established cardiovascular disease or at least two obesity complications or risk factors for cardiovascular disease; participants with chronic kidney disease were eligible if they also had a BMI of 30 kg/m 2 or greater. Participants were randomly assigned by interactive response technology (1:1:1) to once-weekly subcutaneous survodutide (up-titrated to 3·6 mg or 6·0 mg) or placebo. The primary endpoint was a composite of death from cardiovascular causes, non-fatal stroke, non-fatal myocardial infarction, ischaemia-related coronary revascularisation, or heart failure event (targeting 189 primary endpoint events). We assessed the non-inferiority of pooled survodutide compared with placebo with a margin of 1·65 for the upper limit of the two-sided 95% CI of the hazard ratio (HR). Efficacy and safety analyses included all randomly assigned participants who received at least one dose of survodutide or placebo. The primary analysis was performed according to the treatment-regimen estimand, which assessed treatment effects regardless of any early discontinuation of survodutide or placebo, temporary stop, the use of protocol-prohibited obesity medications, or a prolonged dose-escalation period. This completed trial is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT06077864. Findings From Nov 20, 2023, to Nov 8, 2024, we screened 7753 participants, of whom 5530 (71·3%) participants were recruited and randomly assigned to treatment. 23 (0·4%) participants were not treated; 1836 (33·3%) of 5507 participants received survodutide 3·6 mg, 1835 (33·3%) received 6·0 mg, and 1836 (33·3%) received placebo; 2194 (39·8%) were female, 3313 (60·2%) were male, and 4332 (78·7%) were White. Median time in study was 22·0 months (IQR 20·1-23·7). 1029 (56·0%) in the survodutide 3·6 mg group, 1039 (56·6%) in the survodutide 6·0 mg group, and 1083 (59·0%) in the placebo group remained on treatment until study closeout. The primary endpoint occurred in 136 (3·7%) of 3671 participants in the survodutide group and in 76 (4·1%) 1836 participants in the placebo group (HR 0·89 [95% CI 0·67-1·18; p Interpretation In participants with obesity with established cardiovascular disease or chronic kidney disease or at increased risk of cardiovascular disease, survodutide was not associated with increased risk for the primary composite endpoint of death from cardiovascular causes, non-fatal stroke, non-fatal myocardial infarction, ischaemia-related coronary revascularisation, or heart failure event compared with placebo. This cardiovascular safety trial provides clinicians with reassuring data that treatment with survodutide, a novel glucagon receptor-GLP-1 receptor dual agonist, is not associated with increased cardiovascular risk. Funding Boehringer Ingelheim.

items.title: Efinopegdutide: a step towards precision in MASH therapy?
Efficacy and safety of efinopegdutide in adults with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis and stage 2–3 fibrosis: a phase 2b, randomised, placebo-controlled study
items.abstract: Background Efinopegdutide is a pharmacologically distinct once-weekly GLP-1-glucagon receptor co-agonist with a relative receptor potency balance of approximately 2:1 under development for metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH). We aimed to investigate the efficacy and safety of efinopegdutide in adults with non-cirrhotic MASH. Methods We did a phase 2b, randomised, placebo-controlled, double-blind study conducted at 176 academic and community centres in 26 countries. We included adults (aged ≥18 years) with biopsy-confirmed MASH and stage 2 or stage 3 fibrosis. Eligible participants were randomly assigned (1:1:1:1:1) to receive either efinopegdutide (4 mg, 7 mg, or 10 mg), placebo, or open-label semaglutide 2·4 mg, all administered subcutaneously once weekly. Randomisation was performed centrally. The primary endpoint was MASH resolution without worsening of fibrosis at week 52. The key secondary histological endpoint was fibrosis improvement of at least one stage without worsening of steatohepatitis. Missing end-of-treatment biopsies were considered as failure for the primary analysis. This study is registered with EU CT, 2022-502647-35-00, and ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT05877547, and is complete. Findings Between June 23, 2023, and Dec 29, 2025, we screened 1704 participants. We randomly assigned 386 (23%) participants, of whom 381 (99%; 194 [51%] women and 187 [49%] men) received at least one dose of study intervention and were included in the analysis. Baseline characteristics were similar across groups; 239 (63%) of 381 participants had F2 fibrosis and 142 (37%) had F3 fibrosis; the mean age of participants was 53 years (SD 13). At week 52, MASH resolution without worsening of fibrosis occurred in 31 (56%) of 55 participants in the 4 mg efinopegdutide group, 31 (63%) of 49 participants in the 7 mg efinopegdutide group, and 35 (61%) of 57 participants in the 10 mg efinopegdutide group versus seven (13%) of 53 participants in the placebo group (difference vs placebo 43·0 percentage points [95% CI 25·7 to 57·8; p Interpretation Treatment with efinopegdutide resulted in a significantly greater proportion of participants with MASH resolution without worsening of fibrosis compared with placebo. The 7 mg dose showed the most favourable benefit-risk profile, improving fibrosis by at least one stage without worsening steatohepatitis in approximately half of participants after 1 year of treatment. These findings support the potential utility of efinopegdutide as a once-weekly GLP-1-glucagon receptor co-agonist in MASH. Funding Merck Sharp & Dohme, a subsidiary of Merck & Co.

items.title: A digital intervention to strengthening parenting in Tanzania
A blended digital parenting intervention for the prevention of sexual violence, exploitative sex, and maltreatment of children at scale in Tanzania: a cluster-randomised, controlled trial
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Childhood sexual, physical, and verbal violence are global public health priorities, affecting 1 billion children each year. ParentApp integrates sexual violence prevention into WHO-UNICEF's open-access Parenting for Lifelong Health programme, using innovative blended digital delivery. We aimed to test the efficacy of ParentApp in preventing sexual violence and maltreatment against adolescent-aged children and improving preventive mechanisms such as family mental health and adolescent-caregiver relationships. METHODS: This cluster-randomised, controlled trial was conducted in 80 Tanzanian sub-wards. Participants were primary caregivers aged 18 years and older and their adolescents (aged 10-17 years). Sub-wards were randomly assigned (1:1) to receive either ParentApp (intervention group) or a control WASHApp programme. Clusters were randomly assigned in blocks of six, stratified by urban versus rural location. Statisticians carrying out randomisation and data analysts were masked; it was not possible to mask participants or researchers. Intervention groups received a low-cost Android phone installed with ParentApp, a 12-module offline-first app, with one in-person orientation session and remote support via WhatsApp group chats, at a delivery cost of US$6 per family at scale, or $10 with 20% smartphone provision. Control groups received a low-cost Android phone installed with WASHApp, a 12-module offline-first app for water, sanitation, and hygiene, with one in-person orientation session. The primary outcomes were adolescent sexual violence victimisation and maltreatment and high-risk situations for sexual violence, assessed in all participants irrespective of uptake and engagement at 5 months and 18 months post-baseline. The trial was registered on March 14, 2023, with OSF (https://osf.io/t9fxz) and is completed. FINDINGS: Between May 11 and Oct 9, 2023, 2692 caregiver-adolescent dyads were screened for study eligibility; 2396 adolescents (1217 [50·8%] female and 1179 [49·2%] male) and 2396 caregivers (1795 [74·9%] female and 601 [25·1%] male) were recruited. 2145 (89·5%) adolescents and 2252 (94·0%) caregivers were retained in the study and included in analyses at 18 months. Adolescent girls in ParentApp clusters had a substantial reduction in past-month sexual violence victimisation compared with those in control clusters (incidence rate ratio [IRR] 0·43 [95% CI 0·21-0·86]; p=0·018), with no effect for boys (1·21 [0·59-2·43]; p=0·60). Past-month maltreatment (physical abuse, verbal abuse, and neglect) was lower in ParentApp clusters than in control clusters (adolescent report IRR 0·92 [0·88-0·96]; p<0·0001, caregiver report 0·87 [0·82-0·92]; p<0·0001). Past-month exposure to high-risk situations for sexual violence was lower in ParentApp clusters than in control clusters (adolescent girls IRR 0·87 [0·77-0·97]; p=0·012, adolescent boys 0·85 [0·79-0·91]; p<0·0001, caregiver report 0·81 [0·75-0·88]; p<0·0001). There were no reported adverse events. INTERPRETATION: A low-cost blended digital parenting programme in countries such as Tanzania could simultaneously reduce childhood sexual violence (for girls) and maltreatment and sexual violence risk situations (for girls and boys). FUNDING: UK Research and Innovation Global Challenges Research Fund, The Oak Foundation, The LEGO Foundation, The European Research Council, and an anonymous donor.

items.title: Reframing disease elimination: an update from the Lancet Commission on chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
items.abstract: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) remains a leading cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide, with increasing global burden driven by population growth and ageing, persistent harmful exposures, and substantial health inequities. The Lancet Commission on COPD articulated an ambitious vision for disease elimination with prevention, early detection, and intervention. This Review revisits that vision, assesses progress since 2022, and calls for a broader commitment to lifelong lung health as an update of the Commission. Across seven sections, this Review advances a unified framework integrating the biology of lung development and ageing, precision medicine, patient-centred outcomes, and regulatory reform. COPD is not a single, uniform disease; rather, a biologically complex condition shaped by genetic, developmental, environmental, infectious, and behavioural factors across the entire life course. Effective prevention and care should therefore move beyond the detection and treatment of late physiological impairment toward earlier disease recognition, biological stratification, and interventions to preserve lung health, reduce symptoms, and prevent morbidity and premature mortality. The Review charts a path from reactive, late-stage management toward proactive, equitable, precision-based prevention and care. The central premise is unequivocal: the global burden of COPD can be substantially reduced. Success should be measured not only by gains in lung function and survival but also by improvements in daily functioning, quality of life, and wellbeing. In this expanded vision, COPD is no longer viewed solely as a chronic disease to be managed but as a preventable and modifiable condition within a broader commitment to lifelong lung health.

items.title: Trevogrumab (anti-GDF8) with or without garetosmab (anti-activin A) for prevention of muscle loss during semaglutide-induced weight reduction in people with obesity (COURAGE): a two-part, phase 2, double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomised trial
items.abstract: Background Rapid weight loss, as induced by GLP-1 receptor agonists, is accompanied by pronounced muscle loss. GDF8 (myostatin) and activin A (ActA), acting via ActRIIA/B receptors, are negative regulators of muscle mass. The aim of this study was to evaluate the effect of antibodies blocking GDF8 (trevogrumab) and ActA (garetosmab) on semaglutide-induced weight and muscle loss. Methods COURAGE is a two-part, phase 2, double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomised trial. This multicentre (60 sites), US-based trial enrolled participants aged 18-80 years with obesity (BMI ≥30 kg/m 2 ). In part A, participants were treated for 26 weeks with semaglutide (titrated to 2·4 mg subcutaneously weekly) in addition to a randomly assigned (1:1:1:1) concomitant treatment: placebo, trevogrumab 200 mg, trevogrumab 400 mg, or trevogrumab 400 mg and garetosmab 10 mg/kg. Trevogrumab was administered subcutaneously weekly and garetosmab was administered intravenously every 4 weeks. Part A also included a subsequent semaglutide withdrawal period, at which point participants (randomly assigned at baseline 1:1 within each group) received either trevogrumab 400 mg or placebo for an additional 26 weeks. In part B, participants were treated with semaglutide for 52 weeks and randomly assigned (1:2:2) to concomitant treatment with placebo, trevogrumab 25 mg, or trevogrumab 75 mg. Groups were stratified according to sex, BMI ( 2 vs ≥35 kg/m 2 ), and participation in an exploratory MRI substudy assessing thigh muscle volume. Study participants, the principal investigators, and study site personnel were masked to all randomisation assignments throughout the study. Primary endpoints were percent change in lean mass, fat mass, and bodyweight from baseline to week 26 (part A) or week 52 (part B). Efficacy and safety analyses were done in all randomly assigned participants who received at least one dose of a study drug (efficacy, as randomly assigned; safety, as treated). COURAGE is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT06299098, and is currently active, not recruiting. Findings 975 participants were enrolled between June 21, 2024, and April 14, 2025. Mean age was 49·0 years (SD 13·2) and mean BMI was 36·7 kg/m 2 (SD 5·0); 627 (64%) of 975 participants were female and 348 (36%) were male. In part A (n=605, of whom n=599 received at least one dose of study drug), a substantial decrease in lean mass was observed in the semaglutide plus placebo group at week 26 (-6·6% [95% CI -7·4 to -5·7]); the estimated treatment difference (ETD) versus semaglutide plus placebo was +3·1% (95% CI 1·9 to 4·3) with semaglutide plus trevogrumab 200 mg, +2·7% (1·5 to 4·0) with semaglutide plus trevogrumab 400 mg, and +4·5% (3·1 to 5·9) with semaglutide plus trevogrumab 400 mg plus garetosmab 10 mg/kg. In part B (n=376), lean mass percent change from baseline to week 52 for semaglutide plus placebo was -7·3% (-8·8 to -5·8); the ETD versus semaglutide plus placebo was +1·5% (-0·3 to 3·3) for semaglutide plus trevogrumab 25 mg, and +3·1% (1·3 to 4·9) for semaglutide plus trevogrumab 75 mg. Change from baseline in fat mass in part A was -15·6% (-17·4 to -13·9) in the semaglutide plus placebo group; the ETD was significant in the semaglutide plus trevogrumab 400 mg group (-3·4% [-5·9 to -0·9]) and the semaglutide plus trevogrumab 400 mg plus garetosmab 10 mg/kg group (-11·7% [-14·4 to -9·0]) in part A. No other groups in part A nor any in part B had significantly different changes in fat mass compared with semaglutide plus placebo. Percent change in bodyweight in part A was -10·6 (-11·6 to -9·7) in the semaglutide plus placebo group; the ETD was significant for the semaglutide plus trevogrumab 400 mg plus garetosmab 10 mg/kg group (-2·7 [-4·1 to -1·2]). No other groups in part A nor any in part B had significantly different changes in bodyweight compared with semaglutide plus placebo. Semaglutide plus trevogrumab (25 mg, 75 mg, 200 mg, or 400 mg) was generally well tolerated with a safety profile similar to semaglutide plus placebo; however, semaglutide plus trevogrumab 400 mg plus garetosmab 10 mg/kg had a high incidence of serious adverse events (14 [9%] of 149) and treatment discontinuations (48 [32%] of 149). Gastrointestinal adverse events were the most commonly reported, and they occurred with similar incidence across treatment groups. Muscle spasms occurred more frequently in the semaglutide plus trevogrumab 400 mg plus garetosmab 10 mg/kg group (61 [41%] of 149) compared with the semaglutide plus trevogrumab 200 mg or 400 mg groups (23 [8%] of 299) and semaglutide plus placebo groups (seven [5%] of 151). Most adverse events were mild to moderate in severity. Two deaths occurred during the study, both in the semaglutide plus trevogrumab 400 mg plus garetosmab 10 mg/kg group; a causal association between treatment and these events was not identified. Interpretation This study establishes proof of concept for GDF8 inhibition by trevogrumab alone as a generally well tolerated strategy to preserve lean mass during GLP-1 receptor agonist-induced weight loss. Although the addition of ActA inhibition by garetosmab further improved body composition and weight loss, the combination did not have favourable safety and tolerability. Further study is required to understand whether improved body composition during weight loss might preserve physical function and overall metabolic health. Funding Regeneron Pharmaceuticals, Inc.

items.title: Lynch syndrome
items.abstract: Lynch syndrome is the most common inherited cancer predisposition syndrome, affecting approximately one in 350-450 individuals, yet the majority of carriers remain undiagnosed, representing a substantial and preventable public health burden. Caused by germline pathogenic variants in DNA mismatch repair (MMR) genes, Lynch syndrome confers markedly elevated and heterogeneous risks of colorectal, endometrial, and multiple extracolonic cancers. Advances in molecular diagnostics, particularly universal tumour testing for MMR deficiency, have transformed case identification and enabled targeted germline testing and cascade screening of relatives at risk. Despite these advances, implementation remains inconsistent, with substantial attrition across diagnostic pathways and inequities in access to care. Preventive strategies-including colonoscopic surveillance, aspirin chemoprevention, and risk-reducing surgery-are effective but require gene-specific and individualised application. Therapeutically, the immunogenic biology of MMR-deficient tumours has positioned Lynch syndrome at the forefront of precision oncology, with immune checkpoint inhibitors delivering substantial benefit and emerging vaccine strategies offering promise for cancer interception. In this Review, we provide an integrated overview of Lynch syndrome across the continuum of care, highlighting advances in biology, diagnosis, prevention, and treatment, while emphasising the crucial need to align scientific progress with equitable and effective health-system delivery.

items.title: Empirical tuberculosis treatment in infants living with HIV hospitalised with severe pneumonia in Africa (EMPIRICAL): a multicentre, randomised, open-label, 2 × 2 factorial, controlled superiority trial
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Mortality among infants with severe HIV-associated pneumonia remains high globally. The EMPIRICAL trial evaluated whether empirical tuberculosis treatment (eTB-T) improves survival compared with the currently recommended microbiologically and clinically guided strategy. METHODS: This multicentre, open-label, group-sequential designed, 2×2 factorial, randomised, controlled, superiority trial was conducted in 19 hospitals across Côte d'Ivoire, Malawi, Mozambique, Uganda, Zambia, and Zimbabwe. Infants aged 28-365 days admitted with severe HIV-associated pneumonia, without a current tuberculosis diagnosis or contact, were centrally and individually randomly assigned (1:1:1:1) using a secure web-based system stratified by site and severity. A computer-generated block randomisation schedule was used, with fixed blocks of eight allocations (two allocations to each factorial treatment group) within each stratum. Participants received standard of care (SoC) comprising treatment for bacterial (WHO-recommended antibiotics) and Pneumocystis jirovecii (cotrimoxazole and steroids) pneumonia, SoC plus 15 days of oral valganciclovir (16 mg/kg per 12 h), or SoC plus 6 months of tuberculosis treatment (isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol for 2 months, plus isoniazid and rifampicin for 4 subsequent months), or both interventions combined. Here, we report the comparison between the eTB-T (ie, SoC plus tuberculosis treatment and SoC plus oral valganciclovir plus tuberculosis treatment) and non-eTB-T (ie, SoC or SoC plus 15 days of oral valganciclovir) groups. Nasopharyngeal aspirates, stools for Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra testing, and urine for tuberculosis lipoarabinomannan assay were collected at recruitment. In the non-eTB-T groups, tuberculosis treatment was initiated if microbiological results collected at recruitment yielded positive results or if, during follow-up, the treating clinician suspected tuberculosis on clinical grounds, including radiological findings, in accordance with routine clinical practice and guidelines. The primary endpoint was all-cause mortality (at 15 days and 360 days). Survival was estimated using flexible parametric models with covariate-adjusted conditional estimates; missing data were imputed by chained equations. The trial is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT03915366) and is now complete. FINDINGS: Between March 15, 2020, and Jan 31, 2024, 563 participants were enrolled; 558 were analysed after excluding five patients who did not meet eligibility criteria. 276 participants were allocated to the eTB-T groups (n=140 eTB-T and n=136 valganciclovir plus eTB-T) and 282 to the non-eTB-T groups (n=142 SoC and n=140 valganciclovir). 17 (6%) of 276 in the eTB-T groups and 20 (7%) of 282 in the non-eTB-T groups were lost to follow-up. Median age was 4·4 months (IQR 3·2-7·4) and 274 (49%) of participants were female and 284 (51%) were male. In the non-eTB-T groups, 130 (46%) of 282 participants eventually initiated tuberculosis treatment at a median of 4·0 days (IQR 3·0-15·0) after recruitment due to positive microbiological findings in 55 (20%) cases (53 confirmed by tuberculosis lipoarabinomannan assay and two by nasopharyngeal aspirates Xpert MTB/RIF) or clinical decision in 75 (27%) cases. There was no evidence of interaction between valganciclovir and eTB-T (adjusted hazard ratio 1·19, 95% CI 0·73-1·95; pheterogeneity=0·4836). At 12 months, 132 (48%) of 276 participants in eTB-T groups and 121 (43%) of 282 participants in non-eTB-T groups died. In the eTB-T groups, the adjusted hazard ratio for death was 1·12 (95% CI 0·87-1·43; p=0·3868). At 15 days, the odds ratio was 1·24 (95% CI 0·83-1·84; p=0·2950). Serious adverse events did not differ between groups (1·19, 0·82-1·73; p=0·3523). There were no treatment-related deaths. The most common adverse events were elevation of transaminases (72 [26%] cases in the eTB-T groups and 74 [26%] in the non-eTB-T group), anaemia (163 [59%] cases in the eTB-T groups and 169 [60%] in the non-eTB-T groups), and infectious disease requiring antimicrobial treatment (161 [58%] cases in the eTB-T groups and 176 [62%] in the non-eTB-T groups). INTERPRETATION: In contrast to empirical treatment with valganciclovir, there was no evidence that eTB-T was superior to a clinically and microbiologically guided strategy in reducing all-cause mortality among infants with HIV-associated pneumonia. However, the high proportion of infants who eventually initiated tuberculosis treatment during follow-up in the non-eTB-T groups might have reduced the contrast between strategies and attenuated the ability to detect differences in outcomes. FUNDING: European and Developing Countries Clinical Trials Partnership.
