Primary Tumor Biology, Recurrence and Survival After Colorectal Liver Metastasis Resection: The BIO-CRLM Study
items.abstract: Objective: To evaluate whether integrated primary tumor biology, combining primary tumor location and RAS/BRAF status, defines recurrence phenotypes and survival trajectories after liver resection for colorectal liver metastases (CRLM). Summary Background Data: Selection for resection remains largely morphology-based, although tumor biology strongly influences post-hepatectomy outcomes. Primary tumor site and RAS/BRAF status are individually prognostic, but whether their integration identifies distinct post-resection trajectories is unclear. Methods: An international multicenter cohort of patients undergoing liver resection for CRLM between 2017 and 2023 was analyzed. Integrated biology was defined a priori as left-sided-wild-type, right-sided-wild-type, rectal-wild-type, left-sided-RAS-mutant, right-sided-RAS-mutant, rectal RAS-mutant, and BRAF-mutant disease. Primary outcomes were recurrence-free survival (RFS) and overall survival (OS). Secondary outcomes included early recurrence, disseminated first recurrence, and first recurrence phenotype. Results: Among 3162 patients from 44 centers, 2415 (76.4%) developed recurrence and 1342 (42.4%) died. Integrated biology was independently associated with both RFS and OS (global P <0.001 for both). Compared with left-WT tumors, the highest mortality risks were observed in BRAF-mutant disease [hazard ratio (HR): 2.68, 95% CI: 2.02–3.57, P <0.001] and right-RAS-mutant disease (HR: 2.32, 95% CI: 1.94–2.79, P <0.001). Integrated biology was also associated with early recurrence, disseminated first recurrence, and first recurrence phenotype. Rectal-RAS-mutant tumors had the strongest association with lung-only recurrence [relative risk ratio (RRR): 3.38, 95% CI: 2.22–5.13, P <0.001] and disseminated recurrence (RRR: 2.57, 95% CI: 1.86–3.55, P <0.001) relative to liver-only recurrence. Conclusions: Integrated primary tumor biology identifies clinically distinct post-hepatectomy disease trajectories after CRLM resection. Combining primary tumor site with RAS/BRAF status may support preoperative counseling, surveillance planning, and trial stratification.

items.title: Postpancreatectomy Mortality (PPM) Following Minimally Invasive Pancreatic Surgery Is Mainly Driven by Pancreatectomy-Specific Complications
items.abstract: Background: Postpancreatectomy mortality (PPM) remains relatively unexplored after minimally invasive pancreatic surgery (MIPS). The International Study Group for Pancreatic Surgery (ISGPS) recently proposed a consensus definition and classification of PPM based on root-cause analysis. We aimed to assess the applicability of this classification and characterize mechanisms of PPM following MIPS. Methods: This study retrospectively analyzed consecutive patients undergoing MIPS enrolled in the Italian IGoMIPS registry (October 2019–July 2025). All PPM events were reviewed and attributed specific PPM types using structured root-cause analysis according to ISGPS criteria. Multivariable logistic regression identified predictors of PPM, and PPM type distributions were compared across procedures. Results: Out of 3590 patients, the PPM rate was 2.7%. Specifically, PPM occurred in 5.9% following minimally invasive pancreatoduodenectomy (MIPD), 0.8% following left pancreatectomy (MILP), and 4.8% following total pancreatectomy (MITP), while no PPM events occurred after parenchyma-sparing resections. Increased age and American Society of Anesthesiology Physical Status (ASA-PS) ≥3 independently predicted PPM. Root-cause analysis showed that most PPM followed cascades of multiple pancreatectomy-specific complications, predominantly postoperative pancreatic fistula (POPF) and postpancreatectomy hemorrhage (PPH). PPM 2 accounted for approximately two-thirds of deaths, particularly after MIPD and MITP, whereas PPM 1 and PPM 3 accounted for 13.3% and 15.3%, respectively. Conclusions: Mortality after MIPS predominantly occurs after a cascade of pancreatectomy-specific complications rather than technical failure or isolated medical events. Centers performing MIPS should invest in strategies to mitigate POPF and PPH and minimize failure to rescue once they occur.

items.title: Aborted Minimally Invasive Cholecystectomy Signals Complex Biliary Disease
items.abstract: Objective: Evaluate operative complexity, clinical outcomes, and drivers of health care utilization after aborted minimally invasive cholecystectomy (MIC). Background: Although MIC is a standard approach, minimally invasive techniques cannot always be completed safely. Operative complexity, patient characteristics, and clinical outcomes after aborted MIC remain poorly defined. Methods: We conducted a retrospective review of patients referred to our tertiary medical center between 2015 and 2025 after aborted MIC. All patients subsequently underwent definitive open cholecystectomy. Multivariable regression models were used to identify predictors of hospital length of stay (LOS), postoperative complications, and 30-day readmission. Results: The cohort included 176 patients. The most common reasons for aborting MIC were fibrotic, contracted, and intrahepatic gallbladder (38.6%), dense adhesions (23.3%), inability to safely separate the gallbladder from adjacent organs (22.7%), and unsafe anatomy (19.3%). Complex biliary pathology was confirmed intraoperatively in 30.6% of patients; concomitant procedures were required in 43.4%, and the overall complication rate was 18.7%, including a bile leak rate of 5.1%. No bile duct injury was observed. Median LOS was 2 days, the readmission rate was 6.3%, and mortality was 0.5%. Higher comorbidity burden, greater blood loss, and performance of concomitant procedures independently predicted longer LOS. No variables were independently associated with complications or readmission. Conclusions: Aborted MIC often reflects unrecognized complex biliary pathology rather than technical failure. A definitive open surgical approach with biliary reconstructive capability achieves acceptable short-term outcomes. Early conversion or referral should be considered a proactive safety strategy, with important implications for surgical training, decision-making, and system-level escalation and referral pathways.

items.title: Ex Vivo Lung Perfusion and Allograft Failure After Lung Transplantation
items.abstract: Objective: Ex vivo lung perfusion (EVLP) has been championed as a disruptive strategy to expand the lung transplantation (LT) donor pool, yet contemporary evidence remains limited. Using a real-world cohort, we emulated a randomized controlled trial (RCT) to characterize the causal effect of EVLP on post-LT survival. Methods: LT recipients ≥18 years were identified from the 2018–2025 Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network. Annual hospital LT volume was computed; centers in the top quartile (>54 LT/y) were designated high-volume centers (HVCs). Using target trial emulation with clone-censor-weight methodology, we simulated a pragmatic, open-label RCT comparing EVLP with standard allografts at HVCs and non-HVCs. Survival was evaluated using Kaplan-Meier and multivariable Cox models. Results: Among 20,627 LTs, 1419 (7%) received EVLP allografts. The proportion of EVLP allografts increased across all centers, from 5% in 2018 to 10% in 2024 and 8% in 2025 ( P trend <0.001). In the Lung Allocation Score era, LT using EVLP allografts yielded similar 2-year outcomes at HVC, but inferior outcomes at non-HVC. In the Composite Allocation Score period, however, EVLP was associated with significantly worse survival at non-HVC. In the emulated RCT among CAS-era recipients, EVLP remained independently associated with similar outcomes at HVC, but increased 2-year hazards of patient mortality (HR: 2.43, CI: 1.36–4.34, P =0.003) and allograft failure at non-HVC (HR: 2.52, CI: 1.31–4.84, P =0.005). Conclusions: EVLP was associated with comparable survival at HVC but inferior outcomes at non-HVC. These findings highlight the critical role of hospital context and center experience in determining the effectiveness and safety of EVLP and call for standardization of protocols across centers.

items.title: Prospective Evidence of Concomitant Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma Risk Among Patients With Branch-duct Intraductal Papillary Mucinous Neoplasms Without Worrisome Features/High-risk Stigmata at Baseline
items.abstract: Objective: To evaluate the natural history, especially concomitant pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (cPDAC) risk in patients with branch-duct intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm (BD-IPMN) without worrisome features (WF) or high-risk stigmata (HRS). Summary Background Data: BD-IPMNs without WF/HRS are considered low-risk, yet optimal surveillance strategies remain uncertain. Methods: In a prospective multicenter Japan Pancreas Society registry, 1234 patients with BD-IPMN without WF/HRS underwent imaging and laboratory surveillance every 6 months for up to 5.17 years. Cumulative incidence, standardized incidence ratios (SIRs), and competing-risk analyses were performed to assess advanced pancreatic neoplasia, defined as IPMN high-grade dysplasia (IPMN-HGD), invasive IPMN, or cPDAC, and associated risk factors. Outcomes were also evaluated under simulated guideline-recommended extended surveillance intervals. Results: During 5.17 years of follow-up, advanced pancreatic neoplasia developed in 26 patients: 10 IPMN-HGD/invasive IPMN and 16 cPDAC. The 5.17-year cumulative incidence was 2.48%; SIRs relative to the general population were 8.01 overall, 3.07 for IPMN-HGD/invasive IPMN, and 4.91 for cPDAC. The cPDAC SIRs were 6.21 and 3.02 for cysts <20 mm and ≥20 mm, respectively. Diabetes history and mural nodule development predicted IPMN-HGD/invasive IPMN, whereas CA19-9 elevation and new or worsening diabetes predicted cPDAC. Of 19 patients eligible for surveillance interval extension, 13 (68%) had a later simulated detection date. Conclusion: Patients with BD-IPMN without WF/HRS at baseline had 3.07 and 4.91 times the incidences of IPMN-HGD/invasive IPMN and cPDAC expected in the general population, respectively. Surveillance based solely on cyst stability may warrant caution regarding the timely detection of surgically resectable pancreatic cancer.

items.title: Transformation of Retroperitoneal Well-Differentiated to Dedifferentiated Liposarcoma
items.abstract: Background: While the majority of primary retroperitoneal (pRP) dedifferentiated liposarcoma (DDLPS) appear to occur de novo, the rate of transformation of pRP well-differentiated (WD) LPS to DDLPS has not been well defined. This study aims to understand the natural history of RP WDLPS and investigate the rate of transformation to DDLPS. Methods: We identified all patients with RP WDLPS treated at 24 participating sites between January 2002 and December 2017. Patients with DDLPS on primary surgery pathology were excluded. Crude cumulative incidence (CCI) of transformation to DDLPS and overall survival (OS) were analyzed. Recurrence data were collected for up to 5 disease recurrences per patient. Results: Of 584 patients in our study cohort, 40% (n=235) developed recurrent disease at a median of 31.4 months from surgery. Transformation to DDLPS was observed in 81 patients (14% of all patients, 35% of patients who underwent surgery for recurrent disease, with a median follow-up of 73 mo and 5- and 8 y CCI of 12% and 15%, respectively). Transformation was observed at first recurrence in 59 patients (25%), second in 16 patients (13%), third in 6 patients (4%), and none at fourth or fifth. The 5- and 8-year OS for patients with transformation to DDLPS was 79% and 61%, respectively, compared to 85% and 71%, respectively, for patients without transformation ( P =0.05). Conclusion: Approximately 1 in 7 patients with pRP WDLPS will transform to DDLPS over time, accounting for over one third of those who develop recurrent disease. Transformation to DDLPS does not portend worse OS among those patients who recur.

items.title: Deeper Inside the “M” of the TNM in Patients With Colorectal Liver Metastases: Proposition of the B-PLEC Classification
Hallmarks of Oncological Radicality in Perihilar Cholangiocarcinoma: International Investigation of Margin Clearance and Resection Extent
items.abstract: Objective: To define a clinically relevant threshold for pR0 and determine the oncological relevance of individual margins. Summary Background Data: No uniform definition of pR0 exists for perihilar cholangiocarcinoma (pCCA), and it is uncertain which patients benefit the most from wider margin clearances. Methods: This retrospective international cohort study included patients undergoing curative-intent major hepatectomy for pCCA in 23 expert centers across North America and Europe (2004-2024). Overall survival (OS), and initial recurrence patterns were compared across proximal, distal, and radial (RM) margins with clearance categorized as 0 mm, submillimeter (>0–<1 mm), or ≥1 mm. Results: Among 1475 included patients, the 5-year OS decreased from 46.6% for ≥1 mm clearance to 36.6% for submillimeter clearance and 26.3% for 0 mm clearance. Both submillimeter and 0 mm clearance were associated with worse OS (adjusted hazard ratio [HR], 1.24 [95% CI, 1.03–1.50] and 1.58 [95% CI, 1.36–1.84]). Only progressively narrower RM clearance from submillimeter to 0 mm conferred an increased risk of local recurrence (subdistribution HR, 1.70 [95% CI, 1.11–2.61] and 2.37 [95% CI, 1.58–3.56]). Nodal metastasis influenced RM submillimeter–OS association (P interaction =0.02), and RM 0 mm remained adverse regardless of nodal status (P interaction =0.28). Conclusions: Margin clearance at ≥1 mm appears to define pR0. Survival worsened from submillimeter to 0 mm radial margin clearance, with tumor biology refining this distinction. Narrowing clearance was associated with local recurrence but had limited relevance to nonlocal recurrence. Operative strategy should balance greater clearance against tumor biology and risks of extending resection.

items.title: Surgeons’ Outcomes Before Early Exit From Surgical Practice
items.abstract: Objective: To determine whether postoperative outcomes differ between patients treated by surgeons who exit operative practice early and those treated by surgeons who remain in active practice. Summary/Background: Amid a growing US surgeon shortage, early departure from operative practice may further strain the surgical workforce. Whether early practice exit is associated with declining clinical performance is unknown. Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using Medicare claims from 2015 to 2023. We categorized surgeons as remaining in active practice, exiting at presumed retirement, or exiting early. We compared 30-day and 90-day readmission, postoperative complications, reoperation, and mortality using adjusted multivariable logistic regression. Among surgeons who exited practice, we evaluated postoperative outcomes during the 5 years preceding exit. Results: Among 23,575 surgeons, 7119 (30.2%) exited operative practice, including 5383 (22.8%) who exited before age 65 years. After adjustment, rates of postoperative complications, 30-day and 90-day readmission, reoperation, and 90-day mortality were similar among patients treated by surgeons who remained in active practice, exited early, or exited at presumed retirement. Among surgeons who exited practice, each additional year of age at exit was associated with a 0.06 percentage point lower rate of postoperative complications and a 0.04 percentage point lower rate of reoperation during the preceding 5 years. Conclusions: Patients treated by surgeons who exited operative practice early had postoperative outcomes comparable to those who remained in active practice. Early practice exit was not consistently preceded by declining surgical outcomes, suggesting that factors other than measurable postoperative performance may contribute to surgeons’ decisions to leave operative practice.

items.title: Early Postoperative Microbiota Transplantation is Feasible and Associated With Microbial and Metabolic Recovery Following Colorectal Surgery
items.abstract: Background Microbiota disruption following colorectal surgery contributes to impaired gastrointestinal recovery and postoperative inflammation. Perioperative interventions essential for surgical safety, including mechanical bowel preparation and antibiotic prophylaxis, profoundly suppress microbial community diversity and fermentative metabolic activity, creating a window of ecological vulnerability during the early postoperative period. Despite growing recognition of the microbiome’s role in postoperative physiology, including its contributions to epithelial repair, immune regulation, and gastrointestinal motility, no standardized strategies exist to restore gut microbial composition and function after surgery. Here, we evaluated the safety, feasibility, and exploratory biological effects of early postoperative microbiota transplant therapy (MTT) following colorectal surgery. Results In this phase I clinical study, twelve patients undergoing sigmoid colectomy for diverticular disease or colon cancer received MTT via nasojejunal feeding tube on postoperative day 2 and were compared with matched non-MTT patients from a prior cohort undergoing identical surgery. Longitudinal microbiome, metabolomic, and immune profiling identified sustained donor-attributed microbial community similarity at 16S resolution and recovery-associated increases in fecal short-chain and branched-chain fatty acids by postoperative day 14, consistent with restoration of microbial metabolic activity. Exploratory integrated microbiome-metabolite modeling identified a dominant recovery-associated latent axis reflecting shared variation between microbial community structure and metabolite profiles across the postoperative period. Longitudinal immune profiling within MTT recipients demonstrated temporally structured immune remodeling characterized by early innate immune shifts followed by later adaptive immune transitions consistent with immune resolution. Cross-omic integration revealed time-stratified associations linking microbial and metabolic recovery trajectories with staged immune remodeling. No adverse events were attributed to MTT. Conclusions Early postoperative MTT was feasible, well tolerated, and associated with exploratory microbial, metabolic, and within-recipient immune recovery dynamics following colorectal surgery. Together, these findings suggest that postoperative recovery may involve temporally aligned microbial, metabolic, and immune dynamics, and that MTT may serve as a useful biological perturbation model for investigating host-microbiome interactions during surgical recovery. Prospective controlled studies are needed to determine whether these observations are MTT-specific and whether microbiome restoration strategies can improve clinical outcomes such as reduced ileus, surgical site infection, or anastomotic complications.

items.title: Robotic Versus Open Pancreatoduodenectomy
items.abstract: Objective: To synthesize randomized controlled trial (RCT) evidence comparing robotic pancreatoduodenectomy (RPD) with open pancreatoduodenectomy (OPD) and use IDEAL developmental mapping to contextualize clinical heterogeneity. Background: Whether procedural maturity modifies interpretation of randomized treatment effects remains uncertain. Methods: MEDLINE, Embase, CENTRAL, and registries were searched through July 2026 for RCTs comparing RPD with OPD in adults. Primary outcomes were severe postoperative morbidity, postoperative pancreatic fistula (POPF) grade B/C, and 90-day mortality. Secondary outcomes included estimated blood loss (EBL), length of stay, functional recovery, and hospital costs. Random-effects meta-analyses, RoB-2, GRADE, and IDEAL assessments were performed; costs were synthesized descriptively by trial. Results: Four RCTs involving 765 patients were included. RPD showed no significant differences versus OPD in severe morbidity (RR: 0.92; 95% CI: 0.75–1.13; P =0.43; I ²=0%), POPF grade B/C (RR: 0.88; 95% CI: 0.58–1.32; P =0.52; I ²=50%), or 90-day mortality (RR: 0.81; 95% CI: 0.24–2.79; P =0.74; I ²=19%). RPD was associated with lower EBL (MD −70.6 mL; 95% CI: −134.7 to −6.5 mL; P =0.03; I ²=78%). Reported direct procedural costs were higher with RPD across contributing trials, whereas total admission costs varied by setting. GRADE certainty was moderate for severe morbidity and low for POPF grade B/C, mortality, and EBL. IDEAL mapping classified 3 trials as Stage 3 and one as Stage 2b. Stage 3 sensitivity analysis showed lower POPF grade B/C rates and shorter hospital stay with RPD. Conclusions: In experienced programs, RPD shows comparable perioperative safety to OPD, with a modest but heterogeneous EBL reduction and consistently higher direct procedural costs. IDEAL assessment complements quantitative synthesis, contextualizing between-trial heterogeneity and procedural maturity.

items.title: Overload: Impact of Trainer Incivility on Resident Cognition and Operative Performance
items.abstract: Objective: Incivility is frequent in the operating room (OR), yet its impact on the cognition and performance of surgical residents remains unknown. This study aimed to determine the effect of intraoperative trainer incivility on resident cognitive load and performance during routine surgery and subsequent independent management of major hemorrhage. Methods: In this parallel-arm randomized controlled trial, all enrolled vascular residents were randomized to operate with a trainer demonstrating either constructive or uncivil behaviors during a standardized femoral anastomosis in a high-fidelity simulated OR (simulation 1). Senior residents then returned to independently manage a major hemorrhage (simulation 2). The primary outcome was cognitive load, represented objectively by the heart rate variability metric standard deviation of normal-to-normal intervals (SDNN) and subjectively by the Surgery Task Load Index (SURG-TLX). Expert raters assessed nontechnical skills [Non-Technical Skills for Surgeons (NOTSS)] and technical skills (Technical Score). Results: Fifty-eight residents were enrolled [20 (34%) women; mean (SD) age: 35.2 (4.4) years], with 29 in each trial arm for simulation 1. Eleven senior residents from each group (n=22) completed simulation 2. The uncivil group demonstrated significantly higher objective cognitive load across both simulations (SDNN group×phase interaction F ₂,₄₀=6.51; P =0.004) versus the constructive group, equating to a 46% divergence. During simulation 1, residents reported significantly higher SURG-TLX scores (median difference: 31; 95% CI: 20.0–42.0; P <0.001) and achieved significantly lower NOTSS scores (difference: −1.66; 95% CI: −2.40 to −0.95; P <0.001) versus the constructive group. Self-reported cognitive load in the uncivil group did not differ significantly between simulations 1 and 2 (SURG-TLX difference: 14.0; 95% CI: −0.83 to 28.83; P =0.06). Extraversion was independently associated with higher simulation 2 NOTSS ( β =0.27; 95% CI: 0.16–0.37; P <.001) and technical score ( β =0.53; 95% CI: 0.09–0.98; P =0.03). Conclusions: Trainer incivility during operative surgery causes persistent, cognitively induced cardiac autonomic dysregulation in surgical residents and is associated with degradation of vital nontechnical skills during the acute interaction. The self-reported cognitive burden of trainer incivility was comparable to that incurred during independent management of profuse simulated bleeding. Trainer-induced cognitive overload can spill across time and task domains, highlighting immediate and residual impacts of dysfunctional training dynamics with implications for surgical performance.

items.title: From sirens to systems: Characterizing EMS and trauma care across America
items.containerTitle: Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: State emergency medical services (EMS) and trauma systems determine prehospital triage, transport, trauma center designation, data reporting, and quality improvement, yet their contemporary organization has not been systematically characterized. We sought to describe state-level EMS and trauma system structures, policies, resources, and perceived gaps across the United States. METHODS: We conducted a cross-sectional survey of EMS and trauma system leaders in all 50 states and the District of Columbia from July 2025 through March 2026. A 56-item instrument utilizing categorical, Likert-type, rank-order, and free-text items assessed oversight, prehospital triage and transport, clinical protocols, trauma center verification, registries, quality improvement, and funding. Respondents were recruited by email and phone. Multiple respondents could contribute complementary domain-level information to a single state profile. Responses were summarized descriptively. RESULTS: All 51 jurisdictions participated. Most states reported a state EMS medical director (84%), statewide trauma triage protocols (84%), and mandatory participation in their state trauma registry (88%). However, operational coordination varied: only 29% had a centralized trauma communications center, only 6% of states reported a single point of contact for helicopter EMS dispatch, and 35% required a certificate of need for new helicopter services. Trauma center verification relied on American College of Surgeons (ACS) verification in 59% of states, while others used state-administered processes. More than half of states rated EMS financial resources in the two lowest adequacy categories, and 55% reported that their trauma system required at least moderate improvement. Rural populations were most frequently identified as underserved (96%) and as experiencing worse outcomes (92%). CONCLUSIONS: State EMS and trauma systems share broad adoption of national clinical standards but differ substantially in governance, coordination, verification, data integration, and funding. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE AND STUDY TYPE: Level V, Prognostic/epidemiological.

items.title: Resuscitation using fresh-frozen plasma is associated with improved contextual fear memory in a non-TBI mouse model of trauma and hemorrhagic shock
items.containerTitle: Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Cognitive dysfunction is a consequence of traumatic injury with lasting impacts. Even without direct brain injury, trauma and hemorrhagic shock (T/HS) can cause malperfusion, inflammation, and neuronal injury. Disruption of the endothelial glycocalyx (eGC), a key regulator of vascular homeostasis, contributes to trauma-induced endotheliopathy and may influence secondary neurologic injury. Prior work demonstrated that fresh-frozen plasma (FFP) resuscitation preserves eGC expression and reduces maladaptive vascular repair in a murine T/HS model. This study evaluates post-injury cognition and FFP protection against cognitive impairment compared with lactated Ringer’s (LR). METHODS: Male C57BL/6 mice were randomized to sham procedure or T/HS followed by a volume-driven LR or pressure-directed FFP resuscitation approach. T/HS mice underwent laparotomy, femoral artery cannulation, hemorrhagic shock, pseudofractures via bone homogenate injection, and hindlimb muscle crush injuries. Sham mice received laparotomy and femoral artery cutdown. Four days postsurgery, open field testing assessed locomotion, followed by fear conditioning on days 7 to 8 to assess cognition. Brains were collected to analyze hippocampal glycosaminoglycans hyaluronan, heparan sulfate (HS), and chondroitin sulfate (CS). RESULTS: Open field testing showed intact locomotion at post-injury day 4 in all groups. On day 8, mice resuscitated with FFP had significantly greater contextual freezing compared with mice resuscitated with LR, consistent with improved hippocampal-dependent contextual memory. Cued fear conditioning did not differ between groups. LR and FFP resuscitation strategies resulted in distinct hippocampal hyaluronan and HS staining patterns, without synthesis gene expression differences. T/HS+LR brains showed increased 4- O -sulfated CS (CS-4S), a neurologically detrimental sulfation pattern, whereas FFP decreased CS-4S and increased CS-6S. CONCLUSIONS: Goal-directed plasma resuscitation is associated with improved spatial memory and distinct eGC structural remodeling compared with volume-driven crystalloid resuscitation following T/HS. These findings highlight the potential for resuscitation strategy after hemorrhagic shock to influence neurological recovery, even in the absence of direct brain injury.

items.title: Carboxypeptidase B1: A novel, targetable contributor to thromboembolic complications in severe acute pancreatitis?
items.containerTitle: Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Severe acute pancreatitis (SAP) is associated with increased thrombotic risk. Systemic release of pancreatic proteases in SAP may alter susceptibility to endogenous fibrinolysis, but this remains unexplored. Pancreatic carboxypeptidase B1 (CPB1) is a protease activated by trypsin that shares cleavage specificity with thrombin-activatable fibrinolysis inhibitor, which cleaves C-terminal lysine residues off fibrin, impairing co-localization of tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) and plasminogen and rendering clots resistant to fibrinolysis. We hypothesized that circulating CPB1 would be elevated in SAP patients and contribute to fibrinolytic resistance. METHODS: Plasma and clinical data were prospectively collected from SAP patients (n=15), matched critically ill controls without pancreatitis (n=13), and healthy controls (n=4) with IRB approval and informed consent. CPB1 levels were measured through ELISA. Clot lysis assays assessed fibrinolysis in response to tPA. Healthy control plasma was tested with and without porcine pancreas CPB1 to assess the effect of CPB1 on fibrinolysis. Transition midpoints (T M ’s) were defined as the time to 50% clot lysis. Clinical data were analyzed using Mann-Whitney U and Fisher exact tests. Assay results were analyzed using Kruskall-Wallis test. Significance was set at P <0.05. RESULTS: Demographics were similar between groups. SAP patients had markedly elevated CPB1 levels (154.0 [58.4–388.0] ng/mL) compared with sick (7.0 [4.1–15.6] ng/mL, P <0.0001) and healthy controls (4.0 [2.1–4.4], P <0.001). Healthy control plasma supplemented with porcine pancreas CPB1 demonstrated complete disruption of fibrinolysis compared with healthy plasma without CPB1. SAP patients had the highest resistance to tPA-induced fibrinolysis, with significantly higher baseline TMs than critically ill controls (42.0 [21.7–126.6] vs. 22.8 [18.3–33.7], P =0.04). CONCLUSIONS: Patients with SAP have uniquely elevated circulating levels of CPB1, which may contribute to thromboembolism in SAP through fibrinolytic resistance. Further investigation into targeted CPB1 inhibition as a potential therapeutic strategy in SAP is warranted to potentially reduce development of organ failure and mortality. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: N/A (Basic Science).

items.title: Propranolol administration following traumatic brain injury induces distinct neuroinflammatory gene expression profiles
items.containerTitle: Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) remains a major cause of morbidity and is frequently followed by prolonged intensive care stays with sustained physiologic stress. Beta-blockade has been investigated as an adjunct therapy for TBI given its potential to reduce sympathetic hyperactivation. The molecular mechanisms underlying neuroinflammatory signaling remain incompletely defined. We hypothesized that propranolol (BB) administration following TBI would modify neuroinflammatory transcriptional responses consistent with attenuation of maladaptive inflammatory signaling. METHODS: Male Sprague-Dawley rats (n=6–8/group) were divided into 6 groups: (1) TBI7d (controlled cortical impact) followed by 7 days of daily handling, (2) TBI7d with daily propranolol administration (TBI BB7d), (3) TBI with chronic restraint stress for 7 days (TBI CRS7d), (4) TBI CRS7d with daily propranolol administration (TBI CRS BB7d), (5) CRS7d (n=7) who underwent daily stress exposure for 7 days; and (6) CRS BB7d (n=7) underwent daily stress exposure with propranolol injections for 7 days. RNA was extracted from the injured frontal lobe and analyzed using the NanoString Neuroinflammation panel. Differential gene expression was analyzed using ROSALIND. Significant differentially expressed genes (sDEGs) were defined as fold change ≥1.5 or ≤−1.5 with p <0.05. Functional pathway analysis was performed using Qiagen Ingenuity Pathway Analysis. RESULTS: Compared with TBI alone, TBI BB7d demonstrated 83 sDEGs, including genes associated with neuronal signaling, neurotransmitter regulation, and epigenetic modulation. Pathway analysis identified significant involvement of the IL8 signaling and FXR/RXR. In the TBI CRS7d model, propranolol treatment yielded 21 sDEGs. These genes were enriched in pathways related to cellular stress responses and inflammatory regulation. Propranolol downregulated IL6, IL8, and neuroinflammation signaling pathways. CONCLUSIONS: Propranolol administration following TBI, with and without stress, resulted in distinct neuroinflammatory transcriptional profiles. Propranolol was associated with alterations in multiple pathways involved in stress response, immune regulation, and neurorecovery. These findings suggest beta-blockade may modulate stress-related neuroinflammatory signaling following TBI.

items.title: Bending the learning curve: Achieving faster proficiency with intrathoracic surgical stabilization of rib fractures
items.containerTitle: Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Surgical stabilization of rib fractures (SSRF) is a technique for repairing the chest wall after trauma. Two primary SSRF techniques exist—intrathoracic and extrathoracic plating. This study compares our institution’s proficiency acquisition and operative reference times for both techniques. METHODS: A retrospective, single-institution cohort study was conducted at a level 1 trauma center to analyze the learning curves of SSRF among 12 attending surgeons who performed the extrathoracic technique and 9 who performed the intrathoracic technique from May 2015 to September 2025. Four hundred fifty-three cases were assessed, and operative times were averaged across each surgeon’s cases. Plating time and exposure/closure times were reported. Cumulative sum (CUSUM) analyses with Savitzky-Golay filtering were performed to find proficiency points and operative reference times. Statistical significance was determined using parametric or nonparametric tests and multivariable linear regression. RESULTS: Surgeons demonstrated faster proficiency acquisition with the intrathoracic technique. When no co-surgeon was present, plating proficiency occurred after 7 cases for the intrathoracic approach and 17 cases for the extrathoracic approach. The reference time per plate was achieved at 17:03 min/plate for the intrathoracic technique and 16:56 min/plate for the extrathoracic technique. For exposure/closure times, proficiency occurred after 35 cases for the intrathoracic approach and 68 cases for the extrathoracic approach. Reference exposure/closure times were 78:57 min for the intrathoracic approach and 80:13 min for the extrathoracic approach. CONCLUSIONS: Intrathoracic SSRF demonstrated more rapid proficiency in both rib plating and exposure. Once proficiency has been attained, operative times are expected to align with reference times, and continued improvement towards mastery is anticipated afterwards. These findings can help establish a framework for setting expectations when onboarding new surgeons using these techniques. ( J Trauma Acute Care Surg . 2026;00: 000–000. Copyright © 2026 Wolters Kluwer Health, LLC. All rights reserved.) LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Retrospective Comparative Study; Level III.

items.title: Simultaneous clavicle and rib fracture fixation in patients with severe chest wall injuries is associated with improved outcomes: A pilot study
items.containerTitle: Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Simultaneous clavicle open reduction and internal fixation (Clavicle-ORIF) with surgical stabilization of rib fractures (SSRFs) is an understudied but potentially beneficial strategy. We compared outcomes between patients undergoing simultaneous Clavicle-ORIF with SSRF (Clavicle-ORIF+SSRF) and those undergoing SSRF alone (SSRF-Alone) for severe chest wall injury in a pilot study to determine if there is a benefit for further research on this approach. METHODS: A prospective, 2016–2025 IRB–approved database of adults undergoing SSRF at a Chest Wall Injury Collaborative Center was queried for patients with displaced clavicle fractures. Patients undergoing Clavicle-ORIF simultaneously with SSRF were compared with patients with displaced clavicle fractures for a retrospective cohort. Outcomes were daily morphine milligram equivalents, mechanical ventilation, intensive care unit days, and hospital length of stay. RESULTS: Of 60 consecutive patients with displaced clavicle fractures, 52 (86.7%) had complete data, of whom 17.3% underwent simultaneous Clavicle-ORIF+SSRF. The groups were similar in age (52 vs. 57 y) and injury severity (New Injury Severity Score 22 vs. 27; RibScore 4 vs. 3). Mortality was low, with 2 deaths, both in SSRF-Alone. Clavicle-ORIF+SSRF was associated with significantly fewer intensive care unit days (2 [1–3] vs. 5 [3–11], p =0.005) and less mechanical ventilation requirement (0% vs. 42%, p =0.02). Median and maximum daily morphine milligram equivalents were lower but not statistically different for Clavicle-ORIF+SSRF (38 [30–59] vs. 62 [30–83], p =0.25; and 67 [45–155] vs. 112 [61–140], p =0.61). CONCLUSIONS: This pilot study demonstrated that in patients with combined rib and clavicle fractures undergoing SSRF, simultaneous clavicle fixation has the potential to improve outcomes. The study was limited by a small sample size, but it justifies further research on the benefits of simultaneous clavicle fixation with SSRF. ( J Trauma Acute Care Surg . 2026;00: 000–000 Copyright © 2026 Wolters Kluwer Health, LLC. All rights reserved.) LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Pilot Retrospective Cohort; Level III.

items.title: Antithrombin III outperforms fresh frozen plasma and improves memory recovery after severe isolated traumatic brain injury
items.containerTitle: Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Fresh frozen plasma (FFP) administered after severe isolated traumatic brain injury (TBI) has been shown to affect subsequent neurological recovery. One component of FFP, antithrombin III (AT3), demonstrates anti-inflammatory effects on the injured brain and may be a key FFP element that supports post-TBI recovery. We hypothesized that AT3 better improves cognition following severe, isolated TBI when compared with FFP. METHODS: Male CD1 mice (n=29) underwent sham craniectomy (S) or craniectomy followed by severe TBI via controlled cortical impact. Mice received saline (placebo, P), FFP (10 mL/kg), or AT3 (250 IU/kg) 30 minutes after injury. Morris water maze exercises on days 6 to 14 characterized cued/spatial learning and memory. Decreased latency/distance and increased frequency/duration across four zones [zone 5 (escape platform), zone 6/zone 7 (concentric circular areas surrounding zone 5)], and zone 1 (quadrant containing zone 5) indicated superior learning and memory. The Garcia Neurological Test (GNT) allowed scoring of global animal neurological function following surgery on days 1 to 14. RESULTS: Mice treated with FFP or AT3 had consistent improvements in GNT scores back to sham levels across all the post-TBI experimental period from day 1 through 14 ( p <0.01). Cued learning was unaffected by FFP or AT3. Spatial learning was consistently worsened by FFP but not by AT3, which, in comparison, demonstrated reduced latency to zones 5, 6, and 7 ( p <0.01). FFP had no effect on memory, but AT3 consistently improved memory, decreasing latency to zones 1, 5, 6, and 7 ( p <0.01) and increasing frequency into zones 1, 6, and 7 ( p <0.01). There were no differences in brain or lung edema between groups. CONCLUSION: FFP after severe TBI improves global neurological recovery but appears to worsen spatial learning. Instead, AT3 confers better neurological recuperation, particularly through improved memory recovery. Further inquiry is warranted to identify beneficial and deleterious components of commonly transfused FFP to enhance recovery after severe blunt TBI.

items.title: Infectious complications are preceded by specific longitudinal neutrophil cell surface patterns after polytrauma: Preliminary results of a prospective analysis
items.containerTitle: Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Alterations in neutrophil receptors provide valuable insights into the immune response after polytrauma. Point-of-care (POC) technologies enable rapid on-site analysis of neutrophils. Previous studies demonstrated individual neutrophil surface patterns after trauma, depending on injury severity and metabolic status. We hypothesized that infectious complications after polytrauma are preceded by specific neutrophil cell surface receptor alterations. METHODS: A POC neutrophil analysis system (AQUIOS ® Flow Cytometer) was implemented at a Level 1 trauma center. Polytrauma patients with an Injury Severity Score (ISS)≥25 were prospectively included. Neutrophil cell surface expression of CD10, CD11b, CD64, CD62L, and CD16 was analyzed immediately after admission and after 8 hours, 24 hours, 48 hours, and 5 days. Patients were grouped according to the occurrence or absence of infectious complications. RESULTS: Thirty-two polytrauma patients with a median ISS of 34.5 were included in this study. Trauma sequelae included spine fractures, long bone fractures, and traumatic brain injury. During hospitalization, 13 out of 32 patients developed infectious complications. Patients who subsequently developed infectious complications showed significantly higher CD64 expression throughout the observation period, and CD62L demonstrated a trend toward higher expression. In addition, CD11b expression was elevated 8 hours after trauma. CONCLUSIONS: Longitudinal assessment of multiple selected neutrophil markers draws an individual neutrophil surface profile, with specific patterns associated with the development of infectious complications. This offers a promising tool for early risk stratification and identification of trauma patients vulnerable to post-traumatic infectious complications and allows for future immune-protective trauma surgery. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Prognostic and Epidemiological; Level III.

items.title: Hospital volume and outcomes in after-hours emergency general surgery: a nationwide retrospective cohort study
items.containerTitle: Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: High-volume hospitals are associated with better outcomes in some surgical fields, including emergency general surgery (EGS). However, the association of hospital volume with outcomes in after-hours EGS remains unclear. This study aimed to evaluate the association between hospital-year volume of after-hours EGS and in-hospital mortality and total healthcare costs. METHODS: We conducted a nationwide retrospective cohort study using the Japanese Diagnosis Procedure Combination database. We included patients aged ≥16 years who were directly admitted from outpatient settings and underwent after-hours EGS on or the day after admission between April 2014 and March 2023. The primary outcome was in-hospital mortality; the secondary outcome was total healthcare costs during hospitalization. Associations were evaluated using mixed-effects models. Hospital-year volume was analyzed continuously using natural cubic splines and categorically (1–19, 20–49, 50–99, and ≥100 cases/year). RESULTS: Overall, 235,465 patients were included. In the mixed-effects logistic regression model, each 10-case increase in hospital-year volume was associated with lower in-hospital mortality (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 0.97; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.96–0.98; p <0.001). Spline analyses showed that the adjusted odds of in-hospital mortality generally decreased with increasing hospital-year volume, although this decline became less pronounced at higher-volume levels. Adjusted healthcare costs decreased across most of the volume range before increasing slightly at the highest levels. Compared with 1 to 19 cases/year, the aORs for in-hospital mortality were 0.77 (95% CI, 0.71–0.83), 0.72 (95% CI, 0.66–0.78), and 0.66 (95% CI, 0.59–0.74) for 20–49, 50–99, and ≥100 cases/year, respectively (all p <0.001). The corresponding adjusted relative costs were 0.99 (95% CI, 0.99–1.00; p =0.205), 0.98 (95% CI, 0.97–0.99; p =0.001), and 0.97 (95% CI, 0.96–0.99; p <0.001). CONCLUSIONS: Higher hospital-year after-hours EGS volume was associated with lower in-hospital mortality and modestly lower healthcare costs. These associations varied across the volume range. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Prognostic/epidemiological; Level III.

items.title: Is the H-index an adequate measure of trauma surgeon research productivity?
items.containerTitle: Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery
items.abstract: The H-index is a widely used objective metric by academia to make critical decisions such as grant funding, hiring, promotion, and retention. The H-index is defined as the largest number (h) of publications that have received at least h citations. Unfortunately, the H-index presents many limitations including its inherent cumulative nature, incompatibility among specialties, its potential opaqueness to landmark research, and gender disparity among other potential threats to its validity. Alternatives to H-index that potentially address some of its core weaknesses are the relative citation ratio (RCR), fractional H-index, and the altmetric-index. The altmetric-index measures social and internet engagement rather than citations but has the advantage over H-index in providing more immediate feedback on a paper potential impact, especially among the general public. Trauma surgeons rank in the mid-to-low median H-index, driven primarily by low H-index among young faculty. H-index has value as an objective measure of research productivity, but stakeholders must understand its limitations, and it should only be used as one component of the total holistic assessment of an individual contribution to an academic surgical department.

items.title: Evaluation of the ACS Trauma Quality Improvement Program benchmark for intracranial pressure monitoring across trauma centers
items.containerTitle: Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: In severe traumatic brain injury (sTBI), intracranial pressure (ICP) monitoring detects and directs management for intracranial hypertension. ICP monitoring is recommended for sTBI patients and is included as a benchmarked quality metric by the American College of Surgeons Trauma Quality Improvement Programs (ACS-TQIP), which reports annual ICP monitor usage across all participating trauma centers. We evaluated whether greater institutional ICP utilization was associated with lower center-level mortality. METHODS: For this retrospective observational study, adult patients aged 18 years and older meeting the ACS-TQIP definition of sTBI admitted to Level I or II trauma centers from 2013 to 2023 were identified. Patient data were aggregated by trauma center and calendar year to mirror the ACS-TQIP benchmarking framework. Annual institutional ICP monitor utilization and in-hospital mortality rates were calculated for each center-year combination. Multivariable generalized linear mixed-effects models evaluated whether centers with higher ICP monitor utilization had lower mortality after adjusting for patient demographics, injury severity, neurological status, operative intervention, injury mechanism, and hospital length of stay. RESULTS: Among 191,686 sTBI patients, 29,224 (15.2%) underwent ICP monitoring. ICP monitor utilization ranged from 11% to 21% during the study period with a notable increase in 2017, whereas overall mortality remained largely unchanged. Year-specific analyses demonstrated a protective association between greater ICP monitor utilization and mortality in 2015 and an association with increased mortality in 2023. After adjustment for differences in patient and institutional characteristics, higher institutional ICP monitor utilization was not associated with lower center-level mortality (odds ratio=0.99, 95% CI=0.97–1.00; P =0.128). CONCLUSIONS: Using over a decade of TQIP data, greater institutional ICP monitor utilization was not associated with lower mortality across ACS-TQIP centers. These findings suggest that greater institutional adoption of ICP monitoring alone may not improve center-level outcomes and support periodic reassessment of ICP monitoring as a benchmarked ACS-TQIP quality metric. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level IV, prognostic & epidemiological.

items.title: Secondary traumatic stress: A threat to surgeons and the patients they serve
items.containerTitle: Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery
items.abstract: Secondary traumatic stress (STS) can present with symptoms nearly identical to post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). However, instead of resulting from direct exposure to trauma as the victim, STS develops after repeated indirect exposure to severe injury, death, and human suffering. This can cause significant psychological distress and ultimately contribute to PTSD-like symptoms and burnout. Evidence suggests that STS is common among trauma surgeons, although its prevalence remains poorly characterized. STS should be considered an occupational hazard of trauma surgery rather than a failure of individual determination or resilience and may have important consequences for the surgical workforce and, ultimately, patient care. We argue that institutions should consider a framework that incorporates monitoring of measurable workload and trauma-related risk factors at the individual surgeon level. These factors could prompt preventive measures such as protected recovery time and confidential screening using validated tools. When psychological injury is identified, surgeons should be afforded rapid access to mental health resources and formal peer support. Existing institutional programs demonstrate that these interventions can be operationalized, but their effectiveness in preventing, identifying, and treating STS requires further study. Addressing STS must be taken seriously as an institutional responsibility if we are to protect the trauma surgery workforce while supporting the quality and sustainability of patient care.

items.title: Loss of plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 activity during liquid plasma storage is associated with increased fibrinolysis in response to tissue plasminogen activator
items.containerTitle: Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: In trauma, hyperfibrinolysis influences the need for massive transfusion and mortality. Tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) sensitivity increases during whole blood storage despite rising plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 (PAI-1) activity. Liquid plasma demonstrates preserved fibrinogen function in storage, but fibrinolytic regulation in stored liquid plasma remains undescribed. METHODS: Liquid plasma tails (n = 28) were obtained and stored at 4 °C. Thromboelastography was challenged with 75 ng/mL exogenous tPA at three storage time points (day 1–3, 7–10, and 28) to assess resistance to fibrinolysis. PAI-1 activity was measured through a modified enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) that captures only active PAI-1 utilizing immobilized active urokinase. Statistical analysis included two-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) and Spearman correlation. Significance was set at p <0.05. RESULTS: Aging liquid plasma units demonstrated a significant, progressive increase in fibrinolysis (LY30) in response to tPA over time ( p = 0.008). Alpha angle gradually increased, and maximum amplitude remained stable with storage. PAI-1 activity decreased with storage ( p < 0.001) and inversely correlated with tPA-thromboelastography LY30 (Spearman r = -0.40, p = 0.04). CONCLUSIONS: Stored liquid plasma demonstrates declining PAI-1 activity, increased tPA-mediated fibrinolysis, and preserved clot strength, highlighting differences in fibrinolytic regulation compared with previously reported findings in stored whole blood. Further investigation into fibrinolytic regulation for the spectrum of blood products during storage and the implications for trauma resuscitation is warranted. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Basic Science.

items.title: Intraoperative peri-incisional hypothermia is a risk factor for surgical site infection in acute care surgery: a prospective cohort study
items.containerTitle: Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Surgical site infection (SSI) prevention has plateaued despite decades of prophylaxis and care bundles, suggesting the pathogen-focused paradigm has reached its limits. Contamination at closure is near universal; whether it progresses to infection depends on the defensive competence of the incision, which no current tool measures. We hypothesized that preclosure peri-incisional hypothermia, reflecting compromised perfusion, is associated with increased risk of 30-day SSI. METHODS: In this prospective single-center cohort, adults undergoing acute care surgery (with incision >5 cm) underwent intraoperative infrared thermography immediately before fascial closure. A peri-incisional temperature gradient (near minus far zone) was derived, with negative values indicating local hypothermia. The primary outcome was 30-day SSI. Associations were tested by logistic regression with adjustment for clinical, systemic, and ambient factors. RESULTS: Of 126 analytic patients, 18 (14%) developed SSI. Preclosure gradients were negative in patients who developed SSI and positive in those who did not (−0.97±1.07 vs. +0.51±0.94°C; p <0.001). Each 1°C colder gradient was associated with fourfold higher odds of SSI (odds ratio 4.2; 95% CI: 2.2–8.0), an association stable after adjustment for clinical risk factors (odds ratio 4.5; 95% CI: 2.1–9.6), core temperature, and systemic-hypothermia status (odds ratio 4.3; 95% CI: 2.2–8.4). Focal cold spots were more frequent among SSI patients (83% vs. 16%; p <0.001). Exploratory discrimination was high (area under the curve 0.87), with a negative predictive value of 98%. CONCLUSION: Preclosure peri-incisional hypothermia is a biologically grounded, intraoperatively measurable risk factor for SSI. These findings warrant prospective multicenter validation before clinical application. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Prognostic; Level III. STUDY TYPE: Prospective observational cohort.

items.title: Beyond the national average: Demographically stratified estimates of resource utilization for trauma systems planning
items.containerTitle: Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Trauma systems are planned for populations, but resources are consumed by individual patients whose needs vary by age, sex, and injury pattern. To estimate the resources a population will need, existing tools often apply simple national averages of what admissions consume, creating a potential mismatch between the resources needed and those available. We compared simple population size-based estimates against estimates stratified by patient demographics. METHODS: Using the American College of Surgeons Trauma Quality Programs Participant Use Files (2022–2024), we conducted a retrospective analysis of adult admissions to 502 Level I/II trauma centers. Per-admission estimates for seven resources were derived from pooled 2022–2023 admissions using three approaches: simple estimates based on population size, singularly stratified estimates by age, sex, or payer alone, and jointly stratified estimates combining all three. Estimates were applied to held-out 2024 admissions and percent error calculated, with a 2017–2019 sensitivity analysis. RESULTS: Among 1,803,746 derivation and 947,281 validation admissions, the simple estimate fell outside 10% of observed utilization in 40 of 63 subgroup and metric combinations, 21 higher than observed and 19 lower. Blood product estimates were 236% higher than observed among Medicare-covered patients. Stratifying on one characteristic corrected error chiefly within its own subgroups (59 of 63 within 10%). Applied jointly, age, sex, and payer brought 62 of 63 combinations within 10%, reducing median absolute error from 13.8% to 3.0%. CONCLUSIONS: Simple estimates differed from observed resource use by 10% or more for nearly every patient group examined, failing in both directions in a manner no single adjustment can correct. Stratification by age, sex, and payer, characteristics knowable before injury, substantially reduced this error. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Prognostic/Epidemiological; Level III.

icm-2026-bicarbonate-bayesian-meta-analy.limitations: Finally, although the Bayesian framework provides a probabilistic interpretation of treatment effects that may facilitate clinical decision-making, it cannot overcome the limitations of the underlying evidence, including the small number of available trials and their clinical heterogeneity. Findings from individual trials help contextualise these results. In BICAR-ICU, treatment effects appeared more favourable in patients with concomitant AKI, including lower RRT use. BICARICU-2 similarly showed a directional reduction in RRT among patients with severe acidaemia and stage 2–3 AKI, without a clear mortality benefit. The SODa-BIC pilot and the SODa-BIC trial enrolled patients with less severe acidaemia and lower baseline event rates and were not individually powered to detect definitive differences in mortality or RRT. Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, only four trials were available, limiting precision for several outcomes and for heterogeneity estimates. Second, the included trials enrolled clinically distinct patient populations, which may limit the generalisability of the pooled estimates. BICAR-ICU and BICARICU-2 enrolled patients with more severe acidaemia, with BICARICU-2 additionally requIring stage 2–3 AKI, whereas the SODa-BIC trials enrolled vasopressor-treated patients with less severe acidaemia and did not require advanced AKI. These differences in eligibility criteria likely influenced baseline risk and treatment responsiveness and contribute to the clinical heterogeneity across the available randomised evidence.

Publications
A variety of publications and other educational resources are available through the Society and contain the latest information in cardiovascular anesthesiology. Discount subscriptions to the publications listed below are available for those who are members of both the SCA and the IARS.

SCA Newsletter
The SCA newsletter serves as a valuable resource for its members, offering updates on the latest advancements, educational events, and leadership messages relevant to cardiovascular anesthesiology. Each edition typically includes previews of upcoming conferences, such as the annual Echo and Thoracic Anesthesia Symposiums, important policy and guideline changes, and opportunities for professional development through hands-on workshops and scientific discussions. The newsletter also features announcements of society activities, member achievements, and committee updates, helping practitioners stay informed and engaged within the SCA community.
Read more

Anesthesia and Analgesia
The official journal of the International Anesthesia Research Society hosts three sections of interest to SCA membership: Cardiovascular Anesthesiology, Hemostasis, and Perioperative Echocardiography and Cardiovascular Education.
Discount subscriptions are available for those who are members of both the SCA and the IARS.
Free Access Articles
Read more

Journal of Cardiothoracic and Vascular Anesthesia
Aimed primarily at anesthesiologists who deal with patients undergoing cardiac, thoracic, or vascular surgical procedures.
The Red Journal features a multidisciplinary approach, with contributions from cardiac, vascular and thoracic surgeons, cardiologists, and other related specialists.
Emphasis is placed on rapid publication of clinically relevant material.
The journal is international in scope and encourages innovative submissions from all continents.
Read more

OpenAnesthesia
Sponsored by the IARS, this comprehensive resource for anesthesiology residents and physicians offers online and mobile education resources.

Guideline FAQs
How do I obtain copyright permission to use a table/figure from an ASE Guideline?Expand
To use images or tables from any ASE guideline (or JASE article) you must apply for permission to the JASE publisher, Elsevier. This is done via CCC RightsLink(opens in new tab).
A shortcut is to find the guideline or article you need on JASE (onlinejase.com) and then select the “get rights” link (which looks like a copyright symbol) and it will take you to the CCC RightsLink form for that specific guideline or article. Note that you may request more than one image/table from a guideline on the same form, but you will need separate forms for each guideline or article.
How do I submit an idea for an ASE Guideline?Expand
ASE members may become involved in proposing an ASE Guideline through participation in one of the ASE Councils(opens in new tab) or ASE Specialty Interest Groups(opens in new tab). ASE members may also login to the member portal to download the ASE Guideline Development Manual (updated June 2023) and download the ASE Guideline Proposal Template (see instructions here(opens in new tab)) for more information. Note that guideline proposals are reviewed, prioritized, and approved by ASE leadership depending on topic.
What is ASE’s Endorsement Policy? Expand
ASE supports collaboration with other medical societies and organizations that develop clinical practice guidelines, appropriate use criteria, position statements, and other communications related to echocardiographic imaging. ASE views collaboration as an opportunity to harmonize clinical recommendations, improve the delivery of patient care, and advance cardiovascular ultrasound to improve lives.
Guidelines and other clinical guidance documents developed by external organizations may be considered for ASE endorsement when they address topics relevant to ASE and its membership and meet the basic criteria for review, including:
Medical and scientific soundness.
Alignment with ASE policies.
Alignment with the ASE strategic plan.
At the discretion of the ASE Executive Committee, a request for review of a submitted clinical guidance document may not be accepted. Submission and review do not guarantee endorsement, and ASE endorsement does not guarantee publication in the Journal of the American Society of Echocardiography (JASE).
ASE Endorsement Process
ASE endorsement requires:
Formal review by the ASE Guidelines and Standards Committee to assess the appropriateness of endorsement.
Approval by the ASE Executive Committee.
External organizations may approach ASE to request review and endorsement of guidelines developed without ASE involvement. Although such documents may be considered, the likelihood of consideration is increased when ASE has been involved in, and has knowledge of, the development process.
Organizations seeking ASE endorsement must submit the guideline to ASE Guidelines staff for consideration and complete ASE’s Endorsement Letter of Agreement (LOA). The requesting organization should submit the final manuscript along with the endorsement request.
Categories of ASE Recognition
Clinical guidelines developed by external organizations that are relevant to patient care in cardiovascular ultrasound may be categorized as follows:
Endorsed
The guideline meets ASE’s criteria for endorsement, and ASE fully endorses the document.
Whenever feasible, ASE’s involvement in the development and review of an endorsed document should include one or more of the following:
ASE representation on the writing committee, with at least one member appointed by the ASE Executive Committee.
ASE participation in peer review of the final document.
The sponsoring organization’s written response to ASE peer-review comments and provision of the final document to ASE for review.
Affirmation of Value
The guideline does not meet the requirements for full endorsement, or ASE cannot endorse all of the recommendations. However, ASE determines that the guideline provides value in improving patient care as it relates to the advancement of cardiovascular ultrasound.
Not Endorsed
ASE does not endorse the guideline.
Dissemination of Endorsed Documents
If ASE fully endorses a document:
ASE may disseminate the document to its members with permission from the primary organization.
ASE may request permission to publish the full document, a portion of the document, or a summary on the ASE website, or to provide a link to the article after publication by the primary organization.
The requesting organization should submit the endorsement request and final manuscript to ASE Guidelines staff for consideration.
Who can participate in developing an ASE Guideline?Expand
Writing Group members should represent communities of interest for the topic being addressed. Careful consideration should be given to representation from different ASE Councils, Task Forces, and Interest Groups. Recommendations on such representation should be considered by the writing group Chair but may also come from the Guidelines and Standards Committee, Council Chair, or Executive Committee. To learn more about getting involved with ASE, visit the ASE member portal(opens in new tab).
How do I find an ASE Guideline on a specific topic?Expand
The ASE Guidelines webpage has search and filter options for narrowing the list by topic, technique, disease, anatomy, audience, resource type, language, and date. Filters can be used alone or combined. Selecting a Guideline from the results opens options to view or download it.
Can I download or print an ASE Guideline?Expand
To view, download, or print an ASE Guideline, click the publication you want on the ASE Guidelines webpage and select Download Guideline. The Guideline will open as a PDF, where you can use the download or print options provided by your browser or PDF viewer.
Are ASE Guidelines available in other languages?Expand
Translated versions are available for select ASE Guidelines. Availability varies by Guideline. Check the individual Guideline listing on the ASE Guidelines webpage to see whether a translated version is available.
Are educational resources available for ASE Guidelines?Expand
ASE offers educational resources related to selected Guidelines, including the Guidelines in Practice Webinar Series, which explores the recommendations and their practical applications. ASE Guidelines may also be used as educational resources for healthcare professionals and trainees. Explore the ASE Learning Hub(opens in new tab) to find webinars and other educational activities related to ASE Guidelines.
How do I cite an ASE Guideline?Expand
ASE Guidelines are published in the Journal of the American Society of Echocardiography (JASE)(opens in new tab). Use the full reference information from the journal where the Guideline was published, including the title, authors, journal, year, volume, pages, and DOI. Follow the reference style your journal, institution, or program requires.
How can I provide feedback or ask a question about an ASE Guideline?Expand
For questions or feedback about an ASE Guideline, please email [email protected].

Clinical Practice Documents and Policies
Scroll to top
The Society of Thoracic Surgeons Workforce on Evidence Based Surgery develops clinical practice documents including clinical practice guidelines, expert consensus documents, and expert opinion/white papers to provide practical assistance to the STS membership. These documents are intended to assist physicians and other health care providers in clinical decision-making by describing a range of generally acceptable approaches for the diagnosis, management, or prevention of specific diseases or conditions.
Clinical practice guideline documents are thoroughly reviewed, and the conclusions and recommendations are based on a systematic review of scientific evidence published in medical literature.
Expert consensus documents represent the collective opinions of an expert panel on a clinical topic. The opinions expressed in the statement(s) are not generally developed in accordance with the formal evidence review process outline for clinical practice guidelines. The authors may suggest treatment strategies based on their collective knowledge and clinical experience.
An expert opinion/white paper is authored by leading experts on clinical topics with scarce data and significant uncertainty. These documents are intended to synthesize existing scientific literature, divergent opinions, and other treatment strategies, rather than provide recommendations.

Disclaimer: These guidelines are intended for educational use to build the knowledge of physicians and other health professionals in assessing the conditions and managing the treatment of patients undergoing ECLS / ECMO and describe what are believed to be useful and safe practice for extracorporeal life support (ECLS, ECMO) but these are not necessarily consensus recommendations. The aim of clinical guidelines are to help clinicians to make informed decisions about their patients. However, adherence to a guideline does not guarantee a successful outcome. Ultimately, healthcare professionals must make their own treatment decisions about care on a case-by-case basis, after consultation with their patients, using their clinical judgement, knowledge and expertise. These guidelines do not take the place of physicians’ and other health professionals’ judgment in diagnosing and treatment of particular patients. These guidelines are not intended to and should not be interpreted as setting a standard of care, or be deemed inclusive of all proper methods of care nor exclusive of other methods of care reasonably directed to obtaining the same results. The ultimate judgment must be made by the physician and other health professionals and the patient in light of all the circumstances presented by the individual patient, and the known variability and biological behavior of the clinical condition. These guidelines reflects the data at the time the guidelines were prepared; the results of subsequent studies or other information may cause revisions to the recommendations in these guidelines to be prudent to reflect new data, but ELSO is under no obligation to provide updates. In no event will ELSO be liable for any decision made or action taken in reliance upon the information provided through these guidelines.

Out of these cookies, the cookies that are categorized as necessary are stored on your browser as they are essential for the working of basic functionalities of the website. We also use third-party cookies that help us analyze and understand how you use this website. These cookies will be stored in your browser only with your consent. You also have the option to opt-out of these cookies. But opting out of some of these cookies may have an effect on your browsing experience.
Necessary
Always Enabled
Necessary cookies are absolutely essential for the website to function properly. This category only includes cookies that ensures basic functionalities and security features of the website. These cookies do not store any personal information.
Cookie
Description
PHPSESSID
This cookie is native to PHP applications. The cookie is used to store and identify a users' unique session ID for the purpose of managing user session on the website. The cookie is a session cookies and is deleted when all the browser windows are closed.
viewed_cookie_policy
The cookie is set by the GDPR Cookie Consent plugin and is used to store whether or not user has consented to the use of cookies. It does not store any personal data.
__stripe_mid
This cookie is set by Stripe payment gateway. This cookie is used to enable payment on the website without storing any payment information on a server.
__stripe_sid
This cookie is set by Stripe payment gateway. This cookie is used to enable payment on the website without storing any payment information on a server.
_wpfuuid
This cookie is used by the WPForms WordPress plugin. The cookie is used to allow the paid version of the plugin to connect entries by the same user and is used for some additional features like the Form Abandonment addon.
__cfduid
The cookie is set by CloudFare. The cookie is used to identify individual clients behind a shared IP address and apply security settings on a per-client basis. It does not correspond to any user ID in the web application and does not store any personally identifiable information.
Analytics
analytics
Analytics cookies help us understand how our visitors interact with the website. It helps us understand the number of visitors, where the visitors are coming from, and the pages they navigate. The cookies collect this data and are reported anonymously.
Cookie
Description
GPS
This cookie is set by Youtube and registers a unique ID for tracking users based on their geographical location
_ga
This cookie is installed by Google Analytics. The cookie is used to calculate visitor, session, campaign data and keep track of site usage for the site's analytics report. The cookies store information anonymously and assign a randomly generated number to identify unique visitors.
_gid
This cookie is installed by Google Analytics. The cookie is used to store information of how visitors use a website and helps in creating an analytics report of how the website is doing. The data collected including the number visitors, the source where they have come from, and the pages visited in an anonymous form.
Performance
performance
Collects anonymous data about how visitors use our site and how it performs. We use this to improve our products, services and user experience.
Cookie
Description
YSC
This cookies is set by Youtube and is used to track the views of embedded videos.
__utmz
This cookie is set by Google analytics and is used to store the traffic source or campaign through which the visitor reached your site.
__utmb
The cookie is set by Google Analytics. The cookie is used to determine new sessions/visits. The cookie is created when the JavaScript library executes and there are no existing __utma cookies. The cookie is updated every time data is sent to Google Analytics.
__utma
This cookie is set by Google Analytics and is used to distinguish users and sessions. The cookie is created when the JavaScript library executes and there are no existing __utma cookies. The cookie is updated every time data is sent to Google Analytics.
__utmc
The cookie is set by Google Analytics and is deleted when the user closes the browser. The cookie is not used by ga.js. The cookie is used to enable interoperability with urchin.js which is an older version of Google analytics and used in conjunction with the __utmb cookie to determine new sessions/visits.
_gat
This cookies is installed by Google Universal Analytics to throttle the request rate to limit the colllection of data on high traffic sites.
Advertisement
advertisement
Advertisement cookies help us provide our visitors with relevant ads and marketing campaigns.
Cookie
Description
VISITOR_INFO1_LIVE
This cookie is set by Youtube. Used to track the information of the embedded YouTube videos on a website.
IDE
Used by Google DoubleClick and stores information about how the user uses the website and any other advertisement before visiting the website. This is used to present users with ads that are relevant to them according to the user profile.
NID
This cookie is used to a profile based on user's interest and display personalized ads to the users.
